trait.name: Gear (Dropped)
entries: Bag of Holding (containing hundreds of research notes and several large academic books), Hand Crossbow, Formal Wear (Fine Clothes, 15 gp.).

trait.name: Fey Ancestry
entries: Professor Primula, Palaeontologist has Advantage on saving throws to resist being {@condition charmed|XPHB|Charmed}, and magic cannot put her to sleep.

trait.name: Trance
entries: Professor Primula, Palaeontologist does not require sleep and instead meditates deeply, remaining semiconscious for 4 hours per day. Resting in this manner grants her the same benefits as a human gains from 8 hours of sleep.

trait.name: Voice of Authority
entries: Professor Primula, Palaeontologist has Advantage on Persuasion and {@skill Deception} checks when talking to someone who speaks the same language as her.

trait.name: Research Notes
entries: If Professor Primula, Palaeontologist spends 10 minutes performing a research ritual, she gains an additional +3 to a skill of her choice for the next 1 hour, or until she uses this ability again.

trait.name: Bag of Research Holding
entries: Professor Primula, Palaeontologist is in possession of a Bag of Holding. However, it is already half-full (holding her research notes and books) and she is not willing to put anything in there that might damage her research notes.

spellcasting.name: Spellcasting
headerEntries: Professor Primula, Palaeontologist is a 9th level spellcaster and her spellcasting ability is Intelligence. Her spell save DC is 14, and she has {@hit 6} to hit with spell attacks.

action.name: Take Note
entries: As an Action, Professor Primula, Palaeontologist can take notes of anything she has witnessed or heard in that moment. Her notes provide an accurate record of the event in great detail, but are written in a shorthand form of Common that requires her assistance to decipher (or succeeding a {@dc 15} {@skill Investigation} check per note). Her notes can include a creature's appearance, a location, what has been said, how something has behaved, etc.

action.name: Curate
entries: As an Action, Professor Primula, Palaeontologist can curate a tiny hand-held sized object. The object is preserved in a timeless state (optionally within a glass container) and will cease to decay or deteriorate, so long as it remains undisturbed.

action.name: Letter Deliverer
entries: {@atk rw} {@hit 5} to hit, Range 120 ft., one target. {@h}4 ({@damage 1d4 + 2}) non-lethal Piercing damage. This hand crossbow has been modified to shoot bolts with small paper rolls attached, most often used to deliver notes through colleague's windows, but sometimes used to deliver a note with a Glyph of Warding to particularly bothersome foes. Once loaded into the Letter Deliverer, a Glyph of Warding will not break when moved more than 10 ft. from its starting location but cannot be unloaded from the weapon (it can only be fired and activates on impact).

Professor Elizabeth Primula is an elven scientist, senior research professor, and head of department at the University of Urgleshire. Her research topics are numerous, given her exceedingly long career (over 200 years), although she is currently most fascinated by how the functional morphology of vertebrates and arthropods impacts their behavioural tendencies.

Historically, Professor Primula has been a desk-based palaeontologist, preferring to scour literature and analyse museum-quality fossils in the comfort of her office or in archive rooms. Easy access to her personal library and other museum records have allowed her to undertake large-scale complex analyses with relative ease, and she has published numerous articles and books across all fields of palaeontology. Such prominent works include: "{@i The Ostracod Fauna of Urgleshire: A Comprehensive Review}", "{@i 'Will It Blend?' Helicoprion Feeding Mechanics}", and "{@i On The Origin of Dragons: Dinosaur Hybridisation?}". While Professor Primula has less practical fossil excavation experience than her colleagues, her extensive publication record renders her one of the most influential palaeontologists on the continent and certainly the senior-most palaeontologist at the University of Urgleshire.

"When establishing a research career, it is most important to ensure that you are well-read on a subject prior to publication. I suggest spending at least 10 years studying the literature before dabbling in any particular topic. At least, that is my "gold standard" and what I recommend to our students. The practical requirements of this can lead to an academic advantage for us longer-lived peoples, but also a much slower rate of publication."

Recently, the antics of her colleague Dr Dhrolin on his latest sabbatical highlighted that practical fieldwork beyond fossil collecting is entirely possible for palaeontology. Previous accounts of time travel and prehistoric creatures found hidden within secluded regions were dismissed as folklore, myth, and hoaxes. Professor Primula now has it on good authority that, under the right circumstances, it is actually possible to travel through, or observe creatures from, Deep Time. As such, the University of Urgleshire has granted Professor Primula summer leave to undertake a series of short field excursions between teaching terms, all fully funded by the university.
This book recounts both Professor Primula's notes from these field excursions and her notes from the background literature review she undertook prior to setting out.

"As the head of department, I do have some sway with university management. Dr Dhrolin, myself, and Master Marzogg put together a proposal to the university board to undertake a series of small research excursions. These will allow us to verify some of my hypotheses and, ultimately, to produce some truly groundbreaking research. The suggestion that this in turn might bring in a considerable number of large research grants in the future seemed to seal the deal. While I don't tend to dirty my hands with such fieldwork, I must admit that I am excited about the prospect of seeing some of these animals in the flesh."

trait.name: Gear (Dropped)
entries: Staff of Unspared Expense (page 298 in DDDD), Torn White Suit (Fine Clothes, 15 gp.).

trait.name: Spared No Expense
entries: John Hammorc has a personal wealth of about 100,000 gp. and will spend it frivolously (although he doesn't carry it on him). He can arrange for gp. to be transferred to other NPCs or player characters by courier at a later date.

trait.name: Poor Decisive Choices
entries: John Hammorc has a -2 modifier to Wisdom saving throws and {@skill Insight} checks (both included above). John Hammorc's Proficiency Bonus is +3.

spellcasting.name: Spellcasting (2/Day)
headerEntries: John Hammorc may cast the following unique spell. He may cast this twice a day, then must complete a Long Rest before he may cast it again:

action.name: Reanimate Extinct Creature
entries: Level 5 Conjuration spell. Casting time: 4 hours Range: Touch Components: S, M (Laboratory equipment worth 5000 gp. (not consumed) and a mostly-complete skeleton or other remains of an extinct Beast (consumed)). Duration: Unlimited Effect: When John Hammorc begins casting this spell, he summons a humanoid scientist called "Wu". Using the remains of the extinct Beast and the laboratory equipment, Wu is able to create a clone of that creature at a location within 200 ft. of himself. The clone may be created in its adult form, or as a younger version, behaves in a normal manner for that creature, and is not necessarily loyal to John Hammorc or Wu. The clone is non-magical in nature and so cannot be dispelled. However, John Hammorc may choose for it to have the optional magical rules associated with that creature's stat block and/or may be mutated using the Minor or Major mutation tables (pages 218228 in DDDD). The clone is usually created within an enclosure adjacent to his laboratory. Once the spellcasting is complete, Wu disappears.

action.name: Staff of Unspared Expense (+3)
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 6} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}7 ({@damage 1d8 + 3}) Bludgeoning damage.

While wielding the Staff of Unspared Expense, John Hammorc has Advantage on all Charisma checks and Charisma saving throws. However, vendors sell their wares to John Hammorc at prices 50% more expensive than normal. This item is also cursed (see Staff of Unspared Expense on page 298 in DDDD).

In our first book, {@i Dr Dhrolin's Dictionary of Dinosaurs}, we included a piece of artwork lovingly named "John Hammorc" by our community ({@b page 23 in DDDD}). By popular demand, we have created a stat block for John Hammorc and included him in this book. This NPC can either be used with the suggested "Necromancer Island" story hook ({@b also page 23 in DDDD}), or as a wealthy benefactor to hire a party to investigate "Skull Island" ({@b page 30-47}). Alternatively, you can use him in any other way you wish to help introduce prehistoric creatures into your campaigns.

entries.name: Story Hooks
entries: Now that these story hook NPCs have been introduced, we can outline some further ideas on how prehistoric elements can be introduced into your campaign. Here are some choice examples pulled from popular culture:

"I consider myself a relatively well-connected scientist, with contacts in other scientific fields, in governments, and with various organisations, as well as with entrepreneurs who may offer funding. Among those I've met, one individual stands out as particularly... eccentric. Mr John Hammorc is, by far, the most friendly and philanthropic person I have ever met and was exceptionally interested in the research notes of my peers and myself. He was keen to shower us with financial assistance in exchange for more details about our knowledge on time travel and prehistoric creatures. We, of course, complied with his generous offer. I am sure that other trained scientists could have deduced the same additional information from our published research, but I suppose he valued hearing it unfiltered from the original authors.
Nevertheless, I cannot shake this feeling that we may regret working with this unusual man."

entries.name: Dino-planet
entries: While DnD is traditionally a mediaeval inspired fantasy setting, there's nothing stopping you from sprinkling a little sci-fi into your games. Magical portals need not just lead to other planes of existence, they can also transport players across the universe/multiverse to other planets. One planet (or several planets) could be a prehistoric, primal Dino-World, where enormous beasts rule and players find themselves in a dire fight for survival in a primitive environment.

Portals are just one means to implement this idea. Magically enchanted spaceship-like vessels are already well-established in DnD, allowing for an alternative and more interactive means of transport to such worlds, perhaps forming a story arc in their own right.

Using this story hook allows you to build independent settings that can be populated with all manner of alien, futuristic, or prehistoric creatures (potentially intermingling all three) without having to directly impact your established game world. Unlike time travel, there is little potential for direct impact on your world's timeline from your player's actions (unless of course you want there to be!).

entries.name: Nighttime at the Museum
entries: Based on the modern classic family film of a very similar name, having your campaign focus on (or just include) a magically enchanted museum that animates its housed displays overnight allows for some epic and diverse storytelling in a confined space. Much like in the film, animated creatures can be "defeated" by completing specific tasks or in a traditional combat encounter - being either destroyed or magically returned to their displays when they are defeated. This story hook could also be combined with our new museum system ({@b pages 57-62}) that allows players to build up their own awesome museum, then ultimately be faced with surviving their creation in a cruel ironic twist - the better their museum is, the more dangerous it is.

This approach also allows you to include animals, plants, and peoples from vastly different periods of time or locations without any need for time travel shenanigans or other plot points. Their presence in the museum alone is reason enough to include them. The only challenge is determining the boundary of the museum, either in terms of duration of the animated effect or physical limits. We recommend the traditional story approach for this plot hook of sundown to sunrise and that the animated creatures are entirely restricted to the museum's grounds, unable to leave them on their own.

However you implement this idea, this approach can allow you to introduce all possible encounters long before the players actually face them, allowing for some seriously intimidating "Chekhov's gun" moments. Having your low-level party wandering around a museum, seeing the remains and displays of high-CR creatures, only to have that museum later come to life will make the players painfully aware of the dangers that await them. One of our highest-tier pledgers requested a creature design that is perfect for this story hook. On {@b pages 346-349}, you can find the Skeletal {@i Tyrannosaurus}, an ideal centrepiece for such a storyline.

entries.name: The Waste Nexus
entries: On the theme of portals and interdimensional magic, what happens when portals malfunction? Is there a demiplane or location where they divert to? Would this location be a nexus for the universe's waste and unwanted things? Such locations exist in many different fictional universes, often being timeless spaces that combine creatures, objects, and themes from a variety of times - from prehistoric, to mediaeval, to modern, to futuristic. In these locations, you can take creatures from all of history that are found in our books and lump them together in a chaotic mishmash of time periods, resulting in a particularly violent and chaotic environment.

Such locations are also excellent for recovering campaigns where the party has been defeated. A total party kill need not result in the players having to design new characters. Instead, they could find their characters awakening in this waste nexus world, greeted with the new challenge of clawing their way back into their original plane. In the same vein, this waste nexus can allow the introduction of a long-term villainous higher-power or pantheon that functions as a long-term (perhaps multi-campaign) BBEG. That is, the players are faced with the impossible task of killing a god and are immediately discarded into the waste nexus, where they work together with unlikely allies to escape and rally against the unkillable.

As part of our Time Travel Butterfly Effects ({@b pages 75-77}), we've introduced the Institution of Chronological Stability (ICS) ({@b pages 80-82}). This faction and its associated NPC stat blocks can be the perfect means to introduce the party to the concept of the waste nexus, and even send them there, should the party fall on their bad side.

entries.name: Skull Island
entries: Skull Island is a common feature in many fantasy and sci-fi settings. Originally featured in the 1932 novel and 1933 film both named {@i King Kong}, it has been a staple of speculative fiction ever since. The island generally takes its name from a large skull-shaped mountain found at its centre. Although this name and imagery has been repeated in dozens of unrelated stories since its inception, the original idea of it being an island of pure primal violence inhabited by strange often over-sized creatures and isolated tribal peoples ruled by the giant ape {@i Kong} remains consistent.

We love this setting. It allows you to include an isolated, totally outrageous environment of extremes. You can mix real prehistoric animals with wild creature designs, kaiju, and elemental magic to form this mythological setting. There is a vast array of options available to make the creatures on Skull Island unique and interesting in dramatic ways. So much so that we have opted to dedicate a significant portion of this book to suggesting how you might implement this idea. In the next section, we dive into far more detail about Skull Island and its monstrous inhabitants.

trait.name: Ultra-Gigantism
entries: Mammugore cannot be killed by any means other than an attack or ability from another creature with Ultra-Gigantism. If it is reduced to 0 Hit Points or otherwise defeated by any other means, it flees to its home to recover over 24 hours.
Mammugore can optionally speak, understand languages, and problem solve as though its Intelligence score was 10.

trait.name: Legendary Resistance (5/Day)
entries: If Mammugore fails a saving throw, it can choose to succeed instead.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: When Mammugore chooses the Attack action, it may make three attacks of any combination with its Goring Strike or Goring Cleave.

action.name: Goring Strike
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 24} to hit, reach 15 ft., one target. {@h}54 ({@damage 8d10 + 10}) Cold damage.

action.name: Goring Cleave
entries: Each creature within a 30 ft. cone in front of Mammugore must make a {@dc 32} Dexterity saving throw, taking 32 ({@damage 4d10 + 10}) Cold damage on a failed save, or half as much damage on a successful save.

bonus.name: Trample
entries: One creature within 5 ft. of Mammugore must make a {@dc 34} Dexterity Saving Throw, taking 29 ({@damage 4d10 + 7}) Bludgeoning damage and be knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone} on a failed save, or taking half as much damage and not knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone} on a success.

A bribed Hired Goon will leave peacefully without stealing anything and may even reveal who hired them (so long as they don't fear that individual more than the party).

Uncommon rarity. If a Rare, Very Rare, or Legendary object is randomly determined to be stolen by the Petty Robber, reroll that result until an object of Common or Uncommon rarity is selected instead. If no suitable objects are available, the Petty Robber leaves with nothing.

action.name: Ignorant

action.name: Clobber

action.name: Heavy Crossbow

action.name: Wreck

Before they do, they will typically threaten to destroy the object or item first as a means of bargaining for their escape.

trait.name: Bombastic Display
entries: The Criminal Mastermind seeks an audience for their heists, preferring to outmanoeuvre an active foe. They will often opt to wait for guards or players to show up.

trait.name: Criminal Gang
entries: Any Hired Goon hired by the Criminal Mastermind loses its Unfaithful Mercenary for the duration of the Criminal Mastermind's Burglary.

Haul the goods! The Criminal Mastermind can instruct two or more Hired Goons to work together to move objects of Huge size. Those Hired Goons count as a single creature for the purposes of determining the number of creatures stealing objects during the Burglary and only roll for Large or larger objects when randomly determining which object may be stolen by them.

trait.name: Until We Meet Again! (1/Three Months)
entries: If the Criminal Mastermind would be knocked {@condition unconscious|XPHB|Unconscious} or captured by law enforcement (even if passed over by the player characters), they instead escape in an elaborate and ridiculous fashion that cannot be interrupted or prevented.

trait.name: Mastermind
entries: The Criminal Mastermind makes Burglary checks at Advantage.

action.name: Mastermind Flavouring
entries: A Criminal Mastermind can be flavoured in many ways. They might be an acrobatic rogue,

fantastical sorcerer, or brutish barbarian. Their skill check bonuses can be described as enhanced by skill, tools, or magical means. However you describe their appearance and abilities, they can use the following spells as an Action, as if they were spellcasters, but do not require any components and spells cast in this way cannot be countered. Any spell cast in this manner is cast at its lowest level.

Their spell save DC is 16, with {@hit 8} to hit with spell attacks. Outmanoeuvre (2/Day each): Web, Spider Climb, Jump, Grease. Great Escape (2/Day): Haste, Fly, Misty Step. Mass Destruction (2/Day): Fireball, Shatter, Lightning Bolt. Targeted Attack (2/Day): Scorching Ray, Magic Missile, Flame Blade. Beguile (2/Day): Entangle, Suggestion, Charm Person.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If the Criminal Mastermind chooses the Attack action (excluding as a Bonus Action attack from Master Multiattacker), it may make two attacks with any combination of Powerful Attack, Agile Attack, or Brilliant Attack.

When Criminal Mastermind attacks with one of these attacks, choose a damage type for this attack befitting the flavouring that you have given this Criminal Mastermind. Once selected, this damage type cannot be changed.

action.name: Powerful Attack
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}17 ({@damage 2d12 + 4}) (see above) damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 16} Strength saving throw or be {@condition stunned|XPHB|Stunned} for one round.

action.name: Agile Attack
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 8} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}13 ({@damage 2d8 + 4}) (see above) damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 16} Constitution saving throw or be {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned} for 1 minute.

action.name: Brilliant Attack

A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 12} Wisdom saving throw or be {@condition charmed|XPHB|Charmed} for 1 minute.

bonus.name: Master Multiattacker

entries: The Expert Thief will not steal Common or Uncommon objects. If a Common or Uncommon object is randomly determined to be stolen by the Expert Thief, reroll that result until an object of Rare, Very Rare, or Legendary rarity is selected. If no suitable objects are available, the Expert Thief leaves with nothing.
Alarm Systems do not alert players to a Burglary (even if triggered by other members of the Burglary).
The Expert Thief can carry museum objects up to Medium in size.

trait.name: Leave Calling Card
entries: The Expert Thief will always leave a unique "calling card" in place of a stolen object. This is generally a very small and unusual object, such as a jigsaw piece, a single white glove, or a rose petal. Alternatively, they may leave another trace of their presence, such as leaving a tap turned on or painting graffiti on a wall.

Their skill check bonuses can be described as enhanced by skill, tools, or magical means. However you describe their appearance and abilities, they can use the following spells each once per day as an Action, as if they were spellcasters, but do not require any components and spells cast in this way cannot be countered.
Their spell save DC is 13, with {@hit 5} to hit with spell attacks.
Tricky Escape (1/Day each): Web, Spider Climb, Jump, Grease.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: When the Expert Thief chooses the Attack action, it may make three attacks in any combination with their Expert Attack (Melee) or Expert Attack (Ranged).

When Expert Thief attacks with one of these attacks, choose a damage type for this attack befitting the flavouring that you have given this Expert Thief. Once selected, this damage type cannot be changed.

action.name: Expert Attack (Ranged)

Whenever Aenocyon deals damage to a creature larger than itself, it deals an additional {@dice 1d6} Piercing damage to that creature.

A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 11} Strength saving throw or have its speed reduced by 10 ft. for the next 1 minute. This effect can stack to reduce a creature's speed to 0.
{@i "A-NO-SIGH-ON"} {@b (TERRIBLE WOLF)}

The La Brea nights are breath-taking. When the skies are clear and lit by a full moon, the scenery really is beautiful. Normally, a wolf howl in the distance in such a setting would be calming natural background noise. However, here such a sound carries a deadly warning. For the wolves of La Brea are enormous and no less savvy than regular wolves. When the wolf cries here, you make ready for combat!

{@i Aenocyon} is a large canine from the Americas that first appeared in the Late Pleistocene (125,000 years ago). Although commonly known as dire wolves, these large carnivorans are thought to be the last members of an extinct canine lineage that did not survive into the modern day.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: While {@i Aenocyon} was similar to the modern wolf in many ways, it had several key differences. It was on average larger than most living wolves, weighing between 130-150 lb., with some individuals reaching 200 lb. or more. Adults were usually between 3-4 ft. tall and about 6 ft. long. {@i Aenocyon} was more robust than wolves, with a bigger skull and more powerful jaws. The strong jaw combined with large teeth gave it a powerful bite, comparable to, or possibly exceeding, that of hyenas although with much of the power towards the front of the jaw rather than the middle. This means they may not have been as good at cracking bones as hyenas, but would have been able to bite and hold onto larger prey with more force than other canines. Like many dogs, {@i Aenocyon} was a cursorial (running) predator, capable of moving at speed for long periods of time. This would have allowed them to hunt prey over great distances, killing through exhaustion as much as through inflicted injury.

{@i Aenocyon} is the most common predator found within the La Brea tar pits. Studies into the radioactive isotope composition of their bones suggest they were generalist rather than specialist hunters, feeding on a variety of prey such as bison, horses, camels, pigs, and even mammoths ({@b page 98}). The same studies suggest that {@i Aenocyon} was in direct competition for food with several other predators found in the tar pits, like {@i Smilodon} ({@b page 105}), although whether this competition was widespread or exaggerated by the unique conditions of the tar pits is up for interpretation.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: The large number of {@i Aenocyon} fossils found in La Brea has led many to believe that these animals were highly social. Studies into their morphology and sexual dimorphism suggest that {@i Aenocyon} was similar enough to modern wolves that they likely lived together in at least temporarily monogamous pairs with several years' worth of offspring. Like wolves, older siblings may have acted as babysitters for this year's puppies and also worked alongside their parents to bring down prey. During a chase, they may have taken a relay approach, taking turns to harass an animal until it was too tired to defend itself from an attack.

We suggest playing {@i Aenocyon} similarly to wolves. They should be intelligent, effective hunters that invest a lot of time into their families, often seen playing or sleeping together. Any other large predator should be seen as a possible threat or competitor and may be mobbed if it gets too close. Humanoids should fall into this category, and they should not normally be seen as prey unless there is little else to predate upon. In fact, the natural curiosity of {@i Aenocyon} makes it more easily tamed than most animals. A party may find a curious youngster visiting their camp at night, following the smell of food who, with care and patience, can become a loyal companion.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Aenocyon} first appeared in the fossil record approximately 125,000 years ago in North America. Originally classed as a member of the genus {@i Canis}, it has recently been identified as the last known member of a separate family of canines that first appeared in the Americas almost 6 million years ago. {@i Aenocyon} was a highly successful predator, found across both North and South America, with some evidence they may have migrated to Eurasia, although these fossils are in need of reassessment since the reclassification. As with many La Brea animals, {@i Aenocyon} went extinct approximately 10,000 years ago. This was likely caused by a combination of climate change and a loss of the larger prey that they preferred to hunt, although human activity may also have played a part.

As a Bonus Action, the Mammuthus can pick up, use, or attack with a weapon or object, so long as that weapon does not require ammunition.
{@i "MAH-MUT-US KOH-LUM-BEE"} {@b (COLUMBIAN MAMMOTH)}

Columbian mammoths are a common sight along the rolling plains and harsh barrens of this continent. While woolly mammoths are well-known to inhabit frigid tundras, these bare skinned cousins are better adapted to harsher dry conditions, much like their other elephant relatives, but also seem to enjoy sparse forests. Be wary of them in regions inhabited by humanoids, as they quickly learn how dangerous we can be.

{@i Mammuthus columbi}, more commonly known as the Columbian mammoth, is a Pleistocene era (1.5 million to 13,000 years ago) elephant from North and Central America. One of the largest elephants in the fossil record, it was the closest known relative of the woolly mammoth, and the two species are thought to have hybridised frequently where their ranges overlapped.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: The Columbian mammoth was an extremely large animal with males reaching 14 ft. tall at the shoulder, 13 ft. long, and weighing between 10 and 12 tonnes. Its vertebrae had tall spines at the shoulders, giving it a sloping back, and its skull was tall with a domed appearance. The Columbian mammoth's tusks grew to exceptional lengths, reaching 13 ft. in some males and weighing as much as 500 lb. They were usually slightly asymmetrical with one tusk overlapping the other as the tips curved inwards towards the skull. While females also had large tusks, they were smaller and lighter than the males. Unlike the woolly mammoth, very little is known of the Columbian's soft tissue, although one currently undescribed sample of potential mammoth hair suggests that their sparser hair might have been lightly coloured. Studies into the wear on their teeth, as well as isotopic analyses of their bones, suggests that they were generalist herbivores, not specialising on any one plant type.

Despite its name, the Columbian mammoth was a very widespread animal with fossils recovered from multiple sites throughout America, ranging from Canada to Costa Rica. They inhabited a variety of environments including temperate grasslands, prairies, savannas, and forests. This wide range of habitats meant that Columbian mammoths lived alongside a very wide variety of animals, including deer, bison, antelope, horses, ground sloths, camels, dire wolves, sabre-toothed cats, and humans. It also cohabited with several other proboscideans such as woolly mammoths, mastodons, and gomphotheres. Most of the carnivores present would not have been a threat to adult mammoths, although evidence suggests they gathered at natural traps like the La Brea Tar Pits to feed on the carcasses of trapped mammoths. However, the Columbian mammoth also co-evolved alongside humans, with multiple sites showing evidence of active hunting with large animal traps or harvested mammoth corpses.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Fossil associations of multiple individuals indicate that Columbian mammoths were a social species, with specimens recovered from the Waco Mammoth National Monument in Texas suggesting that they lived in matriarchal herds like modern elephants. Mammoths were migratory animals that travelled hundreds of kilometres every year. Like woolly mammoths, their tusks may have been useful in clearing ground coverage to expose edible plants, however there is strong evidence they were also used in combat between individuals. A pair of adult males were found with their tusks locked together. Such an occurrence is also seen in other animals with asymmetrical ornamentation, like deer. This shows that mammoths sometimes got their tusks trapped together when fighting, which led to the animals either dying together through injuries inflicted on each other or by dehydration/starvation.

We suggest playing the Columbian mammoth as an adaptable and curious creature. In regions where humanoids are rare, healthy adults should show little fear of them and may approach a party as a novel interest in their environment. In areas where humanoids are more common, and the mammoth is more likely to have been hunted by them, they should be highly aggressive. These individuals may attempt to scare players off with mock charges or launch full on attacks if they feel threatened. The most dangerous individuals should be males in musth (a state of heightened aggression during mating seasons) who are exceptionally temperamental and unpredictable.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Both the Columbian and woolly mammoths are believed to have evolved from the Steppe mammoth. This large mammoth first arose approximately 1.8 million years ago in Eurasia before migrating to North America 300 thousand years later and giving rise to the Columbian mammoth there. On the mainland, this species maintained its large ancestral size, however populations on the Channel Islands near California underwent insular dwarfism, giving rise to the Pygmy mammoth. Columbian mammoths had a large amount of variation within their populations, which was likely a result of hybridisation with woolly mammoths.

The Columbian mammoth went extinct approximately 13,000 years ago and debate continues over the exact cause. Climate change leading to deglaciation at the end of the ice age resulted in less favourable conditions for large mammals, however it has also been suggested that overkilling from human hunters may be the main factor in their extinction. Nevertheless, there remains a lack of consensus on whether the evidence of human interaction is from hunting or scavenging. It is also very possible that mammoths died out due to a variety of factors, with both climatic change and human activity contributing to their eventual downfall.

{@i "PAR-AH-MI-LOH-DON"} {@b (BESIDE NEAR TOOTH)}

The sight of a large herbivore lumbering out of a nearby bush is often met with fear and panic. While not quite as frightening as a large carnivore doing so, most big herbivores can be quite aggressive and so attack may be imminent. This fear is not so prevalent for the slow-moving giant ground sloths, which are relatively easily escaped from. However, should one find oneself in its grasp, the fear returns posthaste.

{@i Paramylodon} is a ground sloth that first appeared in the Pliocene (4.9 million years ago) of North America. Sometimes known as Harlan's ground sloth, this large herbivore was descended from ground sloths that migrated from South America during the Great Faunal Interchange (when animals from North America migrated South and vice versa after the two continents connected).

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Paramylodon} was a large animal, although not exceptionally big for a ground sloth. It was up to 10 ft. tall and weighed between 1-1.5 tonnes once fully grown. Like other ground sloths, it was a powerfully built animal with a squat body, long muscular forelimbs tipped with curving claws, stocky hind legs, and a short neck topped by a boxy skull. Within its skin, {@i Paramylodon} had a layer of osteoderms that formed a scattered disconnected armour. {@i Paramylodon} was quadrupedal and had a rather unusual posture. Its fingers were reinforced along the knuckles, allowing it to use them to support its weight with the claws facing inwards and held above the ground. Its hind feet were also turned so that the sole of the foot faced inwards, so it supported its weight primarily on the outer edge of its foot, giving it a strange walking style.

Specimens from the La Brea Tar Pits seem to occur in two different morphotypes, broadly described as a robust type and a gracile type. The robust type is larger with thicker bones, a tall sagittal crest running down the midline of their skull and pointed canine teeth. The more gracile form is smaller, lacks the crest, and has blunted canines. While these features have been hypothesised to be due to individual or species variation, it is considered much more likely that these differences are a result of sexual dimorphism (physical differences between males and females of the same species). Sexual dimorphism can be difficult to determine with confidence in the fossil record. In the case of {@i Paramylodon}, we can say that, based on examples of their living relatives like sloths and anteaters where males are bigger than females, it is likely that the larger crested {@i Paramylodon} are probably the males.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: As with all ground sloths, {@i Paramylodon} was a herbivore. It had a broad snout which suggests it was primarily a grazer. Based on the structure and position of the hyoid bone (the bone that connects to the tongue and helps it move) we can say {@i Paramylodon} had a very mobile tongue that it probably used to pull up grass. Recent studies into its dental wear also suggest it may have supplemented its diet with edible roots and tubers.

We suggest playing {@i Paramylodon} as a solitary animal, spending most of its life grazing in grasslands or open woods. It should be a ponderous animal, moving slowly from place to place and rarely leaving its home territory. During the breeding season, males should compete over females by displaying using their canines or entering shoving matches. If it feels threatened a {@i Paramylodon} should rear up to its full height and spread its arms wide in a threat display. If attacked, it will not chase its aggressor. Rather it should hold its ground and wait for them to get close enough to be crushed by its bulk or snatched by its claws.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Paramylodon} is a member of the Mylodontidae, a group of ground sloths distantly related to the modern two-toed sloths. It has been hypothesised to be descended from a South American taxon named {@i Glossotherium}, which may have migrated into North America during the Great Faunal Interchange. While many South American species seem to have struggled to establish a foothold in North America beyond the southern parts of the continent, {@i Paramylodon} proved to be very successful, with populations established across the continent from Mexico to Canada. Along with the majority of ground sloths, {@i Paramylodon} went extinct during the Late Pleistocene approximately 14,000 years ago. As with many of La Brea's mammals, there is some debate over whether the primary driver of their extinction was environmental change or human activity. Ground sloths were known to be eaten by humans, but that may have been just one of several factors that drove the group to extinction. A small handful of ground sloths living on islands in the Caribbean outlived their continental relatives, with the last species dying in Cuba only 5000 years ago.

{@i "S-MY-LOW-DON"} {@b (SCALPEL TOOTH)}

Saber-toothed cats are fearsome predators. These large felids display all of the hunting prowess of other big cats but are armed with far more dangerous weapons. Those elongate teeth are utterly lethal. Should one find oneself prone and open to attack, a swift death is almost guaranteed.

{@i Smilodon,} commonly known as the saber-toothed cat, from the Pleistocene to Holocene eras (2.5 million years ago to 10,000 years ago) of North and South America is one of the most iconic extinct mammals.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: Fossil remains of {@i Smilodon} have been divided into 3 species: {@i Smilodon gracilis} from North America, {@i Smilodon populator} from South America and {@i Smilodon fatalis} which has been found in both continents. While {@i S}. {@i populator} was by far the largest species, {@i S}. {@i fatalis} was the species found in the La Brea Tar Pits and therefore will be the main one we discuss here. It was a robust cat about the same size as a large African Lion, with its body reaching 6 ft. long and a weight of 400-600 lb. {@i Smilodon} was a powerfully built animal, with tall shoulders, strong forelimbs and a heavily muscled neck. Its tail was very short, much like a modern lynx. Its head was boxy with a short muzzle and widely positioned eyes, reducing its depth perception but giving it a very broad field of vision. {@i Smilodon}'s most distinctive feature is its long, sword-like fangs. These were elongated (7 in. or more) teeth with a blade-like appearance, hence the name "saber-toothed". While strong (see below), these teeth would have been delicate as they developed, and {@i Smilodon}'s milk canines (baby teeth) remained in the jaw until the new sabres were at least 50% erupted. This resulted in young {@i Smilodon} having four fangs in their upper jaw during their adolescence.

{@i S}. {@i fatalis} is a common carnivore in the North American fossil record, with a recent specimen showing that it successfully migrated as far south as Uruguay. Thousands of fossils of {@i S. fatalis} have been collected from the La Brea Tar Pits. While it is found in several environments (particularly grasslands) and was a diverse predator, analyses of its preferred prey suggest that it was biased towards larger prey that are associated with tree cover. This means that it was more likely to be found in woods or forests.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Smilodon's} preference for forest dwelling prey, combined with its stocky build and reduced binocular vision, strongly suggest it was not built for prolonged or explosive chases, relying instead on ambush tactics. Being unsuitable for pursuits, it likely would have given up on a hunt if the initial charge failed. Whether they hunted alone or in groups is a topic of some debate. While thousands of fossils have been found in association in La Brea, these may have been coincidental associations rather than natural groups. However, there is some evidence of social behaviour, namely pathological evidence (records of trauma or disease preserved on the bone) such as saber-tooth bite wounds or evidence of animals living through otherwise debilitating chronic conditions, with the strongest evidence being three individuals in association with each other, an adult and two juvenile siblings who were at least two years old. This association has been interpreted as a mother and her two older, but not yet independent, offspring.

We suggest playing {@i Smilodon} as a patient ambush predator. Like all modern cats, it should spend most of its day resting, becoming more active in the early morning and late afternoon. It should not charge until prey is very close and, unless starving, will not give chase if the initial attack fails. Females can be found with several mixed age cubs from different litters and occasionally from their wider family. Males are more likely to be solitary but might still be found living in small groups of brothers well into old age. While {@i Smilodon} prefers large prey, a hungry animal will not turn its nose up at a humanoid who wanders too close. If a party has any large animals with them, this will likely result in them being stalked and attacked.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Smilodon} is the most well-known member of the Machairodontinae, a group of extinct felines from a separate lineage to modern cats that first evolved in Europe approximately 15 million years ago, before spreading across much of the northern hemisphere. During this time, {@i Smilodon} arose in North America, then spread to South America 2.5 million years later during the North and South America Great Faunal Interchange. The last {@i Smilodon} went extinct at the end of the last Ice Age approximately 10,000 years ago. The cause of their extinction is the subject of debate, with disagreement over whether it was caused by climate change, reduction in the numbers of larger prey, pressure from increasing human populations, or some combination of these factors.

entries.name: Wielding a Weapon
entries: The fossil record is full of examples of biological structures that seem odd to us today and become the focus of much scientific study. {@i Smilodon}'s saber-teeth are one such example and their durability has been a key topic of discussion. Previously, it was argued that the teeth would have been very resistant to downwards (vertical) force, but much weaker to sideways (lateral) stress. This means they would have been very good at shearing through flesh but could easily break if bent from the side. Their enormous size also led authors to suggest that they may have obstructed feeding, causing {@i Smilodon} to avoid eating flesh close to bone, resulting in inefficient feeding and lots of wasted food. More recent research has examined the teeth in more detail and found that the teeth were much stronger than previously predicted and may be more robust than the conical canines seen in most cats. Furthermore, the jaws themselves were surprisingly weak with the association being the longer the canines, the weaker the bite. {@i Smilodon} did not have the bite strength to sever spinal cords or crush windpipes, like modern cats. Instead, they likely used what is known as the "canine shear bite" where {@i Smilodon} would pull its prey to the ground and pin them with its powerful forelimbs before delivering a single massive killing bite. Possessing a gape twice as big as that of a lion, it would open its jaws wide and use the muscles in the neck and shoulder to power the canines through the neck. This would sever major arteries and the windpipe, quickly leading to the prey dying of trauma or shock. Based on bite marks on bone, {@i Smilodon} would be much more efficient at defleshing carcasses than previously thought too, meaning the canines didn't hinder feeding. Interestingly, this type of tooth adaptation is also seen in multiple unrelated groups of carnivores, such as gorgonopsids and the metatherian saber-tooth {@i Thylacosmilus}.

"TER-AH-TORN-IS"
{@b (WONDER BIRD)}

Just like modern vultures circling a weak animal, awaiting its death, Teratornis is an unwelcome sight above an adventuring party. A bad omen, if you will. The difference here, however, is that Teratornis is enormous and would be a formidable foe if it decided to attack. Thankfully, it seems to prefer to wait - a preferential choice, despite the omen.
{@i Teratornis} is a large bird from the Late Pleistocene (40,000 years ago) of North America. A distant relative of vultures and hawks, it was one of the heaviest flying birds in the fossil record.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Teratornis} was exceptionally large for a fully flighted bird. Its wingspan is estimated to have been up to 14 ft. in length and it may have weighed over 30 lb. This makes it bigger than the Andean condor, the heaviest flying bird alive today, which has a maximum weight of around 28 lbs. Like modern vultures, its wings would have been very broad and were adapted for long soaring flight on air currents. Its overall appearance would have been similar to a large vulture, with a heavyset torso, a long thin neck, and an elongated beak, although it had longer and stronger legs. In fact, some studies suggest it was an adept walker, with abilities comparable to ground living birds like turkeys. Like vultures, its eyes were placed on the sides of its head, giving it a very wide field of vision at the cost of poor depth perception.

While fossils of {@i Teratornis} are known from several Pleistocene formations in North America, the vast majority were discovered in the La Brea Tar Pits. Like many other predators in this assemblage, {@i Teratornis} is thought to have been drawn there by the large number of animals that died in the traps. As it could fly, it could more safely penetrate the pits than other carnivores, allowing it to feed on carcasses that mammalian predators may struggle to reach.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Teratornis} has several features in common with modern vultures and this has led many to argue that it was, like them, a specialist scavenger that soared over grasslands looking for carcasses.

However, it may also have caught small prey like lizards or even fish to supplement its diet. When scavenging a carcass, it likely used its large size to drive smaller competitor animals away. Given its remains are found in large numbers in La Brea, it may have been a gregarious animal that descended on corpses in mobs working together to strip away digestible meat and bones quickly. Like vultures, it likely had very strong stomach acids to help break down rotten food and bone without risk of being poisoned.

We suggest playing {@i Teratornis} as a large, mostly unaggressive bird when not eating. It should be most often seen soaring high over open areas, scanning the ground for an easy meal. When one spots food and dives to feed, any {@i Teratornis} in the area should quickly follow suit. During a feeding frenzy, they should be more pushy and more likely to attack if approached, but they will be more likely to bluff than to rush to violence. They could make for an ideal encounter where players are trying to recover an item from a corpse (perhaps even swallowing said item). Sometimes, {@i Teratornis} can be found following parties or caravans, roosting in trees above them at night in the hopes of snatching any scraps of food left behind. With effort, it may be possible to tame one of these hangers on to gain an exceptional aerial scout.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Teratornis} belongs to the Teratornithidae. This is a clade of large birds from the Americas that first arose approximately 25 million years ago during the Late Oligocene. They are part of the Accipitriformes which includes vultures, condors, eagles, hawks, and secretary birds. While teratorns are best known from North America, the oldest remains have been found in Sao Paulo, Brazil. This suggests the group originally evolved in South America, then moved north during the Miocene (23 million years ago). Teratorns include the heaviest non-pterosaurian flying animal in the fossil record, {@i Argentavis}, which may have weighed more than 150 lb. {@i Teratornis} went extinct approximately 10,000 years ago, likely due to climate change impacting large mammal numbers in its habitat. With the reduction of large prey carcasses, {@i Teratornis'} large body size became a hindrance instead of a help.

trait.name: Agile Attacker
entries: If Dyoplax succeeds on a Dexterity saving throw to take half damage from an attack, spell, or effect, it instead takes no damage.
If Dyoplax takes the Dash action, it also Disengages.

trait.name: Pseudosuchid Resilience
entries: Dyoplax has Advantage on any check or saving throw to avoid or end the {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned} condition.

action.name: Needle Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}3 ({@damage 1d4 + 1}) Piercing damage.
{@i "DYE-OH-PLAX"} {@b (FROM THE GREEK FOR TWO AND FLAT, REFERENCING ITS DOUBLE ARMOUR)}

Between damp brush and flowing waterways, strange predatory archosaurs hunt. One example is Dyoplax, which, while small, is unusually agile for a pseudosuchid. Although it is of little concern to a seasoned adventurer, several of these mobbing a novice party can lead to a bloody mess indeed.
{@i Dyoplax} is a small pseudosuchian found within the Stuttgart Formation. A tiny and heavily-armoured predator, its exact evolutionary relationships remain uncertain.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Dyoplax} was a small animal, growing to only about 2 ft. long as an adult. It was gracile, with long legs and an overlapping twinned set of armoured scutes running along its back. How heavy it was is uncertain but, given its gracile build and armour, it likely weighed around 10 lb. Its head was broad at the back but had a relatively long and narrow snout with a blunt tip and small nostrils. It had short, curving, needle-like teeth set in the front of its mouth.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Its small teeth suggest that {@i Dyoplax} was likely either fully or partially insectivorous (eats insects). However, it may have also hunted small, fast vertebrates, like reptiles and synapsids, that it could have chased down using its long, slender legs. It likely spent the hottest parts of the day resting, coming out in the cooler afternoon and evening to hunt.

We suggest playing {@i Dyoplax} as an animal that spends most of the day sheltering in cool covered undergrowth. It should be resting during the hottest parts of the day, then becoming more active in the early morning and late afternoon when the temperatures are lower. It should spend much of its time patrolling for prey along riverbanks and within foliage, either snapping at insects as they try to fly away or sprinting (briefly) after small, terrified reptiles. It poses very little threat to humanoids and may, in fact, be drawn to buzzing insect activity around a lit campfire. Anyone sitting first or last watch should have no trouble spotting this small animal, snapping at moths and midges around the camp.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Dyoplax}'s placement within pseudosuchia (the group that eventually gave rise to the crocodylomorphs) is surprisingly controversial for such a small animal. When the original fossil was discovered, the researcher in 1867 described it as a cross between a lizard and a gharial (a long-snouted crocodilian). Initially, it was placed in the Aetosauria, a group of heavily armoured omnivorous/ herbivorous pseudosuchians. However, various factors such as the placement of the teeth and the lack of a shovel-shaped jaw makes this unlikely. Another analysis suggested that it belonged to Sphenosuchia, a group of basal crocodylomorphs with gracile bodies and erected postures. They argued {@i Dyoplax} had features of crocodylomorphs in the structure of its nasal bone and the jugal (cheek) bone.

A more recent study in 2013 argued against this placement and instead identified it as a erpetosuchid. These are long-legged pseudosuchians related to, but not part of, Crocodylomorpha, with long legs and heavily armoured backs. They argued that {@i Dyoplax} should be placed in the group due to cranial characters like the shape of the orbits (eyes) and how slender its legs are, but they noted that ultimately the preservation of the {@i Dyoplax} holotype (a high-quality mold made in sandstone) made reliable analyses difficult.

trait.name: Heavyset Skull
entries: Metoposaurus cannot be critically hit.

trait.name: Aestivate
entries: While in a burrow underground, Metoposaurus can enter a trance-like state of hibernation for several months. During this time it can survive without food or water and is treated as though it were unconscious, although it is aware of its surroundings.

action.name: Wide-Gaped Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}6 ({@damage 1d10 + 1}) Piercing damage.
A Medium or smaller creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} (escape {@dc 11}). Until this Grapple ends, Metoposaurus cannot attack another target.

bonus.name: Adaptive Hunting
entries: As a Bonus Action, Metoposaurus may do one of the following things:

- Lunge: Metoposaurus Dashes. - Snap: Metoposaurus makes a single Wide-Gaped Bite attack against a creature that is within 5 ft. of it. - Gape-suck: If Metoposaurus is within water, pick another creature also in water within 15 ft. of it. That creature must succeed a {@dc 11} Strength saving throw or be pulled 10 ft. towards to Metoposaurus.

reaction.name: Reactive Attack
entries: If another creature comes within 5 ft. of Metoposaurus (including from Gape-suck), it can use its Reaction to make a single Wide-Gaped Bite attack against that creature.
{@i "MEH-TOP-OH-SORE-US"} {@b (FRONT REPTILE)}

Research records indicate that the majority of dangerous predators in the Stuttgart Formation are aquatic, dwelling within the waterways of the region. What they don't note, however, is that some of those predators are fully capable of lunging out of the water and snatching oblivious creatures drinking at the river's edge or inattentive adventures.
{@i Metoposaurus} is a temnospondyl amphibian from the Late Triassic (227 million years ago) of western Europe. A sizable aquatic predator, it is known to be found in multiple mass death assemblages.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Metoposaurus} was a strangely shaped animal, between 5 to 10 ft. in length with a flat shovel-like head and disproportionately large jaws full of tiny needle-like teeth. Its eyes were small but positioned much further forward than in most temnospondyls. Its legs were tiny relative to its body size but they had wide palms and good musculature. When swimming it is thought that these were used for steering while the tail provided locomotion.

There are several {@i Metoposaurus} mass death assemblages scattered across Europe. These are bonebeds (sediments filled with fragmentary bone fossils) dominated by dozens or hundreds of {@i Metoposaurus} remains. Studies show that these bonebeds were probably deposited in temporary lakes that disappeared during the dry season. Research suggests that, in order to survive these changes in environment, {@i Metoposaurus} burrowed deep into the mud once the lakes started to dry up and entered a period of dormancy. This strategy allowed them to wait for wetter seasons to return but came with risks, not least the chance that the rains may be delayed and the animals would be trapped, their burrows eventually becoming their tombs.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Studies into the kinetics (how forces affect the skeleton) of the skull show that {@i Metoposaurus} had an impressively wide gape and was able to bite with considerable force. It also suggests it may have used both ambush and active pursuit tactics when hunting. This ability to adapt its attack strategy based on circumstances would have allowed it to feed on a wider range of prey, from chasing down fleeing fish to snatching unfortunate animals coming to the water's edge to drink.

We suggest playing {@i Metoposaurus} as an opportunistic predator, taking advantage of any chance to snatch prey. This should make them highly unpredictable and it should be difficult for even a seasoned adventurer to guess how they will react. During the wet season, they should be found patrolling waterways, either following shoals of fish or staying near the water's edge in the hopes of finding a larger meal. When the rains stop and their homes start to dry up, many {@i Metoposaurus} may be forced into close contact and fighting should be commonplace. Eventually, they will be forced to burrow into the mud in the hopes of being able to wait out the dry period. Once the rainy season returns, they should rise from dormancy and overnight a new lake might be filled with dozens of hungry individuals.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Metoposaurus} is the name sake of the Metoposauridae. This is a group of temnospondyls that first appeared about 235 million years ago, in what is now North Africa, before spreading across much of Pangea. Within Metoposauridae, mass death assemblages are common and have been identified for at least four taxa, including {@i Metoposaurus} itself. Metoposaurids, despite their success, died out around 215 million years ago, before the Triassic-Jurassic extinction. The cause is uncertain, but it has been suggested that it may be linked to the Manicougan Crater, formed by an asteroid impact event that has been linked to a notable rise in the extinction rate during the Late Triassic.

trait.name: Electrosense
entries: Palaeobates has a Blindsight of 5 ft. while in water (included above).

trait.name: Euryhaline
entries: Palaeobates can only breathe in water. It can tolerate both salty and brackish water.

trait.name: Dermal Denticles
entries: If a creature Grapples or otherwise holds Palaeobates, that creature takes 1 Piercing damage.

action.name: Crushing Nip
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 0} to hit, Reach 5 ft, one target. {@h}2 (2) Bludgeoning damage.
{@i "PAY-LEE-OH-BAH-TES"} {@b (ANCIENT WALKER)}

Throughout the Triassic, strange shark-like fish can be found along coastal waters and in estuaries. Rather than hunting prey viciously like the sharks we are familiar with today, they cruise the ocean floor in search of shelly prey to crush with their specialised teeth. More than once they've mistaken an armoured boot for prey. That wouldn't be such an issue on its own if it wasn't for the commotion of such a mistake attracting larger predators.

{@i Palaeobates} is a hybodont cartilaginous fish from the Triassic (252 to 205 million years ago) of Europe and North America. A member of the sibling group to modern sharks, it had distinctive teeth designed more for crushing shells than tearing flesh.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Palaeobates} was a small animal, growing no more than 3 ft. long. In most ways it resembled a modern shark with a long torpedo-shaped body and an asymmetrical crescent moon shaped tail where the upper half was much larger than the lower half. It had two large dorsal fins, each with a bony spine supporting it. Male {@i Palaeobates} also had two pairs of hook-like spines just behind their eyes, giving them an almost devilish appearance. In its mouth were tightly compacted rows with dozens of flat, domed teeth which evolved for crushing prey rather than tearing pieces off of it.

{@i Palaeobates} has been found in Triassic formations across the Northern Hemisphere. It generally occurs in marine environments or, as is the case in the Stuttgart Formation, in the saltier waters found at the entrance to river deltas. It was likely euryhaline, meaning that it was capable of tolerating different salinities and would have been comfortable in the mix of fresh and saltwater found in a deltaic system.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Palaeobates} is best known for its durophagous (crushing) teeth. Durophagous teeth are able to robustly exert a large amount of pressure over a small area and are used to crack hard-shelled organisms like crustaceans, molluscs, bivalves, and brachiopods. {@i Palaeobates} may have specialised in feeding close to the sea floor either by digging out shelled animals or hunting ammonoids that floated above the ocean floor.

We suggest playing {@i Palaeobates} as a solitary hunter that is most commonly found close to the ocean floor. It should spend most of its day lazily drifting just above the seabed, using the electrical sensors around its snout to detect prey hidden in the sediment below. Sometimes, if food is scarce it may move into the shallower waters of a delta in search of a meal. Occasionally, a {@i Palaeobates} will make an investigatory bite on the toes or fingers of a humanoid swimmer, and although it's almost never followed by a full attack, it is a potentially bone breaking injury with the subsequent commotion risking drawing the attention of much more dangerous predators.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Palaeobates} is a member of the Hybodontiformes or hybodonts. This is a group of cartilaginous fish that is the sister group to the Neoselachians, the group that includes modern sharks and rays. Hybodonts first appeared in the Devonian (360 million years ago) and had a global distribution. They were very successful, found in both fresh and saltwater environments and occupied a variety of niches, from pursuit predators to slow opportunists to shell-crushing durophages. These highly adaptive carnivores had an enormous temporal range, surviving for more than 290 million years. However, like so many other organisms, they were driven into extinction during the end Cretaceous extinction event 66 million years ago.

trait.name: Latrinic
entries: Woznikella has Vulnerability to Poison damage (included above).

Over the course of 24 hours, Woznikella may create a 5 ft. by 5 ft. latrine that is 2 to 3 ft. deep. Once created, Woznikella does not need to create another latrine for at least a month, or until it moves to a new area.
A creature that starts its turn in this latrine must succeed a
{@dc 11} Constitution saving throw or become {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned} for 1 minute.

trait.name: Adaptive Hardy Herbivore
entries: Woznikella has Advantage on all saving throws.

action.name: Tusk and Horn Gore
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}11 ({@damage 4d4 + 1}) Piercing damage plus 2 ({@damage 1d4}) Bludgeoning damage.

action.name: Shove into Shite
entries: If Woznikella is within 5 ft. of a creature that is within 10 ft. of Woznikella's latrine, it can attempt to push that creature into the latrine.
The target creature must succeed a {@dc 11} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}, pushed up to 10 ft. into the latrine, and take {@dice 1d8} Poison damage.
Additionally, after a failed save but before the creature is moved, Woznikella may use its Bonus Action to make a Tusk and Horn Gore against that creature.
{@i "VOZ-NI-KEH-LAH"} {@b (NAMED FOR THE TOWN OF WOŹNIKI IN POLAND)}

In the sodden mists of the Stuttgart Formation, strange grunting sounds can sometimes be heard carried on the wind. These originate from herbivorous dicynodonts that rummage through the wet soils and muds in search of fresh plant growth. While not particularly bothersome animals, be wary not to step in one of their latrines.

{@i Woznikella} is a medium-sized dicynodont from the Middle-Late Triassic (around 230 million years ago) of Poland. While the holotype is from the Grabowa Formation, partial remains of a dicynodont were discovered in the Stuttgart Formation which, in recent years, have tentatively been identified as belonging to {@i Woznikella.}

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Woznikella} is only known from a partial immature specimen. This animal would have been at least 5 ft. long and may have reached 6 or 7 ft. as an adult. It was a squat animal, with a tubby body, short tail, and a semi-erect gait. Based on dicynodont remains in fossil carnivore dung, it is thought that it may have been covered in sparse, wiry hair (not depicted here). Its head was tall at the back and had pointed jaws that ended in a keratinous beak. The sides of the skull jutted out and forward, forming two downward pointing horn-like triangular extensions that were also covered in keratin. These horn-like protrusions appear to have had two distinct morphologies in dicynodonts and it is thought that they were probably sexually dimorphic (different shapes for males and females). While much of the upper part of the jaw is not preserved in {@i Woznikella}, based on comparisons with other dicynodonts, it is very likely that it also had a large set of tusks (continuously growing, elongate and pointed teeth). These were true tusks (unlike {@i Mastodonsaurus'} ({@b page 146 in DDDD}) pseudotusks, for example), which are only found in mammals and dicynodonts. They can serve a variety of functions including defence, intraspecific (same species) combat, and digging.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Based on dicynodont bonebeds preserving the remains of dozens of individuals together, {@i Woznikella} was likely a social animal that lived in sizable herds. They would have fed by browsing, using their beaks to cut through low-growing ferns. Interestingly, dicynodonts are one of the only animals in the fossil record with strong evidence of their toileting habits. Analyses of large deposits of coprolites (fossil dung) have indicated that animals such as {@i Woznikella} were latrinic. This meant that, rather than randomly defecating as they fed, {@i Woznikella} would have communal latrines - designated spots to defecate that are away from feeding grounds. This behaviour is well documented in mammals and is thought to be beneficial as it helps establish territorial boundaries and reduces the spread of disease. As with their tusks, the dicynodont latrines are the first non-mammalian example of this behaviour.

We suggest playing {@i Woznikella} as a relatively calm animal that is rarely found alone. Herds should be seen grazing across large areas and, for the most part, they should not be prone to conflict. If a fight does break out over food or a mate, they should swing their heads back and forth to show the size of their facial "horns", or yawn widely to expose their tusks. Only if one of the animals refuses to back down should a full-on fight ensue. As long as it is given a respectful distance, {@i Woznikella} should not be a threat to humanoids. However, as with any sizable herbivore, they may still attack if they feel threatened or if they are approached during their mating season.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Dicynodonts first appeared in the fossil record in the Permian (268 million years ago) of South Africa. They are members of the Synapsida, a highly diverse group of animals that includes mammals. They were incredibly successful herbivores, spreading across much of Pangea and, by the end of the Permian, were one of the most abundant animals in the fossil record. However, the end-Permian extinction event devastated Dicynodont numbers and only a handful of taxa survived into the Triassic. While those that survived the extinction event would once again become the dominant herbivores, they eventually declined towards the Late Triassic. It has been hypothesised that this may have been due to climate change, and the spread of increasingly arid conditions. Their numbers dwindled and they finally went extinct approximately 201 million years ago.

trait.name: Unknown Anatomy
entries: As little is known about Zanclodon beyond it being a carnivorous archosaur, we're unsure what its adaptations might have been. Choose from one of the three adaptations listed below. Zanclodon gains that adaptation. Alternatively, you may roll twice on the Minor Mutations table (pages 218-226 in DDDD) and apply those adaptations to Zanclodon (do not adjust its CR).
- Durable Defender. Zanclodon's AC is increased to 16. It has Advantage on Constitution saving throws.
- Frenzied Feeder. Zanclodon may make three Blade-Toothed Bite attacks with its multiattack, rather than two.
- Nocturnal Nightmare. Zanclodon has a Darkvision of 60 ft. If Zanclodon begins its turn Hidden, its first attack this turn deals an additional {@dice 1d6} Piercing damage.
- Aquatic Ambusher. Zanclodon gains a swim speed of 30 ft. and has Advantage on {@skill Stealth} checks while in water.

trait.name: Wastebasket Taxon
entries: All other archosaurs (crocodiles, dinosaurs, pterosaurs, birds, and their kin) treat Zanclodon as an ally unless Zanclodon attacks them or one of their other allies.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Zanclodon chooses the Attack action, it may make two Blade-Toothed Bite attacks.

action.name: Blade-Toothed Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}5 ({@damage 1d6 + 2}) Piercing damage.
{@i "ZANK-LOW-DON"} {@b (SCYTHE TOOTH)}

Sometimes, there were strange murmurings and rummagings in the sodden undergrowth of the Stuttgart Formation that we never fully identified. More than once, our party found itself accosted by a strange predatory archosaur that, in the chaos of battle, none of us were able to fully see. Only brief moments of clarity revealed a maw agape lunging at us, revealing blade-like teeth, before each of us flinched and darted back in terror - only to find the animal already vanished into the rain.

{@i Zanclodon} is a fairly obscure, and poorly understood, archosaurian reptile from the Stuttgart Formation. Below, we discuss the challenges in palaeontology of working with fragmentary remains. Interestingly, {@i Zanclodon} is surprisingly relevant to a theropod discovery in 2025.

entries.name: Working with Fragmentary Fossils
entries: The field of palaeontology is really not too different from classic detective work. Like Hercule Poirot and Sherlock Holmes, we piece together evidence to make deductions about ancient beasts, long-gone ecosystems, and significant moments in time. Unfortunately, we do not have the benefit of our stories ending in neat little drawing room scenes. Instead, we try to bring fossils together to create brief glimpses into the complex history of life on our planet. Mistakes are frequent, particularly in taxonomy. Thousands of taxa have been erected only to be re-evaluated, re-diagnosed, or rendered entirely invalid. One key issue is the identification, description, and placement of undiagnosable material. Many fossils are simply too heavily damaged or incomplete to determine the full anatomy or taxonomic placement of a newly discovered organism.

Some scientists take a simplified approach, noting that the specimen is unplaceable. Others achieve the best placement they can and assign the fossil to an established taxon, despite it not meeting all of the criteria. This can result in a taxon containing examples that are likely from other, perhaps new, taxa. When this happens a lot to a single taxon, we call it a "wastebasket taxon" - as all of the "junk" is thrown in it. {@i Zanclodon} is one such wastebasket taxon.

entries.name: The History of Zanclodon as a Wastebasket
entries: The original material assigned to {@i Zanclodon} was described in the 1840s by notable palaeontologist Theodor Plieniger. He was describing several isolated Triassic archosaur fossils including teeth, vertebrae, and a jaw with teeth still in the sockets. The most notable feature of these bones was that the teeth lacked serrations, which was seemingly unique among archosaurs. He initially wanted to name his new animal {@i Smilodon} but, unsurprisingly to modern readers, found that the name was already occupied. He instead settled on {@i Zanclodon} and, over the next 70 years, eight species were erected within this genus for isolated teeth and jaw remains, despite having little in common with the holotype material.

The placement of {@i Zanclodon} within Archosauria was equally muddled. It was first identified as a dinosaur, then a teratosaurid (now called rauisuchians) and later, despite its clearly carnivorous teeth, a herbivorous plateosaurid. Like many wastebasket taxa from the 1800s, interest in {@i Zanclodon} dropped for most of the 20thcentury and it was not until 1998 when the first proper taxonomic revision occurred after a single jaw assigned to the genus was noted to have serrated teeth and therefore could not be {@i Zanclodon}. For the subsequent 10 years, a handful of publications reappraised specific fossils assigned to {@i Zanclodon} as various indeterminate archosaurs, culminating in a 2011 paper that removed all but the original fossils. Of those original fossils, only the jaw remained and the other components had been lost. Nevertheless, the initial unique dentition allowed {@i Zanclodon} to remain a valid genus of indeterminate primitive archosaur.

In 2025, the original jaw described in 1998 that was initially assigned to {@i Zanclodon} was revised and identified as a (for the Triassic) exceptionally large theropod (perhaps 23 ft. long). A new distinct genus, {@i Newtonsaurus}, was erected for that specimen.

This history of rushed early assignment of fragmentary or unrelated remains followed by a period of re-evaluation is typical of a wastebasket taxon and is, unfortunately, common in palaeontology. In fact, by remaining a valid, even if very poorly understood, taxon, {@i Zanclodon} is one of the lucky few to be revised and survive the experience.

entries.name: What Do We Know About Zanclodon?
entries: {@i Zanclodon}'s jaw was about 11 inches long and it has the conical, recurved teeth of a predator, albeit without serrations. This means that it was likely a major predator in the Stuttgart Formation about the size of a very large dog or wolf and, as a Triassic archosaur, it was probably covered in scales or scutes. However, without the rest of its body, we can't determine how it hunted, if it stood on two or four legs, or if it had any specialised adaptations. Given the environment of the Stuttgart Formation, it may have spent a lot of time in water.

Each of the adaptations presented in {@i Zanclodon}'s "{@b Unknown Anatomy}" ability convey a different role within its ecosystem. We suggest that you trust your own instincts on how an animal with those adaptations might behave, or defer to the behaviour of another known animal that fills the same niche.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: Our artwork for Zanclodon is based on the Aquatic Ambusher adaptation.
