monster.name: Australovenator

trait.name: Prey Dragger
entries: Australovenator may move at its normal speed while grappling a creature smaller than itself, dragging the creature with it.

trait.name: Muscular Forearms
entries: Australovenator has Advantage on {@skill Athletics} checks and Strength saving throws.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Australovenator chooses the Attack action, it may make two Gracile Bite attacks and one Powerful Claws attack. Alternatively, it may make one Gracile Bite attack and one Dismembering Kick. attack.

action.name: Gracile Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 6} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}5 ({@damage 1d6 + 2}) Piercing damage.

action.name: Powerful Claws
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 6} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}10 ({@damage 2d6 + 3}) Piercing damage plus 3 ({@damage 1d6}) Slashing damage.
A creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled}.

action.name: Dismembering Kick
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 6} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}14 ({@damage 2d10 + 3}) Slashing damage plus 8 ({@damage 1d10 + 3}) Bludgeoning damage.
A creature hit by this attack that is currently {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} by Australovenator takes an additional {@dice 1d10} Slashing damage.

legendary.name: Clawed Squeeze
entries: Australovenator squeezes a creature that is currently Grappling with its powerful clawed hands. That creature takes {@dice 2d6} Piercing damage.

legendary.name: Dragging Stride
entries: Australovenator moves up to 10 ft. If it is Grappling a creature, that creature is dragged with it.

legendaryHeader: Australovenator can take 1 Legendary Action, choosing from the options below. Only one legendary option can be used at a time and only at the end of another creature's turn. The Australovenator regains spent Legendary Actions at the start of its turn.

entries: "AUS-TRAH-LOW-VEN-AH-TOR"
{@b (SOUTHERN HUNTER)}

The journal of another researcher who travelled through these polar regions reports the presence of a large predatory dinosaur, a megaraptor of some sort, that patrols the winter forests. Presumably, it sustains itself through the harsh winter months by excavating lungfish... Although I would rather not test that hypothesis by encountering it during the long night.

{@i Australovenator} was a megaraptorid from the Cretaceous (100 to 95 million years ago) Winton and Eumeralla formations in eastern Australia. A lightly built theropod, it is best known for the pair of enormous hooked claws it had on each hand.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: While it is the largest theropod known from Australia, {@i Australovenator} is one of the smallest megaraptorids. It grew to approximately 20 ft. long and would have weighed about 700 lb. Its body was lightly built and gracile with a long snout. Its thin jaws had a relatively weak bite and were not built for handling large struggling prey, but could slash effectively. By comparison, its arms were robust and powerful with the typical three fingers of theropods. While the claw on the third digit was relatively small, those on the first two fingers were enormous. They looked superficially like the toe claws of a dromaeosaur but were much larger and more robust. The claw on the first digit was so big it dwarfed the finger itself. Studies show these arms were very well muscled and had a wide range of movement. They are also known to have been very resistant to the stresses created when the fingers extended or flexed.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: The strength and flexibility of {@i Australovenator's} arms naturally raises the question of what they were used for. Most researchers agree that the arms were its primary hunting tool and would have been used to grapple prey such as {@i Leaellynasaura} ({@b page 140}). The claws would have either pierced the skin to better hold them in place or opened blood vessels, causing the animal to die of blood loss and shock. They may also have been useful in dismembering prey, holding the prey still so that the weaker jaws could access softer delicate areas of the prey's body.

We suggest playing {@i Australovenator} as a largely solitary hunter, following herds of ornithischians waiting for an opportunity to ambush stragglers and drag them into the undergrowth. If challenged, rather than immediately attacking, an {@i Australovenator} should use its muscular arms and large claws as part of a threat display.

Humanoids may be seen as easy slow prey, or threats to be warded off by {@i Australovenator} waving its claws and stomping its feet aggressively. If a challenge turns into a fight, an {@i Australovenator} will grapple its enemy with its claws then attempt to dismember them or bite their neck. Rival fights should rarely be fatal however, with the loser quick to back off to avoid serious injury.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Australovenator} is the smallest member of the Megaraptoridae. These unusual dinosaurs were first described in the late 90s based on fragmentary remains that included a massive claw. These claws were first thought to be from a giant dromaeosaurid, but in the early 2010s they were recognised as originating from a distinct group of theropods which the most recent studies suggests were probably a sister group to the Tyrannosauroidea.

While their earliest relatives come from Japan and Thailand, the first true megaraptorids appear in the fossil record approximately 120 million years ago in eastern Australia. Within 30 million years, they had migrated to South America where they appear to have been part of a large diversification event alongside several other dinosaur groups. By the Late Cretaceous (70 million years ago) the largest megaraptorids grew to more than 30 ft. long. While {@i Australovenator} itself is thought to have gone extinct approximately 95 million years ago, the megaraptorids were successful enough to outlive some other major theropod groups like the carcharodontosaurids and were still part of the South American dinosaur fauna right up until the end Cretaceous extinction.

trait.name: Lungfish
entries: Ceratodus can breathe in both air and water.

trait.name: Aestivate
entries: While in its burrow, Ceratodus can enter a trance-like state of hibernation for several months.
During this time, it can survive without food or water. If collected, it can be kept as a fresh source of food in this aestivated state (2 day's rations for one person).

action.name: Fishy Nip
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 2} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}1 (1) Piercing damage.

action.name: Create Burrow
entries: As an Action, Ceratodus can create a burrow in mud, sand, or silt that is large enough for it to fit in (typically 1-3 ft. deep and 6 inches in diameter).
If already in a burrow, it can instead use its Action to cover the entrance, concealing it ({@skill Survival} or Investigation {@dc 12} to reveal it).
"SER-AH-TOE-DUS"
{@b (HORN TOOTH)}

The harsh winters of the polar Eumeralla forest can be made a little easier with some knowledge of Ceratodus' habits. These freshwater lungfish aestivate, or rather hibernate in a burrow during dry periods, and are a valuable source of food during the long night, that is, if you know where to find them.

{@i Ceratodus} was a lungfish that was present globally throughout the Mesozoic and early Cenozoic (250 to 55 million years ago). One of several species of fish capable of breathing air, it represents a window into how vertebrates originally transitioned from the water to the land.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Ceratodus} is known only from fossilised tooth plates (broad, flat teeth) and therefore we can only speculate about its overall body morphology by looking at other extinct and living lungfish. Based on comparisons with modern tooth plates, {@i Ceratodus} has been estimated to average about 3 ft. long, although some giant examples may have been as large as 13 ft. in length. Lungfish typically have a similar appearance, and it's generally assumed that {@i Ceratodus} should have been similar to at least some modern species, such as the Australian lungfish. They likely had long cylindrical bodies that transitioned into a muscular tail with a low rounded fin running along its length. Their pectoral and pelvic fins are unusually fleshy and strong, able to support the fish's weight as they dragged themselves along the ground. As a lungfish, {@i Ceratodus} possessed a set of working lungs as well as gills, allowing it to breathe both in and outside of water.
While it still spent most of its life in water, it would have been able to travel short distances to nearby bodies of water if its pond dried up or in search of food.

{@i Ceratodus} is a globally present genus, found on every continent except Antarctica. It preferred living in shallow pools and swampy regions. When their water sources dry up and there are no other nearby pools to migrate to, some lungfish species dig burrows into the mud to aestivate (the summer equivalent of hibernation). Fossil burrows have been attributed to {@i Ceratodus,} although without body fossils, this is still speculative.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Based on its tooth plates, {@i Ceratodus} would have been primarily carnivorous while also occasionally eating aquatic plants. Their plates would have allowed them to crush hard shelled organisms like small crustaceans and aquatic insects, although it may also have fed on smaller fish and amphibians. Based on the behaviour of modern lungfish, when breeding, a male {@i Ceratodus} may have dug a breeding burrow where it would be able to fertilise the eggs of several females. After the female laid eggs in a small nest, the male would remain and oxygenate the eggs until they hatch, while also providing protection from small predators. {@i Ceratodus}, like modern lungfish, was likely exceptionally long-lived and some individuals may have lived for over a century, if in good health.

We suggest playing {@i Ceratodus} as a freshwater fish that primarily feeds at the bottoms of ponds or in the mud of swampy flats. It should be relatively placid towards large animals, ignoring them unless they approach too close whereby it should make a dash for deeper water. A {@i Ceratodus} caught on land and unable to reach the water may attempt to bite anyone that picks it up. They make for an ideal source of food for travelling adventurers and can be easily dug up from their muddy burrows. When cooked, {@i Ceratodus} should taste like salmon, the consumption of which grants wisdom according to some myths.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Ceratodus} is a member of the Dipnoi (lungfish). This group arose in the Early Devonian, more than 400 million years ago, and persists to the modern day. One of several groups of fish that can breathe out of water, they were originally a marine family before transitioning into freshwater habitats. They are a sister group to all tetrapods (land vertebrates) and their ability to walk on land while still being tied to water provides insight into the early stages of terrestrialisation (moving to land) of vertebrates. {@i Ceratodus} survived the end Cretaceous extinction, but died out approximately 55 million years ago. The cause of their extinction is still unknown.

trait.name: Amphibian Ambusher
entries: Koolasuchus can breathe in both air and water, has Advantage on {@skill Stealth} checks while in water, and has a Blindsight of 10 ft. while in water (included above).

trait.name: Frozen Torpor
entries: Koolasuchus is functionally immune to Cold damage (included above). If Koolasuchus would take Cold damage, instead prevent that damage and, for every 10 points of Cold damage prevented (cumulative), reduce its walking and swimming speed by 5 ft. for 1 minute. If its walking speed is reduced to 0 by this effect, it falls unconscious.

action.name: Grab and Drag
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}11 ({@damage 2d8 + 2}) Piercing damage.

A creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} (escape {@dc 12}). Koolasuchus may move up to 10 ft. after hitting with this attack, dragging a {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} creature with it.
"COOL-AH-SOO-KUS"
{@b (KOOL'S CROCODILE)}
Many adventurers expect frozen polar rivers and ponds to be devoid of large predators, particularly reptiles and amphibians.
They presume that their physiology is not suited to the cold waters and they can be fished or swam in without fear.
However, I can attest that this is very much NOT the case in some regions. Some amphibians have adaptations, such as natural antifreeze, that allows them to tolerate such extreme colds comfortably.

{@i Koolasuchus} is a large chigutisaurid temnospondyl amphibian. Roughly the size of a large crocodile, this giant amphibian was the last surviving member of a group which had successfully established in Gondwana during the Early Triassic (252 million years ago).

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Koolasuchus} was very big for an amphibian, reaching 10 ft. long and weighing at least 1000 lb. It looked similar to an enormous salamander, with a flat, moist, scaleless body. Its tail was compressed and likely had dorsal (upper) and ventral (lower) fins. Its legs were small and short, giving it a slow sprawling gait, although it was capable of moving fast in short explosive bursts. Although the skull is incomplete, its head was clearly enormous compared to its body and would likely have been about 2 ft. wide with large jaws, numerous sharp, curving teeth, and small eyes set right at the front of the head.

As an amphibian, {@i Koolasuchus} would have been ectothermic ("cold blooded"). This has raised the question of how it could survive in a region as cold as the Eumeralla Formation. It was closely tied to local water sources and would have been very unlikely to migrate to warmer climates during the winter freeze. One possibility is that {@i Koolasuchus} was able to enter a state of torpor, in the same manner as modern overwintering amphibians. This would require {@i Koolasuchus} to build up fat stores prior to the cold and submerge itself beneath ice near the shore. As amphibians can breathe through their skin, they can remain underwater for months on end if they reduce their metabolic activities. {@i Koolasuchus} could have used a similar strategy, but it inherently comes with a high risk. Modern frogs frequently die due to changes in conditions or being discovered by predators while in this form of hibernation and, if {@i Koolasuchus} used a similar strategy, it would have been an enormous and easy meal for a scavenging predator like {@i Australovenator} ({@b page 134}).

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Koolasuchus} is a large aquatic carnivore, similar in size to a modern crocodile and is thought to have occupied a similar ecological niche. It may have hunted by snapping at fish and invertebrates that passed by, or laid in wait near the shore with only its eyes poking above the water's surface. If an animal came too close, {@i Koolasuchus} would have lurched out to grab it and drag it back into the water.

We suggest playing {@i Koolasuchus} as a patient, inactive animal. It should spend most of its day in the water, unmoving, and watching for prey. Rather than chasing prey, it should remain still until either fish or some unlucky land animal strays too close. Then with a sudden snap, the prey should be grabbed and devoured immediately, leaving an eerie stillness. With larger prey, it should try to drag the prey underwater to either hold onto it until it drowns or bleeds to death from the bite wound.
A humanoid, especially a smaller one, approaching too close to the water's edge may suddenly find a 10 ft. monster amphibian latched onto their legs before they have a chance to flee.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Koolasuchus} was a chigutisaurid, a late surviving group of temnospondyls that was one of the only temnospondyl groups to survive the Permo-Triassic extinction. Found exclusively in Gondwana (South America, Australia, Madagascar, Africa, Antarctica and India), their long-term survival into the Early Cretaceous has been attributed to the relative isolation of the Gondwanan landmasses, particularly Australia which was ultimately their last stronghold. Their extinction has been attributed to climate change, with an increase in temperatures allowing animals such as crocodiles to fully establish themselves as competition. It has been speculated that crocodiles, which occupied a similar niche but were better adapted for the increasingly warm conditions, outcompeted {@i Koolasuchus}, resulting in not only its extinction but the final fall of a group that had persisted for 230 million years.

trait.name: Burrow Builder
entries: Leaellynasaura has a burrowing speed of 5 ft. (included above). It can only burrow through soft dirt, mud, and sand.

trait.name: Alert Polar Prey
entries: Leaellynasaura has a Darkvision of 120 ft., Resistance to Cold damage (both included above), gains +5 to Initiative rolls, and other creatures can't gain Advantage on attack rolls against it as a result of starting their turn Hidden from it.

action.name: Wriggling Scratch
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}2 ({@damage 1d4}) Slashing damage.
If Leaellynasaura hits a creature that is grappling it with this attack, the Grapple ends.
"LEE-AE-LIN-AH-SORA-AH"
{@b (LEAELLYN'S REPTILE)}

If you traverse the polar forests with the utmost stealth in the darkest long-nights, you might be so lucky as to glimpse a small herd of Leaellynasaura. These delightful little dinosaurs are exceptionally skittish and very, very cute. I can only imagine what horrible hunting pressures have pushed them to evolve such fearfulness.

{@i Leaellynasaura} is a small ornithischian dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous (118 million years ago) of Australia. An animal adapted for living in polar climates, there has been a lot of debate about where it falls on the dinosaur family tree.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: For a Cretaceous dinosaur, {@i Leaellynasaura} was not a large animal, growing to only 6 ft. long and probably weighing less than 20 lb. In most respects it was similar to other small-bodied ornithischians, being a lightly built biped with a tall skull and jaws tipped by a keratinous beak. However, its tail was distinctive, which was exceptionally long with at least 70 vertebrae and almost three times the length of the body. This gave it the greatest tail-to-body ratio of any ornithischian.

There has been some debate about whether {@i Leaellynasaura} was a diurnal (daytime) or nocturnal (nighttime) animal. A partial skull shows evidence that it had very large eyes for its size, which may have given it good night vision. This would have been useful as it inhabited polar regions, which included months without sunlight. Another suggestion was that the size of the eyes had more to do with the age of the animal than its habits, as the skull came from a young individual and juvenile animals almost always have proportionally larger eyes than adults. However, a study into the growth patterns of {@i Leaellynasaura}'s bones show that it did not have periods of arrested development (periods with slowed growth). This indicates that it was probably active throughout the year and, regardless of the maturity of the specimen in question, it certainly would have had to cope with months of darkness.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Leaellynasaura} was a herbivore and, with its narrow jaws, was probably a selective browser. It would have used its hard beak to snip the fronds off of ground-level ferns and small cycads. Several burrows have been found near where {@i Leaellynasaura} was discovered which may have been made by the small dinosaur, serving as shelter from predators and a place to escape the coldest wintery weather.

We suggest playing {@i Leaellynasaura} as a highly alert and extremely skittish animal. It should move through the undergrowth in groups of 3 to 6 individuals with at least one animal always scanning for danger as the others feed. Any threat should make them scatter into the nearest bushes or burrow for safety. On the very rare occasion one is cornered or picked up by a humanoid, it can do little more than bite and scratch in the hopes of breaking free.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Where exactly {@i Leaellynasaura} falls on the ornithischian family tree is not certain. It has been placed in multiple different positions within the group, such as it being a late surviving basal form to being a generic member of the more derived Neornithischia. The most recent study to look at its relationships placed it in Elasmaria, a subgroup of Iguanodontia made up of small bipedal Gondwanan (southern hemisphere) ornithischians that are the sibling group to the Dryomorpha (which includes the larger, more well known ornithopods). As with all phylogenetic studies of contentiously placed animals, this interpretation could be overturned by a new study at any point.

Chinsamy, A., Rich, T. and Vickers-Rich, P. 1998. Polar dinosaur bone histology. {@i Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology}, {@b 18 (2)}, pp.385-390.

Duncan, R.J., Evans, A.R., Vickers-Rich, P., Rich, T.H. and Poropat, S.F. 2021. Ornithopod jaws from the Lower Cretaceous Eumeralla Formation, Victoria, Australia, and their implications for polar neornithischian dinosaur diversity. {@i Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology}, {@b 41 (3)}, pp.e1946551.
Martin, A.J. 2009. Dinosaur burrows in the Otway Group (Albian) of Victoria, Australia, and their relation to Cretaceous polar environments. {@i Cretaceous Research}, {@b 30 (5)}, pp.1223-1237.

trait.name: Electrolocation
entries: Steropodon has a Blindsight of 5 ft., this is increased to 10 ft. while in water. It also has Expertise in Perception and passive {@skill Perception} (all included above).

trait.name: Small Semi-Aquatic Animal
entries: Steropodon can hold its breath for up to 10 minutes and has a swim speed of 25 ft.

action.name: Venomous Spur
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}1 (1) Piercing damage plus 2 ({@damage 1d4}) Poison damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 7} Constitution saving throw or be {@condition stunned|XPHB|Stunned} until the start of Steropodon's next turn.
"STER-OHP-OH-DON"
{@b (LIGHTNING TOOTH)}

Most adventurers envisage thundering titanic dinosaurs when we discuss travelling through the Cretaceous. However, with patience, calmness, and a bit of luck, waiting quietly for a few hours may allow them to glimpse rare and skittish early mammals that live in the shadows of these giants. The aquatic Steropodon is one such animal, requiring hours of silence next to a shallow river. I believe that the wait is well worth it.

{@i Steropodon} is a monotreme from around the Early Cretaceous (105 million years ago) of New South Wales, Australia. Known from a single jaw, it is considered to be an early relative of the platypus.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: With only a fragmentary fossil on record, it is difficult to accurately judge the size of {@i Steropodon} but estimates have been made through comparison with both fossil and living monotremes. It may have grown to a length of 1.5-2 ft. and weighed as much as 4-5 lb. As the largest known Cretaceous mammal was only a little over 3 ft. long, this makes {@i Steropodon} a relative giant of its time. The jaw is from an adult and has 3 molars, which is distinct from derived monotremes that lose their teeth as adults. Based on a lateral canal in the jaw, {@i Steropodon} is thought to have had a soft-tissue bill which was likely extremely sensitive. The platypus uses its bill to not only sense things through touch, but also to detect the electrical field of organisms in the water. This electrolocation is a valuable hunting tool in environments with poor visibility and it seems likely that {@i Steropodo}n's bill had a similar function.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Based on what little information we have on {@i Steropodon} and other related extinct monotremes, we can assume that it was behaviourally similar to the platypus. It would have hunted in muddy water and used its sensitive bill rather than its eyes to find food. It likely fed primarily on invertebrates it dug up from the bottom of the river such as worms, larvae, and shelly arthropods. As it was a monotreme, it would have laid soft-shelled eggs in burrows instead of giving birth to live young and fed them through milk secreted from specialised glands beneath the skin. While we do not know whether it possessed a venomous spur like the platypus, we consider it plausible based on their relatively close relationship.

We suggest playing {@i Steropodon} as an animal constantly in search of food. Most of its day should be spent with its bill buried in the muddy bottom of a river or lake searching for prey. Its electrolocation should make it a hard animal to sneak up on, and it will be common for it to dart into hiding without ever being seen by an approaching humanoid. If it is caught it should be relatively harmless, although it will try to scratch attackers with its envenomed spur, the venom of which causes severe pain.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Steropodon} is a member of the Monotremata and was the oldest known monotreme species when it was first described in the 80s. Since then, many more monotreme fossils have been discovered, with the oldest coming from the Early Cretaceous of Australia approximately 130 million years ago (although it has been suggested that their origins date back to the Late Jurassic, we do not have the fossil evidence yet to support this). They are primarily known from Australasia, with some fossils from South America suggesting a historically wider range. They are generally considered more basal than other mammals, retaining plesiomorphic (ancestral) traits like a cloaca and laying eggs. While somewhat diverse in the past, only the platypus and echidna survive today, which are both considered vulnerable to extinction due to climate change, pollution, and habitat reduction.

trait.name: Heavyset
entries: Barilium has Advantage on Constitution saving throws and saving throws to resist being {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled}.

trait.name: Trampling Retreat
entries: If Barilium takes the Dash Action, it also Disengages and may move through spaces occupied
by creatures smaller than itself. If it does so, once during its turn, it may make a Trample attack against a creature whose space it moves through.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Barilium chooses the Attack action, it may make two Blunt Gore attacks.

action.name: Blunt Clawed Gore
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}4 ({@damage 1d4 + 2}) Piercing damage plus 5 ({@damage 1d6 + 2}) Bludgeoning damage.

action.name: Trample
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 6} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}13 ({@damage 2d10 + 2}) Bludgeoning damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 14} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.
{@i "BAR-ILL-E-UM"} {@b (HEAVY ILIUM)}

In areas that lack tree cover, large herds of Barilium thunder and holler across the open plains and riverways. These conspicuous animals are the bread and butter of these lands - commonplace and a welcome reminder of where you are. Nevertheless, approach with caution, as their powerful builds and large size renders them dangerous when frightened.

{@i Barilium} is a large iguanodontian ornithopod from the Early Cretaceous (138 to 132 million years ago) of Southeast England. A robust animal, it was originally described as a species of {@i Iguanodon} ({@b page 134 in DDDD}), but is now considered its own genus.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Barilium} is known only from partial remains but has been estimated to be approximately 26 ft. long with a weight of about 4 tonnes. Believed to be an obligate quadruped (had to walk on four legs), it was notably more heavily built than other contemporary iguanodontians, including {@i Iguanodon} itself. Like {@i Iguanodon}, {@i Barilium} possessed a modified claw on its first digit, however, this was a short and blunt stub, instead of a prominent spike like in {@i Iguanodon}. The shape of {@i Barilium}'s bottom jaw suggests that it had an elongate head tipped by a short keratinous beak. Its teeth were laterally thin and leaf shaped and, combined with its robust jaw and ability to chew, suggest it was a browser of tough plants, namely early conifers and ferns.

{@i Barilium} fossils have been recovered from the Wadhurst Clay Formation, an Early Cretaceous unit from East Sussex, England. We include {@i Barilium} here in the Wessex Formation section as both are part of the larger Wealden Group, and {@i Barilium} is both very closely related to, and has a nearly identical environmental preference to, less well-known iguanodontians from the Wessex Formation. The Wadhurst Formation was laid down in a predominantly freshwater environment with some tidal and lagoonal influence, likely within a river delta. Fossils from this formation include a variety of animals like fish, mammals, and dinosaurs such as the smaller hadrosauriforme {@i Hypselospinus}, as well as theropods like {@i Altispinax} and {@i Suchosaurus}.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Barilium} is known only from fragmentary remains that provide little insight into its behaviour. However, as it is similar to {@i Iguanodon}, we can assume some shared attributes. It may have been a somewhat gregarious animal living in small herds, grazing along forest edges or within clearings. Its smaller, blunt thumb claw is ill suited to be used as a weapon, which may have meant that {@i Barilium} had few defences against predators beyond its size and numbers. This could have made it relatively skittish for its size and prone to fleeing if threatened.

We suggest playing {@i Barilium} as a somewhat jumpy animal, easy to spook if surprised. It should live in small herds with one or two animals always on the lookout for threats. If danger is spotted, they should sound alarm calls, which will quickly trigger the herd to flee. While this makes it unlikely that players may be directly attacked by a {@i Barilium}, they could easily be at risk of being trampled by a panicked herd. Individuals should be most likely to attack if they feel cornered with no means of escape and then should use their size to try and crush a potential threat.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Barilium} was originally described as a species of {@i Iguanodon} within the group Iguanodontidae. Years later, {@i Iguanodon} underwent a major review which argued that many of the species included within the genus were actually distinct animals. Several new taxa were erected, among them {@i Barilium}. Where {@i Barilium} falls within the iguanodontian tree is somewhat uncertain. Iguanodontidae is currently considered a dubious grouping and may be paraphyletic (includes organisms from separate branches of the tree of life). Further studies suggest it occupies a position further down the tree than previously suspected, resting amongst groups such as the basal styracosterns or hadrosauriformes.

trait.name: Feeding Lookouts
entries: If Hypsilophodon are present in numbers of 3 or more, increase their passive Perceptions to 14.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Hypsilophodon chooses the Attack action, it may make up to two Self-Sharpening Bite attacks.

action.name: Self-Sharpening Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}4 ({@damage 1d4 + 2}) Piercing damage.
Hypsilophodon's next attack with Self-Sharpening Bite deals an additional 2 damage.

action.name: Opposable Digit
entries: As an Action, Hypsilophodon can grasp and interact with small objects, such as trinkets, wands, door handles, etc., although it may not understand how to use them. Each time Hypsilophodon tries to use an object or item, roll {@dice 1d4} to determine the result:
1 - It fails to use the object, potentially injuring itself or damaging the object (if able), and will not attempt again.
2 - It is unable to use the object.
3 - It uses the object without Proficiency.
4 - It uses the object with Proficiency.
Creatures wilds haped or polymorphed into Hypsilophodon do not need to make this roll if they would normally understand how to use the object.

bonus.name: Cursorial
entries: Hypsilophodon can Dash or Disengage as a Bonus Action.
{@i "HIP-SIH-LOFF-OH-DON"} {@b (HIGH CRESTED TOOTH)}

In the same manner as observing a herd of deer feeding in rural fields on a cold, misty morning, herds of dozens of Hypsilophodon can sometimes be seen picking at low-lying ferns in the Wessex plains. Such animals often employ similar sentry tactics, so that the majority of them can feed in peace.

{@i Hypsilophodon} is a bipedal dinosaur from the Wessex Formation (130 million years ago). It comes from the "{@i Hypsilophodon} beds", a layer of rock named for the dozens of {@i Hypsilophodon} fossils found within it.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Hypsilophodon} was a small dinosaur, up to 3 ft. tall and 5 to 8 ft. long. It had a simple, lightly built body, standing on two legs with a long tail, two short forearms with five fingered hands and a proportionally large head. From the side, the head looked triangular, tall at the back with a small, pointed mouth tipped by a hard beak at the front. At the front of the jaws, its teeth were pointed and triangular while further back they were ridged and chisel-like, which may have been self-sharpening. Like many ornithopods, {@i Hypsilophodon} was able to chew, grinding its teeth against each other to crush softer plants.

{@i Hypsilophodon} has been interpreted in several different ways. While originally reconstructed as a ground living biped, starting in the 1880s a trend emerged where {@i Hypsilophodon} was instead interpreted as an arboreal animal akin to {@i Dendrolagus} (the "tree kangaroo"). This was based on the idea that it may have had a reversed first toe (hallux) that let it perch on branches, despite no real evidence to support this hypothesis. This idea remained popular into the early 1970s. The discovery of fossilised flat plates with the animal have also led to the idea that it was armoured, although these are now known to be cartilaginous structures on the ribs that would have provided no real defence.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Hypsilophodon}'s pointed jaws suggests that it was a very specialist feeder, preferring to eat delicate shoots and saplings rather than tougher plants like cycads. As mentioned above, it was found in large numbers within the "{@i Hypsilophodon} beds". Up until very recently, this was thought to be a mass mortality assemblage, where a huge herd was killed when a river burst its banks. However, a 2025 study re-examined the remains and argued that these accumulated over many years and, while it's likely that {@i Hypsilophodon} was a herding animal, most died alone.

We suggest playing {@i Hypsilophodon} as a herding animal, living in groups of 20 to 50 individuals. They should feed in open spaces, where their excellent vision allows them to quickly spot predators. Some members of the herd should act as sentries and sound an alarm call if danger appears. Once startled they will usually flee, only turning to face an attacker if cornered. A {@i Hypsilophodon} with no other option will bite an attacker, but this will do little to hold off a hungry predator or determined adventurer.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Hypsilophodon}'s classification has seen a lot of revision throughout the years, although it is clearly a dinosaur. It was originally identified as an iguanodontid before later being placed in the Hypsilophodontidae. By the 21st century, Hypsilophodontidae had been re-examined and found to be invalid. Several studies moved {@i Hypsilophodon} around, identifying it as either a late-surviving primitive ornithopod or as an even more primitive animal outside of Ornithopoda altogether. The most recent analyses place it back within the ornithopods and have even suggested the resurrection of Hypsilophodontidae, now made up of {@i Hypsilophodon} and the recently described {@i Vectidromeus}.

Coram, R.A., Radley, J.D. and Martill, D.M. 2017. A cretaceous calamity? The Hypsilophodon bed of the Isle of Wight, southern England. {@i Geology Today}, {@b 33 (2)}, pp.66-70.
Galton, P.M. 1971. {@i Hypsilophodon}, the cursorial non-arboreal dinosaur. {@i Nature}, {@b 231 (5299)}, pp.159-161.

trait.name: Thermal Glider
entries: Istiodactylus can fly for up to 8 hours effortlessly, without requiring rest. Istiodactylus has +6 to {@skill Perception} checks (included above).

trait.name: Carrion Feeder
entries: Istiodactylus has Resistance to Poison and Necrotic damage, and Immunity to the {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned} condition (included above).

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Istiodactylus chooses the Attack action, it may make two attacks with its Toothed Grasp attack.

action.name: Toothed Grasp
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}8 ({@damage 2d6 + 1}) Piercing damage.

A creature hit by this attack must make a {@dc 11} Constitution saving throw. On a failed save, they take an additional {@dice 1d4} Slashing damage and Istiodactylus recovers lost Hit Points equal to this additional damage.

bonus.name: Quad Launch (Istiodactylus)
entries: If not already flying, as a Bonus Action, Istiodactylus can launch itself into the air. Every other creature within 5 ft. of Istiodactylus must succeed a {@dc 11} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}. Istiodactylus then begins to fly and must fly 15 ft. in a straight line (either horizontally, or vertically up).
Istiodactylus can only begin flying by using this ability, or if it is falling.
"ISS-TEE-OH-DAC-TIE-LUS"
{@b (SAIL FINGER)}

Soaring vultures and other scavenging birds are a common, usually unwelcome, sight for many travellers. Our prehistoric past has many similar animals, although they were often larger in size. Istiodactylus is one such animal and may be found gliding along Cretaceous flats in search of carcasses to pick at.

{@i Istiodactylus} is a large pterosaur from the Early Cretaceous (125 million years ago) of the Isle of Wight, England. Possessing distinctive triangular teeth and a strong bite, it is thought to have been a major scavenger within the Wessex Formation.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Istiodactylus} was a large pterosaur, with an adult wingspan reaching up to 16 ft. Its skull was distinctive, looking triangular in lateral (side) view, with the back of the head being relatively tall while the dorsal margin of the skull sloped downwards at a sharp angle. Towards the front, the jaws straighten out into a blunt rounded end. Most of the mouth lacked teeth, but at the tip were 48 very densely packed triangular teeth that formed an interlocking semi-circle. At the front edge of this semi-circle, there was a gap in the teeth, but this was occupied by a downwards projecting piece of bone called an odontoid (pseudo-tooth) that filled in the space. Their jaws appear to have been fairly muscular, giving the animal a powerful bite despite the skull not being particularly well built to handle struggling prey.

{@i Istiodactylus}' wings were elongated and well-adapted for soaring flight. As they were somewhat broader than other soaring pterosaurs, it is thought that they were more likely to be flying over land rather than the sea. {@i Istiodactylus} had awkwardly proportioned limbs that would have made it rather ungainly when walking.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Like many pterosaurs, {@i Istiodactylus} was originally thought to have aquatic habits, perhaps hunting fish by wading through shallow water or plucking them from the ocean's surface on the wing. However, further research showed that its morphology was not in-line with other fish specialists. Instead, it was found to be a primarily terrestrial soarer that would have glided over land for long periods of time. The relatively weak construction of the skull, however, did not support it being an active hunter and instead it is now thought to have been a preferential scavenger of large vertebrates, although it may have taken small prey if it was able to snatch them up. Its strong bite and frontal tooth positioning suggest that it was specialised for biting off chunks of flesh, perhaps deep into a carcass.

We suggest playing {@i Istiodactylus} as a soaring animal, spending hours riding thermals over plains or streams, searching for carcasses in the same manner as a vulture. Upon spotting one, it should quickly land and start tearing into it. If the remains are large enough, it should be a common sight to see several {@i Istiodactylus} feeding off of the same carcass. They should use their large size and impressive wingspan to drive off smaller scavengers, but will retreat quickly if confronted by a carnivore bigger than themselves. However, they should not venture too far away and will quickly return to gorge at the first opportunity. An opportunistic {@i Istiodactylus} may try to take a bite out of a humanoid that approaches too close, but more commonly should only be a major threat if several of them are defending a carcass.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Istiodactylus} is the namesake member of the Istiodactylidae. This is a group of scavenging pterosaurs that first appeared approximately 130 million years ago in China. The occurrence of {@i Istiodactylus} itself in England suggests that the group was present throughout Eurasia. Istiodactylids are themselves part of the Ornithocheiroidea, a highly diverse group of medium-to-large sized Cretaceous pterosaurs with a global distribution. Ornithocheiroids include everything from marine piscivores like {@i Pteranodon}, to omnivorous or frugivorous forms like {@i Tupandactylus} ({@b page 108 in DDDD}) and giant terrestrial stalkers like {@i Quetzalcoatlus} ({@b page 164 in DDDD}). First appearing in the Early Cretaceous, ornithocheiroids would go on to become the dominant group of pterosaurs and survive right up until the end Cretaceous extinction.

monster.name: Neovenator

trait.name: Combative Hunter
entries: Neovenator has Resistance to Slashing and Piercing damage (included above), and has Advantage on attacks against Huge creatures.

trait.name: Potential Hyper-Sensory Skin
entries: Neovenator has a Blindsight of 5 ft. (included above).

trait.name: Ambush Predator
entries: If Neovenator begins its turn Hidden, it can Dash as a Bonus Action this turn.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Neovenator chooses the Attack action, it may make two Rending Bite attacks.

action.name: Rending Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 8} to hit, Reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}18 ({@damage 3d8 + 5}) Piercing damage.
When a creature is hit by this attack, it suffers a horrible rend of their flesh. That creature takes {@dice 2d6} Slashing damage at the beginning of its next turn, then the rend clots.
Multiple instances of this effect do not stack.

legendary.name: Exacerbating Thrash
entries: Neovenator thrashes fiercely, forcing those around it to dodge its outburst.
Every creature within 5 ft. of Neovenator that is currently suffering from a Horrible Rend (from Rending Bite) takes {@dice 1d6} Slashing damage as their wounds bleed from the abrupt movement.

legendary.name: Savvy Manoeuvre
entries: Neovenator may either Disengage, then move up to 15 ft., or it may move up to 15 ft., then attempt to Hide.

legendaryHeader: Neovenator can take 1 Legendary Action, choosing from the options below. Only one legendary option can be used at a time and only at the end of another creature's turn. Neovenator regains spent Legendary Actions at the start of its turn.

entries: {@i "NEE-OH-VEN-AH-TOR"} {@b (NEW HUNTER ONE)}

While dawn break is a stunning sight over the Wessex Formation, it is wise not to let its beauty lower your guard. We've lost more than one travelling companion who wandered away to watch the sunrise, only to be picked off by the arch predator of this region: Neovenator, a patiently stalking giant carnivore that prefers to hunt at dawn and dusk. Despite its size, it can move with remarkable stealth and tact.

{@i Neovenator} is a medium-sized carcharodontosaur that is thought to have been one of the largest predators of the Wessex Formation. With approximately 70% of the skeleton known, it is one of the most complete theropods known from Europe.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Neovenator} was between 20 and 26 ft. long and would have weighed at least 1 tonne. It had the standard theropod body plan, with its most distinctive feature being its unusual head. It had a narrow skull, which was less heavily built than more derived giant carcharodontosaurs like {@i Giganotosaurus} ({@b page 229}) and {@i Carcharodontosaurus} ({@b page 69 in DDDD}). It had a twinned pair of bony ridges running along the upper margin of its head, in front of its eyes. One research study of {@i Neovenator}'s skull hypothesised that it had highly sensitive skin on its face, like a modern crocodile, and that this may have helped it feel-out bone while biting through a carcass to avoid tooth breakage. Alternatively, this sensitivity may have helped in social behaviour by making the skin more easily stimulated by contact. It was even suggested that, like crocodilians, they may have used their skin to test the temperature of their nests to maintain the right conditions for the eggs. However, a later study argued that the face of {@i Neovenator} was no more sensitive than most theropods and the face may have instead supported some kind of soft-tissue structures underneath the skin.

Like some specimens of {@i Allosaurus} ({@b page 197 in DDDD}), the holotype of {@i Neovenator} shows evidence of numerous injuries. This includes broken tail vertebrae, cracked ribs, fractured shoulder blades, and one toe with a large amount of bone overgrowth. Modern carnivores are frequently injured when hunting, and while the wounds on the {@i Neovenator} specimen may have been from intraspecific (same species) fighting, they were more likely incurred as part of the day-to-day risks of hunting their prey.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Neovenator} is generally considered to be the arch predator of the Wessex Formation. It was one of the largest carnivores, with only two spinosaurids reaching a similar or greater size. However, spinosaurs are widely interpreted as specialist wading predators for whom terrestrial prey made up a smaller percentage of their diet. They would have little reason to directly compete with {@i Neovenator} outside of potential scavenging. Based on teeth marks left on bones, {@i Neovenator} fed on iguanodontians that were larger than itself, such as {@i Mantellisaurus}, although whether it hunted them or scavenged their remains is uncertain.

We suggest playing {@i Neovenator} as a solitary ambush hunter. It should be most active in the early morning or late evening, using the poor light conditions to make it easier to sneak up on prey. It should be extremely patient, getting as close as possible before charging. If the target avoids the initial attack and attempts to flee, {@i Neovenator} should only give chase for a short time before breaking off and returning to a safe hiding spot where it can wait for the next potential meal to wander too close. It should be a major threat to humanoids, seeing them as relatively easy meals.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Neovenator} is a member of Carcharodontosauria, with a somewhat uncertain placement just outside of Carcharodontosauridae (the group which would eventually give rise to some of the largest carnivores like {@i Giganotosaurus}). Originally, it was thought to be a potential sister taxon to {@i Allosaurus} itself, however later studies identified it as being more derived. Regardless, it is certainly an allosauroid, which are a group of highly successful theropods that first appeared in the Middle Jurassic and survived into the Late Cretaceous.

entries.name: References

Brusatte, S.L., Benson, R.B. and Hutt, S. 2008. The osteology of {@i Neovenator salerii} (Dinosauria: Theropoda) from the Wealden group (Barremian) of the Isle of Wight. {@i Monographs of the Palaeontographical Society}, {@b 162 (631)}, pp.1-75.

Hutt, S., Martill, D.M. and Barker, M.J. 1996. The first European allosaurid dinosaur (Lower Cretaceous, Wealden Group, England). {@i Neues Jahrbuch für Geologie und Paläontologie-Monatshefte}, {@b 1996}, pp.635-644.
Molnar, R.E. 2001. Theropod paleopathology: a literature survey. {@i In}. Tanke, D.H. and Carpenter, K. (Eds.) {@i Mesozoic Vertebrate Life}. Indiana University Press, pp.337-363.

trait.name: Spined Osteoderms
entries: If a creature touches Polacanthus or hits it with a melee attack, that creature takes {@dice 1d6} Piercing damage.
If a creature touches Polacanthus in an attempt to Grapple or Restrain it, that creature takes {@dice 1d8 + 2} Piercing damage instead.
Polacanthus has Resistance to Bludgeoning, Piercing, and Slashing damage and an AC of 19 (included above).

trait.name: Pelvic Shield
entries: Polacanthus cannot have its movement speed reduced by any attack or ability (excluding difficult terrain and being {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled}).

action.name: Short Charge Tackle
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}9 ({@damage 2d6 + 2}) Bludgeoning damage plus 4 ({@damage 1d8}) Piercing damage.
Polacanthus may move up to 5 ft. immediately before making this attack.
{@i "POLE-AH-KAN-THUS"} {@b (MANY THORNS)}

The clatter of bone and cry of a dinosaur does not always herald imminent danger. Among the Early Cretaceous forests and plains, small herds of armoured dinosaurs often produce excessive noise from their social combat. In these activities, competing individuals shove each other with as much force as they can muster. Despite the abundance of spikes involved, equally abundant armour means that these conflicts rarely leave either party seriously injured.

{@i Polacanthus} was a medium sized polacanthine ankylosaur from the Early Cretaceous (130 million years ago). A well-known, yet incomplete fossil, the holotype only consists of the armoured pelvis, femurs, and tail.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: Reconstructing {@i Polacanthus} has been a challenge as the only definitive specimen consists of the partial remains of the back half of the animal. Different researchers have come up with different interpretations of the front of the animal (e.g. reconstructing it with bare shoulders, giant shoulder spines and a long neck), however more recently described taxa like {@i Gastonia} are now considered reasonable proxies for {@i Polacanthus'} overall anatomy. What we present here is an amalgamated reconstruction using the known features of the {@i Polacanthus} holotype as a base, while incorporating elements of {@i Gastonia} where appropriate.

Estimates for the length of {@i Polacanthus} range between 13 to 16 ft. long with a probable weight of about 1 tonne. In most respects it was similar to other ankylosaurs, but its hind legs were unusually long. It likely had rows of sparse plates and spikes on the front of its body, with a row of spines running along each flank. It had a bony shield made of a rosette of osteoderms that lacked any ornamentation over its pelvis. This armour extended onto the upper surface of the tail, becoming interspersed with spikes and plates. Along the tail, spines were likely arranged in twin parallel rows on each side that ran to the tip. Its head may have had a deep jaw, narrow beaked muzzle, and flat armour running along the top.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Based on the likely narrow shape of the beak and stomach contents found for other ankylosaurs, {@i Polacanthus} was probably a selective browser, preferring to feed on low-lying ferns. While most ankylosaurs are thought to be solitary, evidence from {@i Gastonia} suggests it may have lived in herds of 5 to 10 individuals. This might explain its sparse but elaborate armour, as studies show that the spikes, while certainly a deterrent, were not built for defence and were more likely used in sexual displays or intraspecific (same species) combat.

We suggest playing {@i Polacanthus} as a shrubland or woodland browser. Herds will frequently feed along or within the treeline to hide from predators. When not eating, a herd's members should be relatively playful and might be found having mock shoving matches. While these are almost always benign amongst the old animals, youngsters may take things too far. This could lead to a real fight breaking out where they hold their tails high to show off their spines before ramming their sides into each other. Many immature individuals should be seen with chipped or broken spines.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Polacanthus} is the most well-known member of the Polacanthinae. This is a group of medium-sized ankylosaurs sometimes characterised for having distinctive pelvic shields. The exact content of this group is uncertain as recent studies have found that some defining traits may have originated through convergent evolution (two or more separate lineages giving rise to very similar traits). Some phylogenies find {@i Gastonia} as a polacanthine while others find it as a more primitive ankylosaur. The Polacanthinae arose in the Late Jurassic (~160 million years ago) and appear to have gone extinct in the Early Cretaceous (125 million years ago).

entries.name: References
entries: Arbour, V.M., Burns, M.E. and Currie, P.J. 2011. A review of pelvic shield morphology in ankylosaurs (Dinosauria: Ornithischia). {@i Journal of Paleontology}, {@b 85 (2)}, pp.298-302.

trait.name: Sail Communication
entries: Amargasaurus can communicate with other Amargasaurus using its sail. It can convey complex messages to them without the need to make any sound, so long as they can see it.

trait.name: Sturdy Stature
entries: If Amargasaurus fails a saving throw to avoid being knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}, it may reroll the saving throw but must use the second result.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Amargasaurus chooses the Attack action, it may make one Bulk Crush attack and one Foreleg Stomp attack.

action.name: Bulk Crush
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 7} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}20 ({@damage 3d10 + 4}) Bludgeoning damage.
If this attack hits, Amargasaurus deals {@dice 1d6} Bludgeoning damage to itself and the hit creature is knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.

action.name: Foreleg Stomp
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 7} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}13 ({@damage 2d8 + 4}) Bludgeoning damage.

action.name: Startling Sail Display
entries: As an Action, Amargasaurus may flush its sail with blood, creating strange shapes and colours, confusing potential attackers.

Each non-Amargasaurus creature within 40 ft. of Amargasaurus that can see it must make a {@dc 14} Intelligence saving throw. On a failed save, they are {@condition frightened|XPHB|Frightened} of Amargasaurus for {@dice 1d4} rounds (roll separately for each creature).
"AH-MARR-GAH-SORE-US"
{@b (LA AMARGA REPTILE)}

Sauropods are well-known for their exceptionally long necks and occasional armoured ornamentation. One animal in particular, however, bends (but does not break) this trend. Amargasaurus is relatively short necked for a member of these giants, and sports enormous spikes all along its neck. These spines support a fleshy sail that it is able to flush with blood to create vivid colours - making it quite an exciting animal to behold.

{@i Amargasaurus} was a dicraeosaurid sauropod from the Early Cretaceous (129 million years ago) of the Neuquén Province, Argentina. Small for a sauropod, its most distinctive feature is a prominent paired row of thin spines running in parallel along the back of its relatively short neck.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: Small by sauropod standards, {@i Amargasaurus} grew to approximately 43 ft. long, 8 ft. tall, and weighed about 4 tonnes. While its tail was long, its neck was relatively short (again, in comparison to other sauropods). Fossils of {@i Amargasaurus}' skull are incomplete, but other dicraeosaurid fossils suggest that it was likely elongate with prominent peg-like teeth. Its most striking feature were 10 extremely long paired spikes (neural spines) that ran down the back of the neck. These were formed by the dorsal spines of the vertebrae lengthening and splitting into two. These spines increased in size as they moved away from the head, with the biggest growing to about 2 ft. long. There has been a lot of debate about not only their function, but also their appearance. Some scientists have reconstructed them as spikes jutting out of the neck, covered in a keratinous sheath for protection. However, more recent studies have found strong evidence that the spines supported a fleshy pair of sails that ran along the length of the neck.

{@i Amargasaurus} was discovered in the La Amarga Formation, a large Early Cretaceous sequence that outcrops across several provinces in Argentina. This formation was laid down near a series of braided rivers, however {@i Amargasaurus} likely spent most of its time in more heavily wooded areas with more canopy cover. The La Amarga Formation is an unusual formation as, aside from an unidentified stegosaur and some other small tetrapods, the unit only contains fossils of sauropods. Each of these sauropods would have fed at different levels in the canopy to avoid competition, with {@i Amargasaurus} occupying the niche of a close-to-the-ground browser/grazer.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: As mentioned before the function of the neural spines in {@i Amargasaurus} have, unsurprisingly, been the subject of a lot of debate. When it was first thought that they were bare spikes, it was often suggested that these were defensive structures, but this is not a plausible function given factors such as the underneath of the neck being completely exposed. With the discovery of strong evidence for the fleshy sail, it seems more likely that this was some form of a display structure. The sail may have been quite colourful or {@i Amargasaurus} might have been able to brighten its appearance by flushing it with blood. This could be useful for mating displays, threats to rivals, or to startle potential predators.
We suggest playing {@i Amargasaurus} as a herd animal, travelling in groups of 5-10 individuals.

It should be relatively placid, responding to a perceived threat by flashing its sails as a warning before attacking with its bulky weight. With appropriate caution, it should be a relatively easy animal to approach and might, with care and effort, make an excellent travel mount.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Dicraeosaurids were a group of sauropods closely related to the more well known-diplodocids like {@i Apatosaurus}. They first arose in the Middle Jurassic (approximately 165 million years ago) and were a distinctive group, characterised by their small bodies and relatively short necks, with two genera (including {@i Amargasaurus})

having elongate neural spines. Dicraeosaurids were present in Gondwana (Africa and South America) and Laurasia (North America, China) suggesting that the group originated before the two supercontinents split. The group was hit heavily by the Jurassic-Cretaceous extinction event, with only one species ({@i Amargasaurus}) known to have survived into the Cretaceous.

trait.name: Ultimate Armoured Animal
entries: Ankylosaurus' AC is increased to 22, has Immunity to Bludgeoning, Piercing, and Slashing damage, and Resistance to Force and Thunder damage (all included above). Ranged attacks against Ankylosaurus treat its AC as 26, as the chances of a ranged attack hitting a gap in its armour are exceedingly small.

trait.name: Rotund Mass
entries: Ankylosaurus is immune to being knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}, being Shoved, or being otherwise moved forcibly.
Ankylosaurus cannot climb or jump and has Disadvantage on any Dexterity saving throw.

trait.name: Armoured Legendary Resistance (2/Day)
entries: If Ankylosaurus fails a non-Dexterity saving throw, it can choose to succeed instead. However, if it does so, Ankylosaurus
also replaces its Immunity to Bludgeoning, Piercing, and Slashing damage with Resistance to those damage types instead until the start of its next turn.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Ankylosaurus chooses the Attack action, it may make two Clubbed Tail attacks.

action.name: Clubbed Tail
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 8} to hit, Reach 5 ft. (Large) or 10 ft. (Huge), one target. {@h}18 ({@damage 2d12 + 5}) Bludgeoning damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 16} Constitution saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone} and gain one level of the Shattering Blow condition as described below.

action.name: Condition: Shattering Blow
entries: A creature suffering from a Shattering Blow has its movement speed reduced by 10 ft. (to a minimum of 5 ft.) for each level of Shattering Blow it has. All levels of Shattering Blow can be removed by a Lesser Restoration spell, equivalent effect, or by completing a Long Rest.

reaction.name: Reflect Attack (2/Day)
entries: If Ankylosaurus is hit by a melee attack, it may use its Reaction to shove itself into the attacker, partially reflecting the attack back at the attacker. The attacking creature takes damage equal to half of the damage dealt by the attack (rounded down, before applying any Resistance/Immunity) and of the same type(s) as the attack.
"AN-KAI-LOW-SORE-US"
{@b (FUSED REPTILE)}

Perhaps excluding Triceratops, few non-theropod dinosaurs are as well-known and as well-liked as Ankylosaurus. This living fortress is as close to being indestructible as an animal can achieve. That formidable characteristic renders it largely fearless of humanoids and, reportedly, a generally placid creature to encounter.

{@i Ankylosaurus} is from the Late Cretaceous (68 million years ago) of western North America and is the largest and most famous member of the Ankylosauria. A heavily armoured animal with a tail tipped with a thick bony club, it is the classic example of a living tank.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Ankylosaurus} was a large and heavy animal, growing up to 26 ft. long and weighing somewhere between 6 to 8 tonnes. Like many other ankylosaurs, it had very wide ribs and a broad pelvis giving it a rotund body shape. Its legs were short, resulting in a rather low profile despite its size. The head was triangular, with a relatively broad muzzle covered in a keratinous beak. Its teeth were leaf-shaped with well-developed crenulations (ridges) along their edges which, combined with its wide mouth, suggests that it was a generalist herbivore. Wear patterns on its teeth indicate that it would have nipped at plants before swallowing them mostly whole, breaking them down further in its huge and complicated hindgut.

To say that {@i Ankylosaurus} was heavily armoured is an understatement. Its body was covered in bony osteoderms embedded within its skin that varied in shape from flat plates, to oval domes, triangular spikes, and protective rings. These could reach a thickness of over six inches at the most heavily armoured points and even its eyelids were armour plated. Four large osteoderms jutted backwards from its head and cheeks, giving the skull a characteristic X-shape at the back. At the tip of its tail, these osteoderms were fused into a huge half-metre wide bony club at the end of a stiffened "handle".

{@i Ankylosaurus} is found in several formations in the western United States and Canada, most famously the Hell Creek Formation. These deposits were laid down in a forested floodplain positioned close to the shoreline of the Western Interior Seaway, a huge inland sea that split North America into the Laramidia and Appalachia subcontinents. Dinosaurs are very common in Hell Creek, with multiple species of ceratopsians, hadrosaurs, and theropods present in large numbers. Amongst these are some of the most famous dinosaurs including {@i Tyrannosaurus} ({@b page 192 in DDDD}), {@i Triceratops} ({@b page 324}), {@i Pachycephalosaurus} ({@b page 274}), and {@i Edmontosaurus}.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Ankylosaurus}' most famous characteristics, and the ones that have been subject to the most study, are its armoured body and heavy tail club. From the early days of its discovery, it was believed that these were primarily used for defence against predators like {@i Tyrannosaurus}. This was so ingrained, a 1995 paper specifically deemed it "improbable" that the tail was used for intraspecific (within the same species) fighting. However, recent evidence of healed injuries caused by tail club strikes from ankylosaurs like {@i Zuul} ({@b page 188 in DDDD}) show that these tails were indeed used for intraspecific combat. Nevertheless, they would have undoubtedly also been used to defend against predators. Interestingly, despite them being more vulnerable to predators, juvenile ankylosaurs tended to have less armour than the adults. This may suggest either a different defensive strategy, such as living in small groups to reduce the odds of the individual being attacked or being protected by their parents for an extended period of time.

We suggest playing an adult {@i Ankylosaurus} as a primarily solitary animal, occasionally gathering in small groups in the breeding season but mostly living alone. It should be a slow moving, ponderous animal that spends its days browsing on low lying plants or snuffling through soil for fallen fruits or invertebrates. If approached by a potential threat, it should squat down with its tail held high as a clear warning. This threat should often be enough to ward off an attacker. However, if they persist, a single well-placed blow from the {@i Ankylosaurus}' tail will shatter bone and leave them severely injured. It will largely ignore humanoids unless they come very close to it.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Ankylosaurus} belongs to the Ankylosauridae. This is a group of Cretaceous ankylosaurs that first appeared in East Asia approximately 125 million years ago before migrating into North America and Europe, and (of course) take their name from {@i Ankylosaurus} itself. The group underwent a major diversification event where they seemingly usurped their older relatives, the nodosaurs, as the dominant armoured dinosaurs. {@i Ankylosaurus} is one of the latest surviving ankylosaurids, only appearing in the fossil record 2 million years before the end-Cretaceous extinction. However, given the low number of ankylosaurids preserved in very Late Cretaceous deposits, it is possible that the group was already in decline before the final extinction of the non-avian dinosaurs.

trait.name: Arch-Predator of its Time
entries: Anomalocaris has Immunity to the {@condition frightened|XPHB|Frightened} condition and has a passive Perception of 13 (included above).

trait.name: Aquatic Undulator
entries: Ranged attacks against Anomalocaris are made at Disadvantage. Anomalocaris can only breathe in water.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Anomalocaris chooses the Attack action, it may make one Grasping Appendages attack and one Oral Cone attack.

action.name: Grasping Appendages
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 2} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}1 (1) Piercing damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 7} Strength saving throw or be {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled}.

action.name: Oral Cone
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 2} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}1 (1) Piercing damage.
Anomalocaris may only use this attack against a creature it is Grappling. If Anomalocaris hits with this attack, it regains 1 lost Hit Point.
{@i "AH-NOM-AH-LOW-KAR-IS"} {@b (UNLIKE OTHER SHRIMP)}

Many predators retain their behaviours when brought into the present day. While this is of little consequence for most large predators, animals from our world's early history can find themselves a bit... out of their depth. One such animal is Anomalocaris. For its time, it was a giant and formidable arch predator. However, in the modern era, it is comparable in size to a small house cat. Nevertheless, it still behaves as though it were a giant.

{@i Anomalocaris} is an anomalocarid radiodont from the Middle Cambrian (505 million years ago). It has been found in several deposits around the world, but it is best-known from the Stephen Formation (specifically the Burgess Shale) of British Columbia, Canada. A vicious looking arthropod, it was the largest known predator of the Cambrian seas.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: While {@i Anomalocaris} was small by modern standards, with the largest individuals reaching 1.6 ft. long (average 1 ft.), it was a giant among its native ecosystem, where most animals did not exceed 4 inches in length. It had a squat, wide body with a row of flexible, overlapping flaps (lobes) attached to both sides of each body segment. These were longer moving towards the animal's midline then shortened again towards the tail. By undulating these lobes, {@i Anomalocaris} could swim relatively quickly. Using a fan-shaped tail composed of similar lobes, it was also able to steer well, making it a dexterous aquatic predator. {@i Anomalocaris'} mouth was underneath its body, disc-shaped, and surrounded by rows of overlapping plates. In front of its mouth, it had a pair of elongate flexible appendages. These would usually curl beneath its body but could be uncurled to extend and reveal a series of sharp spines running along their bottom surface. {@i Anomalocaris} also had highly advanced eyes, with 24,000 lenses each, giving it much more advanced vision than other arthropods of its time.

While {@i Anomalocaris} has been found in several formations around the world, it is most famously from the Burgess Shale in Yoho National Park, British Columbia. This rock was deposited at the base of an ancient underwater cliff and gained notoriety for having some of the best preservation of any Cambrian deposit, including the preservation of soft-bodied animals. Thanks to this exceptional preservation, we know that {@i Anomalocaris} shared its environment with a wide array of unusual organisms such as various trilobites, the multilimbed {@i Hallucigenia}, sponges, comb jellies, annelid worms, and dozens of other bizarre arthropods (like {@i Opabinia} and {@i Marrella)}.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: All evidence suggests that {@i Anomalocaris} was not only a predator, but the arch nektonic (free-swimming) hunter of its ecosystem. Dwarfing all other animals in its environment, it likely hunted by quickly grabbing prey with its appendages, before bringing them to its mouth to devour them. Originally, it was thought to have predated on hard-bodied arthropods like trilobites, however observations of the wear patterns on the limbs and mouth parts suggests instead it specialised in tackling soft-bodied prey (although attack marks on trilobite fossils do indicate that something in the Burgess Shale was feeding on them).

We suggest playing {@i Anomalocaris} as an alert, darting predator that is highly sensitive to movement. It should swim freely up and down the water column in search of prey. Any motion it sees should draw its attention and cause it to swiftly strike out in an attempt to grab its victim and pull them in to be devoured. Once it has caught them, it will take its time finishing its meal, drifting lazily on the current. An opportunistic predator, {@i Anomalocaris} should not go to any lengths to distinguish between a soft radiodont or the outstretched hands of an unsuspecting humanoid, who could quickly find their fingers bitten by the ocean's original arch predator.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Anomalocaris} is one of the largest predatory members of the Radiodonta. This is a group of early (stem) arthropods (a sister group to the modern Euarthropoda) that is distinguished by their diverse frontal appendages, which varied wildly in both form and function. {@i Anomalocaris} lived approximately 508 million years ago, although it is currently unclear whether it survived up to the Cambrian-Ordovician extinction event (485 million years ago). Radiodonts as a group survived the event and the remains of filter-feeding forms like the 6.5 ft. long {@i Aegirocassis} can be found all the way through the Ordovician into the Early Devonian (400 million years ago).

monster.name: Aristonectes

trait.name: Agile Aquatic Predator
entries: While submerged in water, Aristonectes has Advantage on Dexterity checks and Dexterity saving throws.

trait.name: Benthic Feeder
entries: Aristonectes can hold its breath for up to 1 hour, has Resistance to Cold and Thunder damage, and a Darkvision of 120 ft. (all included above).

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Aristonectes chooses the Attack action, it may make two Over-sized Paddle Slap attacks and one Needle-Toothed Bite attack

action.name: Over-sized Paddle Slap
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 7} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}15 ({@damage 2d10 + 4}) Bludgeoning damage.

action.name: Needle-Toothed Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, Reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}12 ({@damage 4d4 + 2}) piercing damage.

A Small or smaller creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} (escape {@dc 15}). While grappling a creature in this manner, Aristonectes may only use its Needle-Toothed Bite against the {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} creature.

legendary.name: Gastrolith Grab
entries: Aristonectes Disengages and may swim up to 10 ft. downwards. If it reaches the seabed, it may pick up a gastrolith. If it does so, for the next minute, its Needle-Toothed Bite attack deals an additional {@dice 1d6} Bludgeoning damage (this ability does not stack).

legendaryHeader: Aristonectes can take 1 Legendary Action. Only one legendary option can be used at a time and only at the end of another creature's turn. Aristonectes regains spent Legendary Actions at the start of its turn.

entries: "AH-RIS-TOH-NECK-TEES"
{@b (BEST SWIMMER)}

I've read of strange filter-feeding plesiosaurs that gobble at silty sand in search of arthropods and shelly benthos. Despite this modest and placid diet, these animals can, apparently, reach enormous sizes. However, as I am not much one for diving, I've yet to come across such an animal on my expeditions to verify these reports.

{@i Aristonectes} was an elasmosaurid plesiosaur from the Late Cretaceous (70 million years ago) of Antarctica and South America. It was an unusual animal in many aspects of its morphology and was also one of the biggest plesiosaurs known.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Aristonectes} was a giant plesiosaur, with some evidence suggesting it reached 40 ft. in length and weighed up to 14 tonnes. It was also very unusual for an elasmosaurid, which tended to have short tails and exceptionally long necks (sometimes up to 70% of the total length). {@i Aristonectes} went in the opposite direction, with a longer tail and a proportionally shorter neck (around 50% of the length). Its body was streamlined and its four limbs were modified into long paddles. Its head was flattened and tapered towards the snout, with an unusually simple, oval shaped mouth filled with forward pointing teeth. They were tightly spaced and when the jaws were closed, formed a mesh with small gaps in between. This would have done a great job filtering out materials like sand or debris that were scooped up from the sea, suggesting that it specialised in benthic filter feeding.

{@i Aristonectes} has been found in several Late Cretaceous formations in Patagonia and Antarctica. It is usually found in shallow marine environments, areas with a lot of tidal activity relatively close to land. {@i Aristonectes} has been found alongside a wide variety of animals such as ammonites like {@i Diplomoceras} ({@b page 210}), numerous types of predatory and filter feeding sharks, common shellfish, and several species of bony fish. There were also other marine reptiles present including the closely related {@i Wunyelfia}, and the more cold water adapted {@i Mosasaurus} ({@b page 154 in DDDD}).

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Current studies suggest that {@i Aristonectes} was a manoeuvrable but slow-swimming animal that fed close to the sea bottom. It would have used its large mouth to draw in water and sand from the sea floor which it then pushed out between tightly meshed teeth. Anything too large to fit through the gaps in its teeth such as small fish, bivalves, or crustaceans would be trapped and devoured. It also swallowed stones that it kept inside of its stomach for some time before regurgitating them. The function of these stones is controversial but, in {@i Aristonectes'} case, they were probably used to help grind the tough shells of the invertebrates it swallowed. While we have very little idea of how social they might have been, like most other plesiosaurs they probably gave birth to a single large calf that remained with its mother until it was large enough to fend for itself.

We suggest playing {@i Aristonectes} as a whale-like animal, spending much of its time in shallow water, dipping its head into the sandy seafloor to search for food. It should be a slow-moving, peaceful creature that is more likely to be curious than scared of humanoids. They may approach boats to inspect them, interested in their strangeness and the creatures that mill about upon them. However, while normally calm, their size means that an angry {@i Aristonectes} can be a serious threat. This is particularly so if a mother with a calf considers humanoids to be a threat to her young. She will either ram would-be attackers with her massive body or slam them with her huge paddles.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Aristonectes} is arguably the largest member of the Elasmosauridae. Elasmosaurids first appeared 130 million years ago in the Early Cretaceous. These exceptionally long necked and highly diverse plesiosaurs originally appeared in the Northern hemisphere before later establishing populations in all of the world's oceans. The group survived through most of the Cretaceous, eventually becoming extinct alongside many other terrestrial and marine species during the end-Cretaceous extinction.
Various marine gastropod fossils.
