trait.name: False Rhino
entries: Despite looking like a rhinoceros, Arsinoitherium is more closely related to elephants (as well as manatees and hyraxes). Its elephant-like columnar limbs give Arsinoitherium Advantage on any saving throw to avoid being knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.

trait.name: Mudwalker
entries: Arsinoitherium is not slowed by muddy Difficult Terrain, nor waist-high water.

action.name: Twin Horn Charge
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}19 ({@damage 2d12 + 6}) Piercing damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 13} Constitution saving throw or gain the "Pierced" condition (see below).
Additionally, if Arsinoitherium moved at least 15 ft. in a straight line before making this attack, it deals an additional {@dice 4d4} Bludgeoning damage.

action.name: Condition: Pierced
entries: A creature that is Pierced has been impaled by large horns or thagomisers.

This creatures' speed is reduced by 15 ft. (to a minimum of 5 ft.) and, at the start of its turn in combat or every minute outside of combat while not resting, the creature takes {@dice 1d12} Piercing damage (no save allowed).

This effect persists until the creature completes a Long or Short Rest, until it receives a Lesser Restoration effect, or it falls {@condition unconscious|XPHB|Unconscious}. Multiple instances of this condition do not stack.
"AR-SIN-OI-TEAR-E-UM"
{@b (ARSINOE'S BEAST)}

{@i We were accustomed to fearing the swamps. Many dangerous animals inhabited the murky waters, hidden below the surface. Crocodiles and snakes were often the greatest concern, but sometimes fate surprises you. I must admit that our party wasn't prepared when an ill-tempered, two-tonne rhino-like animal rose out of the depths, with the distinct impression that we were in its favourite feeding spot... Arsinoitherium} was a large rhino-like mammal from the Late Eocene and Early Oligocene (36-27 million years ago) of North Africa and West Asia. An herbivore related to elephants and hyraxes, its most distinctive feature was a pair of giant horns extending out from the front of its skull, accompanied by two much smaller horns behind them.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Arsinoitherium} was a large and heavy animal, about 10 ft. long and weighing more than 2 tonnes. While superficially rhino-like, its legs were proportionally longer and more closely resembled those of elephants. Its boxy skull was shorter and squatter than a rhino's and its distinctive horns were bony, rather than keratinous (made of keratin). These thick horns may also have been covered in a keratinous sheath that extended them even further (although this remains somewhat speculative).

{@i Arsinoitherium} was widespread across what is now Africa and West Asia, known from Tunisia, Kenya, and Angola, as well as Saudi Arabia. While the environments it lived in and the fauna it cohabited with varied, in general it occupied tropical wetland regions. Much like today, these environments were highly productive, supporting a wide variety of organisms. Crocodiles and wading birds like shoebills lived alongside basal marsupials and mammalian predators like the hyaenodonts.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: While physically similar to some large semi-aquatic mammals, isotopic analysis (studies of radioactive decay) of {@i Arsinoitherium} remains suggests that they primarily ate terrestrial (land) plants. The structure of its teeth and jaws were also unusual and this, combined with its narrow snout, suggests that it was a highly selective browser, one that used a powerful stroke as it chewed to break down food. What this food was remains up for speculation, but suggestions have included robust fruits or tough leaves.

We suggest playing {@i Arsinoitherium} as a social animal, living in small groups. While players are more likely to encounter it on dry land, it should not be unusual to see some moving through swamps or rivers, travelling to new feeding grounds or snacking on succulent water plants. Within herds, it should be a common sight to see individuals using their horns to engage in powerful shoving matches, whether in play or competition. Upon encountering a party, protective mothers or large bulls should be highly aggressive, with mock charges that could easily turn into a full-blown attack. A cautious party would be wise to give families a wide berth.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Arsinoitherium} is one of the larger members of the Embrithopoda. This is a group of large-bodied mammals that arose approximately 55 million years ago throughout Africa, West Asia, and Eastern Europe. Their relationships were the subject of debate for some time, as they superficially resemble large artiodactyls (rhinos and hippos). However, the current consensus supports Embrithopoda belonging to the group Afrotheria, a highly diverse group of animals originating in Africa that includes sirenians (manatees and their relatives), elephants, aardvarks, and even the rodent-like hyraxes and elephant shrews. Embrithopods are thought to represent a more basal branch of the group, from before the split between sirenians and elephants. While successful, the group had a smaller range than elephants and ultimately went extinct about 28 million years ago.

trait.name: Suggestive Crest
entries: Augustynolophus takes triple damage from the Vicious Mockery cantrip.

trait.name: Robust Quadruped
entries: So long as Augustynolophus did not Dash on its previous turn, it has Advantage on any saving throw to avoid being knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.

trait.name: Bipedal Shift
entries: If Augustynolophus chooses the Dash action, its base speed is increased to 40 ft. until the start of its next turn (dashing up to 80 ft.).

action.name: Trample
entries: As an Action, Augustynolophus may try to trample smaller creatures. For the rest of the turn, it may move through spaces occupied by creatures smaller than itself. If it does so, any creature it moves over or ends its movement on must succeed a {@dc 14} Dexterity saving throw or take 18 ({@damage 3d10 + 2}) Bludgeoning damage, or half as much on a failed save. A creature that fails this save cannot make Opportunity Attacks until the start of its next turn.
Each creature Augustynolophus moves over only makes one saving throw and is only damaged once in this manner per turn.

If Augustynolophus ends its turn on another creature, that creature is pushed in the shortest direction until it is no longer under Augustynolophus and subtracts the amount it moved by from its speed on its next turn.

action.name: Stomp
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}11 ({@damage 2d8 + 2}) Bludgeoning damage.
{@i "AWE-GUST-TEEN-OH-LOW-FUS"} {@b (AUGSTINE'S CREST)}

Large hadrosaurs are commonplace among the Cretaceous fern plains, sparse forest edges, and lush river deltas. The latter of these offers the chance for carcasses of these hadrosaurs to be washed out into ocean basins and preserved as fossils.
Specimens of Augustynolophus are prime examples of this, having been discovered in marine environments which are, of course, not where the animal lived.

{@i Augustynolophus} is a saurolophine hadrosaur from the Late Cretaceous (73 million years ago) of California, USA. One of the few dinosaurs found along the Pacific coast, it is a rare case of a dinosaur being found in a deeper marine deposit.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Augustynolophus} was a large hadrosaur, growing to about 25 ft. long and weighing about 3 tonnes. In most respects it was a typical hadrosaur, being a large quadruped with the ability to balance on two legs to reach higher browsing. It had a single large hoof on the forelimbs that covered most of its fingers with three separate toes on the hindfeet. An elongated crest rose from the top of its head, curving vertically towards its tip. It also had a well-developed battery of teeth that, by working with a flexible upper jaw, allowed it to chew its food.

There are very few deposits along the Pacific coast of North America that yield dinosaurs. {@i Augustynolophus} is known from one such unit, with several specimens found in the Moreno Formation in California. This was laid down in a marine environment, in an area where river deltas transitioned into deeper ocean waters. It is a highly fossiliferous unit that has yielded numerous excellently preserved specimens of mosasaurs, plesiosaurs, fish, and aquatic invertebrates. Dinosaurs are rare in such deposits, but are not unheard of, as they are thought to only be preserved by dying on a beach and being washed out to sea by the tide, or by being caught up in floods and washed out into the ocean. Once at sea, the dinosaur's carcass would bloat with gas, allowing it to float for some time before it eventually sinks to the ocean floor.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Augustynolophus} was probably a gregarious animal that lived in large herds that included both adult and young animals, although mature males may have alternatively been solitary outside of the breeding season. Based on evidence in other hadrosaurs, they were likely good parents that had a protracted period of parental care. Its crest has been hypothesised to have supported an inflatable skin flap, although this is unconfirmed. Regardless, the crest almost certainly developed through sexual selection and was used to attract a mate.

We suggest playing {@i Augustynolophus} as a sedate browser living in large herds. While feeding, at least one animal should be routinely scanning for threats. If a predator is spotted, the whole herd should stampede. By moving together, each animal has a reduced chance of being the target of a predator's attention. If a player has the misfortune to be standing in the wrong place during a stampede, they could find themselves trampled by several fleeing animals.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Augustynolophus} is closely related to {@i Prosaurolophus} ({@b page 302}). It was originally described as {@i Saurolophus}, with some debate as to whether or not it belonged to the North American existing taxa {@i Saurolophus osborni} or represented a new taxon. A review in 2013 argued that it was a new species, {@i Saurolophus morrisi}, due to differences in its cheek bone and crest. However, within less than a year, the same authors published a correction, identifying the {@i S. morrisi} material as distinct enough to warrant its own genus and it was named {@i Augustynolophus}. This type of reassignment is commonplace in palaeontology, particularly in animals with a lot of morphological overlap like hadrosaurs.

trait.name: Thick Body
entries: Brasinorhynchus has Advantage on saving throws to avoid being {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled}..

trait.name: Roughage Eater
entries: Brasinorhynchus is able to consume tough plant material that other herbivores find inedible. This can include non-magical wooden items, like mundane clubs, and uncommon magical items like a Wand of Magic Missiles.

action.name: Hooked Beak
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}10 ({@damage 2d8 + 1}) Piercing damage.
If Brasinorhynchus hits with this attack, it may immediately make a Jawbone Crush attack against the same creature.

action.name: Jawbone Crush
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}4 ({@damage 1d6 + 1}) Bludgeoning damage.

A creature hit by this attack must make a {@dc 11} Dexterity saving throw. On a failed save, one item that could be destroyed by Brasinorhynchus' Roughage Eater trait, a small potion, or mundane trinket that the creature is carrying and that is visible to Brasinorhynchus (selected by the DM) is grabbed and crushed, destroying it.
If Brasinorhynchus crushes an item in this manner, it deals {@dice 1d6} Piercing damage to itself.
"BRASS-E-NO-RING-KUS"
{@b (RED HORSES BEAK)}

Perhaps one of the most frustrating animals we came across on our Triassic exploration was the humble Brasinorhynchus. Upon camping for the night, more than once we awoke to the sound of coarse chewing and chomping nearby, only to find that one of these creatures had been rummaging through our bags and snacking on any magical wooden items it could find. They seemed to be drawn to them and, over the course of the expedition, our poor wizard lost three rather expensive wands.
{@i Brasinorhynchus} is a large rhynchosaur from the Late Triassic (approximately 233 million years ago) in Rio Grande de Sul, Brazil. It was a heavily built herbivore with a distinctive hooked beak.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Brasinorhynchus} is known only from isolated skull pieces, but it has been estimated to be over 6 ft. long with some giants reaching 10 ft. in length. Rhynchosaurs had long, chunky, lizard-like bodies with thick tails and their legs splayed in a sprawling position. {@i Brasinorhynchus'} skull was short with a distinctive triangular shape, being much broader at the back than the front. Its upper jaw was tipped with a hooked beak that gave it a prominent overbite. It had very well-developed cheeks and a strong bite, with broad teeth that evolved for crushing tough plants. While {@i Brasinorhynchus} wasn't able to chew properly like a mammal, it could crush food by pushing its teeth against its jawbone. This is a rare and destructive mode of feeding that causes a lot of damage to both the teeth and the bone. Unlike a lot of other reptiles, they weren't able to replace their teeth, meaning that once their teeth wore down, they became useless. Elderly {@i Brasinorhynchus} would have eventually been unable to feed and quickly die of starvation.

{@i Brasinorhynchus} was found in the Santa Maria Formation of Brazil, which was deposited in and around the transition of a river delta into open sea. The unit is very fossiliferous and includes a variety of taxa such as temnospondyl amphibians, large herbivorous dicynodonts, large predatory reptiles like {@i Prestosuchus} (that was a probable predator of {@i Brasinorhynchus}), and even several early dinosaurs.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: Brasinorhynchus' Jawbone Crush attack is particularly punishing for low-level players. We suggest that the first time it happens, you choose an item or object that is of very little value to the players to demonstrate the danger of this attack.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: The powerful jaws of {@i Brasinorhynchus} allowed it to process tougher plant matter than many other competitors in its environment. This specialisation, combined with its thin snout, suggest it was a selective browser, using its upper beak to snip tough, but nutritious, branches and leaves that other herbivores couldn't eat from primitive seed ferns. As {@i Brasinorhynchus} was a robust sprawling animal, it was likely not speedy and would have struggled to flee from predators. Its strong bite would have been its only defence from attack but would have been a formidable weapon for a cornered rhynchosaur.

We suggest playing {@i Brasinorhynchus} as a somewhat skittish animal. Feeding in small herds, with one or two animals frequently stopping feeding to scan their surroundings for danger. If a threat is spotted, they should attempt to flee as a skittering group into dense foliage, but they should be quick to turn and fight if their foe is faster than them, snapping furiously in an attempt to injure them, before fleeing again.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Rhynchosaurs were a highly successful group of basal archosauromorphs (close to but outside of the archosaurs - the group that includes dinosaurs, pterosaurs, crocodiles, etc.). The rhynchosaurs first evolved approximately 250 million years ago in Pangea and spread across the continent for much of the Triassic. By the start of the early Late Triassic (230 million years ago) they were particularly numerous, however the group would seemingly go extinct within a few million years (although there are some reports of rhynchosaur material from close to the Triassic/Jurassic boundary). The cause of their extinction is still debated, with some arguing they were outcompeted by early herbivorous dinosaurs, while others suggest they died out when their primary food source, the seed ferns, began reducing in number.

trait.name: Subsurface Animal
entries: Cameroceras has Resistance to Cold damage (included above), and can only breathe in water.

trait.name: Electrosensory Tentacles
entries: Cameroceras has a Blindsight of 10 ft. (included above).

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Cameroceras chooses the Attack action, it may make one Grasping Tentacles attack and one Crushing Beak attack.

action.name: Grasping Tentacles
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 6} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}15 ({@damage 2d10 + 4}) Bludgeoning damage.
A creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} and {@condition restrained|XPHB|Restrained} (escape {@dc 15}).

action.name: Crushing Beak
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 10} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}23 ({@damage 3d12 + 4}) Piercing damage.
This attack may only be used against a creature that is currently {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} by Cameroceras.

action.name: Aquatic Full Jet Propulsion
entries: As an Action, Cameroceras triples its movement speed until the end of its turn. If it does so, it cannot use its Aquatic Jet Bonus Action.

bonus.name: Aquatic Jet
entries: Cameroceras dashes as a Bonus Action. If it does so, it cannot use its Aquatic Full Jet Propulsion Action this turn.
"CAM-AIR-OH-SER-AS"
{@b (CHAMBER HORN)}

Strange cone-shelled organisms with unsettling writhing tentacles lurk at the bottom of Ordovician oceans. In my experience, these large cephalopods usually leave humanoids alone, unless they're being actively disturbed. Nonetheless, it is best to keep one's distance, as a rather sharp beak is concealed behind its wiggling feelers.

{@i Cameroceras} is a cephalopod from the Ordovician (486 to 443 million years ago). Possessing a distinctive long, conical, and pointed shell, it is one of the largest members of the nautiloids, a group which has survived into present times in the form of the modern nautilus.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Cameroceras} is a giant nautiloid that held most of its body in a long, conical shell called an orthocone. Due to a combination of fragmentary material and a messy taxonomy (see below), exactly how big {@i Cameroceras} grew is uncertain. However, the largest confidently identified remains are from an animal at least 6 to 7 ft. in length, while contested fragmentary material suggest it could reach up to 30 ft. in length. A long tube called a siphuncle ran along the inside of the bottom margin of the shell, connecting several internal chambers. Through this, {@i Cameroceras} could rapidly suck in or squirt out water, allowing it to propel itself with jets or to change its buoyancy. {@i Cameroceras} may have held its shell vertically in the water column, although it likely could re-orientate horizontally when needed. While we have no preserved soft tissue remains of {@i Cameroceras}, through comparison with other cephalopods, we can confidently say that it was a multi-tentacled animal with a parrot-like mouth nestled in the middle of them. Like the nautilus, it may not have had strong vision, instead relying on its sense of touch to find its way around.

{@i Cameroceras} is what we call a "wastebasket taxon". This means that numerous specimens have been assigned to this genus based on limited evidence. This over-assignment means that fossils identified as {@i Cameroceras} have been found in rock formations throughout the northern hemisphere, but many likely belong to other genera that will only be described when sufficient analyses are undertaken or more complete specimens found. These fossils have largely been found in formations laid down in either shallow continental or adjacent deeper waters. These areas are especially rich in fauna such as eurypterids, agnathans (jawless fish), trilobites, and dozens of species of cephalopod.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: While one study suggested that {@i Cameroceras} would have been a nektonic (free swimming) filter feeder, research into their buoyancy as well as fossil evidence of attacks on other cephalopods and arthropods instead indicate that {@i Cameroceras} was likely a benthic (sea floor) predator. It would have floated close to the sandy bottom, using its tentacles to search for prey. Anything that brushed against them would be snatched up and their outer shells cracked by its powerful beak.

We suggest playing {@i Cameroceras} as a shallow-to-deep water predator, often found floating near the seafloor or lazily drifting from one hunting ground to the next. They should sometimes be found in large groups with their shells held vertically, looking almost like an underwater forest. While their shells may seem static, their tentacles should be constantly sifting through the sand or rock, searching for prey. They should not be picky about their food, and are likely to eat any creature they can get their tentacles on.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Cameroceras} is a member of the Endocerida. This is a group of shelly nautiloids that first appeared in the Early Ordovician, approximately 475 million years ago. While most species were about the same size as an average octopus or squid, the largest members were amongst the biggest cephalopods in the fossil record. The orthocones of endocerids had variable shell shapes, ranging from very straight to curled. The group underwent several diversity events in the Early and Middle Ordovician before falling into decline in the Late Ordovician. As mentioned above, the wastebasket nature of {@i Cameroceras} taxonomy makes it hard to be certain when it arose exactly, but we do know that it became extinct alongside almost all other endocerids during the Ordovician-Silurian mass extinction caused by a combination of a glaciation event, the reduction in the oxygen content in the seas, and an increase in oceanic sulphur.
Various Orthoceras fossils.

trait.name: Aquatic Animal
entries: Cartorhynchus can hold its breath for up to 30 minutes.

trait.name: Eel-Like Wriggle
entries: Cartorhynchus has Advantage on Dexterity saving throws while in water.

action.name: Shell-Crushing Nip
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}1 (1) Piercing damage.
Tiny or Miniscule creatures hit by this attack take an additional 2 Bludgeoning damage.
"CAR-TOE-REEN-CUS"
{@b (SHORT SNOUT)}

Normally, a well-armoured boot or greave protects any adventurer's foot from biting nuisances in shallow rockpools, as well as more serious stinging threats like coneshells and jellyfish. However, in some Triassic pools, this armament can actually provoke an attack. The specialist shell-feeding Cartorhynchus is liable to nip at passing armoured toes.

{@i Cartorhynchus} is a small ichthyosaur from the Early Triassic (248 million years ago) of China. One of the strangest ichthyosaurs that we know of, it may have retained the ability to move on land.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Cartorhynchus} was tiny for an ichthyosaur, measuring only 16 in. long and weighing as little as 1 to 4 lb. As its name suggests, it had a short snout with molar-like teeth. Its body was squat and plump, almost lizard-like with a long tail. Rather than using just its tail to swim, it is thought to have moved its whole body in a more eel-like manner. Its flippers were proportionally very large and surprisingly flexible. It has been suggested that they were strong enough to allow {@i Cartorhynchus} to drag itself across beaches, although it likely would have remained close to the shoreline for safety.

{@i Cartorhynchus} is found in the Nanlinghu Formation in the Anhui Province, China. This was a shallow near-shore marine environment rich in aquatic fauna. {@i Cartorhynchus} lived alongside a varied assemblage of animals including coelocanths, bizarre long-limbed arthropods, as well as other aquatic reptiles like early sauropterygians and a number of other ichthyosaurs.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Cartorhynchus} possessed rounded molar-like teeth that gave it a crushing bite. Similar teeth are found in a wide variety of aquatic animals and usually indicate that they are durophagus, meaning that they feed on hard shelled prey, usually molluscs or crustaceans. Studies suggest that {@i Cartorhynchus} sucked up shellfish hidden in the sandy seafloor, then cracked them open with its strong bite to reach the soft internal tissues.

We suggest playing {@i Cartorhynchus} as a resident of shallow waters along beaches or within rock pools being fed by the ocean. They should spend most of their time slowly swimming near the bottom of the sea, rummaging through the sand with their snouts. When they sense prey, they should quickly suck it in and crush it. A {@i Cartorhynchus} is no threat to a humanoid and will usually flee if disturbed. Particularly hungry individuals may mistake toes pressed into the sand for shellfish, and unwary players may find themselves on the receiving end of a surprisingly strong nip.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Cartorhynchus} is the smallest member of Nasorostra. This is a small group of short nosed Early Triassic ichthyosaurs. The group first appeared approximately 250 million years ago and had a global distribution. The Early Triassic was a transitionary period for ichthyosaurs, with numerous unusual taxa appearing in the fossil record. They were less dolphin-like in appearance than other ichthyosaurs, lacking the classic dorsal fin and tail flukes. Their size also varied wildly, from the tiny {@i Carthorhynchus} to the whale-sized giants like {@i Shonisaurus} ({@b page 306}). This diversity did not continue beyond the Triassic, with ichthyosaurs undergoing an evolutionary bottle neck and only the much more well-known morphologies surviving into the Jurassic and Cretaceous.

trait.name: Foraging Friend
entries: If Caviramus spends four hours foraging, it can find a day's worth of rations for one person (composed of fish,
fruits, insects, and/or edible plant stems) without requiring a {@skill Survival} check. It may carry these rations in its mouth.

trait.name: Scrambler
entries: So long as Caviramus does not fly on a turn in which it takes the Dash action, it may make a Fanged Bite attack as a Bonus Action for the remainder of that turn.

action.name: Fanged Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}2 (2) Piercing damage.

bonus.name: Head Crest
entries: As a Bonus Action, Caviramus can flush its head crest with blood making it appear a vibrant red colour. If it does so, it gains a +2 modifier (cumulative with other modifiers) to all Charisma checks for 1 minute.
"KAV-IH-RAH-MUS"
{@b (HOLLOW BRANCH)}

One tends to become accustomed to pterosaurs swooping or striding majestically. However, among these noble animals are several smaller species that scramble around uncouthly. Caviramus is one such animal. Despite this, it still makes for a pleasant companion on jungle ventures and is often an indicator of abundant edible fruits in the area.

{@i Caviramus} is an early pterosaur from the Late Triassic (205 million years ago) of the Northern Alps, Switzerland. Originally described based on an isolated jaw, a more complete pterosaur from the same region named {@i Raeticodactylus} is sometimes synonymised with {@i Caviramus}, a viewpoint we follow here.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Caviramus} was a small pterosaur with a wingspan of about 4.5 ft. Its body was fairly typical for a pterosaur, with membranous wings and a long tail likely tipped with a fleshy vane. Its limbs were long and, although it probably held its forelimbs in a sprawling posture when standing, it was quite agile on land. Its head was relatively short compared to later pterosaurs, with a low rounded bony crest on the underside of the bottom jaw. It also had a tall triangular bony projection on its head that probably supported a large soft-tissue crest. It had heterodont (differentiated) teeth with a set of overlapping fangs at the front of the mouth and a series of smaller multicusped (multiple points) teeth towards the middle.

{@i Caviramus} is from the Kossen Formation, a unit that runs along the Northern Alps near the borders of Switzerland, Germany, and Austria. This was laid down in a shallow lagoon that transitioned into deeper waters. While the formation is fossiliferous, it mostly consists of bivalves, echinoderms, and ammonites, although large vertebrate remains, like the giant ichthyosaur {@i Shonisaurus} ({@b page 306}), have been discovered in recent years.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Prior to the explosion in pterosaur research in the new millennium, many researchers assumed that most pterosaurs ate fish. However, more advanced research techniques have revealed that pterosaur diets were just as diverse as any other group of animals. {@i Caviramus,} for instance, has a much more complex dentition than fish specialists like {@i Rhamphorhynchus} {@b (page 168 in DDDD)}. The combination of fangs and multicusped teeth, along with dental wear patterns, suggest it fed on prey like small vertebrates or hard-shelled arthropods.

We suggest playing {@i Caviramus} as a somewhat flighty animal that is always on the lookout for either a meal or threats. When hunting, it should spend a lot of time on the ground, scanning for prey with jerky head motions and scrambling around. While often found inland, it should sometimes visit local beaches to scavenge the shoreline for washed up fish and other remains. An individual {@i Caviramus} may not be much of a threat to a humanoid, but may be very difficult to catch unaware. More often than not, an adventurer might only briefly glimpse one before it launches into the air.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Caviramus}' placement in the pterosaur family tree varies between research studies, but it has most recently been placed in the Caviramidae. Pterosaur phylogenies (especially for the earliest members) are famously variable between publications, with several conflicting family trees recovered by different researchers. This is partly because of the lack of transitional pterosaur fossils. The earliest pterosaurs in the fossil record date to about 228 million years ago and already have all of the features that we consider pterosaurian. We are yet to find an example of an animal that represents a middle-ground between pterosaurs and their flightless ancestors. The current consensus is that pterosaurs are most closely related to a group of long-legged archosaurs called the lagerpetids, but how these animals evolved flight and became pterosaurs remains unknown.

trait.name: Defensive Formation
entries: Chasmosaurus has +2 to its AC if one other Chasmosaurus is within 5 ft. of it. If two or more other Chasmosaurus are within 5 ft. of it, it instead gains +4 to its AC.

trait.name: Blood-filled Frill Fenestrae
entries: Attacks that target Chasmosaurus critically hit on a roll 1 lower than normal (i.e. on a roll of 19 and 20 if there are no other modifiers).

action.name: Frill Display
entries: As an Action, Chasmosaurus can flood its membranous frill with blood, giving it a vivid colour rapidly. Each other non-Chasmosaurus creature with 50 ft. that can see it must succeed a {@dc 13} Intelligence saving throw. On a failed save, the creature is {@condition frightened|XPHB|Frightened} of Chasmosaurus for 1 minute. It may repeat this saving throw at the end of each of its turns and becomes immune to Chasmosaurus' Frill Display for 24 hours on a successful save.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Chasmosaurus chooses the Attack action, it may make one Small Horned Gore attack and one Powerful Beak attack.

action.name: Small Horned Gore
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}7 ({@damage 1d10 + 2}) Bludgeoning damage plus 5 ({@damage 1d6 + 2}) Piercing damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 12} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.

action.name: Powerful Beak
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}12 ({@damage 1d12 + 6}) Piercing damage.
"KAS-MOH-SORE-US"
{@b (OPENING REPTILE)}

In our ventures through the northern coastline, we encountered a curious cadaver. This large animal appeared to be a ceratopsian of some kind and our druid determined that it died as a result of a large carnivore attack. Its skull was most intriguing to me. Unlike other ceratopsians, this creature had short, dullish horns and its large frill was long and almost boxy in appearance. It looked almost frail, the poor beast.

{@i Chasmosaurus} is a medium-sized ceratopsian from the Late Cretaceous of Alberta, Canada (76 million years ago). A distinctive looking animal, {@i Chasmosaurus} was known for the contrast of its comparatively small horns compared to its large, angular frill.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Chasmosaurus} was a smaller relative of {@i Triceratops} ({@b page 324}) and {@i Centrosaurus} ({@b page 116 in DDDD}), growing up to 16 ft. long and weighing 2 tonnes. Its appearance was typical of ceratopsians, with a large, elongate, and beaked head, prominent horns, a bony frill, a quadrupedal stance, bulky body, and a relatively short tail. The horns on {@i Chasmosaurus} were shorter and less prominent than in most other ceratopsians, and its frill was long and somewhat rectangular, rather than the more rounded shape of its relatives, although the back of the frill was quite variable between individuals, depending on age. {@i Chasmosaurus} gets its name from its most striking feature - two large openings in its frill. In life, these would have been covered by soft tissue.

{@i Chasmosaurus} has been found exclusively in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, Canada (77-74 million years ago). This is believed to have been laid down in a transitional environment where meandering rivers changed into a swampy coastal setting along the edge of the Western Interior Seaway over time. The formation has produced an abundance of dinosaur fossils, with large herbivores being especially common. {@i Chasmosaurus} lived alongside a diverse community of ankylosaurs, hadrosaurs, pachycephalosaurs, and several other ceratopsians including {@i Centrosaurus}. Theropods were also present within the assemblage, dominated by small dromaeosaurs and troodontids. Two large predators have also been identified, {@i Daspletosaurus} and {@i Gorgosaurus}. These are both tyrannosaurs which were large enough to be potential predators of {@i Chasmosaurus}.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Chasmosaurus} was a herbivore that lived alongside a variety of comparatively sized competitors. While evidence for niche partitioning among the Dinosaur Park Formation ceratopsians is limited, it has been suggested that the more elongate face, combined with less worn teeth than other herbivores, is evidence that {@i Chasmosaurus} was a selective browser that preferred to eat softer plant material. This allowed it to live alongside the likes of {@i Centrosaurus}, which may have preferred to eat tougher plants. {@i Chasmosaurus} remains have not been found in large enough numbers to suggest the animals lived in large herds, but it is uncertain whether they were solitary or lived in small groups. The large frill is believed to have been a social and/ or sexual signalling device, which would suggest some social behaviour.

We suggest playing {@i Chasmosaurus} as a less social animal, with groups consisting of two or three adults with several juveniles and babies. They should spend most of their lives browsing in open plains, however once a year they should gather in communal breeding grounds to reproduce. Males and females form tight knit bonds which are renewed each season by ritualistic displays. When nesting, {@i Chasmosaurus} pairs should be fiercely territorial. If an intruder approaches the nest, they will be at risk of attack from either adult. Once the eggs have hatched and the young have grown large enough to travel, the family will leave the breeding grounds to return to the plains.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Chasmosaurus} is the namesake of the Chasmosaurinae, a diverse group of ceratopsians that evolved in North America during the Late Cretaceous approximately 78 million years ago. Chasmosaurines are extremely variable but can broadly be identified by their elongate frills lacking prominent spikes and their brow horns being more prominent than their nose horns. Somewhat ironically, neither {@i Chasmosaurus} itself nor the most famous chasmosaurine, {@i Triceratops,} wholly conform to this standard. The group proved extremely successful and diverse, spreading across western North America. However, like all non-avian dinosaurs, they went extinct at the end of the Cretaceous.

monster.name: Coelodonta

trait.name: Polar Adaptations
entries: Coelodonta is not slowed by snowy Difficult Terrain, can tolerate temperatures as low as -20°C comfortably, and has Immunity to Cold damage (included above).

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Coelodonta chooses the Attack action, it may make one Horned Pierce attack and one Crushing Gore attack.

action.name: Crushing Gore
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}9 ({@damage 1d8 + 5}) Bludgeoning damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 13} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.

action.name: Horned Pierce
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}11 ({@damage 1d12 + 5}) Piercing damage.
If Coelodonta moved at least 15 ft. in a straight line immediately before making this attack, a hit creature gains the Run Through condition.

action.name: Condition: Run Through
entries: A creature that is Run Through has been impaled by massive horns.

At the start of its turn in combat or every minute outside of combat while not resting, the creature must succeed a {@dc 13} Constitution saving throw or take {@dice 2d6} Piercing damage. On a successful save it takes half as much damage.
This effect persists until one of the following occurs:

- The creature is healed by at least 10 Hit Points (cumulatively). - The creature finishes a Long Rest. - A {@dc 15} {@skill Medicine} check is passed on the creature. - A Lesser Restoration spell is cast on the creature. - It dies.

legendary.name: Goring Shuffle
entries: Coelodonta may move up to 5 ft. then make a single Crushing Gore attack.

legendaryHeader: Coelodonta can take 1 Legendary Action, choosing from the options below. Only one legendary option can be used at a time and only at the end of another creature's turn. The Coelodonta regains spent Legendary Actions at the start of its turn.

entries: "SEAL-OH-DON-TAH"
{@b (HOLLOW TOOTH)}

Being charged by a rhino, mock or otherwise, is an unpleasant experience. I can assure you that it is not made any better by the presence of a woolly coat on said rhino. If anything, the musky smell that the coat carries makes it even more unpleasant.

{@i Coelodonta}, more commonly known as the woolly rhino, was a Pliocene to Pleistocene (3.7 million years ago to 14,000 years ago) rhinoceros from the Eurasian mammoth steppes. A highly successful animal, it was known for its dense fur coat and large nose horns.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: The woolly rhino was about the same size of the modern white rhino, weighing approximately 2 tonnes with a 12 ft. long body. Like the woolly mammoth, exceptionally preserved fossils show it was covered in a thick coat of double layered reddish fur that provided insulation against the cold. It had two prominent nose horns, the first of which was very long and curved, and the second of which was shorter and straighter. Unlike living rhinos, which have quite rounded horns in cross-section, the woolly rhino's horns were thinner and more blade-like. It also had a large fatty hump over its shoulders, which would have been able to sustain the animal through leaner winter months when food was scarce.

The woolly rhino was an inhabitant of the mammoth steppe environments across Eurasia. These were cold grasslands with intermittent rain and snow. It shared its home with several other herbivores like bison, mammoths, deer, and other cold-to-temperate adapted rhinos, such as the single horned giant {@i Elasmotherium}. It encountered predators like the cave lion and short-faced bears, which were large enough to prey on young {@i Coelodonta}. Additionally, it lived alongside humans and evidence suggests that they were hunted, with their horns used as tips for spears.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Like its modern relatives, the woolly rhino was an herbivore and, based on stomach contents and radioactive isotope analysis of its horns, it spent the summers grazing on grasses and herbs, then switched to browsing on shrubbery in the winters. Abrasive marks on the sides of the horns suggest that they were used to sweep snow away in the cold months to expose hidden greenery, as well as for defence. There is little direct fossil evidence on whether woolly rhinos were solitary or social animals, although contemporary Pleistocene cave art shows several depictions of multiple rhinos associated together, which can be taken as anecdotal evidence of social behaviour. Modern white rhinos typically only form herds composed of females and calves, with bulls living either solitarily or in loose male-only aggregations. Research into the skulls of woolly rhinos, particularly males, shows evidence of trauma that matches well with similar injuries seen in modern rhinos. This, along with cave art depictions, suggests that woolly rhinos were quite combative with each other. In fact, one study suggested that woolly rhinos appeared to have suffered more head trauma than their living relatives, which may indicate that they were more aggressive.

We suggest playing the woolly rhino as a relatively gregarious animal, often found in small herds of females and calves. When observed from a distance, they should be seen to spend most of their time digging beneath snow for food or engaging in short, violent headbutting contests. Bulls should primarily be found alone, only joining herds during the mating season, where they will often compete with rivals for females. They should be much quicker to feel threatened or angry than other animals when encountering player characters, as well as be much more unpredictable. A party that surprises a rhino should be just as likely to be met with sudden intense violence as they are to be greeted by fear or a simple mock charge. This makes moving through rhino territory very risky for an inexperienced traveller.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Coelodonta} are part of the Rhinocerotinae group, which includes all modern rhinos and, of which, it is most closely related to the critically endangered (less than 50 individuals) Sumatran rhino. The oldest fossils of {@i Coelodonta} are from China, where it first evolved before eventually migrating to Europe during the Middle Pleistocene (approximately 450,000 to 500,000 years ago). The species proved quite successful but eventually went extinct about 14,000 years ago. While it has long been speculated that humans hunted them to extinction, genetic evidence suggests that, despite coexisting alongside our predecessors for several thousand years, rhino populations remained relatively stable. It was instead the retreat of the glaciers and the severe climate change at the end of the last ice age that was the most likely extinction driver, although humans may still have contributed by being an added pressure upon an already dwindling population.

trait.name: Gigantic Guts
entries: Cotylorhynchus' massive guts process large volumes of food very slowly, diminishing the effects of consumed toxins. It has Advantage on saving throws to avoid the {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned} condition caused by consuming something.

trait.name: Wide Sprawler
entries: Cotylorhynchus has Advantage on saving throws to avoid being {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} and attacks made against it that would also apply the {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} condition are made at Disadvantage.

trait.name: Lazy Feeder
entries: Cotylorhynchus focuses on feeding constantly (unless in breeding season). While feeding, it cannot be intimidated.

action.name: Powerful Claw Rake
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}6 ({@damage 1d10 + 1}) Slashing damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 11} Strength saving throw or drop an item it is wielding.
{@i "COH-TEA-LOW-RHEEN-CUS"} {@b (CUP SNOUT)}

This preposterous animal lumbers around the dry scrub devouring all plant life that it can reach. I mused to my travelling companions that I'd never seen such a ridiculously proportioned creature, only for them to remind me that it is strangely similar to a giant Galápagos tortoise. I now see the resemblance and accept that there are niches for all sorts of body types.

{@i Cotylorhynchus} was a large, bizarre looking animal from the Permian (280 to 270 million years ago) of Texas and Oklahoma, USA. A member of the Caseidae, its most distinctive feature was a long bulky body tipped with a disproportionately small head.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: With a body length of up to 20 ft. for the largest fossils, {@i Cotylorhynchus} was a giant and one of the largest land animals of its time. In appearance, it looked vaguely like a giant, rotund iguana. Its body was thick and round, with wide ribs suggesting a large digestive tract. Its limbs were squat and splayed, with powerful extensor muscles and large curving claws. Its tail was long and tapering, accounting for nearly half the animal's total length. {@i Cotylorhynchus'} head was tiny in comparison to the body, held upright on a short but strong neck. It was shaped like a parallelogram, with a bulbous snout that stuck out in front of the jawline giving the front of the skull a steeply angled appearance. The jaws contained numerous peg-like teeth tipped with three cusps, as well as smaller teeth on the roof of the mouth and a robust tongue. The dentition and enormous belly indicate {@i Cotylorhynchus} was not only herbivorous, but that it was eating large volumes of plants with relatively low nutritional value. It needed large guts in order to process this food and, while it has been suggested to be a grazer, the high positioning of its tiny head suggests that lowering it to ground level would not have been viable for hours on end. Instead, rather like modern Galapagos tortoises, it may have held its head up and browsed from fern bushes and the lower branches of trees. It may have also used its powerful limbs and claws to pull branches within range of its jaws, stripping them, then using its muscular tongue to crush tough leaves against the teeth in the roof of its mouth.

{@i Cotylorhynchus} was found in several formations in the southern parts of the United States, including the San Angelo and Chickasha formations. These were laid down in dry tropical environments with influence from rivers, lagoons, and seasonal monsoons. {@i Cotylorhynchus} was one of the largest animals in the faunal assemblage, sharing its environment with temnospondyls (large carnivorous amphibians), other basal synapsids, and even mudfish. The largest animals would have had few predators, but some localities do include {@i Dimetrodon}, which could reach 15 ft. in length and would have almost certainly preyed on immature {@i Cotylorhynchus}.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: There is some ongoing debate as to whether {@i Cotylorhynchus} was perhaps semi-aquatic. This has been touched upon as far back as the 1960s, where one study, while largely arguing that it was terrestrial, noted that it wasn't impossible the animal spent some of its time in water. Two studies have argued for potential aquatic or semi-aquatic habits, with one stating that {@i Cotylorhynchus} had low bone density and a bone thickness comparable to known aquatic animals. They suggested that it was likely living in rivers or lagoons, where the difficulties of diving or swimming may have led to the development of a primitive diaphragm. {@i Cotylorhynchus}' remains being found in fluvial or lagoonal deposits may represent unfortunate victims dying in their natural environment. A second study suggested that it and its relatives (the caseids) were more hippo-like, living in water but coming onto land to feed. An in-depth third study highlighted that, while the formations these animals were found in did have some aquatic environments, they were primarily dry and arid. They also noted that the bone density of {@i Cotylorhynchus} should, if it was semi-aquatic, be high density, rather than low density and that the animal did not possess any other morphological adaptations for life in the water. Instead, they argued that it was fully terrestrial and fossils found in water environments represent individuals washed in during monsoonal flooding. In general, a terrestrial lifestyle is considered the most plausible and the one we support here.

We suggest playing {@i Cotylorhynchus} as a methodical, slow moving animal. It should spend large portions of the day wandering in small herds constantly searching for food, only stopping to rest or engage in brief shoving matches with an irritating rival. Humanoids should be of very little interest to it and it should react with bemused curiosity if approached. Only if strongly pressed should one lash out and, even then, it is more likely to simply make a warning slash with its claws than full-on attack. This rather amiable nature should make it a prime candidate for domestication.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Cotylorhynchus} was one of the largest members of the Caseidae. This was a group of synapsids (which also produced the ancestors of living mammals) that appeared in the Late Carboniferous (around 300 million years ago) and survived up until the Middle Permian (260 million years ago). Caseids were initially quite small carnivorous and omnivorous animals that transitioned into significantly larger herbivorous forms. The larger species developed their distinctive giant body/tiny head combination and the group proved relatively successful, with remains found throughout Pangea, although they did not survive as far as the Permo-Triassic extinction event.

entries.name: References
entries: Lambertz, M., Shelton, C.D., Spindler, F. and Perry, S.F. 2016. A caseian point for the evolution of a diaphragm homologue among the earliest synapsids. {@i Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences}, {@b 1385 (1)}, pp.3-20.
Olson, E.C. 1968. The family Caseidae. Fieldiana. {@i Geology}, {@b 17}, pp.225-349.

Reisz, R.R., Scott, D. and Modesto, S.P. 2022. Cranial anatomy of the caseid synapsid Cotylorhynchus romeri, a large terrestrial herbivore from the Lower Permian of Oklahoma, USA. {@i Frontiers in Earth Science}, {@b 10}, pp.847560.

Werneburg, R., Spindler, F., Falconnet, J., Steyer, J.S., Vianey-Liaud, M. and Schneider, J.W. 2022. A new caseid synapsid from the Permian (Guadalupian) of the Lodève basin (Occitanie, France). {@i Palaeovertebrata}, {@b 45 (2)}, pp 1-36.

trait.name: Opportunistic Omnivore
entries: Daeodon is able to consume a variety of plants, fungi, carrion (sometimes), and fresh meat. It cannot be {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned} by tainted or laced food or drink.

trait.name: Cursorial Predator
entries: Daeodon can Dash as a Bonus Action. Additionally, If Daeodon moves at least 20 ft. in a straight line, any creature subsequently hit by its melee attacks this turn is knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.

trait.name: Neck Strength
entries: Daeodon has Advantage on saving throws to resist or escape the {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} condition.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Daeodon chooses the Attack action, it may make two Face-Bite attacks.

action.name: Face-Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}13 ({@damage 2d10 + 2}) Piercing damage.
This attack critically hits on the roll of a natural 19 or 20.

bonus.name: Neck Throw
entries: As a Bonus Action, Daeodon can use its powerful neck muscles to rend and fling a Medium or smaller creature that has been hit by its Face-Bite attack this turn.
The hit creature must succeed a {@dc 12} Strength saving throw or be thrown up to 10 ft. in any direction of Daeodon's choosing and then knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.

bonus.name: Cursorial Run
entries: Daeodon may Dash as a Bonus Action.
"DAY-OH-DON"
{@b (DREADFUL TOOTH)}

Ferocity comes in many forms within the fossil record. One such vicious animal is the pig-like entelodontid Daeodon. This vicious predator would give all but the largest predatory dinosaurs a run for their money. My encounters with this animal have been short and exceedingly violent.

{@i Daeodon} is a member of the Entelodontidae that is from the Oligocene (29 million years ago) of western and central North America. Looking a bit like a pig with a massive head, its large teeth and powerful jaws have earned it the moniker the "Hell Pig".

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Daeodon} is the largest entelodont known, reaching 6 ft. tall at the shoulder, 12 ft. long, and weighing up to 1600 lb. It was quadrupedal (walked on four legs) with thin legs and two-toed pig-like hooves. The neural spines on its vertebrae were very tall around the shoulders, giving it a sloping back like that of a bison. Its head was 3 ft. long and boxy, with cheek bones modified into large projecting flanges that anchored powerful jaw muscles. The lower jaw was robust, with a small pair of bumps (tubercles) positioned around the middle point of the lower surface. This deep jaw gave it a bite strong enough to crack bone and its teeth were equally large and robust, topped off with large interlocking canines at the front of its mouth.

{@i Daeodon} is known from several Oligocene and Miocene formations across the USA, such as the John Day Formation in Oregon and the Agate Fossil Beds in Nebraska. These deposits were generally laid down in forested regions or open grassland. It was part of a rich faunal assemblage alongside a wide variety of animals such as the strange long armed calicotheres, the bear-dog {@i Daphoenodon}, various species of dogs and mustelids, the false-sabre toothed cat (nimravids) {@i Dinictis}, the hornless rhino {@i Diceratherium}, as well as species of grazing oreodonts and early camels.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Despite its vicious and powerful jaws, based on the wear patterns of its enamel and analysis of the carbon isotope composition of its bones, {@i Daeodon} is considered to have been an omnivore. It is thought to have been a generalist that fed on grass, fruit, or leaves, and shifted its diet with the seasons. There is some debate over how much meat it ate and how it acquired it. However, bite marks left on calicothere bones indicate that it was certainly feeding on the remains of large animals at least on occasion, although this may have been from scavenging rather than active hunting. Some have argued that its particularly large and awkward skull suggests that attacking prey could have been difficult and it is more likely that its bone-crushing bite was needed to scavenge carcasses. Others instead argue that it would have been capable of running prey down and, while the skull was very big, the muscular neck and shoulder muscles provided ample support for it. Perhaps, as often happens, the truth lies somewhere in the middle with {@i Daeodon} being an opportunistic animal, adapting its approach as needed.

We suggest playing {@i Daeodon} as a somewhat social animal, living in small, scattered groups which individuals frequently leave and join. They should be found grazing on tall grasses or mobbing a carcass, often stopping to snap at either other {@i Daeodon} or any animal foolish enough to get too close. Aggression should be common, with adults threatening each other with wide yawns that expose their canines. When fighting breaks out, it should be vicious, and many individuals should bear scars or deep puncture wounds along their snout and flank from attacks. Any humanoid foolish enough to approach a {@i Daeodon} will find it fearless, barrelling down without hesitation, hoping to kill them either by trampling or with a powerful bone-crushing bite.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Despite frequently being associated with pigs, entelodonts are not closely related to the Suidae (pigs, hogs, and swine). Instead, they are part of another group of artiodactyls (even-toed ungulates), the Cetancodontamorpha. This group first appeared at least 47 million years ago in the Eocene and consists of a wide variety of animals including both hippos and whales. Entelodontidae first arose in the Middle Eocene, around 37 million years ago in Asia. The group appears to have enjoyed moderate success, with nine genera found throughout the Northern hemisphere. Entelodonts, including {@i Daeodon}, survived up until the Early Miocene (15 to 16 million years ago). The cause of their extinction is somewhat uncertain, but may have been due to a combination of environmental shifts leading to an influx of new predators which ultimately outcompeted them.

entries.name: References
entries: Joeckel, R.M. 1990. A functional interpretation of the masticatory system and paleoecology of entelodonts. {@i Paleobiology}, {@b 16 (4)}, pp.459-482.

Lucas, S.G., Emry, R.J. and Foss, S.E. 1998. Taxonomy and distribution of {@i Daeodon}, an Oligocene-Miocene entelodont (Mammalia: Artiodactyla) from North America. {@i Proceedings of the Biological Society of Washington}, {@b 111}, pp.425-435.

Spaulding, M., O'Leary, M.A. and Gatesy, J. 2009. Relationships of Cetacea (Artiodactyla) among mammals: increased taxon sampling alters interpretations of key fossils and character evolution. {@i Plos one}, {@b 4 (9)}, pp.e7062.

trait.name: Tree Raker
entries: Deinotherium has Advantage on attacks against plants and creatures composed of plants.

trait.name: Revenge Memory
entries: Deinotherium has Advantage on {@skill Survival} checks to track creatures that have previously attacked it and will generally actively seek them out.

action.name: Tusk Rake
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 8} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}16 ({@damage 2d10 + 5}) Bludgeoning damage plus 9 ({@damage 2d8}) Piercing damage.

A Large or smaller creature hit by this attack is knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone} and dragged underneath Deinotherium. That creature temporarily occupies the same space as Deinotherium and must crawl out before it can stand up again.

bonus.name: Crush Stomp
entries: If a creature is lying {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone} underneath Deinotherium, it can use its Bonus Action to try and stomp on that creature. That creature must succeed a {@dc 11} Dexterity saving throw or take 11 ({@damage 2d10}) Bludgeoning damage.

bonus.name: Trunk Grab
entries: Deinotherium can attempt to Grapple a Medium or smaller creature using its trunk as a Bonus Action ({@dc 16} Strength or Dexterity saving throw (target's choice)). It may attack other creatures without breaking this Grapple, but if it attempts to attack the {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} creature, the Grapple ends.
"DIE-NO-THER-E-UM"
{@b (TERRIBLE BEAST)}

We are all very much used to seeing proboscideans, elephants and their kin, with their usual forward facing long tusks - either as savannah elephants, jungle elephants, or tundra mammoths. However, the fossil record reveals that their ancestors had all manner of bizarre toothed ornamentation. One such animal is the invert-horned Deinotherium.

{@i Deinotherium} is a giant proboscidean mammal from the Miocene (13 million years ago) of Africa, Europe, and Asia. Bigger than any living elephant, {@i Deinotherium} is best known for its distinctive downward turning tusks that protrude from the front of its lower jaw.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Deinotherium} was one of the largest proboscideans, comparable to the Columbian Mammoth ({@b page 98}). Adults stood about 13 ft. tall at the shoulder and weighed 10 to 13 tonnes, with the largest fossils belonging to older males and it is likely that, like modern elephants, {@i Deinotherium} had slow continuous growth for most of its life. It had columnar and proportionally thin legs. Its back was relatively straight and didn't have the prominent shoulder hump found in mammoths, giving it less of a sloped back in comparison. The lower jaw in {@i Deinotherium} was tipped with characteristic downward facing tusks formed from the lower incisors. These were shorter than other large proboscidean tusks and curved backwards. Their function has been the subject of debate, as their position seems to suggest that they were less well-adapted for foraging or fighting compared to the tusks of other elephants and mammoths. It has been suggested that they were primarily used to strip away bark or excess branches from trees, however they were also likely used for display. Although they are awkwardly positioned to be used as weapons, it is possible that {@i Deinotherium} could have used them to stab at challengers during a fight. Although {@i Deinotherium} had a trunk, how long it was is not known. Current research suggests that its trunk was shorter and thicker than an elephant's, but would still have been long enough to reach the ground if it bent down. This shorter trunk may have evolved, in part, because {@i Deinotherium} was a browser, preferring to strip trees of their foliage, rather than reaching down and pulling up tall grasses.

{@i Deinotherium} is known from numerous Middle Miocene to Early Pleistocene formations in Africa and Eurasia. It is consistently found in environments with heavy tree cover, ranging from damp forests to subtropical semi-open woodlands. With such a broad range, it lived alongside a variety of other animals. This included other large proboscideans, amphycionid bear-dogs, the giant hyenadont {@i Megistotherium}, multiple species of bizarre giraffids, small basal horses, and several species of primates including some hominids.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Given their size, adult {@i Deinotherium} would have had few, if any, predators, although younger animals would have been vulnerable to attack. {@i Deinotherium} may have lived in small herds for protection although we have limited direct evidence to support this. One possible indicator can be found in their cranial endocasts (casts of the brain), which shows a comparable level of intelligence to modern elephants, which are highly social with very complex societies. This, alongside the ubiquity of the single sex herd structure amongst elephantiformes, leads most researchers to assume an elephant-like social structure. Herds would have been made of several generations of related females and their calves while older bulls spent most of their lives alone.

We suggest playing {@i Deinotherium} as an animal that spends most of its time in small groups browsing within forested regions. They should be destructive to the forest, knocking trees over and goring bark away with their tusks. Within the group, juveniles should be treated with immense care, often seen playfully swinging their trunk under the watchful eye of their mother and her sisters. While {@i Deinotherium} may seem placid, it should be quick to defend itself if approached by a potential threat. It has evolved alongside humanoids and is well aware of the threat they may pose, although some {@i Deinotherium} should be able to quickly distinguish between a benign group of wandering travellers and a hunting/poaching party. Once attacked, a {@i Deinotherium} should be able to remember their assailant and, if angry enough, may track them down for miles to seek revenge. Many a would-be hunter has woken from their beds to the sounds of a rampaging herd destroying their home.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Deinotherium} is the largest member of the Deinotheridae. This is a small but successful group of proboscideans which were the sister group to the Elephantiformes. The oldest fossils were found in Late Oligocene (28 million years ago) rocks from Ethiopia, and the group later migrated to other parts of Africa and Eurasia. The exact reason for their extinction is uncertain, but around the time of their disappearance, there was an increase in arid environments and a reduction in heavy tree cover. It is likely that {@i Deinotherium} suffered from a lack of food and declined rapidly. Populations first reduced in Europe and India, before eventually the last members died off in Africa approximately 1 million years ago.

Springer International Publishing, pp. 579-644.
Nabavizadeh, A. 2024. Of tusks and trunks: A review of craniofacial evolutionary anatomy in elephants and extinct Proboscidea. {@i The Anatomical Record}, {@b 308 (11)}, pp.1-20.

trait.name: Salamander-like Poison
entries: Diplocaulus secretes a powerful poison in its skin. If a creature hits Diplocaulus with a melee attack or otherwise touches Diplocaulus (excluding from Toxic Nip), that creature must succeed a {@dc 9} Constitution saving throw or take {@dice 2d4} Poison damage.

trait.name: Aestivation
entries: Diplocaulus can survive periods of drought by sealing itself in a burrow. It has a burrowing speed of 5 ft. (included above) and may enter a catatonic state for up to 2 months where it does not require food or drink. They typically only burrow 5 ft. into soft sediments.

action.name: Toxic Nip
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}4 ({@damage 1d4 + 2}) Piercing damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 9} Constitution saving throw or take {@dice 2d6} Poison damage.

bonus.name: Hydrofoil Head
entries: If Diplocaulus is swimming, it can Dash as a Bonus Action.
"DIP-LOH-CAW-LUS"
{@b (DOUBLE STALK)}

Long before snakes slithered across the world, other small creatures filled the role of "watch where you're stepping". This is particularly so in the swamplands of the Carboniferous, where slimy salamander-like lepospondyls rest in the shallows. One ill-placed misstep can result in rather nasty poisoning, if you should accidentally stand on a lurking Diplocaulus.

{@i Diplocaulus} is a large lepospondyl from the Late Carboniferous (307 million years ago) of North America and Africa. One of the quintessential Palaeozoic amphibians, its most distinctive feature is its bizarre boomerang-shaped head.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Diplocaulus} is the largest lepospondyl known, growing up to 3 to 4 ft. in length. Its body looked similar to a salamander or newt, with broad ribs, short limbs with web toes, and a long paddle-like tail. Its most recognizable feature was its head, which was extremely broad with a small, concealed mouth. The sides were modified into two triangular backwards pointing projections, which are referred to as tabular horns (named for the tabular bone that makes up most of the structure), giving it an overall boomerang shape. The function of these horns has been the subject of a lot of research over the years. Some have argued that they may have played a role in social behaviour or that they, via their awkward shape, may have served as a predator deterrent. Studies into them in the 1980s argued that they were essentially hydrofoils and allowed the animal to move more easily in water, allowing {@i Diplocaulus} to swim more easily in slow moving water.

{@i Diplocaulus} has been found in several Carboniferous and Permian formations across North America and Africa. Typically, it is found in formations that were laid down in coastal swamps or in freshwater lakes. It lived alongside a diverse assemblage of animals, including giant insects, a variety of both fresh and marine fish, other lepospondyls, and various synapsids.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Due to their superficial similarities, {@i Diplocaulus} is usually thought to have been quite salamander-like in its behaviour. It lived in wet, moist environments and would have hunted similar prey, like small fish or arthropods. It may have been a suction feeder, opening its mouth quickly and rapidly sucking in prey. Fossils show that it was able to dig burrows and aestivated (entered torpor) in order to survive droughts. These burrows were communal and were used not only by multiple {@i Diplocaulus,} but sometimes other lepospondyls.

While this allowed them to survive up until the rainy season, it also left them very vulnerable to predators, with one fossil burrow preserving a half-eaten {@i Diplocaulus} inside. Like salamanders, it is possible that {@i Diplocaulus'} defence against such attacks included foul-tasting toxins in its skin - a common adaptation amongst amphibians.

We suggest that {@i Diplocaulus} should mostly be found in swamps or lakes, either slowly gliding through the water searching for food or resting on a shoreline rock. They should be easily spooked and, if they spot a potential predator, quickly escape into murky waters. If caught, they should primarily rely on their toxic secretions to protect themselves and otherwise only wriggle and nip at attackers in the hopes of making them let go.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Lepospondyli, a somewhat contested group which is broadly defined as modern amphibians and their extinct relatives, was one of the first major groups of basal tetrapods to evolve in the Early Carboniferous (347 million years ago). First appearing in what is now Europe and North America, the group eventually had a global distribution. While many lepospondyls like {@i Diplocaulus} were aquatic or semi aquatic, several families transitioned into permanently terrestrial lifestyles. While they were very successful in the Carboniferous, the change to a much drier climate in the Early Permian (298 million years ago) led to a severe drop in numbers. Most families quickly disappeared with only one species of {@i Diplocaulus} surviving into the Late Permian (202 million years ago).

entries.name: References
entries: Cruickshank, A. R. I. and Skews, B. W. 1980. The functional significance of Nectridean tabular horns (Amphibia: Lepospondyli). {@i Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences}, {@b 209 (1177)}, pp.513–537 Germain, D. 2010. The Moroccan diplocaulid: the last lepospondyl, the single one on Gondwana. {@i Historical Biology}, {@b 22 (1-3)}, pp.4-39.

Harris, S.K., Lucas, S.G., Berman, D.S. and Henrici, A.C. 2005. Diplocaulus cranial material from the lower Abo Formation (Wolfcampian) of New Mexico and the stratigraphic distribution of the genus. {@i New Mexico Museum of Natural History and Science Bulletin}, {@b 30}, pp.101-3.

Zoehfeld, K.W., Bakker, R.T., Flis, C.J. Pettersson, C.B. and Bell, T.H. 2013. Burrows and break-ins on the Texas Permian delta: stacked aestivating amphibians and attacks by Dimetrodon. In: {@i 2013 GSA Annual Meeting in Denver}.

trait.name: Deep Sea Drifter
entries: Diplomoceras can only breathe in water and has Resistance to Cold and Thunder damage (included above). It can swim up to 10 ft. in any direction, but if moving only vertically, its swim speed is increased to 30 ft.
If a strong current is present in the water, Diplomoceras will drift with it and will not attempt to swim against it.

action.name: Ink Blot
entries: As an Action, Diplomoceras can release a jet of ink into the water adjacent to it. It may select a 10 ft. diameter sphere of water adjacent to itself. That area of water becomes filled with black ink, rendering it opaque and obscuring line of sight into and through the water. This effect persists for 30 seconds, unless a particularly strong current disperses the water.

action.name: Raspy Radula
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 1} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}2 ({@damage 1d4}) Slashing damage plus 2 ({@damage 1d4}) Bludgeoning damage.
A creature hit by this attack that is smaller than Diplomoceras is {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} and {@condition restrained|XPHB|Restrained} (escape {@dc 9}).
"DIP-LOW-MOH-SER-AS"
{@b (DOUBLE HORN)}

Among the horrors of most ancient oceans, there are some animals that stand out as more comical than terrifying. The group known as "heteromorph ammonites" all fit into this category, as their bizarre, uncoiled shells make them look quite ridiculous indeed.

{@i Diplomoceras} is an ammonite from the Late Cretaceous (83 million years ago) with a global distribution. It belongs to the loosely associated "heteromorph ammonites", which encompasses several different ammonite groups that have modified their shells into bizarre shapes and patterns, rather than being the usual tightly coiled circular shells.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Diplomoceras} was a large ammonite with the biggest individuals growing to nearly 7 ft. long. While we do not have the soft tissue preserved, based on comparisons with other cephalopods, we can safely presume that it had multiple tentacles formed from its mantle. Most of the body was made up of a multi-chambered (septa) shell that was connected to the outside via the siphuncle (a long tube that ran along the base of the shell which allowed the animal to draw in or push out water). The shell itself made up more than 90% of {@i Diplomoceras'} length and was bizarrely shaped, looking remarkably like a paperclip. Why it looked like this remains a mystery, with some arguing it allowed for easier movement through the water column, or helped keep benthic species on the seafloor {@i Diplomoceras} had a global distribution and is found in geological formations from Canada to Greenland to Japan, and even Antarctica. It is generally found in shallow seas but lived in a variety of different climates. This meant it also lived alongside a huge variety of other animals, including numerous species of fish, crustaceans, mosasaurs, and plesiosaurs, like the benthic filter feeder {@i Aristonectes} ({@b page 172}).

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Like the giant orthocone {@i Cameroceras} ({@b page 184}), {@i Diplomoceras} probably held its shell vertically in the water column. Stomach contents show that it specialised in feeding on zooplankton (tiny free-swimming animals). Evidence suggests that it spent most of its time close to the seafloor but was able to rise or fall within the water column by controlling the amount of water in its shell. It wasn't a strong swimmer, however, and likely drifted on the currents with less active movement than other animals.

We suggest playing {@i Diplomoceras} as a largely passive animal, floating gently above the ocean floor. They should be found in groups which tend to be same sex, with smaller males being found higher in the water column than the much larger females. Humanoids are more likely to encounter them in the day when they feed on plankton closer to the surface, but a {@i Diplomoceras} is not particularly threatening. Still, if surprised, they may use their tentacles to grab onto a potential threat and use their raspy tongue-like radula to inflict injuries. They might also release a cloud of blotting ink to mask them shooting down into deeper water in the hopes that a predator won't follow.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Diplomoceras} is a heteromorph ammonite. This means that it has a shell that has been modified away from the classic tightly curled whorl. Heteromorphs evolved into a huge variety of shapes and sizes and, historically, have been treated as a broadly related assemblage. However, more recent phylogenetic analyses show that heteromorphs are polyphyletic (not a single lineage ({@b see Phylogenetics on page 9)}) and are grouped together more for their morphology than their biological relationships. {@i Diplomoceras,} for example, is more accurately placed in the Ancyloceratina, a group that includes several ammonites with both the normal shell morphology and heteromorph variants. The Ancyloceratina appeared in the Late Jurassic (around 149 million years ago) and went on to become extremely diverse during the Cretaceous. The group survived right up until the end of the Cretaceous, with some recent evidence suggesting that they may have even survived into the earliest Paleocene (64 million years ago).
