trait.name: Swarm
entries: The Trilobite Swarm can occupy another creature's space and vice versa, and it can move through any opening large enough for a Tiny beast. The swarm can't regain Hit Points or gain Temporary Hit Points, and has Immunity to the {@condition charmed|XPHB|Charmed}, {@condition frightened|XPHB|Frightened}, {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled}, {@condition paralyzed|XPHB|Paralyzed}, {@condition petrified|XPHB|Petrified}, {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}, {@condition restrained|XPHB|Restrained}, and {@condition stunned|XPHB|Stunned} conditions (included above).

trait.name: Hidden Gills
entries: The Trilobite Swarm can breathe in water. Additionally, it may breathe for up to an hour after leaving the water, then must return to water or begin to suffocate.

trait.name: Complex Eyes
entries: The Trilobite Swarm has Darkvision 10 ft. and Expertise in {@skill Perception} (both included above).

action.name: Swarming Consumption
entries: The Trilobite Swarm scurries over a creature within 5 ft. That creature must succeed a {@dc 6} Dexterity saving throw or lose {@dice 1d4 + 1} days' worth of rations.

action.name: Tickling Spikey Feet
entries: The Trilobite Swarm crawls all over a Small or Medium sized creature that it is within 5 ft. of.
That creature must succeed a {@dc 8} Constitution saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}, drop an item they are wielding, and take 1 point of Piercing damage.
{@i "TRY-LOW-BITE"} {@b (THREE LOBES)}

For much of our history, you can find small unfamiliar shells washed up on the shores of ancient beaches. The strange, segmented remains are of the abundant trilobites that inhabit all manner of ocean environments. From shallow rock pools to the crushing depths, these little creatures scuttling around in search of food. For experienced adventurers, these shells are a stark reminder to not leave rations unattended near the sea, lest they be unwantedly devoured.

Trilobita (more commonly known as trilobites) are one of the most well-known non-dinosaurian fossil groups. These arthropods first appeared in the fossil record in the Cambrian (520 million years ago) and became a global phenomenon, surviving until their extinction in the Permian (252 million years ago). They were an incredibly diverse group with thousands of research papers dedicated to their study. Here, we have opted to discuss them as a group, rather than picking a single genus to focus on.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: Trilobites range widely in length, from as small as 1 mm to as big as 2 ft. As their name suggests, their body can be divided into three sections: the cephalon (head), thorax (body) and pygidium (tail). These sections are subdivided into multiple segments and can have a lot of variation in ornamentation. Several groups developed large spines along the length of their body, while others grew elaborate "horns" similar to those found on some beetles.

Thanks to exceptionally preserved specimens, we know they had sensory antennae attached to the ventral side of the cephalon. Each segment had a pair of legs, with the cephalon having 4 to 5 pairs of endoprites (walking legs) that also supported exopodites (gills) to keep the animal oxygenated. Trilobites had complex compound eyes with calcite lenses. These eyes varied widely in morphology and number of lenses, with some relatively flat against the body, others huge and bulb-like protruding from the sides of their cephalons, and others still standing erect on stalks with overhanging "shades". While early trilobites likely only had relatively simple vision, more derived forms would have had very advanced vision and were probably able to clearly see objects and judge distance.

Trilobites were exclusively marine organisms, being either benthic (seafloor) walkers or pelagic (open ocean) swimmers. With their long history, they shared their habitats with a vast array of different organisms, from the predatory Cambrian giant {@i Anomalocaris} ({@b page 169}) to the Devonian armoured fish like {@i Dunkleosteus} ({@b page 216}). They are also commonly found alongside more other long surviving animals like corals, shelly fauna like brachiopods, and crinoids (sea lilies).

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: The behaviour of trilobites was as variable as their morphology but broadly speaking they had three main feeding strategies. Some were active predators with large mouths and hooked raspers to scrape off flesh. These hunters tended to feed on benthic worms, large plankton, or other trilobites. Others were scavengers, moving along the seafloor and sifting through sediment with wing-like limbs in search of organic detritus. Finally, the pelagic trilobites tended to be filter feeders, possessing a chamber under their exoskeleton that helped filter plankton out of the surrounding water.

We suggest playing trilobites as a common sight in the ocean, whether you are swimming close to shore or diving in the deep, oxygen-poor depths. Trilobites should not pay much attention to other organisms unless they are small enough to eat or they are perceived as approaching to attack. If startled, they should roll up into a ball to protect their soft underbelly, similar to a Woodlouse (Oniscidea). A single trilobite is not a threat to a humanoid of any size, however large numbers of trilobites can swarm inactive or unsuspecting humanoids. While not particularly dangerous, they can certainly be a nuisance and consume or soil food supplies.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Trilobites are the most well-known members of the Artiopoda. This extinct group of arthropods first evolved in the Early Cambrian 520 million years ago in what is now China. Most are not well known outside of fossil lagerstätten (sites of exceptional preservation) due to most of their bodies being composed of non-mineralised tissues. Trilobites, with their hard mineralised exoskeleton, are an exception to this and have the highest preservation potential within the group, allowing them to be preserved in many deposits. After enjoying success in the Cambrian, trilobite diversity went into sharp decline in the Middle Devonian due to the group being heavily impacted by several extinction events. Only one family, the Proetida, survived into the Permian. However, the group as a whole never recovered and died out 252 million years ago in the Permo-Triassic Extinction.

trait.name: Clumsy Glider
entries: While falling and not {@condition incapacitated|XPHB|Incapacitated}, Yi can glide (albeit not particularly well). While doing so it may move 5 ft. horizontally for every 5 ft. it descends. If it moves in this manner, Yi takes no damage from falling this turn.

action.name: Downturned Nip
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 2} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}1 ({@damage 1d2}) Piercing damage.
{@i "EE"} {@b (MANDARIN FOR WING)}

The coniferous canopy above us was alive with a cacophony of alert calls. These strange bat-like dinosaurs sailed clumsily between the branches, following our party and making sure everything in the forest knew we were there. Despite the frustration caused by their alert calls, they were nonetheless adorable travelling companions. When we settled for the rest for the night, I was able to hand feed three of them!
{@i Yi} is a small theropod dinosaur from the Jurassic (164-159 million years ago) of Hebei, China. It is unusual in several ways, not least because its forelimbs were modified into bat-like wings.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Yi} is a small dinosaur known from a single exceptionally well-preserved specimen. It weighed only about 13 oz. and stood about 1 ft. tall. Its skull was quite short and squat, with a downturned lower jaw towards the end. It only had teeth in the front of its jaw, which were long, straight, and forward pointing. Its arms were enormous for its size with a total span just shy of 2 ft. Its fingers were long with curved claws. It also had an unusual rod-like structure projecting backwards from its wrist, called a styliform element, which supported a membranous wing. This wing was functional but, due to the lack of strong chest muscles, it's unlikely {@i Yi} was a powerful flyer. Studies suggest it may have been a somewhat awkward glider that moved through the air with limited control, perhaps similar to {@i Microraptor} ({@b page 50 of DDDD}).

{@i Yi}'s diet has been subject to debate, due to its unusual skull and reduced number of teeth compared to most other small theropods. Studies into the structure of the skull, as well as possible stomach contents from related animals, suggests that it ate mostly plants and insects. {@i Yi} was discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation in the Hebei province in North China. The formation was laid down in a subtropical environment and, based on the large number and variety of terrestrial plants, was likely a forested area.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: The lifestyle of {@i Yi} and its relatives has been the subject to much research over the years. Evidence such as its hallux (first toe) being reversed which allowed the feet to grip or perch, the elongated fingers with claws, and the gliding membrane has led scientists to consider {@i Yi} to be an arboreal animal, climbing through the treetops and using its wings to glide from tree to tree. It may have done this in search of food or to escape predators. Unlike most modern arboreal birds, it would have relied on all four limbs to climb.

We suggest playing {@i Yi} as an agile (albeit slightly clumsy) animal, flitting between branches as it moves through the canopy. Individuals should make trilling calls to communicate throughout the forest and a party might expect to be greeted by the warning shrieks of {@i Yi} jumping between the treetops once they have been spotted. Like many arboreal animals, they should be willing to come down to the ground in search of food and may find themselves drawn to a campsite if there is the chance of an easy meal. This could be just the opening to try and tame this otherwise cautious animal.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Yi} is a member of the Scansoriopterygidae. This is a group of small theropod dinosaurs with some members showing adaptations for climbing or gliding. The group has an extremely restricted range, known only from the Middle-Late Jurassic Tiaojishan Formation of China. The reason for this very limited fossil record has been considered by several authors, with some hypothesising that they were outcompeted by more efficient dinosaurs. Their membranous wings were less efficient and harder to control than feathered wings, so animals like {@i Microraptor} and birds may have outcompeted {@i Yi} for food. The Scansoriopterygidae seem to have been an evolutionary lineage with limited success that couldn't compete with other airborne archosaurs.

monster.name: Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted

trait.name: Undead Swamp Titan
entries: Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted is not slowed by Difficult Terrain from a swampy or marshy environment. She cannot be knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone} or forcibly moved.

trait.name: Magical Legendary Resistance (3/Day)
entries: If Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted fails a saving throw, she can choose to succeed instead. However, if she does so, she expends one unspent spell slot of 2nd level or higher. If she has no spell slots available, then this ability fails.

spellcasting.name: Spellcasting
headerEntries: Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted is a 7th level spellcaster. Her spellcasting ability is Wisdom (spell save {@dc 18}, {@hit 10} to hit with spell attacks). She may cast the following spells:

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted chooses the Attack action, she may make two Crushing Undead Stomp attacks.

action.name: Crushing Undead Stomp
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 14} to hit, Reach 15 ft., one target. {@h}24 ({@damage 3d10 + 8}) Bludgeoning damage plus 13 ({@damage 2d12}) Necrotic damage.
A creature hit by this attack is affected by the "Haunted Hunter" curse.

action.name: Curse: Haunted Hunter
entries: The cursed creature is haunted by its aggressive actions against innocent animals. Whenever the cursed creature's spells or attacks cause damage to a creature with the Beast creature type that has no alignment (or is unaligned), the cursed creature takes {@dice 1d12} Psychic damage (no save allowed).
This curse is only removed when the cursed creature dies or if it is removed by a Wish spell.

reaction.name: Protect the Hunted
entries: When an allied creature within 100 ft. of Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted takes damage, Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted can use her Reaction to redirect that damage from the allied creature to herself (applying her own Resistances and Immunities instead of the allied creature's).

legendary.name: Rotten Tailswipe
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 14} to hit, Reach 15 ft., one target. {@h}19 ({@damage 2d10 + 8}) Bludgeoning damage plus 6 ({@damage 1d12}) Necrotic damage.
A creature hit by this attack is knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.

legendary.name: Magic Swell
entries: Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted uses the Magic action to cast a spell, following the normal restrictions for spellcasting and spell slot usage.

legendaryHeader: Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted can take 2 Legendary Actions, choosing from the options below. Only one legendary option can be used at a time and only at the end of another creature's turn. Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted regains spent Legendary Actions at the start of her turn.

entries: Chosen by Diana Lester

In rare cases, mundane animals can be magically augmented by external supernatural sources, typically demigods, magical objects, or primal forces of nature. This can have all manner of unusual effects, ranging from empowering their attacks with magical energies, to granting them supernatural defences, or even just destroying them altogether. Throughout our excursions, aside from the numerous monstrosities on Skull Island, we only encountered one other example of a creature modified in this way. An enormous undead Brachiosaurus that the locals referred to as "Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted". Apparently, this creature is some sort of guardian of nature, protecting the wilds from hunters and poachers.

We were advised long before entering the swamplands to ensure that we take ample rations with us so that we weren't forced to resort to hunting. After seeing Dreadfoot in the (rotting) flesh, I am very glad indeed that we heeded that warning.

entries.name: Origin
entries: Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted was a particularly large female {@i Brachiosaurus} in life. She inhabited the sparse forests and swamps of the Late Jurassic where she had a reputation for being a highly territorial animal. She would routinely see off predators and hunters stalking prey in an almost maternal fashion - using her colossal bulk to protect smaller animals. The archosaurian peoples of the region dubbed her "Dreadfoot", taken from her ability to inspire dread in trespassers with her stomping feet.

Eventually, a group of particularly cruel and greedy poachers banded together to attempt to rid the region of her. With a series of titanic snares made from thick marine rope, they set a lethal trap hidden within the murky waters of her swamp. In an act of pure brutality, they drew the beast out and into this trap by wounding smaller animals, causing their cries of pain to attract Dreadfoot. Snared by their cunning trap, she was left injured and died slowly as the swamp began to rot her body away. However, in their greed to rid the region of its protector, they birthed something far worse, for the deities of the swamp were watching with scornful eyes. Repulsed by the actions of these humanoids, several minor deities pooled their powers to grant Dreadfoot a new, much more resilient, body and allow her to enact vengeance on those who wronged both her and the innocent animals of the wilds.

Those poachers secured themselves just a single night of clear hunting before Dreadfoot descended upon their camp in the early hours of the morning. All but one was slain in a brutal display of strength, magic, and vengeance. That lone survivor stumbled back to civilization to tell their story and the tale of Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted quickly spread throughout the region.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted is a particularly aggressive animal, violently defending both herself and others in her care from potential threats. That said, humanoids who clearly demonstrate that they are not a danger to Dreadfoot or the animals that she watches over can pass through her territory without fear of attack. Unfortunately, most adventuring parties are highly threatening in appearance and their first encounter with Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted is usually a rather hostile one.

As an undead entity, Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted does not require food or rest. Consequently, unlike a living {@i Brachiosaurus}, she does not need to spend massive amounts of time feeding and digesting. This frees her up to spend her time patrolling the gloomy Late Jurassic swamplands, actively searching for threats to quell. Her constant presence renders these regions devoid of large settlements, which would face constant attack from her. Only small groups of druidic humanoids are able to persist in these areas for prolonged periods, as they are able to sustain themselves without garnering Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted's ire.

We recommend playing Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted as either a direct threat that continuously hunts down a player party that is moving through her territory, or as an NPC that must be appeased to allow players to pass. In either case, she is an extremely dangerous creature, and direct combat should be avoided where possible for all but the highest-level adventurers.

monster.name: Nessie, Spirit of the Loch

trait.name: Dynamic Counter Shading
entries: Nessie, Spirit of the Loch can change the hues of her skin to give her dynamic counter shading, making her particularly difficult to spot from above or below.
While in water, Nessie, Spirit of the Loch has Advantage on {@skill Stealth} checks.

trait.name: White Eyed-Lurker
entries: Nessie, Spirit of the Loch can breathe in both air and water and has Immunity to Cold and Thunder damage (included above).
Any attempt to record, illustrate, or otherwise recount Nessie, Spirit of the Loch results in a blurred image with two white piercing eyes.

trait.name: Vital Legendary Resistance (3/Day)
entries: If Nessie, Spirit of the Loch fails a saving throw, she can choose to succeed instead. However, if she uses this ability, she also loses 25 Hit Points.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Nessie, Spirit of the Loch chooses the Attack action, she may make one Nessie Maw attack and two Nessie Paddle attacks.

action.name: Nessie Maw
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 9} to hit, Reach 15 ft., one target. {@h}17 ({@damage 2d12 + 4}) Piercing damage plus 7 ({@damage 2d6}) Poison damage.
A Medium or smaller creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} (escape {@dc 17}). Nessie, Spirit of the Loch
cannot use her Nessie Maw attack against another target until this Grapple ends.

action.name: Nessie Paddle
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 9} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}15 ({@damage 2d10 + 4}) Bludgeoning damage plus 9 ({@damage 1d10 + 4}) Thunder damage.

action.name: Illusive Form
entries: Nessie, Spirit of the Loch can choose to appear as many different mundane objects or animals. As an Action, she may take on the appearance of a mundane Huge animal (such as a whale), group of animals (such as a school of fish or flock of waterbirds), driftwood, a capsized boat, or another mundane Huge object that might be in the loch.
This disguise can only be revealed by a {@dc 18} {@skill Perception} or {@skill Investigation} check when within 50 ft. of Nessie, Spirit of the Loch.

action.name: Seafoam
entries: As an Action, Nessie, Spirit of the Loch can summon thick sticky seafoam that fills a 30 ft. radius of water around her. Creatures within the seafoam have half-cover (+2 AC) and creatures other than Nessie, Spirit of the Loch have their swim speed reduced by 20 ft. (to a minimum of 0).

legendary.name: Thundering Screech
entries: Each other creature within 30 ft., of Nessie, Spirit of the Loch must make a {@dc 18} Constitution saving throw, taking {@dice 1d10} Psychic damage and {@dice 1d10} Thunder damage on a failed save, or half as much damage on a successful save.

legendary.name: Skulking Mystery
entries: Nessie, Spirit of the Loch Disengages and may swim up to 30 ft.

legendary.name: Lurch
entries: Nessie, Spirit of the Loch lunges up to 15 ft. (regardless of whether she is on land or water). If she moves in this way, she is not slowed by Difficult Terrain.

legendaryHeader: Nessie, Spirit of the Loch can take 2 Legendary Actions, choosing from the options below. Only one legendary option can be used at a time and only at the end of another creature's turn. Nessie, Spirit of the Loch regains spent Legendary Actions at the start of her turn.

entries: Chosen by CinDere FeLL

In addition to the prehistoric animals that we can observe in their own times, there are also many reports of ancient lineages that survived in isolated communities within secluded vales, remote islands, or hidden valleys. Most of these are mere legends or folklore, although some do seem to have more merit than others. The most prominent example of a creature like this is the legendary Nessie, otherwise known as the Loch Ness Monster.

Every country has its own legends of strange elusive creatures, commonly referred to as cryptids. These are animals (or monsters) whose existence is not accepted by professional scientists but are still studied by researchers called cryptozoologists who hope to prove that the organism is real. Many cryptids have become quite famous, with the likes of Bigfoot and the Chupacabra being household names. However, few have entered the public consciousness quite as much as Nessie, the Loch Ness Monster. Here we explain Nessie's history as well as our own fictional account of her behaviour.

entries.name: Celts, Catholics, and the Water Monsters of the British Isles
entries: Lake and river monsters were a common component of mythology for thousands of years on the British Isles. Celtic folklore is rich with them, with the most well-known of these being the Kelpie, the water horse that lures people into lakes to drown them. Aquatic reptiles inhabiting various waterways were also common, like Cata who lived in the Irish River Shannon, or the Oilliphéist, an ancient dragon-like creature. Later Catholic parables also include sea monsters, one example being the account of Saint Colomba driving a man-eating serpent out of the River Ness. Tempting though it may be to suggest that this story laid the groundwork for the legend of Nessie, it is probably wishful thinking and was simply one of many pieces of Celtic mythology integrated into Catholic lore. For the origins of Nessie, we must instead look at the 1930s, almost 1,500 years after these other legends.

entries.name: Origin of the Legend
entries: The Loch Ness monster, as it is described today, first hit headlines in 1933 when Aldie Mckay claimed to have seen a whale-like creature in the loch. However, it was the famous Spicer sighting that more prominently established the rumour of a lake monster. Mr and Mrs Spicer described seeing a strange animal with a thick body and long serpentine appendage lurching across a road near the Loch, carrying some poor animal it had killed back to its watery lair. A year later in 1934, a photograph emerged showing a mysterious plesiosaur-like creature swimming in Loch Ness. Nicknamed the Surgeon's Photo (after the supposed photographer, gynaecologist Robert Wilson), it shows the tall neck and small, pointed head of some unknown creature held high above the water's surface. This image was so striking that the legend of the Loch Ness monster was a near-overnight extravaganza and it was quickly given the feminine moniker "Nessie". Many concluded that she must be a plesiosaur "ghost lineage", a creature (or rather small population) that was thought to be extinct, but persists to the modern day despite a lack of recent fossils. Such ghost lineages are extremely rare indeed (with the coelacanth being the most famous real example), but not impossible.

entries.name: Media Darling
entries: In the 1930s and 40s, Loch Ness quickly became a tourist hotspot. People arrived from all over the world, hoping to get a glimpse of the elusive creature. In 1934, the first of many large-scale hunts for Nessie took place, with twenty men scouring the waters in the hopes of finding her. While they had no luck, the growing foot traffic around the loch resulted in many more supposed sightings. These ranged from glimpses of ripples, suggesting that something was moving just beneath the surface, to the gripping photos in 1972 supposedly showing plesiosaur-like flippers. Over the years, many more hunts were carried out, some of which were sponsored by major media outlets like the BBC and used advanced sonar technology to map as much of the loch as possible. The most recent of these occurred in 2023, celebrating 90 years since Aldie McKay's sighting.

entries.name: The Truth Behind Nessie
entries: While it would be nice to say that Nessie remains a mystery and images like the Surgeon's Photo are tantalising hints at a mysterious creature living in Loch Ness, time has not been kind to her legend. Many classic stories have been proven to be either cases of mistaken identity (confusing a mundane animal for the monster) or full-fledged hoaxes. Spicer's sighting is now thought to be a case of the couple coming across a herd of deer crossing the road in the dark and misinterpreting what they were seeing. The 1972 photos bear little resemblance to the paddles of plesiosaurs and were in fact taken from scans of the loch floor which were then embellished to look like flippers. Most damning of all was the confession in the early 90s that the Surgeon's Photo was a practical joke carried out by Christian Spurling, his family, and his friends. After his stepfather was mocked by his employer, the {@i Daily Mail}, Spurling's group modified a toy submarine to look like a creature, photographed it and then had an acquaintance, Dr. Robert Wilson, sell the photo to the paper as a practical joke, which triggered a media firestorm. Finally, a comprehensive scientific analysis of the loch itself in 2006 revealed that it couldn't consistently support a population of predatory plesiosaur-like animals, rendering the presence of animals like Nessie living within it impossible.

Today, Nessie is seen more as folklore than zoology in scientific circles, but we shouldn't underestimate the hold she has on the public. Every year, thousands travel to Loch Ness to try and find her and, even after the truth of the Surgeon's Photo was revealed, there are still many enthusiasts who dedicate their lives to finding Nessie, in the hope that there is still some mystery left in the world.

Most British palaeontologists have at some point in their lives had at least a passing fascination with the Loch Ness Monster, and so we are happy to honour her here with our own take on the potential behaviour of this illustrious cryptid.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Nessie, Spirit of the Loch is a bizarre plesiosaur that has adapted to life in the deep waters of Loch Ness, a gigantic lake almost 25 miles long that stretches through the Scottish highlands and is over 750 ft. deep. She lives concealed within the loch, using a variety of magical abilities to remain unseen. At least 25 ft. long, she spends much of her days at the lake bottom, sifting through the sediment in search of food. Her hide is counter shaded, with a pale belly and a pitch-black back. If seen from below with the sun behind her, Nessie's form is largely obscured as she flickers between beams of light. From above, she is almost invisible, with only her ghostly white eyes hinting at the presence of something moving within the water. On the rare occasion she surfaces during the day, if someone is close enough to spot her, Nessie will disguise herself as something more mundane. Many fishermen have seen a reptilian shape ahead of them seemingly become a piece of driftwood or an innocent-looking seal. At night, Nessie more routinely rises to the surface, using ancient magic to spread a rolling fog across the lake to better conceal herself. This cover boosts her confidence, making her much more aggressive. She scours the surface of the lake looking for fish, otters, and seals, although she will occasionally lurch onto land and attack deer or sheep that come too close to the water's edge. Although uncommon, Nessie may attack humanoids foolish enough to sail the lake (particularly at night). In most cases, the last thing those fools hear is wailing ghostly shrieks as Nessie attacks before she drags them to a watery grave.

entries: Binns, R. 1984. {@i The Loch Ness Mystery Solved}. New York, Prometheus Books, pp. 228.
Gould, R.T. 1934. {@i The Loch Ness Monster and Others}. London: Geoffrey Bles, pp. 228.
Naish, D. 2016. {@i Hunting monsters: Cryptozoology and the reality behind the myths}. London: Arcturus Publishing, pp. 240.

monster.name: Skeletal Tyrannosaurus

trait.name: Skeletal Form
entries: Skeletal Tyrannosaurus has Immunity to Necrotic and Poison damage, Immunity to the {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned} and Exhausted conditions, and Resistance to Piercing and Slashing damage (all included above).

trait.name: Museum Guardian
entries: Skeletal Tyrannosaurus may be the guardian of a museum, tomb, or other location. If so, then when Skeletal Tyrannosaurus is reduced to 0 Hit Points, rather than falling {@condition unconscious|XPHB|Unconscious} or dying it instead disassembles into a pile of bones and rolls away to a display stand or hidden chamber to recover. After 24 hours in this location, it revives back to full Hit Points.

trait.name: Sue's Charm
entries: Skeletal Tyrannosaurus has Expertise in Deception, Performance, and {@skill Persuasion} (included above), and has Advantage on Charisma saving throws.
Skeletal Tyrannosaurus can understand Common and Archosauric, but can't speak.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Skeletal Tyrannosaurus chooses the Attack action, it may make one Skeletal Bite attack and one Skeletal Tail attack.

action.name: Skeletal Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 11} to hit, Reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}33 ({@damage 4d12 + 7}) Piercing damage.

legendary.name: Rolling Bones
entries: The Skeletal Tyrannosaurus disassembles itself into a pile of bones, which can roll across the ground. It may move up to 50 ft. and then reassemble itself in an unoccupied space.

entries: Chosen by tyLer bonD
{@i "TIE-RAN-O-SORE-US"} {@b (TYRANT LIZARD KING)}

Museums are, by their very nature, places of history and legacy. Artefacts from across the world are gathered in one place to be viewed and admired. The risks involved in obtaining such relics are great. However, many neglect to take into account the risks of simply housing particularly unusual pieces, especially if they are cursed. Several institutions have filed reports of glowing specimens that may animate and attempt to break from their displays. Many museums now employ magical counter measures, but these may struggle to hold back the oldest or most powerful artefacts.

I have read of a particular case where the skeleton of a large Tyrannosaurus broke through the museum's defensive wards and stalked the halls, surrounded by an eerie glow. This was to the horror of an unfortunate nightwatchman who narrowly avoided (almost certain) death by dashing to the safety of an unlocked ticketing office. Who knows what carnage an unchecked undead Tyrannosaurus could have wrought while chasing prey around the museum. Thankfully, as morning broke, the skeleton appeared to return to its display without protest.

Such events may be the result of external undead forces possessing a fossil, an intrinsic trait of the fossil itself, or perhaps animating magic originating from another artefact within the museum. Regardless, I co-authored a publication shortly afterwards outlining suggested steps that museums can take to mitigate such events. Worryingly, I suspect that this is not the last time that we will hear of mishaps with this particular skeletal Tyrannosaurus.

entries.name: Description and Plot Ideas
entries: The Skeletal {@i Tyrannosaurus} is a {@i Tyrannosaurus rex} ({@b page 195 in DDDD, or page 372 in the 5.5e Monster Manual}) fossil that has been animated by powerful magic. It appears as a rusty brown intact {@i Tyrannosaurus} skeleton that is bathed in a hue of magical energies, with piercing glowing eyes. While sharing several fundamental features with a living {@i Tyrannosaurus rex}, the skeletal version has several augmentations that make it more dangerous, ranging from damage resistances to novel ways to fight in combat.

There are several ways that you can use the Skeletal {@i Tyrannosaurus} in your games. It can be used as an undead minion for a powerful necromancer, lich, or other magical enemy that your party is facing, with its unique abilities differentiating it from other undead minions and animated objects. Alternatively, it can be used as a supernatural guardian for a sacred place, perhaps an ancient temple of a lost civilisation or the entranceway to a primal grove filled with prehistoric creatures. However, our preferred use for the Skeletal {@i Tyrannosaurus} is as a "boss" creature for the "Nighttime at the Museum" plot hook ({@b page 28}), where it can be either a deadly recurring combat encounter in an enchanted museum, or an NPC that needs to be continuously appeased through unusual tasks.

entries.name: The Real Skeletal Tyrannosaurus
entries: Originally discovered in the late 1800s by Edward Cope, the first {@i Tyrannosaurus rex} skeleton to be publicly displayed was a specimen called AMNH 5027, which was found by renowned fossil collector Barnum Brown in 1908. This specimen was about 50% complete and included the first well-preserved skull. In preparation for its display in the American Museum of Natural History in New York, the team opted to combine specimen AMNH 5027 with other parts to create a complete composite, rather than displaying an incomplete skeleton. They used components taken from the original {@i Tyrannosaurus rex} holotype (the specimen used to describe the species), as well as casts from {@i Allosaurus} to fill in any missing pieces. This resulted in a rather famous error, where the display composite had three fingers instead of two.

The display was opened to the public in 1915 and was an overnight success. It became the quintessential example of {@i Tyrannosaurus rex} and, as time passed, new discoveries allowed the display to be updated, fixing anatomical errors and freeing the Holotype specimen to be stored at the Carnegie Museum in Pittsburgh. Specimen AMNH 5027 remains hugely influential and was even used as the basis for the logo of the New York Times best-selling novel {@i Jurassic Park} in the 1980s, immortalising it forever in the world of palaeo-media.

We strongly recommend visiting the American Museum of Natural History in New York, if you can (or any other museum with dinosaurs on display if you can't). There is no better way to experience the true majesty of animals like {@i Tyrannosaurus rex} than seeing their fossils in person. Books, films, and artwork do not adequately reflect the sheer size and power of these magnificent animals. It is not until you are standing next to the skeleton of a dinosaur that you can truly appreciate just how unique these animals were.

Chosen by Kevin LauCK
{@i "TEN-ON-TOH-SORE-US"} {@b (SINEW REPTILE)}

Great nesting herds of Tenontosaurus gather annually in open fern plains and sparse forests to reproduce. While magnificent to behold, these animals are fiercely territorial during nesting season and are best avoided. Unfortunately, this often results in a detour of several hours of walking, as the nest grounds can stretch for miles upon miles.

{@i Tenonotosaurus} is an iguanodontian ornithopod from the Early Cretaceous (115 million years ago) of North America. An earlier evolutionary branch of its relatives {@i Iguanodon} ({@b page 134 in DDDD}) and {@i Parasaurolophus} ({@b page 283}), it is famous for how often its remains are found alongside those of multiple individuals of the dromaeosaurid {@i Deinonychus}.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Tenontosaurus} was a medium-sized ornithopod, growing up to 23 ft. long and weighing about 1 tonne. It had a standard ornithopod body, with large hind legs and more lightly built forelimbs. Its tail was broad and long, making up nearly half the animal's total length. Its head was elongate and horse-like, tipped with a keratinous beak. This narrow beak, combined with its posture, suggests that {@i Tenontosaurus} was a browser that specialised in eating low growing ferns, cycads, and ginkgo trees. Based on research into the structure of its legs and wrists, {@i Tenontosaurus} is thought to have been able to rear up and walk on two legs (facultatively bipedal), although one study suggested that, based on its mass, it would have been preferentially quadrupedal. It is possible that younger animals were more prone to moving bipedally while the bigger adults spent most of their time on all fours.

{@i Tenontosaurus} has been found in several formations across the USA, such as the Cedar Mountain, Cloverly, and Antlers formations, some of which are extensive and span multiple states. These formations were deposited in environments rich in rivers and lakes that supported a wide diversity of overlapping dinosaur fauna, including multiple ornithopod species, late surviving brachiosaurid sauropods, small ceratopsians, nodosaurid ankylosaurs, and theropods like the small tyrannosauroid {@i Moros}, early therizinosaurs like {@i Falcarius}, the giant carcharodontosaurid {@i Acrocanthosaurus,} and the dromaeosaurid {@i Deinonychus}. The latter is especially noteworthy due to its frequent association with {@i Tenontosaurus} fossils (see below).

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: There is evidence that {@i Tenontosaurus} was gregarious for at least part of its life, as fossil deposits have been found containing the remains of multiple juveniles that died together. These may represent fully precocious (independent) infants that grouped together for protection until they were old enough to defend themselves, or maybe these juveniles were still cared for by their parents, whether as part of a herd or in a creche with a small number of guardian adults. {@i Tenontosaurus}' young would have taken several years to grow to maturity, as studies of bone histology (internal structure) show that they were slower to grow than their larger cousins and took more time to reach their adult size. Despite this, we know that they were capable of breeding before reaching physical maturity as remains have been found from animals estimated to be about 8 years old that were still growing but had medullary bone (bone used for forming eggshells).

We suggest playing {@i Tenontosaurus} as an animal that comes together annually at communal nesting sites where many females build their nests. They should be very territorial of the area surrounding their nests, threatening or attacking any animal that approaches too close. After the eggs hatch, the mothers should spend several weeks feeding their young but once they are large enough, many of the adults should abandon the nests. A few younger males and females should remain to act as guardians to the now largely independent offspring, but eventually they too should move on. Once on their own, the youngsters should divide into multiple small herds and may stay together for years before eventually joining larger herds or striking out independently. If attacked by a predator, {@i Tenontosaurus} should either flee or use its powerful tail as a weapon, striking with enough force to knock a humanoid-sized creature flying. The greatest danger, however, may not be the animal itself, but rather the predators that accompany it. Many {@i Tenontosaurus} herds are followed by predatory mobs of {@i Deinonychus} waiting for an opportunity to strike and are not particularly picky about whetting their appetite on any unsuspecting passing prey first.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Tenontosaurus} was an early branching iguanodontian, currently found within the Rhabdodontomorpha. The exact content of this group is currently in flux as it was originally thought to include animals from America, Europe, and Australia, but recently some of the Australian species have been moved to a separate clade. Most rhabdodontomorphs were small-to-medium sized, with {@i Tenontosaurus} being one of the largest members. While {@i Tenontosaurus} itself appears to have died out approximately 108 million years ago, the rhabdodontomorphs survived right up to the end Cretaceous extinction.

entries.name: Pack Hunting Raptors
entries: One of the most famous concepts in palaeontology is that of the pack-hunting dromaeosaur. While popularised through {@i Jurassic Park}, the original hypothesis came from studies of the remains of {@i Tenontosaurus}, which were frequently found in association with multiple individuals of {@i Deinonychus}. Analyses of tooth marks strongly suggests that {@i Deinonychus} not only hunted {@i Tenontosaurus}, but that it was amongst their preferred prey. {@i Deinonychus} weighed approximately 200 lb. and was dwarfed by even a sub-adult {@i Tenontosaurus,} so these {@i Deinonychus} likely had to work together if they were to bring this large prey down.

However, this presumption was challenged in the 2000s by a study that looked at the taphonomy of {@i Deinonychus} bones and gregarious behaviour in modern archosaurs like raptorial birds and crocodiles. They argued that the {@i Deinonychus} remains showed strong evidence of both in-fighting and cannibalism, which is evidence against organised pack hunting. They also noted that modern archosaurs and lizards do not show co-operative hunting and instead gather at kill sites simply to take advantage of an abundant food source, frequently fighting and may cannibalise younger animals, which aligns with many of the cannibalised {@i Deinonychus} remains being sub-adults.

Later research challenged this position too, highlighting that social predators can also be highly aggressive and cannibalistic at kill sites. Others noted that crocodiles, while not strictly pack hunters, frequently live in large groups and have been seen co-operatively hunting. While tightknit wolf-like predators working in-sync to bring down a {@i Tenontosaurus} may be more fantasy than fact, perhaps {@i Deinonychus} was socially complex enough to work together when needed as long as the reward provided a banquet for all.

{@i "TROW-OH-DON"} {@b (WOUNDING TOOTH)}

Night watches in the Cretaceous are often eerie affairs. None so much so, however, as a night where a flock of Troodon take interest in the campsite. These nocturnal animals will sit motionless in the undergrowth, watching with shimmering, forward-facing eyes that reflect firelight and moonlight alike. While not particularly bothersome when faced alone, they usually move in flocks of 6 to 10 animals, making them bolder and much more formidable - particularly so when most of the party are still asleep.

{@i Troodon} is a troodontid theropod from the Late Cretaceous (77 million years ago) of North America, whose taxonomic validity has been debated repeatedly. As of 2026, the most recent study argues that newly described material from Montana should be the new neotype (new name holder), along with material currently assigned to {@i Stenonychosaurus}. As this is the most recent publication, we follow its recommendations and use {@i Stenonychosaurus} as our reference for {@i Troodon} biology and ecology.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Troodon} was a small theropod, growing to about 8 ft. long and weighing 60 to 80 lb. While similar in size to dromaeosaurs like {@i Deinonychus} (and also having a retractable sickle-shaped claw on each foot), it was a more lightly built animal. Its legs were longer and thinner, its torso more gracile, it had smaller hands, and it had a shorter tail. {@i Troodon}'s skull was thin and pointed, with very large and slightly forward-facing eyes. This not only gave it good binocular vision, but may have allowed it to see more clearly at night. {@i Troodon} may have been an omnivore that fed on a fairly large amount of plant matter, based on its prominent teeth serrations and stress-resistant jaw tips.

Material that has been assigned to either {@i Troodon} or {@i Stenonychosaurus} has been found in several exceptionally well-known fossil locations in the USA, such as the Judith River Formation in Montana and the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, Canada. These were deposited in forested floodplains positioned not too far from the coast of an inland sea. They are extremely fossil rich locales that have produced a wide variety of dinosaur taxa, including ceratopsians (the most common), ankylosaurs, and ornithopods, as well as multiple theropod lineages like ornithomimids, oviraptorsaurs, maniraptorans, and several tyrannosaurs. Freshwater plesiosaurs and azhdarchid pterosaurs are also present in much smaller numbers, alongside various non-dinosaurian reptiles. Of relevance for {@i Troodon}, the Dinosaur Park Formation contains several lineages of mammals which likely made up a significant proportion of their diet.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Several nests containing more than 20 eggs have been attributed to a troodontid. While this is impressive, recent research suggests that female {@i Troodon} were only capable of laying 4 to 6 eggs at a time. As such, the nests are thought to be communal, with several females using a single nest like rheas or ostriches, and {@i Troodon} may have lived in sizable flocks or gathered seasonally to lay. It also has interesting implications for their parenting behaviour, as communal nests are usually overseen by a dominant male and female who share the brooding and parenting duties for all the eggs and chicks. It is possible that {@i Troodon} behaved similarly and may have had quite complicated social behaviour.

We suggest playing {@i Troodon} as a curious animal, prone to investigating anything new that appears in its environment. They should frequently be found foraging for fruit or chasing down small mammals, pinning them with their sickle claws before swallowing them whole. They should also be common scavengers, picking at carcasses until chased off by a larger carnivore. {@i Troodon} nests and young should be fiercely guarded by the dominant male and female, who may lead a flock of other adults and semi-adults. {@i Troodon} should be curious of humanoids, but keep their distance unless defending a nest.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Troodon} is a member of the Troodontidae, a large group of small theropods best known for their distinctive serrated teeth. The oldest confidently identified troodontid first appeared in the Late Jurassic (156 to 146 million years ago) in North America, but the majority are known from Cretaceous formations. They were a reasonably successful group, found across much of North America, Europe, and China. They were also able to successfully migrate into more extreme climates, as several large troodontid fossils have been found in the polar Prince Creek Formation. While {@i Troodon} itself is not known past 76 million years ago, the troodontids would remain part of the dinosaurian fauna of the Northern Hemisphere up until the end Cretaceous extinction.

entries.name: Identity Crisis
entries: The first {@i Troodon} fossil was found in Montana in 1855, a single tooth with large distinctive serrations. This isolated tooth was named {@i Troodon} and became its holotype (name-bearer). This may not seem like best practice to us today, as no other characteristics of the animal can be used in its description, but this was not uncommon in the early days of palaeontology. Later 1930s expeditions found skeletons with identical teeth in Alberta, Canada, which were named {@i Stenonychosaurus.} By the 1950s, many other Troodontid genera had been described, but these were synonymised together as {@i Troodon} in the 1980s. However, in the 1990s, it was argued that the lack of characteristics in {@i Troodon}'s original description should render it taxonomically invalid as a {@i nomen dubium} (dubious name), with {@i Stenonychosaurus} being the valid name. This was supported by more in-depth research published in 2011. However, a 2025 study argued that {@i Troodon} and {@i Stenonychosaurus} were synonymous with {@i Troodon} bearing seniority. They suggested that material from the Two Medicine Formation be designated as the {@i Troodon} neotype (a new specimen to be the representative of the species). At the time of writing, those authors are preparing a submission to the ICZN ({@b page 10}) to request the erection of the neotype, but this may be rejected or another team may publish a counter argument in the future. All of this highlights that palaeontology is a dynamic science, with new studies constantly challenging older consensus.

entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 2} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}14 ({@damage 4d6}) Piercing damage.
This attack may only be used against a creature of Medium size or smaller that is lying {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.
The DM may decide that hitting with this attack instantly kills a non-player character creature.

trait.name: True Dire Wolf
entries: Aenocyon has advantage on Wisdom (Perception) checks that rely on hearing or smell.
It also has advantage on attack rolls against a creature if at least one of its allies is within 5 ft. of that creature and that ally isn't incapacitated.

trait.name: Long-limbed
entries: When Aenocyon takes the Dash action, double its speed as normal, and it may then move an additional 10 ft. this turn.

trait.name: Megafaunal Tundra Hunter
entries: Aenocyon has Resistance to Cold damage (included above).
Whenever Aenocyon deals damage to a creature larger than itself, it deals an additional {@dice 1d6} Piercing damage to that creature.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, you do not need to change Aenocyon's CR.

trait.name: Origin Of The Curse
entries: If a humanoid is hit by Aenocyon's Bite, Grip, Rip attack, they must succeed on a {@dc 12} Constitution saving throw or be cursed with werewolf lycanthropy.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Aenocyon chooses the Attack action, it may make two Bite, Grip, Rip attacks.

action.name: Bite, Grip, Rip
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}6 ({@damage 1d6 + 3}) Piercing damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 11} Strength saving throw or have its speed reduced by 10 ft. for the next 1 minute. This effect can stack to reduce a creature's speed to 0.
{@i "A-NO-SIGH-ON"} {@b (TERRIBLE WOLF)}

The La Brea nights are breath-taking. When the skies are clear and lit by a full moon, the scenery really is beautiful. Normally, a wolf howl in the distance in such a setting would be calming natural background noise. However, here such a sound carries a deadly warning. For the wolves of La Brea are enormous and no less savvy than regular wolves. When the wolf cries here, you make ready for combat!

{@i Aenocyon} is a large canine from the Americas that first appeared in the Late Pleistocene (125,000 years ago). Although commonly known as dire wolves, these large carnivorans are thought to be the last members of an extinct canine lineage that did not survive into the modern day.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: While {@i Aenocyon} was similar to the modern wolf in many ways, it had several key differences. It was on average larger than most living wolves, weighing between 130-150 lb., with some individuals reaching 200 lb. or more. Adults were usually between 3-4 ft. tall and about 6 ft. long. {@i Aenocyon} was more robust than wolves, with a bigger skull and more powerful jaws. The strong jaw combined with large teeth gave it a powerful bite, comparable to, or possibly exceeding, that of hyenas although with much of the power towards the front of the jaw rather than the middle. This means they may not have been as good at cracking bones as hyenas, but would have been able to bite and hold onto larger prey with more force than other canines. Like many dogs, {@i Aenocyon} was a cursorial (running) predator, capable of moving at speed for long periods of time. This would have allowed them to hunt prey over great distances, killing through exhaustion as much as through inflicted injury.

{@i Aenocyon} is the most common predator found within the La Brea tar pits. Studies into the radioactive isotope composition of their bones suggest they were generalist rather than specialist hunters, feeding on a variety of prey such as bison, horses, camels, pigs, and even mammoths ({@b page 98}). The same studies suggest that {@i Aenocyon} was in direct competition for food with several other predators found in the tar pits, like {@i Smilodon} ({@b page 105}), although whether this competition was widespread or exaggerated by the unique conditions of the tar pits is up for interpretation.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: The large number of {@i Aenocyon} fossils found in La Brea has led many to believe that these animals were highly social. Studies into their morphology and sexual dimorphism suggest that {@i Aenocyon} was similar enough to modern wolves that they likely lived together in at least temporarily monogamous pairs with several years' worth of offspring. Like wolves, older siblings may have acted as babysitters for this year's puppies and also worked alongside their parents to bring down prey. During a chase, they may have taken a relay approach, taking turns to harass an animal until it was too tired to defend itself from an attack.

We suggest playing {@i Aenocyon} similarly to wolves. They should be intelligent, effective hunters that invest a lot of time into their families, often seen playing or sleeping together. Any other large predator should be seen as a possible threat or competitor and may be mobbed if it gets too close. Humanoids should fall into this category, and they should not normally be seen as prey unless there is little else to predate upon. In fact, the natural curiosity of {@i Aenocyon} makes it more easily tamed than most animals. A party may find a curious youngster visiting their camp at night, following the smell of food who, with care and patience, can become a loyal companion.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Aenocyon} first appeared in the fossil record approximately 125,000 years ago in North America. Originally classed as a member of the genus {@i Canis}, it has recently been identified as the last known member of a separate family of canines that first appeared in the Americas almost 6 million years ago. {@i Aenocyon} was a highly successful predator, found across both North and South America, with some evidence they may have migrated to Eurasia, although these fossils are in need of reassessment since the reclassification. As with many La Brea animals, {@i Aenocyon} went extinct approximately 10,000 years ago. This was likely caused by a combination of climate change and a loss of the larger prey that they preferred to hunt, although human activity may also have played a part.

trait.name: Tremortalk
entries: Mammuthus can communicate with any other Mammuthus within 6 miles of itself via a low bass rumble through the ground. To all other creatures (excluding those with a tremor sense, who can hear it up to 6 miles away and recognise it as a form of communication (but can only understand if they can speak with Beasts)), this communication is only audible up to 100 ft. and simply sounds like a monotone rumble.

trait.name: Columnar Limbs
entries: Mammuthus has Advantage on any check to avoid being knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Mammuthus' CR to 7 and increase its XP to 2900 accordingly.

trait.name: An Elephant Never Forgets
entries: Mammuthus can accurately recall anything it has seen or heard throughout its lifetime. If it hears a language for more than an hour, it can understand that language from then onwards, but cannot speak it.

trait.name: Smarty-Pants
entries: Mammuthus has Proficiency with any object or weapon that it is wielding.

action.name: Trumpet
entries: Mammuthus lets out an extremely loud trumpeting sound through its trunk. Each other non-Probosidean creature within 20 ft. of Mammuthus must succeed a {@dc 14} Constitution saving throw or take {@dice 1d6} Psychic and {@dice 1d6} Thunder damage, as well as drop an object they are wielding (as they clutch their ears in pain).

action.name: Mammoth Gore
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 10} to hit, Reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}16 ({@damage 2d8 + 7}) Bludgeoning damage plus 13 ({@damage 2d12}) Piercing damage.
A creature hit by this attack is either knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone} or pushed back 10 ft. in a direction of the Mammuthus' choosing (DM's choice).

bonus.name: Trunk Wield
entries: Mammuthus can wield most one-handed items with its trunk (DM's discretion) and can use them, although does not have Proficiency with them.
As a Bonus Action, the Mammuthus can pick up, use, or attack with a weapon or object, so long as that weapon does not require ammunition.
{@i "MAH-MUT-US KOH-LUM-BEE"} {@b (COLUMBIAN MAMMOTH)}

Columbian mammoths are a common sight along the rolling plains and harsh barrens of this continent. While woolly mammoths are well-known to inhabit frigid tundras, these bare skinned cousins are better adapted to harsher dry conditions, much like their other elephant relatives, but also seem to enjoy sparse forests. Be wary of them in regions inhabited by humanoids, as they quickly learn how dangerous we can be.

{@i Mammuthus columbi}, more commonly known as the Columbian mammoth, is a Pleistocene era (1.5 million to 13,000 years ago) elephant from North and Central America. One of the largest elephants in the fossil record, it was the closest known relative of the woolly mammoth, and the two species are thought to have hybridised frequently where their ranges overlapped.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: The Columbian mammoth was an extremely large animal with males reaching 14 ft. tall at the shoulder, 13 ft. long, and weighing between 10 and 12 tonnes. Its vertebrae had tall spines at the shoulders, giving it a sloping back, and its skull was tall with a domed appearance. The Columbian mammoth's tusks grew to exceptional lengths, reaching 13 ft. in some males and weighing as much as 500 lb. They were usually slightly asymmetrical with one tusk overlapping the other as the tips curved inwards towards the skull. While females also had large tusks, they were smaller and lighter than the males. Unlike the woolly mammoth, very little is known of the Columbian's soft tissue, although one currently undescribed sample of potential mammoth hair suggests that their sparser hair might have been lightly coloured. Studies into the wear on their teeth, as well as isotopic analyses of their bones, suggests that they were generalist herbivores, not specialising on any one plant type.

Despite its name, the Columbian mammoth was a very widespread animal with fossils recovered from multiple sites throughout America, ranging from Canada to Costa Rica. They inhabited a variety of environments including temperate grasslands, prairies, savannas, and forests. This wide range of habitats meant that Columbian mammoths lived alongside a very wide variety of animals, including deer, bison, antelope, horses, ground sloths, camels, dire wolves, sabre-toothed cats, and humans. It also cohabited with several other proboscideans such as woolly mammoths, mastodons, and gomphotheres. Most of the carnivores present would not have been a threat to adult mammoths, although evidence suggests they gathered at natural traps like the La Brea Tar Pits to feed on the carcasses of trapped mammoths. However, the Columbian mammoth also co-evolved alongside humans, with multiple sites showing evidence of active hunting with large animal traps or harvested mammoth corpses.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Fossil associations of multiple individuals indicate that Columbian mammoths were a social species, with specimens recovered from the Waco Mammoth National Monument in Texas suggesting that they lived in matriarchal herds like modern elephants. Mammoths were migratory animals that travelled hundreds of kilometres every year. Like woolly mammoths, their tusks may have been useful in clearing ground coverage to expose edible plants, however there is strong evidence they were also used in combat between individuals. A pair of adult males were found with their tusks locked together. Such an occurrence is also seen in other animals with asymmetrical ornamentation, like deer. This shows that mammoths sometimes got their tusks trapped together when fighting, which led to the animals either dying together through injuries inflicted on each other or by dehydration/starvation.

We suggest playing the Columbian mammoth as an adaptable and curious creature. In regions where humanoids are rare, healthy adults should show little fear of them and may approach a party as a novel interest in their environment. In areas where humanoids are more common, and the mammoth is more likely to have been hunted by them, they should be highly aggressive. These individuals may attempt to scare players off with mock charges or launch full on attacks if they feel threatened. The most dangerous individuals should be males in musth (a state of heightened aggression during mating seasons) who are exceptionally temperamental and unpredictable.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Both the Columbian and woolly mammoths are believed to have evolved from the Steppe mammoth. This large mammoth first arose approximately 1.8 million years ago in Eurasia before migrating to North America 300 thousand years later and giving rise to the Columbian mammoth there. On the mainland, this species maintained its large ancestral size, however populations on the Channel Islands near California underwent insular dwarfism, giving rise to the Pygmy mammoth. Columbian mammoths had a large amount of variation within their populations, which was likely a result of hybridisation with woolly mammoths.

The Columbian mammoth went extinct approximately 13,000 years ago and debate continues over the exact cause. Climate change leading to deglaciation at the end of the ice age resulted in less favourable conditions for large mammals, however it has also been suggested that overkilling from human hunters may be the main factor in their extinction. Nevertheless, there remains a lack of consensus on whether the evidence of human interaction is from hunting or scavenging. It is also very possible that mammoths died out due to a variety of factors, with both climatic change and human activity contributing to their eventual downfall.

trait.name: Slow Metabolism
entries: Paramylodon has Advantage on saving throws to prevent the {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned} condition. However, if it does become {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned}, the duration of that condition is doubled.

trait.name: Robust Build
entries: Paramylodon has Resistance to Bludgeoning damage (included above).

trait.name: Possible Sexual Dimorphism
entries: Select one of the options below, this Paramylodon gains the associated effect:
Gracile: Increase Paramylodon's speed by 10 ft.
Stocky: At the start of combat Paramylodon gains 6 Temporary Hit Points.

entries: Paramylodon gains a Climb speed of 20 ft.
Additionally, if Hidden in a high location (typically a tree) as an Action, Paramylodon can launch a jumping attack on a creature within 40 ft. below it.

That creature must make a {@dc 13} Dexterity saving throw, taking {@dice 2d8} Bludgeoning damage on a failed save and half as much on a successful one. Paramylodon then takes {@dice 2d8} Bludgeoning damage itself and may then use its Bonus Action to make a Bear-like Maul attack this turn.

A creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} (escape {@dc 13}).
{@i "PAR-AH-MI-LOH-DON"} {@b (BESIDE NEAR TOOTH)}

The sight of a large herbivore lumbering out of a nearby bush is often met with fear and panic. While not quite as frightening as a large carnivore doing so, most big herbivores can be quite aggressive and so attack may be imminent. This fear is not so prevalent for the slow-moving giant ground sloths, which are relatively easily escaped from. However, should one find oneself in its grasp, the fear returns posthaste.

{@i Paramylodon} is a ground sloth that first appeared in the Pliocene (4.9 million years ago) of North America. Sometimes known as Harlan's ground sloth, this large herbivore was descended from ground sloths that migrated from South America during the Great Faunal Interchange (when animals from North America migrated South and vice versa after the two continents connected).

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Paramylodon} was a large animal, although not exceptionally big for a ground sloth. It was up to 10 ft. tall and weighed between 1-1.5 tonnes once fully grown. Like other ground sloths, it was a powerfully built animal with a squat body, long muscular forelimbs tipped with curving claws, stocky hind legs, and a short neck topped by a boxy skull. Within its skin, {@i Paramylodon} had a layer of osteoderms that formed a scattered disconnected armour. {@i Paramylodon} was quadrupedal and had a rather unusual posture. Its fingers were reinforced along the knuckles, allowing it to use them to support its weight with the claws facing inwards and held above the ground. Its hind feet were also turned so that the sole of the foot faced inwards, so it supported its weight primarily on the outer edge of its foot, giving it a strange walking style.

Specimens from the La Brea Tar Pits seem to occur in two different morphotypes, broadly described as a robust type and a gracile type. The robust type is larger with thicker bones, a tall sagittal crest running down the midline of their skull and pointed canine teeth. The more gracile form is smaller, lacks the crest, and has blunted canines. While these features have been hypothesised to be due to individual or species variation, it is considered much more likely that these differences are a result of sexual dimorphism (physical differences between males and females of the same species). Sexual dimorphism can be difficult to determine with confidence in the fossil record. In the case of {@i Paramylodon}, we can say that, based on examples of their living relatives like sloths and anteaters where males are bigger than females, it is likely that the larger crested {@i Paramylodon} are probably the males.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: As with all ground sloths, {@i Paramylodon} was a herbivore. It had a broad snout which suggests it was primarily a grazer. Based on the structure and position of the hyoid bone (the bone that connects to the tongue and helps it move) we can say {@i Paramylodon} had a very mobile tongue that it probably used to pull up grass. Recent studies into its dental wear also suggest it may have supplemented its diet with edible roots and tubers.

We suggest playing {@i Paramylodon} as a solitary animal, spending most of its life grazing in grasslands or open woods. It should be a ponderous animal, moving slowly from place to place and rarely leaving its home territory. During the breeding season, males should compete over females by displaying using their canines or entering shoving matches. If it feels threatened a {@i Paramylodon} should rear up to its full height and spread its arms wide in a threat display. If attacked, it will not chase its aggressor. Rather it should hold its ground and wait for them to get close enough to be crushed by its bulk or snatched by its claws.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Paramylodon} is a member of the Mylodontidae, a group of ground sloths distantly related to the modern two-toed sloths. It has been hypothesised to be descended from a South American taxon named {@i Glossotherium}, which may have migrated into North America during the Great Faunal Interchange. While many South American species seem to have struggled to establish a foothold in North America beyond the southern parts of the continent, {@i Paramylodon} proved to be very successful, with populations established across the continent from Mexico to Canada. Along with the majority of ground sloths, {@i Paramylodon} went extinct during the Late Pleistocene approximately 14,000 years ago. As with many of La Brea's mammals, there is some debate over whether the primary driver of their extinction was environmental change or human activity. Ground sloths were known to be eaten by humans, but that may have been just one of several factors that drove the group to extinction. A small handful of ground sloths living on islands in the Caribbean outlived their continental relatives, with the last species dying in Cuba only 5000 years ago.

When Smilodon is reduced to 0 Hit Points, roll a {@dice d20}. On the roll of a 1-9, nothing happens. On the roll of a 10-20, it splits into two Small-sized juvenile Smilodon that have 29 Hit Points each, lose this ability, and lose their Killing Bite attack.

A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 14} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone} and have its speed reduced to 0 until the start of Smilodon's next turn.

{@i "S-MY-LOW-DON"} {@b (SCALPEL TOOTH)}

Saber-toothed cats are fearsome predators. These large felids display all of the hunting prowess of other big cats but are armed with far more dangerous weapons. Those elongate teeth are utterly lethal. Should one find oneself prone and open to attack, a swift death is almost guaranteed.

{@i Smilodon,} commonly known as the saber-toothed cat, from the Pleistocene to Holocene eras (2.5 million years ago to 10,000 years ago) of North and South America is one of the most iconic extinct mammals.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: Fossil remains of {@i Smilodon} have been divided into 3 species: {@i Smilodon gracilis} from North America, {@i Smilodon populator} from South America and {@i Smilodon fatalis} which has been found in both continents. While {@i S}. {@i populator} was by far the largest species, {@i S}. {@i fatalis} was the species found in the La Brea Tar Pits and therefore will be the main one we discuss here. It was a robust cat about the same size as a large African Lion, with its body reaching 6 ft. long and a weight of 400-600 lb. {@i Smilodon} was a powerfully built animal, with tall shoulders, strong forelimbs and a heavily muscled neck. Its tail was very short, much like a modern lynx. Its head was boxy with a short muzzle and widely positioned eyes, reducing its depth perception but giving it a very broad field of vision. {@i Smilodon}'s most distinctive feature is its long, sword-like fangs. These were elongated (7 in. or more) teeth with a blade-like appearance, hence the name "saber-toothed". While strong (see below), these teeth would have been delicate as they developed, and {@i Smilodon}'s milk canines (baby teeth) remained in the jaw until the new sabres were at least 50% erupted. This resulted in young {@i Smilodon} having four fangs in their upper jaw during their adolescence.

{@i S}. {@i fatalis} is a common carnivore in the North American fossil record, with a recent specimen showing that it successfully migrated as far south as Uruguay. Thousands of fossils of {@i S. fatalis} have been collected from the La Brea Tar Pits. While it is found in several environments (particularly grasslands) and was a diverse predator, analyses of its preferred prey suggest that it was biased towards larger prey that are associated with tree cover. This means that it was more likely to be found in woods or forests.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Smilodon's} preference for forest dwelling prey, combined with its stocky build and reduced binocular vision, strongly suggest it was not built for prolonged or explosive chases, relying instead on ambush tactics. Being unsuitable for pursuits, it likely would have given up on a hunt if the initial charge failed. Whether they hunted alone or in groups is a topic of some debate. While thousands of fossils have been found in association in La Brea, these may have been coincidental associations rather than natural groups. However, there is some evidence of social behaviour, namely pathological evidence (records of trauma or disease preserved on the bone) such as saber-tooth bite wounds or evidence of animals living through otherwise debilitating chronic conditions, with the strongest evidence being three individuals in association with each other, an adult and two juvenile siblings who were at least two years old. This association has been interpreted as a mother and her two older, but not yet independent, offspring.

We suggest playing {@i Smilodon} as a patient ambush predator. Like all modern cats, it should spend most of its day resting, becoming more active in the early morning and late afternoon. It should not charge until prey is very close and, unless starving, will not give chase if the initial attack fails. Females can be found with several mixed age cubs from different litters and occasionally from their wider family. Males are more likely to be solitary but might still be found living in small groups of brothers well into old age. While {@i Smilodon} prefers large prey, a hungry animal will not turn its nose up at a humanoid who wanders too close. If a party has any large animals with them, this will likely result in them being stalked and attacked.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Smilodon} is the most well-known member of the Machairodontinae, a group of extinct felines from a separate lineage to modern cats that first evolved in Europe approximately 15 million years ago, before spreading across much of the northern hemisphere. During this time, {@i Smilodon} arose in North America, then spread to South America 2.5 million years later during the North and South America Great Faunal Interchange. The last {@i Smilodon} went extinct at the end of the last Ice Age approximately 10,000 years ago. The cause of their extinction is the subject of debate, with disagreement over whether it was caused by climate change, reduction in the numbers of larger prey, pressure from increasing human populations, or some combination of these factors.

entries.name: Wielding a Weapon
entries: The fossil record is full of examples of biological structures that seem odd to us today and become the focus of much scientific study. {@i Smilodon}'s saber-teeth are one such example and their durability has been a key topic of discussion. Previously, it was argued that the teeth would have been very resistant to downwards (vertical) force, but much weaker to sideways (lateral) stress. This means they would have been very good at shearing through flesh but could easily break if bent from the side. Their enormous size also led authors to suggest that they may have obstructed feeding, causing {@i Smilodon} to avoid eating flesh close to bone, resulting in inefficient feeding and lots of wasted food. More recent research has examined the teeth in more detail and found that the teeth were much stronger than previously predicted and may be more robust than the conical canines seen in most cats. Furthermore, the jaws themselves were surprisingly weak with the association being the longer the canines, the weaker the bite. {@i Smilodon} did not have the bite strength to sever spinal cords or crush windpipes, like modern cats. Instead, they likely used what is known as the "canine shear bite" where {@i Smilodon} would pull its prey to the ground and pin them with its powerful forelimbs before delivering a single massive killing bite. Possessing a gape twice as big as that of a lion, it would open its jaws wide and use the muscles in the neck and shoulder to power the canines through the neck. This would sever major arteries and the windpipe, quickly leading to the prey dying of trauma or shock. Based on bite marks on bone, {@i Smilodon} would be much more efficient at defleshing carcasses than previously thought too, meaning the canines didn't hinder feeding. Interestingly, this type of tooth adaptation is also seen in multiple unrelated groups of carnivores, such as gorgonopsids and the metatherian saber-tooth {@i Thylacosmilus}.

trait.name: Potential Carrion Feeder
entries: Teratornis has Resistance to Necrotic damage and Immunity to the {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned} condition. It can eat spoiled meat without issue.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules

trait.name: Thunderbird
entries: As an Action, Teratornis can use ambient heat from savannah to summon a powerful storm. For the next 1 hour, heavy cloud cover and rolling thunder engulfs a 1-mile radius from Teratornis' location. While the storm is present, Teratornis is immune to Thunder and Lightning damage.

trait.name: Storm Herald (3/Day)
entries: As an Action, Teratornis can cast the spell Call Lightning (at 3rd level). When it does so, it does not require components and its spellcasting ability score is Wisdom (spell save {@dc 12}, +4 to hit with spell attacks).

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Teratornis chooses the Attack action, it may make one Huge Beak attack and one Huge Snatching Talons attack.

action.name: Huge Beak
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}8 ({@damage 1d10 + 3}) Piercing damage.

action.name: Huge Snatching Talons
