A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 13} Strength saving throw or drop an item it is wielding.
"TER-AH-TORN-IS"
{@b (WONDER BIRD)}

Just like modern vultures circling a weak animal, awaiting its death, Teratornis is an unwelcome sight above an adventuring party. A bad omen, if you will. The difference here, however, is that Teratornis is enormous and would be a formidable foe if it decided to attack. Thankfully, it seems to prefer to wait - a preferential choice, despite the omen.
{@i Teratornis} is a large bird from the Late Pleistocene (40,000 years ago) of North America. A distant relative of vultures and hawks, it was one of the heaviest flying birds in the fossil record.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Teratornis} was exceptionally large for a fully flighted bird. Its wingspan is estimated to have been up to 14 ft. in length and it may have weighed over 30 lb. This makes it bigger than the Andean condor, the heaviest flying bird alive today, which has a maximum weight of around 28 lbs. Like modern vultures, its wings would have been very broad and were adapted for long soaring flight on air currents. Its overall appearance would have been similar to a large vulture, with a heavyset torso, a long thin neck, and an elongated beak, although it had longer and stronger legs. In fact, some studies suggest it was an adept walker, with abilities comparable to ground living birds like turkeys. Like vultures, its eyes were placed on the sides of its head, giving it a very wide field of vision at the cost of poor depth perception.

While fossils of {@i Teratornis} are known from several Pleistocene formations in North America, the vast majority were discovered in the La Brea Tar Pits. Like many other predators in this assemblage, {@i Teratornis} is thought to have been drawn there by the large number of animals that died in the traps. As it could fly, it could more safely penetrate the pits than other carnivores, allowing it to feed on carcasses that mammalian predators may struggle to reach.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Teratornis} has several features in common with modern vultures and this has led many to argue that it was, like them, a specialist scavenger that soared over grasslands looking for carcasses.

However, it may also have caught small prey like lizards or even fish to supplement its diet. When scavenging a carcass, it likely used its large size to drive smaller competitor animals away. Given its remains are found in large numbers in La Brea, it may have been a gregarious animal that descended on corpses in mobs working together to strip away digestible meat and bones quickly. Like vultures, it likely had very strong stomach acids to help break down rotten food and bone without risk of being poisoned.

We suggest playing {@i Teratornis} as a large, mostly unaggressive bird when not eating. It should be most often seen soaring high over open areas, scanning the ground for an easy meal. When one spots food and dives to feed, any {@i Teratornis} in the area should quickly follow suit. During a feeding frenzy, they should be more pushy and more likely to attack if approached, but they will be more likely to bluff than to rush to violence. They could make for an ideal encounter where players are trying to recover an item from a corpse (perhaps even swallowing said item). Sometimes, {@i Teratornis} can be found following parties or caravans, roosting in trees above them at night in the hopes of snatching any scraps of food left behind. With effort, it may be possible to tame one of these hangers on to gain an exceptional aerial scout.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Teratornis} belongs to the Teratornithidae. This is a clade of large birds from the Americas that first arose approximately 25 million years ago during the Late Oligocene. They are part of the Accipitriformes which includes vultures, condors, eagles, hawks, and secretary birds. While teratorns are best known from North America, the oldest remains have been found in Sao Paulo, Brazil. This suggests the group originally evolved in South America, then moved north during the Miocene (23 million years ago). Teratorns include the heaviest non-pterosaurian flying animal in the fossil record, {@i Argentavis}, which may have weighed more than 150 lb. {@i Teratornis} went extinct approximately 10,000 years ago, likely due to climate change impacting large mammal numbers in its habitat. With the reduction of large prey carcasses, {@i Teratornis'} large body size became a hindrance instead of a help.

trait.name: Agile Attacker
entries: If Dyoplax succeeds on a Dexterity saving throw to take half damage from an attack, spell, or effect, it instead takes no damage.
If Dyoplax takes the Dash action, it also Disengages.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules

Dyoplax has Immunity to Poison damage.

action.name: Needle Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}3 ({@damage 1d4 + 1}) Piercing damage.
{@i "DYE-OH-PLAX"} {@b (FROM THE GREEK FOR TWO AND FLAT, REFERENCING ITS DOUBLE ARMOUR)}

Between damp brush and flowing waterways, strange predatory archosaurs hunt. One example is Dyoplax, which, while small, is unusually agile for a pseudosuchid. Although it is of little concern to a seasoned adventurer, several of these mobbing a novice party can lead to a bloody mess indeed.
{@i Dyoplax} is a small pseudosuchian found within the Stuttgart Formation. A tiny and heavily-armoured predator, its exact evolutionary relationships remain uncertain.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Dyoplax} was a small animal, growing to only about 2 ft. long as an adult. It was gracile, with long legs and an overlapping twinned set of armoured scutes running along its back. How heavy it was is uncertain but, given its gracile build and armour, it likely weighed around 10 lb. Its head was broad at the back but had a relatively long and narrow snout with a blunt tip and small nostrils. It had short, curving, needle-like teeth set in the front of its mouth.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Its small teeth suggest that {@i Dyoplax} was likely either fully or partially insectivorous (eats insects). However, it may have also hunted small, fast vertebrates, like reptiles and synapsids, that it could have chased down using its long, slender legs. It likely spent the hottest parts of the day resting, coming out in the cooler afternoon and evening to hunt.

We suggest playing {@i Dyoplax} as an animal that spends most of the day sheltering in cool covered undergrowth. It should be resting during the hottest parts of the day, then becoming more active in the early morning and late afternoon when the temperatures are lower. It should spend much of its time patrolling for prey along riverbanks and within foliage, either snapping at insects as they try to fly away or sprinting (briefly) after small, terrified reptiles. It poses very little threat to humanoids and may, in fact, be drawn to buzzing insect activity around a lit campfire. Anyone sitting first or last watch should have no trouble spotting this small animal, snapping at moths and midges around the camp.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Dyoplax}'s placement within pseudosuchia (the group that eventually gave rise to the crocodylomorphs) is surprisingly controversial for such a small animal. When the original fossil was discovered, the researcher in 1867 described it as a cross between a lizard and a gharial (a long-snouted crocodilian). Initially, it was placed in the Aetosauria, a group of heavily armoured omnivorous/ herbivorous pseudosuchians. However, various factors such as the placement of the teeth and the lack of a shovel-shaped jaw makes this unlikely. Another analysis suggested that it belonged to Sphenosuchia, a group of basal crocodylomorphs with gracile bodies and erected postures. They argued {@i Dyoplax} had features of crocodylomorphs in the structure of its nasal bone and the jugal (cheek) bone.

A more recent study in 2013 argued against this placement and instead identified it as a erpetosuchid. These are long-legged pseudosuchians related to, but not part of, Crocodylomorpha, with long legs and heavily armoured backs. They argued that {@i Dyoplax} should be placed in the group due to cranial characters like the shape of the orbits (eyes) and how slender its legs are, but they noted that ultimately the preservation of the {@i Dyoplax} holotype (a high-quality mold made in sandstone) made reliable analyses difficult.

trait.name: Heavyset Skull
entries: Metoposaurus cannot be critically hit.

trait.name: Aestivate
entries: While in a burrow underground, Metoposaurus can enter a trance-like state of hibernation for several months. During this time it can survive without food or water and is treated as though it were unconscious, although it is aware of its surroundings.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Metoposaurus' CR to 2 and increase its XP to 450 accordingly.

trait.name: Mass Death Assemblage
entries: When Metoposaurus dies, it releases deathly energies, trying to bring all other creatures around it with it to the grave. Each creature within 15 ft. of Metoposaurus must succeed a {@dc 11} Constitution saving throw, taking {@dice 2d6} Necrotic damage on a failed save and half as much on a successful save.

action.name: Wide-Gaped Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}6 ({@damage 1d10 + 1}) Piercing damage.
A Medium or smaller creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} (escape {@dc 11}). Until this Grapple ends, Metoposaurus cannot attack another target.

bonus.name: Adaptive Hunting
entries: As a Bonus Action, Metoposaurus may do one of the following things:

- Lunge: Metoposaurus Dashes. - Snap: Metoposaurus makes a single Wide-Gaped Bite attack against a creature that is within 5 ft. of it. - Gape-suck: If Metoposaurus is within water, pick another creature also in water within 15 ft. of it. That creature must succeed a {@dc 11} Strength saving throw or be pulled 10 ft. towards to Metoposaurus.

reaction.name: Reactive Attack
entries: If another creature comes within 5 ft. of Metoposaurus (including from Gape-suck), it can use its Reaction to make a single Wide-Gaped Bite attack against that creature.
{@i "MEH-TOP-OH-SORE-US"} {@b (FRONT REPTILE)}

Research records indicate that the majority of dangerous predators in the Stuttgart Formation are aquatic, dwelling within the waterways of the region. What they don't note, however, is that some of those predators are fully capable of lunging out of the water and snatching oblivious creatures drinking at the river's edge or inattentive adventures.
{@i Metoposaurus} is a temnospondyl amphibian from the Late Triassic (227 million years ago) of western Europe. A sizable aquatic predator, it is known to be found in multiple mass death assemblages.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Metoposaurus} was a strangely shaped animal, between 5 to 10 ft. in length with a flat shovel-like head and disproportionately large jaws full of tiny needle-like teeth. Its eyes were small but positioned much further forward than in most temnospondyls. Its legs were tiny relative to its body size but they had wide palms and good musculature. When swimming it is thought that these were used for steering while the tail provided locomotion.

There are several {@i Metoposaurus} mass death assemblages scattered across Europe. These are bonebeds (sediments filled with fragmentary bone fossils) dominated by dozens or hundreds of {@i Metoposaurus} remains. Studies show that these bonebeds were probably deposited in temporary lakes that disappeared during the dry season. Research suggests that, in order to survive these changes in environment, {@i Metoposaurus} burrowed deep into the mud once the lakes started to dry up and entered a period of dormancy. This strategy allowed them to wait for wetter seasons to return but came with risks, not least the chance that the rains may be delayed and the animals would be trapped, their burrows eventually becoming their tombs.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Studies into the kinetics (how forces affect the skeleton) of the skull show that {@i Metoposaurus} had an impressively wide gape and was able to bite with considerable force. It also suggests it may have used both ambush and active pursuit tactics when hunting. This ability to adapt its attack strategy based on circumstances would have allowed it to feed on a wider range of prey, from chasing down fleeing fish to snatching unfortunate animals coming to the water's edge to drink.

We suggest playing {@i Metoposaurus} as an opportunistic predator, taking advantage of any chance to snatch prey. This should make them highly unpredictable and it should be difficult for even a seasoned adventurer to guess how they will react. During the wet season, they should be found patrolling waterways, either following shoals of fish or staying near the water's edge in the hopes of finding a larger meal. When the rains stop and their homes start to dry up, many {@i Metoposaurus} may be forced into close contact and fighting should be commonplace. Eventually, they will be forced to burrow into the mud in the hopes of being able to wait out the dry period. Once the rainy season returns, they should rise from dormancy and overnight a new lake might be filled with dozens of hungry individuals.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Metoposaurus} is the name sake of the Metoposauridae. This is a group of temnospondyls that first appeared about 235 million years ago, in what is now North Africa, before spreading across much of Pangea. Within Metoposauridae, mass death assemblages are common and have been identified for at least four taxa, including {@i Metoposaurus} itself. Metoposaurids, despite their success, died out around 215 million years ago, before the Triassic-Jurassic extinction. The cause is uncertain, but it has been suggested that it may be linked to the Manicougan Crater, formed by an asteroid impact event that has been linked to a notable rise in the extinction rate during the Late Triassic.

trait.name: Electrosense
entries: Palaeobates has a Blindsight of 5 ft. while in water (included above).

trait.name: Euryhaline
entries: Palaeobates can only breathe in water. It can tolerate both salty and brackish water.

trait.name: Dermal Denticles
entries: If a creature Grapples or otherwise holds Palaeobates, that creature takes 1 Piercing damage.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Palaeobates' CR to 1/4 and increase its XP to 50 accordingly.

trait.name: Devil's Fish
entries: Palaeobates' creature type becomes Devil. It has Immunity to Fire damage and its attacks deal an additional 2 Fire damage (this damage is not reduced by a target being submerged in water).
Additionally, Palaeobates is unaffected by lava. It can swim and breathe within it as though it were water.

action.name: Crushing Nip
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 0} to hit, Reach 5 ft, one target. {@h}2 (2) Bludgeoning damage.
{@i "PAY-LEE-OH-BAH-TES"} {@b (ANCIENT WALKER)}

Throughout the Triassic, strange shark-like fish can be found along coastal waters and in estuaries. Rather than hunting prey viciously like the sharks we are familiar with today, they cruise the ocean floor in search of shelly prey to crush with their specialised teeth. More than once they've mistaken an armoured boot for prey. That wouldn't be such an issue on its own if it wasn't for the commotion of such a mistake attracting larger predators.

{@i Palaeobates} is a hybodont cartilaginous fish from the Triassic (252 to 205 million years ago) of Europe and North America. A member of the sibling group to modern sharks, it had distinctive teeth designed more for crushing shells than tearing flesh.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Palaeobates} was a small animal, growing no more than 3 ft. long. In most ways it resembled a modern shark with a long torpedo-shaped body and an asymmetrical crescent moon shaped tail where the upper half was much larger than the lower half. It had two large dorsal fins, each with a bony spine supporting it. Male {@i Palaeobates} also had two pairs of hook-like spines just behind their eyes, giving them an almost devilish appearance. In its mouth were tightly compacted rows with dozens of flat, domed teeth which evolved for crushing prey rather than tearing pieces off of it.

{@i Palaeobates} has been found in Triassic formations across the Northern Hemisphere. It generally occurs in marine environments or, as is the case in the Stuttgart Formation, in the saltier waters found at the entrance to river deltas. It was likely euryhaline, meaning that it was capable of tolerating different salinities and would have been comfortable in the mix of fresh and saltwater found in a deltaic system.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Palaeobates} is best known for its durophagous (crushing) teeth. Durophagous teeth are able to robustly exert a large amount of pressure over a small area and are used to crack hard-shelled organisms like crustaceans, molluscs, bivalves, and brachiopods. {@i Palaeobates} may have specialised in feeding close to the sea floor either by digging out shelled animals or hunting ammonoids that floated above the ocean floor.

We suggest playing {@i Palaeobates} as a solitary hunter that is most commonly found close to the ocean floor. It should spend most of its day lazily drifting just above the seabed, using the electrical sensors around its snout to detect prey hidden in the sediment below. Sometimes, if food is scarce it may move into the shallower waters of a delta in search of a meal. Occasionally, a {@i Palaeobates} will make an investigatory bite on the toes or fingers of a humanoid swimmer, and although it's almost never followed by a full attack, it is a potentially bone breaking injury with the subsequent commotion risking drawing the attention of much more dangerous predators.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Palaeobates} is a member of the Hybodontiformes or hybodonts. This is a group of cartilaginous fish that is the sister group to the Neoselachians, the group that includes modern sharks and rays. Hybodonts first appeared in the Devonian (360 million years ago) and had a global distribution. They were very successful, found in both fresh and saltwater environments and occupied a variety of niches, from pursuit predators to slow opportunists to shell-crushing durophages. These highly adaptive carnivores had an enormous temporal range, surviving for more than 290 million years. However, like so many other organisms, they were driven into extinction during the end Cretaceous extinction event 66 million years ago.

trait.name: Latrinic
entries: Woznikella has Vulnerability to Poison damage (included above).

Over the course of 24 hours, Woznikella may create a 5 ft. by 5 ft. latrine that is 2 to 3 ft. deep. Once created, Woznikella does not need to create another latrine for at least a month, or until it moves to a new area.
A creature that starts its turn in this latrine must succeed a
{@dc 11} Constitution saving throw or become {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned} for 1 minute.

trait.name: Adaptive Hardy Herbivore
entries: Woznikella has Advantage on all saving throws.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, you do not need to change Woznikella's CR.

trait.name: Disaster Taxon
entries: Woznikella quickly spreads and multiplies in regions after disasters have wiped out other creatures. It can be found in large numbers in regions devastated by natural disasters.
Additionally, when Woznikella is slain, 24 hours later two more Woznikella magically appear in the location that it was slain (these two do not have this ability).

action.name: Tusk and Horn Gore
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}11 ({@damage 4d4 + 1}) Piercing damage plus 2 ({@damage 1d4}) Bludgeoning damage.

action.name: Shove into Shite
entries: If Woznikella is within 5 ft. of a creature that is within 10 ft. of Woznikella's latrine, it can attempt to push that creature into the latrine.
The target creature must succeed a {@dc 11} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}, pushed up to 10 ft. into the latrine, and take {@dice 1d8} Poison damage.
Additionally, after a failed save but before the creature is moved, Woznikella may use its Bonus Action to make a Tusk and Horn Gore against that creature.
{@i "VOZ-NI-KEH-LAH"} {@b (NAMED FOR THE TOWN OF WOŹNIKI IN POLAND)}

In the sodden mists of the Stuttgart Formation, strange grunting sounds can sometimes be heard carried on the wind. These originate from herbivorous dicynodonts that rummage through the wet soils and muds in search of fresh plant growth. While not particularly bothersome animals, be wary not to step in one of their latrines.

{@i Woznikella} is a medium-sized dicynodont from the Middle-Late Triassic (around 230 million years ago) of Poland. While the holotype is from the Grabowa Formation, partial remains of a dicynodont were discovered in the Stuttgart Formation which, in recent years, have tentatively been identified as belonging to {@i Woznikella.}

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Woznikella} is only known from a partial immature specimen. This animal would have been at least 5 ft. long and may have reached 6 or 7 ft. as an adult. It was a squat animal, with a tubby body, short tail, and a semi-erect gait. Based on dicynodont remains in fossil carnivore dung, it is thought that it may have been covered in sparse, wiry hair (not depicted here). Its head was tall at the back and had pointed jaws that ended in a keratinous beak. The sides of the skull jutted out and forward, forming two downward pointing horn-like triangular extensions that were also covered in keratin. These horn-like protrusions appear to have had two distinct morphologies in dicynodonts and it is thought that they were probably sexually dimorphic (different shapes for males and females). While much of the upper part of the jaw is not preserved in {@i Woznikella}, based on comparisons with other dicynodonts, it is very likely that it also had a large set of tusks (continuously growing, elongate and pointed teeth). These were true tusks (unlike {@i Mastodonsaurus'} ({@b page 146 in DDDD}) pseudotusks, for example), which are only found in mammals and dicynodonts. They can serve a variety of functions including defence, intraspecific (same species) combat, and digging.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Based on dicynodont bonebeds preserving the remains of dozens of individuals together, {@i Woznikella} was likely a social animal that lived in sizable herds. They would have fed by browsing, using their beaks to cut through low-growing ferns. Interestingly, dicynodonts are one of the only animals in the fossil record with strong evidence of their toileting habits. Analyses of large deposits of coprolites (fossil dung) have indicated that animals such as {@i Woznikella} were latrinic. This meant that, rather than randomly defecating as they fed, {@i Woznikella} would have communal latrines - designated spots to defecate that are away from feeding grounds. This behaviour is well documented in mammals and is thought to be beneficial as it helps establish territorial boundaries and reduces the spread of disease. As with their tusks, the dicynodont latrines are the first non-mammalian example of this behaviour.

We suggest playing {@i Woznikella} as a relatively calm animal that is rarely found alone. Herds should be seen grazing across large areas and, for the most part, they should not be prone to conflict. If a fight does break out over food or a mate, they should swing their heads back and forth to show the size of their facial "horns", or yawn widely to expose their tusks. Only if one of the animals refuses to back down should a full-on fight ensue. As long as it is given a respectful distance, {@i Woznikella} should not be a threat to humanoids. However, as with any sizable herbivore, they may still attack if they feel threatened or if they are approached during their mating season.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Dicynodonts first appeared in the fossil record in the Permian (268 million years ago) of South Africa. They are members of the Synapsida, a highly diverse group of animals that includes mammals. They were incredibly successful herbivores, spreading across much of Pangea and, by the end of the Permian, were one of the most abundant animals in the fossil record. However, the end-Permian extinction event devastated Dicynodont numbers and only a handful of taxa survived into the Triassic. While those that survived the extinction event would once again become the dominant herbivores, they eventually declined towards the Late Triassic. It has been hypothesised that this may have been due to climate change, and the spread of increasingly arid conditions. Their numbers dwindled and they finally went extinct approximately 201 million years ago.

trait.name: Unknown Anatomy
entries: As little is known about Zanclodon beyond it being a carnivorous archosaur, we're unsure what its adaptations might have been. Choose from one of the three adaptations listed below. Zanclodon gains that adaptation. Alternatively, you may roll twice on the Minor Mutations table (pages 218-226 in DDDD) and apply those adaptations to Zanclodon (do not adjust its CR).
- Durable Defender. Zanclodon's AC is increased to 16. It has Advantage on Constitution saving throws.
- Frenzied Feeder. Zanclodon may make three Blade-Toothed Bite attacks with its multiattack, rather than two.
- Nocturnal Nightmare. Zanclodon has a Darkvision of 60 ft. If Zanclodon begins its turn Hidden, its first attack this turn deals an additional {@dice 1d6} Piercing damage.
- Aquatic Ambusher. Zanclodon gains a swim speed of 30 ft. and has Advantage on {@skill Stealth} checks while in water.

trait.name: Wastebasket Taxon
entries: All other archosaurs (crocodiles, dinosaurs, pterosaurs, birds, and their kin) treat Zanclodon as an ally unless Zanclodon attacks them or one of their other allies.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Zanclodon's CR to 2 and increase its XP to 450 accordingly.

trait.name: Hidden Spirit in the Rain (3/Day)
entries: Zanclodon can cast the spell Misty Step without requiring components or a spell slot. It may cast it as a Bonus Action or, so long as it is raining, as a Reaction if hit by an attack, causing the attack to miss.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Zanclodon chooses the Attack action, it may make two Blade-Toothed Bite attacks.

action.name: Blade-Toothed Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}5 ({@damage 1d6 + 2}) Piercing damage.
{@i "ZANK-LOW-DON"} {@b (SCYTHE TOOTH)}

Sometimes, there were strange murmurings and rummagings in the sodden undergrowth of the Stuttgart Formation that we never fully identified. More than once, our party found itself accosted by a strange predatory archosaur that, in the chaos of battle, none of us were able to fully see. Only brief moments of clarity revealed a maw agape lunging at us, revealing blade-like teeth, before each of us flinched and darted back in terror - only to find the animal already vanished into the rain.

{@i Zanclodon} is a fairly obscure, and poorly understood, archosaurian reptile from the Stuttgart Formation. Below, we discuss the challenges in palaeontology of working with fragmentary remains. Interestingly, {@i Zanclodon} is surprisingly relevant to a theropod discovery in 2025.

entries.name: Working with Fragmentary Fossils
entries: The field of palaeontology is really not too different from classic detective work. Like Hercule Poirot and Sherlock Holmes, we piece together evidence to make deductions about ancient beasts, long-gone ecosystems, and significant moments in time. Unfortunately, we do not have the benefit of our stories ending in neat little drawing room scenes. Instead, we try to bring fossils together to create brief glimpses into the complex history of life on our planet. Mistakes are frequent, particularly in taxonomy. Thousands of taxa have been erected only to be re-evaluated, re-diagnosed, or rendered entirely invalid. One key issue is the identification, description, and placement of undiagnosable material. Many fossils are simply too heavily damaged or incomplete to determine the full anatomy or taxonomic placement of a newly discovered organism.

Some scientists take a simplified approach, noting that the specimen is unplaceable. Others achieve the best placement they can and assign the fossil to an established taxon, despite it not meeting all of the criteria. This can result in a taxon containing examples that are likely from other, perhaps new, taxa. When this happens a lot to a single taxon, we call it a "wastebasket taxon" - as all of the "junk" is thrown in it. {@i Zanclodon} is one such wastebasket taxon.

entries.name: The History of Zanclodon as a Wastebasket
entries: The original material assigned to {@i Zanclodon} was described in the 1840s by notable palaeontologist Theodor Plieniger. He was describing several isolated Triassic archosaur fossils including teeth, vertebrae, and a jaw with teeth still in the sockets. The most notable feature of these bones was that the teeth lacked serrations, which was seemingly unique among archosaurs. He initially wanted to name his new animal {@i Smilodon} but, unsurprisingly to modern readers, found that the name was already occupied. He instead settled on {@i Zanclodon} and, over the next 70 years, eight species were erected within this genus for isolated teeth and jaw remains, despite having little in common with the holotype material.

The placement of {@i Zanclodon} within Archosauria was equally muddled. It was first identified as a dinosaur, then a teratosaurid (now called rauisuchians) and later, despite its clearly carnivorous teeth, a herbivorous plateosaurid. Like many wastebasket taxa from the 1800s, interest in {@i Zanclodon} dropped for most of the 20thcentury and it was not until 1998 when the first proper taxonomic revision occurred after a single jaw assigned to the genus was noted to have serrated teeth and therefore could not be {@i Zanclodon}. For the subsequent 10 years, a handful of publications reappraised specific fossils assigned to {@i Zanclodon} as various indeterminate archosaurs, culminating in a 2011 paper that removed all but the original fossils. Of those original fossils, only the jaw remained and the other components had been lost. Nevertheless, the initial unique dentition allowed {@i Zanclodon} to remain a valid genus of indeterminate primitive archosaur.

In 2025, the original jaw described in 1998 that was initially assigned to {@i Zanclodon} was revised and identified as a (for the Triassic) exceptionally large theropod (perhaps 23 ft. long). A new distinct genus, {@i Newtonsaurus}, was erected for that specimen.

This history of rushed early assignment of fragmentary or unrelated remains followed by a period of re-evaluation is typical of a wastebasket taxon and is, unfortunately, common in palaeontology. In fact, by remaining a valid, even if very poorly understood, taxon, {@i Zanclodon} is one of the lucky few to be revised and survive the experience.

entries.name: What Do We Know About Zanclodon?
entries: {@i Zanclodon}'s jaw was about 11 inches long and it has the conical, recurved teeth of a predator, albeit without serrations. This means that it was likely a major predator in the Stuttgart Formation about the size of a very large dog or wolf and, as a Triassic archosaur, it was probably covered in scales or scutes. However, without the rest of its body, we can't determine how it hunted, if it stood on two or four legs, or if it had any specialised adaptations. Given the environment of the Stuttgart Formation, it may have spent a lot of time in water.

Each of the adaptations presented in {@i Zanclodon}'s "{@b Unknown Anatomy}" ability convey a different role within its ecosystem. We suggest that you trust your own instincts on how an animal with those adaptations might behave, or defer to the behaviour of another known animal that fills the same niche.

monster.name: Australovenator (Magical Variant)

trait.name: Prey Dragger
entries: Australovenator may move at its normal speed while grappling a creature smaller than itself, dragging the creature with it.

trait.name: Muscular Forearms

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Australovenator's CR to 6 and increase its XP to 2300 accordingly.
{@b {@i Crikey!}} {@i Australovenator has a much more crocodilian appearance, with a thick scaled hide, broader head, and a powerful muscular tail.}
Its AC is increased to 17, it gains a swim speed of 30 ft., and its Gracile Bite deals an additional {@dice 1d6} Piercing damage.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Australovenator chooses the Attack action, it may make two Gracile Bite attacks and one Powerful Claws attack. Alternatively, it may make one Gracile Bite attack and one Dismembering Kick. attack.

action.name: Gracile Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 6} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}5 ({@damage 1d6 + 2}) Piercing damage.

action.name: Powerful Claws
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 6} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}10 ({@damage 2d6 + 3}) Piercing damage plus 3 ({@damage 1d6}) Slashing damage.
A creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled}.

action.name: Dismembering Kick
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 6} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}14 ({@damage 2d10 + 3}) Slashing damage plus 8 ({@damage 1d10 + 3}) Bludgeoning damage.
A creature hit by this attack that is currently {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} by Australovenator takes an additional {@dice 1d10} Slashing damage.

legendary.name: Clawed Squeeze
entries: Australovenator squeezes a creature that is currently Grappling with its powerful clawed hands. That creature takes {@dice 2d6} Piercing damage.

legendary.name: Dragging Stride
entries: Australovenator moves up to 10 ft. If it is Grappling a creature, that creature is dragged with it.

legendaryHeader: Australovenator can take 1 Legendary Action, choosing from the options below. Only one legendary option can be used at a time and only at the end of another creature's turn. The Australovenator regains spent Legendary Actions at the start of its turn.

entries: "AUS-TRAH-LOW-VEN-AH-TOR"
{@b (SOUTHERN HUNTER)}

The journal of another researcher who travelled through these polar regions reports the presence of a large predatory dinosaur, a megaraptor of some sort, that patrols the winter forests. Presumably, it sustains itself through the harsh winter months by excavating lungfish... Although I would rather not test that hypothesis by encountering it during the long night.

{@i Australovenator} was a megaraptorid from the Cretaceous (100 to 95 million years ago) Winton and Eumeralla formations in eastern Australia. A lightly built theropod, it is best known for the pair of enormous hooked claws it had on each hand.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: While it is the largest theropod known from Australia, {@i Australovenator} is one of the smallest megaraptorids. It grew to approximately 20 ft. long and would have weighed about 700 lb. Its body was lightly built and gracile with a long snout. Its thin jaws had a relatively weak bite and were not built for handling large struggling prey, but could slash effectively. By comparison, its arms were robust and powerful with the typical three fingers of theropods. While the claw on the third digit was relatively small, those on the first two fingers were enormous. They looked superficially like the toe claws of a dromaeosaur but were much larger and more robust. The claw on the first digit was so big it dwarfed the finger itself. Studies show these arms were very well muscled and had a wide range of movement. They are also known to have been very resistant to the stresses created when the fingers extended or flexed.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: The strength and flexibility of {@i Australovenator's} arms naturally raises the question of what they were used for. Most researchers agree that the arms were its primary hunting tool and would have been used to grapple prey such as {@i Leaellynasaura} ({@b page 140}). The claws would have either pierced the skin to better hold them in place or opened blood vessels, causing the animal to die of blood loss and shock. They may also have been useful in dismembering prey, holding the prey still so that the weaker jaws could access softer delicate areas of the prey's body.

We suggest playing {@i Australovenator} as a largely solitary hunter, following herds of ornithischians waiting for an opportunity to ambush stragglers and drag them into the undergrowth. If challenged, rather than immediately attacking, an {@i Australovenator} should use its muscular arms and large claws as part of a threat display.

Humanoids may be seen as easy slow prey, or threats to be warded off by {@i Australovenator} waving its claws and stomping its feet aggressively. If a challenge turns into a fight, an {@i Australovenator} will grapple its enemy with its claws then attempt to dismember them or bite their neck. Rival fights should rarely be fatal however, with the loser quick to back off to avoid serious injury.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Australovenator} is the smallest member of the Megaraptoridae. These unusual dinosaurs were first described in the late 90s based on fragmentary remains that included a massive claw. These claws were first thought to be from a giant dromaeosaurid, but in the early 2010s they were recognised as originating from a distinct group of theropods which the most recent studies suggests were probably a sister group to the Tyrannosauroidea.

While their earliest relatives come from Japan and Thailand, the first true megaraptorids appear in the fossil record approximately 120 million years ago in eastern Australia. Within 30 million years, they had migrated to South America where they appear to have been part of a large diversification event alongside several other dinosaur groups. By the Late Cretaceous (70 million years ago) the largest megaraptorids grew to more than 30 ft. long. While {@i Australovenator} itself is thought to have gone extinct approximately 95 million years ago, the megaraptorids were successful enough to outlive some other major theropod groups like the carcharodontosaurids and were still part of the South American dinosaur fauna right up until the end Cretaceous extinction.

trait.name: Lungfish
entries: Ceratodus can breathe in both air and water.

trait.name: Aestivate
entries: While in its burrow, Ceratodus can enter a trance-like state of hibernation for several months.
During this time, it can survive without food or water. If collected, it can be kept as a fresh source of food in this aestivated state (2 day's rations for one person).

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, you do not need to change Ceratodus' CR.

trait.name: Salmon of Wisdom
entries: If a creature consumes a day's ration worth of Ceratodus, its Wisdom ability score is increased to 21 for one hour. If the creature instead consumes two day's ration worth of Ceratodus in a single sitting, its Wisdom ability score is instead increased to 25 for one hour.

action.name: Fishy Nip
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 2} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}1 (1) Piercing damage.

action.name: Create Burrow
entries: As an Action, Ceratodus can create a burrow in mud, sand, or silt that is large enough for it to fit in (typically 1-3 ft. deep and 6 inches in diameter).
If already in a burrow, it can instead use its Action to cover the entrance, concealing it ({@skill Survival} or Investigation {@dc 12} to reveal it).
"SER-AH-TOE-DUS"
{@b (HORN TOOTH)}

The harsh winters of the polar Eumeralla forest can be made a little easier with some knowledge of Ceratodus' habits. These freshwater lungfish aestivate, or rather hibernate in a burrow during dry periods, and are a valuable source of food during the long night, that is, if you know where to find them.

{@i Ceratodus} was a lungfish that was present globally throughout the Mesozoic and early Cenozoic (250 to 55 million years ago). One of several species of fish capable of breathing air, it represents a window into how vertebrates originally transitioned from the water to the land.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Ceratodus} is known only from fossilised tooth plates (broad, flat teeth) and therefore we can only speculate about its overall body morphology by looking at other extinct and living lungfish. Based on comparisons with modern tooth plates, {@i Ceratodus} has been estimated to average about 3 ft. long, although some giant examples may have been as large as 13 ft. in length. Lungfish typically have a similar appearance, and it's generally assumed that {@i Ceratodus} should have been similar to at least some modern species, such as the Australian lungfish. They likely had long cylindrical bodies that transitioned into a muscular tail with a low rounded fin running along its length. Their pectoral and pelvic fins are unusually fleshy and strong, able to support the fish's weight as they dragged themselves along the ground. As a lungfish, {@i Ceratodus} possessed a set of working lungs as well as gills, allowing it to breathe both in and outside of water.
While it still spent most of its life in water, it would have been able to travel short distances to nearby bodies of water if its pond dried up or in search of food.

{@i Ceratodus} is a globally present genus, found on every continent except Antarctica. It preferred living in shallow pools and swampy regions. When their water sources dry up and there are no other nearby pools to migrate to, some lungfish species dig burrows into the mud to aestivate (the summer equivalent of hibernation). Fossil burrows have been attributed to {@i Ceratodus,} although without body fossils, this is still speculative.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Based on its tooth plates, {@i Ceratodus} would have been primarily carnivorous while also occasionally eating aquatic plants. Their plates would have allowed them to crush hard shelled organisms like small crustaceans and aquatic insects, although it may also have fed on smaller fish and amphibians. Based on the behaviour of modern lungfish, when breeding, a male {@i Ceratodus} may have dug a breeding burrow where it would be able to fertilise the eggs of several females. After the female laid eggs in a small nest, the male would remain and oxygenate the eggs until they hatch, while also providing protection from small predators. {@i Ceratodus}, like modern lungfish, was likely exceptionally long-lived and some individuals may have lived for over a century, if in good health.

We suggest playing {@i Ceratodus} as a freshwater fish that primarily feeds at the bottoms of ponds or in the mud of swampy flats. It should be relatively placid towards large animals, ignoring them unless they approach too close whereby it should make a dash for deeper water. A {@i Ceratodus} caught on land and unable to reach the water may attempt to bite anyone that picks it up. They make for an ideal source of food for travelling adventurers and can be easily dug up from their muddy burrows. When cooked, {@i Ceratodus} should taste like salmon, the consumption of which grants wisdom according to some myths.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Ceratodus} is a member of the Dipnoi (lungfish). This group arose in the Early Devonian, more than 400 million years ago, and persists to the modern day. One of several groups of fish that can breathe out of water, they were originally a marine family before transitioning into freshwater habitats. They are a sister group to all tetrapods (land vertebrates) and their ability to walk on land while still being tied to water provides insight into the early stages of terrestrialisation (moving to land) of vertebrates. {@i Ceratodus} survived the end Cretaceous extinction, but died out approximately 55 million years ago. The cause of their extinction is still unknown.

trait.name: Amphibian Ambusher
entries: Koolasuchus can breathe in both air and water, has Advantage on {@skill Stealth} checks while in water, and has a Blindsight of 10 ft. while in water (included above).

trait.name: Frozen Torpor
entries: Koolasuchus is functionally immune to Cold damage (included above). If Koolasuchus would take Cold damage, instead prevent that damage and, for every 10 points of Cold damage prevented (cumulative), reduce its walking and swimming speed by 5 ft. for 1 minute. If its walking speed is reduced to 0 by this effect, it falls unconscious.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Koolasuchus' CR to 2 and increase its XP to 450 accordingly.

trait.name: Frozen Core
entries: Koolasuchus' has spent so long frozen in torpor that it has magically adapted to those conditions permanently. Its body is encrusted by large ice crystals and it has a dull blue colouration.
Koolasuchus loses its Frozen Torpor ability and instead has "normal" Immunity to Cold damage. Its AC becomes 15 and its Grab and Drag attack deals an additional {@dice 1d10} Cold damage.

action.name: Grab and Drag
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}11 ({@damage 2d8 + 2}) Piercing damage.

A creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} (escape {@dc 12}). Koolasuchus may move up to 10 ft. after hitting with this attack, dragging a {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} creature with it.
"COOL-AH-SOO-KUS"
{@b (KOOL'S CROCODILE)}
Many adventurers expect frozen polar rivers and ponds to be devoid of large predators, particularly reptiles and amphibians.
They presume that their physiology is not suited to the cold waters and they can be fished or swam in without fear.
However, I can attest that this is very much NOT the case in some regions. Some amphibians have adaptations, such as natural antifreeze, that allows them to tolerate such extreme colds comfortably.

{@i Koolasuchus} is a large chigutisaurid temnospondyl amphibian. Roughly the size of a large crocodile, this giant amphibian was the last surviving member of a group which had successfully established in Gondwana during the Early Triassic (252 million years ago).

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Koolasuchus} was very big for an amphibian, reaching 10 ft. long and weighing at least 1000 lb. It looked similar to an enormous salamander, with a flat, moist, scaleless body. Its tail was compressed and likely had dorsal (upper) and ventral (lower) fins. Its legs were small and short, giving it a slow sprawling gait, although it was capable of moving fast in short explosive bursts. Although the skull is incomplete, its head was clearly enormous compared to its body and would likely have been about 2 ft. wide with large jaws, numerous sharp, curving teeth, and small eyes set right at the front of the head.

As an amphibian, {@i Koolasuchus} would have been ectothermic ("cold blooded"). This has raised the question of how it could survive in a region as cold as the Eumeralla Formation. It was closely tied to local water sources and would have been very unlikely to migrate to warmer climates during the winter freeze. One possibility is that {@i Koolasuchus} was able to enter a state of torpor, in the same manner as modern overwintering amphibians. This would require {@i Koolasuchus} to build up fat stores prior to the cold and submerge itself beneath ice near the shore. As amphibians can breathe through their skin, they can remain underwater for months on end if they reduce their metabolic activities. {@i Koolasuchus} could have used a similar strategy, but it inherently comes with a high risk. Modern frogs frequently die due to changes in conditions or being discovered by predators while in this form of hibernation and, if {@i Koolasuchus} used a similar strategy, it would have been an enormous and easy meal for a scavenging predator like {@i Australovenator} ({@b page 134}).

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Koolasuchus} is a large aquatic carnivore, similar in size to a modern crocodile and is thought to have occupied a similar ecological niche. It may have hunted by snapping at fish and invertebrates that passed by, or laid in wait near the shore with only its eyes poking above the water's surface. If an animal came too close, {@i Koolasuchus} would have lurched out to grab it and drag it back into the water.

We suggest playing {@i Koolasuchus} as a patient, inactive animal. It should spend most of its day in the water, unmoving, and watching for prey. Rather than chasing prey, it should remain still until either fish or some unlucky land animal strays too close. Then with a sudden snap, the prey should be grabbed and devoured immediately, leaving an eerie stillness. With larger prey, it should try to drag the prey underwater to either hold onto it until it drowns or bleeds to death from the bite wound.
A humanoid, especially a smaller one, approaching too close to the water's edge may suddenly find a 10 ft. monster amphibian latched onto their legs before they have a chance to flee.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Koolasuchus} was a chigutisaurid, a late surviving group of temnospondyls that was one of the only temnospondyl groups to survive the Permo-Triassic extinction. Found exclusively in Gondwana (South America, Australia, Madagascar, Africa, Antarctica and India), their long-term survival into the Early Cretaceous has been attributed to the relative isolation of the Gondwanan landmasses, particularly Australia which was ultimately their last stronghold. Their extinction has been attributed to climate change, with an increase in temperatures allowing animals such as crocodiles to fully establish themselves as competition. It has been speculated that crocodiles, which occupied a similar niche but were better adapted for the increasingly warm conditions, outcompeted {@i Koolasuchus}, resulting in not only its extinction but the final fall of a group that had persisted for 230 million years.

entries.name: References
entries: Hart, L.J., Gee, B.M., Smith, P.M. and McCurry, M.R. 2022. A new chigutisaurid (Brachyopoidea, Temnospondyli) with soft tissue preservation from the Triassic Sydney Basin, New South Wales, Australia. {@i Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology}, {@b 42 (6)}, pp.e2232829.

Mehmood, A., Singh, S.A., Elsler, A. and Benton, M.J. 2025. The ecology and geography of temnospondyl recovery after the Permian– Triassic mass extinction. {@i Royal Society Open Science}, {@b 12 (3)}, pp.241200.
Tattersall, G.J. and Ultsch, G.R. 2008. Physiological ecology of aquatic overwintering in ranid frogs. {@i Biological Reviews}, {@b 83 (2)}, pp.119-140.
Warren, A., Rich, T.H. and Vickers-Rich, P. 1997. The last last labyrinthodonts. {@i Palaeontographica Abteilung A - Stuttgart}, {@b 247 (1-4)}, pp.1-24.

trait.name: Burrow Builder
entries: Leaellynasaura has a burrowing speed of 5 ft. (included above). It can only burrow through soft dirt, mud, and sand.

trait.name: Alert Polar Prey
entries: Leaellynasaura has a Darkvision of 120 ft., Resistance to Cold damage (both included above), gains +5 to Initiative rolls, and other creatures can't gain Advantage on attack rolls against it as a result of starting their turn Hidden from it.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Leaellynasaura's CR to 1/4 and increase its XP to 50 accordingly.

trait.name: Internal Warmth
entries: Leaellynasaura survives the long polar winters by stoking magical fire energies within itself. It gains Immunity to Cold damage and its attacks deal an additional {@dice 1d4} Fire damage. Additionally, after each Long Rest, Leaellynasaura gains 6 Temporary Hit Points.

action.name: Wriggling Scratch
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}2 ({@damage 1d4}) Slashing damage.
If Leaellynasaura hits a creature that is grappling it with this attack, the Grapple ends.
"LEE-AE-LIN-AH-SORA-AH"
{@b (LEAELLYN'S REPTILE)}

If you traverse the polar forests with the utmost stealth in the darkest long-nights, you might be so lucky as to glimpse a small herd of Leaellynasaura. These delightful little dinosaurs are exceptionally skittish and very, very cute. I can only imagine what horrible hunting pressures have pushed them to evolve such fearfulness.

{@i Leaellynasaura} is a small ornithischian dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous (118 million years ago) of Australia. An animal adapted for living in polar climates, there has been a lot of debate about where it falls on the dinosaur family tree.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: For a Cretaceous dinosaur, {@i Leaellynasaura} was not a large animal, growing to only 6 ft. long and probably weighing less than 20 lb. In most respects it was similar to other small-bodied ornithischians, being a lightly built biped with a tall skull and jaws tipped by a keratinous beak. However, its tail was distinctive, which was exceptionally long with at least 70 vertebrae and almost three times the length of the body. This gave it the greatest tail-to-body ratio of any ornithischian.

There has been some debate about whether {@i Leaellynasaura} was a diurnal (daytime) or nocturnal (nighttime) animal. A partial skull shows evidence that it had very large eyes for its size, which may have given it good night vision. This would have been useful as it inhabited polar regions, which included months without sunlight. Another suggestion was that the size of the eyes had more to do with the age of the animal than its habits, as the skull came from a young individual and juvenile animals almost always have proportionally larger eyes than adults. However, a study into the growth patterns of {@i Leaellynasaura}'s bones show that it did not have periods of arrested development (periods with slowed growth). This indicates that it was probably active throughout the year and, regardless of the maturity of the specimen in question, it certainly would have had to cope with months of darkness.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Leaellynasaura} was a herbivore and, with its narrow jaws, was probably a selective browser. It would have used its hard beak to snip the fronds off of ground-level ferns and small cycads. Several burrows have been found near where {@i Leaellynasaura} was discovered which may have been made by the small dinosaur, serving as shelter from predators and a place to escape the coldest wintery weather.

We suggest playing {@i Leaellynasaura} as a highly alert and extremely skittish animal. It should move through the undergrowth in groups of 3 to 6 individuals with at least one animal always scanning for danger as the others feed. Any threat should make them scatter into the nearest bushes or burrow for safety. On the very rare occasion one is cornered or picked up by a humanoid, it can do little more than bite and scratch in the hopes of breaking free.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Where exactly {@i Leaellynasaura} falls on the ornithischian family tree is not certain. It has been placed in multiple different positions within the group, such as it being a late surviving basal form to being a generic member of the more derived Neornithischia. The most recent study to look at its relationships placed it in Elasmaria, a subgroup of Iguanodontia made up of small bipedal Gondwanan (southern hemisphere) ornithischians that are the sibling group to the Dryomorpha (which includes the larger, more well known ornithopods). As with all phylogenetic studies of contentiously placed animals, this interpretation could be overturned by a new study at any point.

entries.name: References
entries: Agnolin, F.L., Ezcurra, M.D., Pais, D.F. and Salisbury, S.W. 2010. A reappraisal of the Cretaceous non-avian dinosaur faunas from Australia and New Zealand: evidence for their Gondwanan affinities. {@i Journal of Systematic Palaeontology}, {@b 8 (2)}, pp.257-300.
Chinsamy, A., Rich, T. and Vickers-Rich, P. 1998. Polar dinosaur bone histology. {@i Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology}, {@b 18 (2)}, pp.385-390.

Duncan, R.J., Evans, A.R., Vickers-Rich, P., Rich, T.H. and Poropat, S.F. 2021. Ornithopod jaws from the Lower Cretaceous Eumeralla Formation, Victoria, Australia, and their implications for polar neornithischian dinosaur diversity. {@i Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology}, {@b 41 (3)}, pp.e1946551.
Martin, A.J. 2009. Dinosaur burrows in the Otway Group (Albian) of Victoria, Australia, and their relation to Cretaceous polar environments. {@i Cretaceous Research}, {@b 30 (5)}, pp.1223-1237.

trait.name: Electrolocation
entries: Steropodon has a Blindsight of 5 ft., this is increased to 10 ft. while in water. It also has Expertise in Perception and passive {@skill Perception} (all included above).

trait.name: Small Semi-Aquatic Animal
entries: Steropodon can hold its breath for up to 10 minutes and has a swim speed of 25 ft.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules for Steropodon, select one of the abilities below. It gains that ability and you do not need to change its CR.

trait.name: Familiar
entries: Steropodon may be used as a familiar via the Find Familiar spell or any similar effect.

trait.name: Time-Correcting Essence
entries: If Steropodon is slain by a member of the player party, the party lowers their Chrono-consequence value by 10 (pages 78-79). Alternatively, if you are using the Minor/Major Effects tables instead (pages 75-77), reduce their next rolled result by two stages.
If you are not using these systems, Steropodon instead deals {@dice 1d6} Necrotic damage to the creature that killed it.

action.name: Venomous Spur
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}1 (1) Piercing damage plus 2 ({@damage 1d4}) Poison damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 7} Constitution saving throw or be {@condition stunned|XPHB|Stunned} until the start of Steropodon's next turn.
"STER-OHP-OH-DON"
{@b (LIGHTNING TOOTH)}

Most adventurers envisage thundering titanic dinosaurs when we discuss travelling through the Cretaceous. However, with patience, calmness, and a bit of luck, waiting quietly for a few hours may allow them to glimpse rare and skittish early mammals that live in the shadows of these giants. The aquatic Steropodon is one such animal, requiring hours of silence next to a shallow river. I believe that the wait is well worth it.

{@i Steropodon} is a monotreme from around the Early Cretaceous (105 million years ago) of New South Wales, Australia. Known from a single jaw, it is considered to be an early relative of the platypus.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: With only a fragmentary fossil on record, it is difficult to accurately judge the size of {@i Steropodon} but estimates have been made through comparison with both fossil and living monotremes. It may have grown to a length of 1.5-2 ft. and weighed as much as 4-5 lb. As the largest known Cretaceous mammal was only a little over 3 ft. long, this makes {@i Steropodon} a relative giant of its time. The jaw is from an adult and has 3 molars, which is distinct from derived monotremes that lose their teeth as adults. Based on a lateral canal in the jaw, {@i Steropodon} is thought to have had a soft-tissue bill which was likely extremely sensitive. The platypus uses its bill to not only sense things through touch, but also to detect the electrical field of organisms in the water. This electrolocation is a valuable hunting tool in environments with poor visibility and it seems likely that {@i Steropodo}n's bill had a similar function.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Based on what little information we have on {@i Steropodon} and other related extinct monotremes, we can assume that it was behaviourally similar to the platypus. It would have hunted in muddy water and used its sensitive bill rather than its eyes to find food. It likely fed primarily on invertebrates it dug up from the bottom of the river such as worms, larvae, and shelly arthropods. As it was a monotreme, it would have laid soft-shelled eggs in burrows instead of giving birth to live young and fed them through milk secreted from specialised glands beneath the skin. While we do not know whether it possessed a venomous spur like the platypus, we consider it plausible based on their relatively close relationship.

We suggest playing {@i Steropodon} as an animal constantly in search of food. Most of its day should be spent with its bill buried in the muddy bottom of a river or lake searching for prey. Its electrolocation should make it a hard animal to sneak up on, and it will be common for it to dart into hiding without ever being seen by an approaching humanoid. If it is caught it should be relatively harmless, although it will try to scratch attackers with its envenomed spur, the venom of which causes severe pain.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Steropodon} is a member of the Monotremata and was the oldest known monotreme species when it was first described in the 80s. Since then, many more monotreme fossils have been discovered, with the oldest coming from the Early Cretaceous of Australia approximately 130 million years ago (although it has been suggested that their origins date back to the Late Jurassic, we do not have the fossil evidence yet to support this). They are primarily known from Australasia, with some fossils from South America suggesting a historically wider range. They are generally considered more basal than other mammals, retaining plesiomorphic (ancestral) traits like a cloaca and laying eggs. While somewhat diverse in the past, only the platypus and echidna survive today, which are both considered vulnerable to extinction due to climate change, pollution, and habitat reduction.

trait.name: Heavyset
entries: Barilium has Advantage on Constitution saving throws and saving throws to resist being {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled}.

trait.name: Trampling Retreat
entries: If Barilium takes the Dash Action, it also Disengages and may move through spaces occupied
by creatures smaller than itself. If it does so, once during its turn, it may make a Trample attack against a creature whose space it moves through.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Barilium's CR to 4 and increase its XP to 1100 accordingly.
{@b {@i Rock Hard Barilium.}} {@i Barilium's body is composed of a fictional mineral called "Barilium". It is dark and crystalline in appearance. It gains the following traits:}
- Its AC is increased to 17.
- It gains Resistance to Bludgeoning, Piercing, and Slashing damage.
- It gains Immunity to Poison damage and Immunity to the {@condition petrified|XPHB|Petrified} and {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned} conditions.
- It gains Vulnerability to Thunder and Force damage.
- Its creature type is Elemental.

If Barilium is reduced to 0 Hit Points by an attack that dealt Thunder or Force damage, it shatters violently and each creature within 10 ft. of it must succeed a {@dc 14} Dexterity saving throw or suffers {@dice 2d6} Slashing damage.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Barilium chooses the Attack action, it may make two Blunt Gore attacks.

action.name: Blunt Clawed Gore
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}4 ({@damage 1d4 + 2}) Piercing damage plus 5 ({@damage 1d6 + 2}) Bludgeoning damage.

action.name: Trample
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 6} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}13 ({@damage 2d10 + 2}) Bludgeoning damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 14} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.
{@i "BAR-ILL-E-UM"} {@b (HEAVY ILIUM)}

In areas that lack tree cover, large herds of Barilium thunder and holler across the open plains and riverways. These conspicuous animals are the bread and butter of these lands - commonplace and a welcome reminder of where you are. Nevertheless, approach with caution, as their powerful builds and large size renders them dangerous when frightened.

{@i Barilium} is a large iguanodontian ornithopod from the Early Cretaceous (138 to 132 million years ago) of Southeast England. A robust animal, it was originally described as a species of {@i Iguanodon} ({@b page 134 in DDDD}), but is now considered its own genus.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Barilium} is known only from partial remains but has been estimated to be approximately 26 ft. long with a weight of about 4 tonnes. Believed to be an obligate quadruped (had to walk on four legs), it was notably more heavily built than other contemporary iguanodontians, including {@i Iguanodon} itself. Like {@i Iguanodon}, {@i Barilium} possessed a modified claw on its first digit, however, this was a short and blunt stub, instead of a prominent spike like in {@i Iguanodon}. The shape of {@i Barilium}'s bottom jaw suggests that it had an elongate head tipped by a short keratinous beak. Its teeth were laterally thin and leaf shaped and, combined with its robust jaw and ability to chew, suggest it was a browser of tough plants, namely early conifers and ferns.

{@i Barilium} fossils have been recovered from the Wadhurst Clay Formation, an Early Cretaceous unit from East Sussex, England. We include {@i Barilium} here in the Wessex Formation section as both are part of the larger Wealden Group, and {@i Barilium} is both very closely related to, and has a nearly identical environmental preference to, less well-known iguanodontians from the Wessex Formation. The Wadhurst Formation was laid down in a predominantly freshwater environment with some tidal and lagoonal influence, likely within a river delta. Fossils from this formation include a variety of animals like fish, mammals, and dinosaurs such as the smaller hadrosauriforme {@i Hypselospinus}, as well as theropods like {@i Altispinax} and {@i Suchosaurus}.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Barilium} is known only from fragmentary remains that provide little insight into its behaviour. However, as it is similar to {@i Iguanodon}, we can assume some shared attributes. It may have been a somewhat gregarious animal living in small herds, grazing along forest edges or within clearings. Its smaller, blunt thumb claw is ill suited to be used as a weapon, which may have meant that {@i Barilium} had few defences against predators beyond its size and numbers. This could have made it relatively skittish for its size and prone to fleeing if threatened.

We suggest playing {@i Barilium} as a somewhat jumpy animal, easy to spook if surprised. It should live in small herds with one or two animals always on the lookout for threats. If danger is spotted, they should sound alarm calls, which will quickly trigger the herd to flee. While this makes it unlikely that players may be directly attacked by a {@i Barilium}, they could easily be at risk of being trampled by a panicked herd. Individuals should be most likely to attack if they feel cornered with no means of escape and then should use their size to try and crush a potential threat.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Barilium} was originally described as a species of {@i Iguanodon} within the group Iguanodontidae. Years later, {@i Iguanodon} underwent a major review which argued that many of the species included within the genus were actually distinct animals. Several new taxa were erected, among them {@i Barilium}. Where {@i Barilium} falls within the iguanodontian tree is somewhat uncertain. Iguanodontidae is currently considered a dubious grouping and may be paraphyletic (includes organisms from separate branches of the tree of life). Further studies suggest it occupies a position further down the tree than previously suspected, resting amongst groups such as the basal styracosterns or hadrosauriformes.

trait.name: Feeding Lookouts
entries: If Hypsilophodon are present in numbers of 3 or more, increase their passive Perceptions to 14.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, you do not need to change Hypsilophodon's CR.

trait.name: Misinterpretation
entries: Hypsilophodon has misidentified components on its body, giving it longer grasping hands and armour plating. It gains a climb speed of 25 ft. and has an AC of 14. It becomes a hostile, aggressive armoured tree-climbing animal that will drop onto unsuspecting creatures while hissing loudly.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Hypsilophodon chooses the Attack action, it may make up to two Self-Sharpening Bite attacks.

action.name: Self-Sharpening Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}4 ({@damage 1d4 + 2}) Piercing damage.
Hypsilophodon's next attack with Self-Sharpening Bite deals an additional 2 damage.

action.name: Opposable Digit
entries: As an Action, Hypsilophodon can grasp and interact with small objects, such as trinkets, wands, door handles, etc., although it may not understand how to use them. Each time Hypsilophodon tries to use an object or item, roll {@dice 1d4} to determine the result:
1 - It fails to use the object, potentially injuring itself or damaging the object (if able), and will not attempt again.
2 - It is unable to use the object.
3 - It uses the object without Proficiency.
4 - It uses the object with Proficiency.
Creatures wilds haped or polymorphed into Hypsilophodon do not need to make this roll if they would normally understand how to use the object.

bonus.name: Cursorial
entries: Hypsilophodon can Dash or Disengage as a Bonus Action.
{@i "HIP-SIH-LOFF-OH-DON"} {@b (HIGH CRESTED TOOTH)}

In the same manner as observing a herd of deer feeding in rural fields on a cold, misty morning, herds of dozens of Hypsilophodon can sometimes be seen picking at low-lying ferns in the Wessex plains. Such animals often employ similar sentry tactics, so that the majority of them can feed in peace.

{@i Hypsilophodon} is a bipedal dinosaur from the Wessex Formation (130 million years ago). It comes from the "{@i Hypsilophodon} beds", a layer of rock named for the dozens of {@i Hypsilophodon} fossils found within it.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Hypsilophodon} was a small dinosaur, up to 3 ft. tall and 5 to 8 ft. long. It had a simple, lightly built body, standing on two legs with a long tail, two short forearms with five fingered hands and a proportionally large head. From the side, the head looked triangular, tall at the back with a small, pointed mouth tipped by a hard beak at the front. At the front of the jaws, its teeth were pointed and triangular while further back they were ridged and chisel-like, which may have been self-sharpening. Like many ornithopods, {@i Hypsilophodon} was able to chew, grinding its teeth against each other to crush softer plants.

{@i Hypsilophodon} has been interpreted in several different ways. While originally reconstructed as a ground living biped, starting in the 1880s a trend emerged where {@i Hypsilophodon} was instead interpreted as an arboreal animal akin to {@i Dendrolagus} (the "tree kangaroo"). This was based on the idea that it may have had a reversed first toe (hallux) that let it perch on branches, despite no real evidence to support this hypothesis. This idea remained popular into the early 1970s. The discovery of fossilised flat plates with the animal have also led to the idea that it was armoured, although these are now known to be cartilaginous structures on the ribs that would have provided no real defence.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Hypsilophodon}'s pointed jaws suggests that it was a very specialist feeder, preferring to eat delicate shoots and saplings rather than tougher plants like cycads. As mentioned above, it was found in large numbers within the "{@i Hypsilophodon} beds". Up until very recently, this was thought to be a mass mortality assemblage, where a huge herd was killed when a river burst its banks. However, a 2025 study re-examined the remains and argued that these accumulated over many years and, while it's likely that {@i Hypsilophodon} was a herding animal, most died alone.

We suggest playing {@i Hypsilophodon} as a herding animal, living in groups of 20 to 50 individuals. They should feed in open spaces, where their excellent vision allows them to quickly spot predators. Some members of the herd should act as sentries and sound an alarm call if danger appears. Once startled they will usually flee, only turning to face an attacker if cornered. A {@i Hypsilophodon} with no other option will bite an attacker, but this will do little to hold off a hungry predator or determined adventurer.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Hypsilophodon}'s classification has seen a lot of revision throughout the years, although it is clearly a dinosaur. It was originally identified as an iguanodontid before later being placed in the Hypsilophodontidae. By the 21st century, Hypsilophodontidae had been re-examined and found to be invalid. Several studies moved {@i Hypsilophodon} around, identifying it as either a late-surviving primitive ornithopod or as an even more primitive animal outside of Ornithopoda altogether. The most recent analyses place it back within the ornithopods and have even suggested the resurrection of Hypsilophodontidae, now made up of {@i Hypsilophodon} and the recently described {@i Vectidromeus}.
