trait.name: Crocodile Resilience
entries: Fruitachampsa has Advantage on any checks or saving throws to avoid or end the {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned} condition.

trait.name: Skittish
entries: Fruitachampsa has Advantage on {@skill Perception} checks to spot creatures that are larger than itself.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Fruitachampsa's CR to 1/4 and increase its XP to 50 accordingly.

trait.name: Volcanic Entombment
entries: Fruitachampsa's body is encased in magical burning ash as it teeters on the boundary between life and extinction.
Fruitachampsa has Immunity to Fire damage and Resistance to Bludgeoning, Piercing, and Slashing damage. Its creature type is Elemental.
Any creature that starts its turn within 5 ft. of Fruitachampsa takes 2 Fire damage.

action.name: Pounce
entries: If Fruitachampsa is Hidden, as an Action, it may jump up to 10 ft., then make a Tiny Snap attack. If this attack hits, it deals an additional 2 Piercing damage.

action.name: Tiny Snap
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}2 (2) Piercing damage plus 1 (1) Bludgeoning damage.
"FROO-TAH-CHAMP-SAH"
{@b (FRUITA CROCODILE)}

Most laypersons and undergraduate students think of crocodiles as solely aquatic ambush predators. This is, in fact, only a tiny snippet of their past diversity and they once occupied many niches. One example is Fruitachampsa, which was about the size of a house cat, with the agility and temperament to match. It makes for an excellent demonstration of this past diversity, as it is so vastly different from what is expected of a crocodylomorph.

{@i Fruitachampsa} is a shartegosuchid crocodyliform from the Late Jurassic (149 million years ago) of Colorado, USA. Sometimes referred to as the "housecat of the Jurassic", it had exceptionally long legs for its size that gave it a slender appearance.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Fruitachampsa} may have been a small crocodylomorph at only 3 ft. long, but it was the largest shartegosuchid with a whopping 3.5 in. skull (1.5 times the size of most of its relatives) and large eyes. Its snout was short and slightly upturned, with small fangs around the middle of its jaws and teeth behind these with unusual, flattened tops. It had an elongated body with two rows of osteoderms running down the length of its back. It had tall stilt-like legs that were held perpendicular below the body (rather than sprawling out) with plantigrade (flat) feet, which indicate that it was a relatively agile animal. What it ate is something of a mystery, as its unusual teeth could be indicative of a specialised diet. It may have been an invertebrate specialist, a predator of specifically very small animals, or perhaps just a generalist carnivore.

{@i Fruitachampsa} is found in the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation in Colorado. This is one of the most well-known Jurassic fossil sites in the world and was deposited in an area of freshwater lakes and rivers with volcanic input, as well as a dune-filled desert environment in the southwest. {@i Fruitachampsa} was part of an extremely diverse fauna that includes numerous other terrestrial crocodylomorphs, pterosaurs, basal mammals, fish, and amphibians. Sauropods like {@i Apatosaurus}, {@i Brontosaurus,} and {@i Brachiosaurus} were found alongside theropods like {@i Allosaurus} ({@b page 197 in DDDD}), {@i Torvosaurus} ({@b page 321}){@i,} and {@i Ceratosaurus}. Many species of ornithischians were also present such as nodosaurid ankylosaurs, {@i Stegosaurus} ({@b page 309}), and the heterodontasaurid {@i Fruitadens}.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: There has been very little research into the behaviour of shartegosuchids, which consist of a mix of terrestrial and semi-aquatic forms. With its long legs, {@i Fruitachampsa} is generally considered to have been a carnivore that specialised in chasing prey. The Morrison Formation has a variety of food options for {@i Fruitachampsa} and it may have fed on a mix of mammals, reptiles, fish, invertebrates, and even baby dinosaurs.

We suggest playing {@i Fruitachampsa} as a highly alert animal, always on the lookout for potential prey or threats. When hunting it may move slowly, sometimes almost imperceptibly, towards its prey until it is within striking distance. Attacks should be sudden but not prolonged, with the animal quick to retreat after a failed attempt. Given its small size, it should be very wary of possible predators and, if a {@i Fruitachampsa} hears a larger animal approaching, it should be quick to hide. This means that most humanoids will never see one, as it will have disappeared into the undergrowth at the first sign of a threat.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Fruitachampsa} was part of the Shartegosuchidae. This is a small group of early branching crocodyliformes that are found almost exclusively in Asia, with {@i Fruitachampsa} being the only exception. Most shartegosuchids are known from the Late Jurassic but the group survived the Jurassic-Cretaceous extinction, persisting into the Late Cretaceous. As {@i Fruitachampsa} is only known from a very restricted place and time, we can say little about the cause of its extinction. However, based on the high percentage of ash preserved in the Morrison Formation (and especially the Brushy Basin Member), it was living in a region of high volcanic activity which may have been a contributing factor.

entries.name: References
entries: Clark, J.M. 2011. A new shartegosuchid crocodyliform from the Upper Jurassic Morrison Formation of western Colorado. {@i Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society}, {@b 163 (suppl_1)}, pp.S152-S172.

Dollman, K.N., Clark, J.M., Norell, M.A., Xing, X. and Choiniere, J.N. 2018. Convergent evolution of a eusuchian-type secondary palate within Shartegosuchidae. {@i American Museum Novitates}, {@b 2018 (3901)}, pp.1-23.

Dunagan, S.P. and Turner, C.E. 2004. Regional paleohydrologic and paleoclimatic settings of wetland/lacustrine depositional systems in the Morrison Formation (Upper Jurassic), Western Interior, USA. {@i Sedimentary Geology}, {@b 167 (3-4)}, pp.269-296.

monster.name: Giganotosaurus (Magical Variant)

trait.name: Arch-Predator
entries: Giganotosaurus cannot be easily swayed from attacking its prey. It has Advantage on Wisdom and Charisma saving throws. Additionally, Giganotosaurus cannot be Intimidated and has Immunity to the {@condition frightened|XPHB|Frightened} condition (included above).

trait.name: Tactical Legendary Resistance (2/Day)
entries: If Giganotosaurus fails a saving throw, it can choose to succeed instead. However, it can use 1 fewer Legendary Actions this round if it does so and it cannot use this Legendary Resistance if it has no more Legendary Actions available to use this round.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Giganotosaurus' CR to 11 and increase its XP to 7200 accordingly.

trait.name: Elemental Titan
entries: Giganotosaurus is magically enhanced by an elemental force. Select one element from Cold, Fire, Lightning, or Force (DM's choice).

Giganotosaurus' body is encrusted with crystal shards of that element. Its AC is increased to 17, it gains Immunity to the selected element damage type, and its attacks each deal an additional {@dice 1d12} damage of that element damage type.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Giganotosaurus chooses the Attack action, it may make two Rapid Monstrous Maw attacks.

action.name: Rapid Monstrous Maw
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 11} to hit, Reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}18 ({@damage 2d10 + 7}) Piercing damage.

This attack deals an additional {@dice 1d4} Thunder damage + {@dice 1d4} Thunder damage for each other time Giganotosaurus has attacked with Rapid Monstrous Maw this battle round (including from its Legendary Action).
If this attack misses, the Thunder damage is still dealt to the target creature.

action.name: Grab and Rip
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 11} to hit, Reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}18 ({@damage 2d10 + 7}) Piercing damage plus 18 ({@damage 2d10 + 7}) Slashing damage.

A creature hit by this attack loses all Temporary Hit Points before this attack's damage is dealt. Additionally, the hit creature is {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} (escape {@dc 19}). While grappling a creature with Grab and Rip, Giganotosaurus cannot attack another target.

legendary.name: Feint and Strike
entries: Giganotosaurus Disengages, may move up to 10 ft., then may make a single attack with its Rapid Monstrous Maw.

legendaryHeader: Giganotosaurus can take 1 Legendary Action. Only one legendary option can be used at a time and only at the end of another creature's turn. Giganotosaurus regains spent Legendary Actions at the start of its turn.

entries: "GIG-AH-NOT-OH-SORE-US"
{@b (GIANT SOUTHERN REPTILE)}

Upon undertaking the task to research the behaviour of Giganotosaurus, I suspected that I would be unable to find many records, with most of the would-be researchers devoured in their fieldwork. Interestingly, the records were extensive and many researchers report them as relative docile animals. However, the distinct lack of information regarding juveniles suggests to me that the success of their fieldwork depended entirely on whether they were disturbing the Giganotosaurus' offspring or not.

{@i Giganotosaurus} was a giant theropod from the Late Cretaceous (99 to 95 million years ago) of Argentina in South America. A truly huge animal, it is famous for being one of only a handful of carnivorous dinosaurs to compete with {@i Tyrannosaurus rex} ({@b page 192 in DDDD}) for the title of largest theropod.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: While {@i Giganotosaurus} was inarguably an exceptionally big animal, exactly how large it was is subject to some debate. Due to the incompleteness of the fossil material, its estimated size has varied over the years (see below). In recent years, new sizing techniques have emerged and, with them, has come greater consensus on just how big {@i Giganotosaurus} was. It is now believed that it was likely 41-43 ft. long and weighed approximately 7 tonnes. This makes it larger than its close relative {@i Carcharodontosaurus} ({@b page 68 in DDDD}) and slightly longer than {@i Tyrannosaurus}, although the tyrant king was a heavier, more strongly built animal. The growth strategy of {@i Meraxes} (another relative of {@i Giganotosaurus}) suggests that it grew slowly over a prolonged time frame. This is quite different from {@i Tyrannosaurus}, which is thought to have essentially experienced a teenage growth spurt, increasing rapidly in size over only a few years.
In terms of overall appearance, {@i Giganotosaurus} was very similar to {@i Carcharodontosaurus}, being a large theropod with an elongated skull that was over 5 ft. long.

Its mouth was lined with large, rather thin but serrated teeth. Its lower jaw had a distinctive point on its underside, giving it the appearance of a prominent chin. Its neck was powerfully built and attached to a strong body. While it had relatively long legs for its size, its three-fingered arms would have been quite small. Its size meant that, while its legs were powerful, it was not a particularly speedy animal.

{@i Giganotosaurus} is known from the Candeleros Formation, which was laid down in the desert floodplain of a braided river system. The fauna of the Candeleros Formation is diverse and includes a wide variety of other dinosaurs, from iguanodontians to giant titanosaur sauropods. Within the formation {@i Giganotosaurus} was by far the largest carnivore and likely preyed on most other animals, with only healthy adult titanosaurs safe from attack.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: As its overall anatomy was so similar to {@i Carcharodontosaurus}, with knife-like teeth and wide lateral vision, it's likely that {@i Giganotosaurus} behaved similarly. As it hunted large sauropods, it did not need to be particularly fast, merely able to close the ground between them and kill them with its immense slashing bite. Based on research into its close relative {@i Mapusaurus}, which has been found with several animals of different ages lying in association with each other, it has been suggested that {@i Giganotosaurus} may have hunted prey in small family groups.

We suggest that {@i Giganotosaurus} should be played as a social predator. One or two adults should commonly be found with smaller offspring. Humanoids should be little more than a curiosity to an adult {@i Giganotosaurus}, only considered food if little else is available, or if they stray too close. However, younger animals may view a party as practice prey or with fear, and either of these could trigger their parent(s) to attack. When undisturbed, an adult should largely ignore parties giving them a wide berth and should be found, more often than not, resting under cover or playing with its young.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Giganotosaurus} is one of the largest members of the Carcharodontosauridae. This group arose in the Late Jurassic (154 million years ago) and were widespread throughout Gondwana (the southern hemisphere continents), with some representation during the Cretaceous in North America and Europe. It was at this time that they became truly enormous, reaching sizes only a handful of other theropods achieved. The group died out around 89 million years ago, seemingly as part of a large faunal exchange, and in later years their role as superpredators was filled by the tyrannosaurids.

entries.name: Sizing You Up
entries: Correctly measuring the size of dinosaurs is consistently challenging. As the vast majority of species are known only from partial material, palaeontologists rely on comparative anatomy and data analyses to estimate the sizes of incomplete animals. While these estimates are supported by rigorous research, different scientists can get very different results based on the material available or the techniques used. {@i Giganotosaurus} is an excellent example of this, since it was the first theropod to gain a lot of media attention for potentially being larger than {@i T}. {@i rex}. In fact, much of the research into it is focused on its size. The original description's estimates were based on comparisons with theropods like {@i Torvosaurus} ({@b page 321}) and {@i Allosaurus} ({@b page 197 in DDDD}), suggesting a 5 ft. skull on a 41 ft. long body, with a weight of between 6-8 tonnes. However, later research, informed by other specimens and more comparisons with more closely related carcharodontosaurs, greatly increased its size estimates. Some suggested it was 47 ft. long and could have weighed as much as 20 tonnes. These extreme ranges would then be revised again as more reliable techniques for estimating size were developed (e.g. using more advanced 3D modelling). This has led to {@i Giganotosaurus} being more conservatively measured at the size mentioned in the Ecology section above (interestingly, very close to the first estimate).

trait.name: Handlebars
entries: Gigantspinosaurus can be ridden by a Medium or Small humanoid without the aid of a saddle, although it is rather uncomfortable

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Gigantspinosaurus' CR to 3 and increase its XP to 700 accordingly.
{@b {@i Bilespew (Recharge 4-6)}}{@i. As an Action, Gigantspinosaurus is able to vomit a disgusting mixture of plant material and stomach acid in an arching spray in front of it.}

Any creature within a 20 ft. line directly in front of Gigantspinosaurus must make a {@dc 12} Dexterity saving throw, taking {@dice 4d6} Acid damage on a failed save or half as much damage on a success.

trait.name: Noxious Body
entries: Gigantspinosaurus' creature type becomes Undead and it has Immunity to Necrotic damage.

Gigantspinosaurus is covered in weeping blisters and reeks of foul rot and vomit. Any creature that starts its turn within or moves within 20 ft. of Gigantspinosaurus must succeed a {@dc 12} Constitution saving throw or have Disadvantage on melee attacks against Gigantspinosaurus until the start of their next turn.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Gigantspinosaurus chooses the Attack action, it can make two Tail Swipe attacks. Alternatively, it can make one Tail Swipe and one Spined Shoulder-Bash if it moved at least 15 ft. in a straight line before reaching the target.

action.name: Tail swipe
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}9 ({@damage 2d6 + 2}) Piercing damage.

action.name: Spined Shoulder-Bash
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 6} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}7 ({@damage 1d10 + 2}) Bludgeoning damage plus 7 ({@damage 1d10 + 2}) Piercing damage.
This attack may only be performed if Gigantspinosaurus moved at least 15 ft. in a straight line before reaching the target this turn.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 12} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.

reaction.name: Extreme Defence
entries: If Gigantspinosaurus is hit by a melee attack within 5 ft., as a Reaction, it can push its defensive spines into the attacking creature.

If the attacking creature is larger than Gigantspinosaurus, it takes {@dice 3d6 + 2} Piercing damage. If it is the same size as or smaller than Gigantspinosaurus, it takes {@dice 1d6 + 2} Piercing damage.
"GIG-ANT-SPY-NO-SAUR-US"
{@b (GIANT SPINED REPTILE)}

Armoured slow herbivores can be interesting encounters on an adventure. Their in-built protection affords them a sense of invulnerability that renders the average humanoid a complete non-threat. You do have to be careful, mind you. The spikes and spines of some of those animals are truly preposterous in size and would be quite the disaster to fall upon.

{@i Gigantspinosaurus} was a medium-sized stegosaur from the Middle Jurassic (160 million years ago) Upper Shiaxmo Formation of China. Its greatest distinguishing feature is a pair of giant backwards curving spines jutting out of its shoulders.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Gigantspinosaurus} was a stegosaur measuring about 14 ft. long and weighing 1.5 tonnes. In many ways it was a very typical member of Stegosauria, with short, spiky plates along its back, a small beaked head, powerful tail, and robust limbs. It differed from other members in the shape of its shoulder spines, which were enormous relative to its size and had a strong backwards sweeping curve. This gave them an almost hooked shape. Although structures like this were quite common within Stegosauria ({@i Stegosaurus} itself is unusual for not having them, {@b page 309}), those in {@i Gigantspinosaurus} are particularly extreme.

As with all stegosaurs, {@i Gigantspinosaurus} was a herbivore. It was specialised in feeding at low levels, browsing from thick branches or shrubbery. Its narrow mouth was filled with triangular teeth and ended in a toothless beak. This suggests that it was a highly selective feeder, cropping tough or woody plants. This specialisation is an example of competitive exclusion, whereby it avoided competing for food with other generalist herbivores.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Stegosaurs are not typically found in association with each other and so it is reasonable to suggest that they did not live in social groups. Instead, it seems that they were probably relatively solitary animals that only came together for mating. Their spiked tails would have been useful for display or intraspecific (same species) fighting, as well as defence from predators.

We recommend that {@i Gigantspinosaurus} be played as a relatively peaceful and non-aggressive animal, but with a clear sense of its own personal space. Parties that encroach on this space will draw the animal's ire and it will quickly shift from gentle to aggressive. Rather than retreating, it will almost always stand its ground and fight.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Gigantspinosaurus} is a member of the Stegosauria, a highly successful group of armoured dinosaurs that first appeared in the Middle Jurassic (169 million years ago) and survived into the Early Cretaceous (100 million years ago). Discovered in 1985, {@i Gigantspinosaurus} was originally something of a contested genus. Its remains were first described as the Chinese stegosaur {@i Tuojiangosaurus}, but a year later an unpublished lecture abstract described it as the new genus {@i Gigantspinosaurus}. As the abstract was thought to be lacking sufficient detail and unpublished lectures are rarely treated as adequate for erecting a new genus, the re-identification was generally disregarded. It would not be formally recognised until the 2000s, when researchers reanalysed the holotype and published their confirmation that it was indeed a distinct animal. Following a redescription in 2018, {@i Gigantspinosaurus} is now considered to be a transitional animal, showing characteristics of both the early branching (huayangosaurids) and derived stegosaurids like {@i Kentrosaurus} ({@b page 138 in DDDD}) and {@i Stegosaurus} ({@b page 309}).

entries: Helicoprion has Resistance to Cold and Thunder damage (included above) and can only breathe underwater.

Opportunity Attacks when moving out of an enemy's reach. Additionally, if Helicoprion hits a creature with an attack, then subsequently moves out of that creature's reach this turn, that creature takes {@dice 1d6} Slashing damage.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules

trait.name: Chainsaw Jaw
entries: Helicoprion's jaw spins rapidly, acting like a circular saw. If a creature is hit by Helicoprion's Whorling Bite attack, select one non-magical object that that creature is wearing or wielding and roll a {@dice d20}. On a 1-9, nothing happens. On a roll of 10-20, that object is destroyed.

trait.name: Not-So-Little Mermaid
entries: Helicoprion gains a walking speed of 30 ft. and can breathe in air.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Helicoprion chooses the Attack action, it may make up to two Whorling Bite attacks.

action.name: Whorling Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 6} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}(see below) Piercing damage.

When a creature is hit by Whorling Bite, roll successive 1d8s until you roll a 1. For each dice rolled in this manner, the hit creature takes 2 Piercing damage (up to a maximum of 24 and minimum of 2). Rolling a critical hit doubles this damage amount, rather than doubling the damage dice rolled.
"HEL-EH-COH-PRY-ON"
{@b (SPIRAL SAW)}

Sharks are very ancient organisms and have evolved all manner of unusual adaptations over their long history. One such oddity is Helicoprion. This strange, sleek, and large shark has a bizarre maw with a spiral whorl of teeth.
It is... hypnotic to watch feed. However, don't let the strangeness of this animal lure you into a daze of curiosity.
After all, it is still a very large predator.

{@i Helicoprion} is a large shark-like holocephalian (a group of cartilaginous fish) from the Early Permian (290 million years ago) with a global distribution. A distant relative of the modern chimera or ratfish, its most distinctive feature was the buzzsaw-like ring of fused teeth (termed a whorl) held in its lower jaw.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: As holocephalians are cartilaginous fish, most of their bodies, excluding their teeth and jaws, do not preserve well and are rarely found. Unfortunately, we have only found the hard parts of {@i Helicoprion,} but due to some fossils of related animals with soft tissue, we can make some informed guesses about its anatomy and biology. Size estimates based on the tooth whorls suggest it grew to 16 to 26 ft. long and likely had a long fusiform (torpedo-shaped) body. Like a shark, it would have had a triangular dorsal fin with pointed pectorals (front fins) and its tail would have been forked with equally sized fins. However, its most distinctive feature was the tooth whorl. Looking a little like a buzzsaw made of teeth, up until recently the placement of the whorl has been highly contentious. Researchers have reconstructed it as hanging beneath the lower jaw, curling up from the tip of the head and even as part of the dorsal or tail fins. More recent evidence argues that the whorl was placed centrally in the lower jaw, forming a spiral structure by retaining older teeth and having new ones overgrow them. Based on tooth wear and biomechanics, it's thought that this is a structure specialised for feeding on soft bodied organisms or unarmoured fish, but exactly how the whorl functioned is still poorly understood.

{@i Helicoprion} has been found all around the world, but most specimens have come from the Phosphoria Formation. This is a deep marine deposit that crops out across western North America. Multiple species of shellfish, sponges, ammonoids, and jawless fish are found in this formation, as well as several other cartilaginous fish, including at least one species of shell-crushing (durophagus) holocephalian.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: The function of {@i Helicoprion}'s tooth whorl has been debated for years with many different hypotheses proposed. These range from it being some sort of specialised defence mechanism, to being used to crack ammonoid shells, to scraping flesh off of carcasses. As mentioned above, the evidence strongly supports it specialising in soft-bodied animals, however, one research paper suggested that the whorl was used to hunt armoured cephalopods, like ammonoids, tearing them out of their shells with a quick bite. While this is an interesting idea, it's important to remember that, because we have no modern analogue to {@i Helicoprion}'s tooth whorl, any hypothesis remains speculative.

We suggest playing {@i Helicoprion} as a constantly moving animal, often found cruising in sparse numbers in deeper waters where swarms of ammonites and other cephalopods can be found. When hunting they should rapidly rush at their prey, aiming to bite it before it has a chance to react. While big enough to be a major threat to humanoids, a {@i Helicoprion} should not normally hunt such unusual prey. However, foolish swimmers may still be attacked by a particularly curious or hungry individual, and will be shredded by its razor-toothed whorl.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Helicoprion} is a member of the Holocephali. This is a group of cartilaginous fish that is the sister group to sharks and rays. They first appeared in the Devonian 387 million years ago and were originally a very diverse group with some members leaning more towards shark-like morphology, and others being more ray-like. From the Permian onwards, the group went into a lengthy, but steady, decline with {@i Helicoprion} itself disappearing approximately 270 million years ago. By the Middle Triassic only three families remained, and were reduced to one during the Jurassic. That group, the Chimeroidea, has survived into modern times with 56 extant (living today) species known.

trait.name: Agile Forest Predator
entries: Herrerasaurus can Disengage as a Bonus Action (see Rapid Disengage), has Advantage on {@skill Stealth} checks while in wooded areas, and, if it succeeds on a Dexterity saving throw to take half damage from an effect, it instead takes no damage.

trait.name: Intraspecific Combat
entries: Herrerasaurus treats any other Herrerasaurus as an enemy, unless it is of the opposite sex and seeking to mate.

trait.name: Cathemeral
entries: Herrerasaurus only requires 4 hours of sleep to complete a Long Rest and has a Darkvision of 60 ft. (included above).

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, you do not need to change Herrerasaurus' CR.

trait.name: Confusing Anatomy
entries: Herrerasaurus' confusing phylogenetic affinities render its physical form malleable and disorientating to observe.

As an Action, it can take on the general appearance of another Medium or Large dinosaurian/reptilian Beast. This disguise is quite superficial, and a creature will be alerted to it being unusual if its passive Perception is 14 or higher. The disguise may be revealed in full by a {@dc 10} {@skill Perception} or {@skill Investigation} check, or if Herrerasaurus attacks.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Herrerasaurus chooses the Attack action, it may make two Ripping Grasping Bite attacks.

action.name: Ripping Grasping Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}4 ({@damage 1d6 + 1}) Piercing damage plus 3 ({@damage 1d4 + 1}) Slashing Damage.

A creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} (escape {@dc 11}). While Grappling a creature in this way, Herrerasaurus cannot attack any other creature with its Ripping Grasping Bite attack
A creature {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} by this attack suffers {@dice 1d4 + 1} Slashing damage at the start of that creature's turn.

bonus.name: Rapid Retreat
entries: Herrerasaurus Disengages as a Bonus Action.
"HAIR-RARE-AH-SORE-US"
{@b (HERRERA'S LIZARD)}

Recounts of this strange predatory reptile are often inconsistent. Some describe it skulking in the shadows within dense forests, others as a fast-paced plains hunter chasing down smaller prey. I fear that both are correct and that this adaptable carnivore could be around any corner. I suggest keeping a watchful eye out in these lands, particularly as dusk falls.

{@i Herrerasaurus} was a small carnivorous dinosaur from the Late Triassic (230 million years ago) of San Juan, Argentina. One of the oldest dinosaurs discovered so far, where exactly it falls in the dinosaur family tree has been the subject of debate for many years.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Herrerasaurus} was a bipedal animal that measured between 15 and 20 ft. long, and likely weighed about 200-360 lb. As dinosaurs first appeared in the Late Triassic and the larger forms would not evolve for some time, this made {@i Herrerasaurus} the biggest dinosaurian predator of its time. Its forearms were relatively short, but it had five fingers on each hand. Of these, three ended in sharp grasping claws while the last two were vestigial (non-functional), lacked any claws, and were positioned in such a way that the flesh of the hand would have covered them up. Its legs were strong and suggest {@i Herrerasaurus} was a speedy animal. Its skull was long, somewhat resembling that of pre-dinosaurian archosaurs. Its teeth were small, triangular, and serrated. Unusually for a dinosaur, {@i Herrerasaurus} had a flexible joint at the articulation where the upper and lower jaw met, allowing the jaw to slide backwards and forwards. This would have allowed {@i Herrerasaurus} to flex its jaw as it bit down on struggling prey, making it easier for it to hold.

{@i Herrerasaurus} was discovered in the Ischigualasto Formation. This is a Late Triassic unit from Argentina that was laid down in a forested semi-volcanic seasonal floodplain. The formation is highly fossiliferous and contains numerous other animals, including several other dinosaurs like basal sauropodomorphs and theropods, large archosaurs, small dinosauriformes (non-dinosaurian reptiles that were the sister group to true dinosaurs, see below), basal crocodylomorphs, and mammal-like synapsids.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: While quite large, {@i Herrerasaurus} likely did not specialise in hunting large prey. This niche was already filled by big non-dinosaurian predators, and it is believed that {@i Herrerasaurus} instead primarily fed on smaller speedier prey. Healed bite marks from another large carnivore have also been taken as evidence that {@i Herrerasaurus} itself was preyed upon by bulkier predators. However, it has also been suggested that this bite was the result of one {@i Herrerasaurus} being bitten by another, perhaps in a squabble for mates or territory. Examinations of its sclerotic rings (circles of bone that encapsulate the eye) suggest that it was a cathemeral animal. This means that, rather than being active mostly during the day or night, {@i Herrerasaurus} would be active throughout a 24-hour cycle sleeping 4 or 5 times a day for a few hours at a time.

We suggest playing {@i Herrerasaurus} as a speedy, largely solitary predator that gathers in groups seasonally to mate. When alone they should be alert predators with unpredictable behaviour patterns, as likely to be encountered in the day as at night. When hunting they should rely on their ability to run down their prey and may be willing to chase a potential meal across some distance. If a party passes through their territory during the mating season, the animals should be too engaged in fights or courtship to pay them much mind. Otherwise, Small and Medium humanoids should immediately be seen as potential prey and at high risk of attack.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Herrerasaurus'} phylogeny is complex and poorly understood. As discussed below, ascribing basal and early forms to their correct groups can be difficult. At various times, {@i Herrerasaurus} has been identified as a theropod, a sauropodomorph, an early saurischian, and as a non-dinosaurian member of Dinosauriformes. While some debate remains, the current consensus is that it is an early saurischian belonging to the clade Herrerasauridae. This is a group of Late Triassic (233 million years ago) carnivores that are most well-known from South America but have also been found in both North America and Africa, with some potential evidence in Europe too. They were a successful group, with {@i Herrerasaurus} in particular being quite numerous. However, with the appearance of more derived theropods towards the end of the Triassic, the herrarasaurids seem to have been outcompeted and the group died out approximately 228 million years ago.

entries.name: When Is a Dinosaur Not a Dinosaur?
entries: Dinosaurs are inarguably the most famous and beloved prehistoric animals. Yet, one question that many laypersons and no small number of palaeontologists have struggled to answer is when dinosaurs first appeared and how exactly do we differentiate them from their immediate ancestors and closest relatives. As true dinosaurs are present in the fossil record by the Late Triassic, we can safely say the group must have evolved either at the start of the Late Triassic or sometime in the Middle Triassic. While this is simple enough to give a broad answer to when they evolved, how to separate dinosaurs from more basal dinosauriformes is much more complex to answer. Many of the classic characteristics that we associate with dinosaurs, such as their legs being held underneath the body, are quite common in non-dinosaurian archosaurs. Recent studies identifying potential feathers in pterosaurs might even suggest that these classically dinosaurian structures have their origins earlier in Archosauria. While we do have some features that we can use to identify true dinosaurs, such as the structure of the ankle, the relative length of the radius to the humerus, the number of vertebrae incorporated into the sacrum (fused vertebrae in the pelvis) etc., things become much murkier when you look at more transitional animals, which may have a combination of derived and basal characters.

One reason {@i Herrerasaurus} has been so difficult to place over the years is that it has a combination of dinosaurian (e.g. general structure of the pelvis, shape of the body of the vertebrae) and non-dinosaurian (only two vertebrae in the sacrum, third finger of the hand longer than the second, partially open hip socket) features. Scientists have had to question whether it was a dinosaur that had retained more primitive traits or whether it was a dinosauriform that developed advanced ones. Similar issues arise when studying other groups, such as firmly identifying basal avian dinosaurs (birds) from derived non-avian ones.

We should also be aware that no species appears out of nowhere fully developed. Animals transition from one form to another over many generations, with lengthy periods where species may not neatly fit into our ancestor/ descendent definitions. When considering what makes something a dinosaur, we should be aware that we are looking at how animals best fit in the evolutionary tree of life, rather than creating a hard definition that will let us organise the fossil record into neat little boxes.

trait.name: Swift Stalker
entries: Inostrancevia has Advantage on {@skill Stealth} checks. If it begins its turn Hidden, until the end of its turn it may Dash as a Bonus Action.

entries: Inostrancevia has Resistance to Slashing damage (included above).

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Inostrancevia's CR to 4 and increase its XP to 1100 accordingly.

trait.name: Bonus Actions

entries.name: Gorgon's Gaze (Recharge 3-6)
entries: As a Bonus Action, Inostrancevia may unleash a Medusa-like gaze on its foes.

Each creature in a 30 ft. cone in front of Inostrancevia that can see it must make a {@dc 13} Constitution saving throw. On a failed save, the creature is {@condition restrained|XPHB|Restrained} and must repeat the saving throw at the end of its next turn (ending the effect on a success). If the creature fails this second saving throw, it instead becomes {@condition petrified|XPHB|Petrified} until freed by a Greater Restoration spell or similar effect.
If Inostrancevia can see its reflection when using this ability, it must also make the saving throws.

action.name: Gaping Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 6} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}15 ({@damage 2d8 + 6}) Piercing damage.
A creature smaller than Inostrancevia hit by this attack is {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} (escape {@dc 14}).

action.name: Saber-toothed Rip
entries: Inostrancevia attempts to rip the flesh of a creature that it is currently Grappling. That creature must make a {@dc 14} Constitution saving throw, taking 22 ({@damage 3d10 + 6}) Slashing damage on a failed save or half as much on a successful save.
A creature that takes damage from this attack has Disadvantage on checks to break its Grapple with Inostrancevia for the next 1 minute.
{@i "IN-AUS-TRAN-SEE-VEE-AH"} {@b (IN HONOUR OF GEOLOGIST ALEKSANDR INOSTRANTSEV)}

When we discuss saber-toothedness in lectures, all students invariably defer to Smilodon as the most prominent and first example in the fossil record. This is, of course, incorrect and many taxa throughout history have evolved to have saber teeth.
One such example is the ferocious Inostrancevia, which I have, thus far, had the good fortune to avoid in my expeditions.

{@i Inostrancevia} was a large gorgonopsian from the Late Permian (259 million years ago) of Russia and Africa. It was a carnivorous synapsid with elongated saber-like canines which evolved to carry out a similar function as those seen in later mammals like the famous {@i Smilodon} ({@b page 105}).

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Inostrancevia} was one of the largest gorgonopsians known. It was about the size of a bear, 10 ft. long and weighed more than 750 lb. It had a bulky body with proportionally long limbs and flat feet. Its front legs were semi-sprawling but its hind limbs were more upright and positioned beneath the body. Its tall boxy skull was enormous, making up almost a fifth of its length, with a deep jaw and powerful bite. Its teeth were divided into incisors, canines, and postcanines, although the latter were only present on the upper jaw. The canines on both jaws were elongated and curving, modified into the classic "saber" morphology seen in later carnivores like {@i Smilodon} or the South American marsupial {@i Thylacosmilus}. Like them, it was able to open its jaws extremely wide, with a gape close to 90°.

{@i Inostrancevia} is known from several Late Permian (259 to 252 million years ago) formations such as the Russian Salarevo and the Tanzanian Usili formations. These were generally laid down in semi-arid environments, dry plains interspersed by lakes or rivers. In Russia it was the dominant predator, with the other synapsid carnivores being noticeably smaller. In Africa however, it faced stiffer competition from other large gorgonopsians like {@i Rubidgea}. Alongside these arch predators were amphibious temnospondyls, dicynodonts, large herbivorous reptiles like {@i Scutosaurus}, and in Africa several species of basal archosauromorph.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Inostrancevia} was not built for speed and likely relied on lunging at prey from cover to catch it unaware. Once tackled, researchers think it either delivered a slashing bite or ripped out a chunk of flesh. If this failed to kill the prey, it would have backed off after the initial attack, waiting for them to collapse from either blood loss or shock.

We suggest playing {@i Inostrancevia} as a semi-solitary animal, spending most of the year alone with females approached by multiple males during the breeding season. These encounters can quickly turn violent and fights easily break out, whether between rival males or a female driving off an unwanted suitor. Most {@i Inostrancevia} should bear the scars from these encounters, with some surviving extreme wounds, such as having a snapped-off canine from an attacker still embedded in their snout. When hunting, they should be extremely patient, positioning themselves ahead of a herd and waiting for just the right opportunity to ambush an unsuspecting passerby. Unwary humanoids approaching will be seen as easy prey and may quickly find themselves in a life-or-death battle.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Inostrancevia} is one of the largest members of the Gorgonopsia. This is a group of carnivorous synapsids that first appeared in the fossil record approximately 270 million years ago. The oldest known gorgonopsian material is from the Permian of Mallorca, Spain, but the group eventually spread throughout Eurasia and Africa. Starting out as small fox-sized predators, they rapidly increased in size throughout their evolution with the later species becoming the arch predators of their environments. As one of the largest, {@i Inostrancevia} was highly successful, being the only gorgonopsian known from more than one continent. All gorgonopsians went extinct approximately 252 million years ago during the Permo-Triassic extinction event, where volcanic activity in Siberia led to massive climate change, reduced sunlight, and ocean acidification. The disappearance of the gorgonopsians left the niche of large terrestrial carnivores empty until it was eventually filled by the archosaurs, including dinosaurs.

entries.name: Throughout Time
entries: While numerous synapsid groups have evolved elongated canines throughout evolutionary history, only a small number have convergently evolved the "saber-tooth" morphology. This includes therapsids like the gorgonopsians, the marsupial thylacosmilids, the non-carnivoran mammals the oxyaenids, the cat-like nimravids and barboufelids, and the truly feline machairodonts (such as {@i Smilodon}). The repeated evolution of these teeth has led scientists to wonder what benefits they provide, as the rest of the skull needs to be modified to allow a wide gape in order to use them properly. Having such long canines also makes them more vulnerable to stress and breakage when biting. Several recent studies have looked at the biomechanics of saber-teeth and what their functional advantage is, arguing that these sharp flattened teeth allowed the animal to puncture or slash flesh much more deeply than the more commonly seen conical teeth of modern cats or dogs. Their extreme size not only makes them better weapons but allows the teeth to stand up to more stress without snapping. They also found that, while animals like {@i Smilodon} were well-adapted for the classic canine-sheer bite model ({@b page 105}), this was not a "one size fits all" approach and different species with their own saber morphology would have used distinct hunting strategies, although what these were is still being debated.

bonus.name: Submerge

"EAR-IH-TAY-TOR"
{@b (FROM THE ENGLISH WORD IRRITATION)}

While modern lagoons are generally places of relaxation and respite, Cretaceous lagoons are an entirely different beast. This is solely because of the presence of one group of animals - the spinosaurs. These large, predatory dinosaurs specialise in eating fish, but will happily opportunistically try to eat humanoids. One particularly troublesome member of this group is the aptly named Irritator.

{@i Irritator} was a spinosaurid from the Early Cretaceous (110 million years ago) Romualdo Formation of Brazil, South America. A close relative of the African giant {@i Spinosaurus} ({@b Page 74 in DDDD}), it was amusingly named after just how much irritation the researchers experienced working on the holotype (first described specimen).

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Irritator} is only known from a partial skeleton of a subadult animal, but comparisons with other genera suggest that the adult animal would have been relatively small for a spinosaurid, likely no bigger than 26 ft. long. Its morphology was fairly standard for the group, with long, notched jaws, conical teeth, tall vertebrae, and large claws. Like other spinosaurs, {@i Irritator} had close ties to water. A study on the anatomy of {@i Irritator}'s brain suggests that it may have held its head with the jaws pointed down at about a 45 degree angle. This would have given it a wide visual range without its snout getting in the way, and allowed it to submerge its jaws in water without covering its nostrils, while it scanned the water for passing prey.

{@i Irritator} was originally found in the Romualdo Formation, which is adjacent to the Crato Formation of Brazil ({@b pages 96-111 in DDDD}). This is an Early Cretaceous tropical-to-arid lagoonal and fluvial (river) deposit. The formation has yielded a high number of exceptionally preserved fossils including numerous species of insects, arachnids, fish, pterosaurs, turtles, crocodylomorphs, and a handful of other theropod dinosaurs.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: The distinctive anatomy of {@i Irritator} suggests that it was a large piscivorous predator that may have primarily waded out into coastal lagoons or patiently waited along riverbanks to snap up passing fish. Its jaws were relatively weak but could snap shut extremely quickly and, combined with its well-developed binocular vision, it likely hunted by standing motionlessly in/near water and snapping very rapidly at passing fish. A recent study in 2023 examining the structure of {@i Irritator}'s jaws suggested that {@i Irritator} was able to rotate the sides of its lower jaw, allowing it to widen the back of its jaw and increase the size of its gape. A similar, albeit much more extreme, arrangement is found in modern pelicans. If correct, it is probable that {@i Irritator} had a large, well-developed gular pouch (throat sac) to hold captured prey in. However, it is important to remember that the {@i Irritator} holotype has undergone significant taphonomic changes that may have deformed the bone, so we recommend caution when interpreting unusual results like these.

We suggest that {@i Irritator} be played as an inhabitant of rivers, deltas, and lagoons. It should usually be seen standing in or near shallow water patiently waiting for unwary prey to pass by, or resting in the shade along the edge of a nearby tree-line. Unwary players who wander too close may be seen as an easy meal, but {@i Irritator} should be hesitant to stray too far from the water's edge without a good reason. It should be quick to avoid wasting unnecessary energy chasing prey that's moving away from the water unless it is starving. Smaller humanoids should be at risk of the animal attempting to swallow them whole, even if they're too big to go down easily and may find themselves in the unenviable position of being either stuck struggling in the animal's gullet or being regurgitated up in a pile of fish.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Irritator} was originally identified as a maniraptoran, a broad clade including everything from dromaeosaurs to therizinosaurs to birds. However, it soon became clear that the fossil had been tampered with and this obscured many of the diagnostic features. Re-examination, particularly with knowledge from the then recently discovered British spinosaur {@i Baryonyx}, made it clear that {@i Irritator} was indeed a member of the Spinosauridae. Further research indicated that it, along with several other Brazilian spinosaurs, were members of the Spinosaurinae, the sub group which includes {@i Spinosaurus} itself. Spinosaurs are thought to have first appeared in Europe approximately 140 million years ago. Some taxa migrated into Africa at least 125 million years ago and it has been hypothesised that the close proximity of South America to Africa in the Cretaceous allowed for dispersal of various animals, such as spinosaurs, between the two continents.

{@i "JAH-KAH-PILL"} {@b (SHIELD BEARER)}

Quiet adventurers sneaking through Cretaceous scrubland may catch the sounds of small chirping dinosaurs scrambling through the undergrowth. With enough patience, they may be privy to the comings and goings of a Jakapil herd. These tiny armoured dinosaurs are exceedingly skittish, but delightful to behold.

{@i Jakapil} was a small dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous (97 to 94 million years ago) of Argentina. A strange animal that looked something like a cross between a tiny {@i Ankylosaurus} and a theropod dinosaur, it is an excellent example of how difficult it can be to confirm the relationships of some particularly unusual fossil animals.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Jakapil} is known from a single incomplete specimen. It was a relatively small dinosaur, probably no more than 5 ft. long, and was bipedal, with small forelimbs and a body covered in spiky armour. Its head was quite short and stocky, almost appearing oversized for its body. The lower jaw was especially thick towards the back. At the tip of its jaw, it had a small keratinous beak, as well as no teeth on its premaxilla (the front portion of the jaw). Its teeth instead start in the middle section (maxilla) and were arranged along the jaw into a straight row. These teeth were compressed with a leaf-like shape, with multiple rounded ridges along their top margin. The morphology of {@i Jakapil}'s teeth indicate that it was a herbivore and the thickness of its jaw, combined with the narrow snout, suggest it cropped plants with its beak and chewed them, rather than swallowing them whole.

{@i Jakapil} is from the Candeleros Formation, a Late Cretaceous arid floodplain. It shared its environment with a wide variety of dinosaurs including the giant theropod {@i Giganotosaurus} ({@b page 229}) and giant sauropods. In fact, it was one of the smallest dinosaurs in the assemblage and the only non-sauropod herbivore to be described based on a body fossil.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Jakapil}'s osteoderms (bony armour plating) were undoubtedly a good form of protection against predators, but given its relatively small size, it is unlikely that it stood its ground as a first option. It is more likely that, when threatened, it would flee, only turning on its attacker if given no other options, and even then, relying largely on its spiked armour to injure attackers. Its relatively bulky frame and defences mean that, if it did go on the offensive, it would be capable of driving off predators if they were of a comparable size.

We suggest playing {@i Jakapil} as a rather skittish creature that tends to flee if confronted by a threat. Like some ankylosaurs, it should have a high-pitched, almost bird-like, call, and many player characters should be much more familiar with hearing a {@i Jakapil} rather than seeing one. If cornered, it should be quick to lash out but with gentle coercing could be drawn towards a careful player by the promise of food.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: The relationships of {@i Jakapil} are currently uncertain. The original research paper described it as a thyreophoran (the armoured dinosaurs including ankylosaurids, stegosaurids, nodosaurs, and their relatives), falling as either a very early branching ankylosaurid or a more primitive thyreophoran like {@i Scelidosaurus} ({@b page 172 in DDDD}). At first glance this seems reasonable, given its extensive armour and the fact that some early thyreophorans could also walk bipedally. However, a more recent study in 2023 has called this identification into question. Researchers argued that, based on the lack of teeth in the premaxilla, the depth of the jaw, and the shape of the teeth, that {@i Jakapil} was much more likely to belong to the Marginocephalia. This group includes the likes of {@i Pachycephalosaurus} ({@b page 274}) and {@i Triceratops} ({@b page 324}), as well as a wide range of other animals from horned giants to lightly built bipeds. Further research is clearly necessary to accurately place {@i Jakapil} and establish its significance in dinosaur evolutionary history, but it is far from unique in this. Sadly, due to the limitations of the fossil record, it is just one of many extinct species whose affinities we are still figuring out. Here, we have maintained the original suggestion of a basal thyreophoran.

entries.name: References
entries: Raven, T.J., Barrett, P.M., Joyce, C.B. and Maidment, S.C. 2023. The phylogenetic relationships and evolutionary history of the armoured dinosaurs (Ornithischia: Thyreophora). {@i Journal of Systematic Palaeontology}, {@b 21 (1)}, pp.2205433.

Riguetti, F.J., Apesteguía, S. and Pereda-Suberbiola, X. 2022. A new Cretaceous thyreophoran from Patagonia supports a South American lineage of armoured dinosaurs. {@i Scientific Reports}, {@b 12 (1)}, pp.11621.

"KELL-EN-KEN"
{@b (NAMED AFTER A BIRD-LIKE PATAGONIAN SPIRIT)}

Terror birds rightfully earn their names. These rather large and extremely fast animals are brutal predators that shred both parties and prey (often synonyms as far as the birds are concerned) with lethal kicks and massive beak strikes. I would advise avoiding them, but usually once they're spotted, you're already within charging range.

{@i Kelenken} is a large flightless bird from the Miocene (15 million years ago) of Argentina. It is the tallest member of the Phorusrachidae, a group of carnivores commonly referred to as the terror birds.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Kelenken} has been estimated to be between 6.5 and 10 ft. tall and looked superficially like a predatory ostrich. It had long legs that ended in four-toed feet with the first toe being small and unable to reach the ground. The second toe was held up with a modified sickle-shaped claw, similar to that of a dromaeosaur (like {@i Velociraptor} ({@b page 182 in DDDD})). It had an oval body with tiny wings, a long neck, and an exceptionally large head tipped with an enormous, hooked beak. Its skull was more than 2 ft. long, the longest of any bird, and it has been estimated that {@i Kelenken} weighed more than 200 lb., which while heavy, is lighter than some of its more robust relatives. This comparatively lighter size combined with their long legs meant that {@i Kelenken} was a speedy animal, capable of running down large mammalian prey.

{@i Kelenken} is found in the Collón Curá Formation in Patagonia, Argentina, which was deposited in a floodplain that included rivers, lakes, and a nearby volcano. Overall, {@i Kelenken} inhabited open semi-arid shrublands alongside a wide variety of quite bizarre animals including ground sloths, the saber-toothed marsupial {@i Patagosmilus}, several deer, tapir-like hoofed herbivores, and early new-world monkeys.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Despite the size of its skull, {@i Kelenken} did not possess a powerful bite. Instead it may have hunted prey by using its speed to run them down before pinning them with its talons. It would then kill them with several rapid strikes from its beak to their skull. As they were pursuit predators with high energy demands, it's likely that {@i Kelenken} did not live in large social groups. Instead they may have been solitary or hunted in pairs, perhaps gathering in small flocks during a breeding season.

We suggest playing {@i Kelenken} as a hyper-alert predator, constantly scanning the horizon for food. Once spotted, they should stalk their prey quietly, getting as close as they can, before bursting into a high-speed charge. Pursuits should be sudden but short, with {@i Kelenken} quickly giving up if it fails to reach its prey. Attacks on humanoids should almost always be driven by hunger and it should see slow-moving humanoids as a relatively easy meal, although it will quickly retreat if they fight back. When breeding or socialising, they should be seen doing elaborate mating rituals such as bobbing head movements or energetic dances.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: The Phorusrhacidae was a largely South American group of carnivorous Cariamiforme birds (represented in modern times by seriemas) that arose in the Middle Eocene (43 million years ago). Phorusrhacids were highly successful within South America, but had limited success further afield, with only one definitive species, {@i Titanis}, found in North America. The giant forms of the phorusrhacids went extinct approximately 1.8 million years ago, with some debate over the cause. Competition with migrating mammals from North America has been the most popular hypothesis, but this has been challenged by strong evidence that they lived alongside mammalian predators for several million years in both continents. Smaller forms survived for much longer in countries like Uruguay and Brazil, with the last dying out approximately 25,000 years ago.
Phorusrhacos longissimus skeleton and skull

"KOO-ME-MAH-NEW"
{@b (BIRD MONSTER)}

Penguins are interesting and adorable animals to encounter. Their curious nature brings them to many adventuring camps and their playful vocalisations provide much entertainment (if you can ignore the fishy smell). However, ancient penguins don't carry quite the same charm - particularly the enormous Kumimanu, which towers over shorter adventurers and packs a powerful peck.

{@i Kumimanu} was an enormous early penguin from the Paleocene (60 million years ago) of Canterbury, New Zealand. Growing to the same height as a human, it was the largest penguin in the fossil record.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Kumimanu} was one of several species of giant penguin that evolved in the Paleocene. Large individuals grew to almost 6 ft. tall and could weigh up to 350 lb. It looked very similar to a typical penguin, standing upright with stubby legs and broad webbed feet. Its wings were modified into flippers and it had a long, pointed beak. As all penguins possess countershading (dark feathers on top, pale beneath) that acts as camouflage in water, it is very likely that {@i Kumimanu} did too. Its feathers would have been tightly packed, providing it with insulation when swimming. It also had much denser bones than most birds, making diving easier and more energy efficient.

{@i Kumimanu} was found in the Paleocene Waipara Greensand Formation in Canterbury, New Zealand. This was deposited in a low-energy shallow marine sea at a time when the New Zealand climate was subtropical, with warm wet summers and cool winters. The Waipara Greensand yields relatively few fossils, but those that are found are very species diverse. {@i Kumimanu} lived alongside two species of proto-penguins, transitional forms that had become flightless but were not yet fully adapted for a marine environment. One of these, {@i Waimanu}, is the oldest species of penguin in the fossil record and only co-existed with {@i Kumimanu} for a short time. Other notable fossils are early tropicbirds and at least 16 species of neoselachian sharks.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: While {@i Kumimanu} appears early in the evolution of penguins, it was already morphologically comparable to its modern descendants and was probably very behaviourally similar. It likely spent most of its time at sea, but formed large shoreline colonies in the breeding season, with birds pairing off to raise their chicks and defend their nesting territory. It is thought to have specialised in hunting large prey, catching fish at the surface and diving deep to feed on cephalopods and jellyfish.

We suggest playing {@i Kumimanu} as a marine species that nests on pebbly beaches. They should spend most of their time at sea hunting, only coming to shore infrequently throughout most of the year. Every breeding season, they should gather in huge colonies, with birds forming mated pairs that are fiercely protective of their nests. If approached by humanoids or predators, they should begin an elaborate display full of head bobbing and exaggerated neck movements. A fight should only break out if the intruder refuses to back away. Their enormous size should render them less scared of humanoids than other penguins.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Penguins, more accurately known as the Sphenisciformes, first appear in the fossil record approximately 62 million years ago in New Zealand. Within a few million years, several lineages had independently evolved giant forms. This is in keeping with Cope's Rule that states animals will generally trend towards larger sizes with each generation as long as environmental pressures allow it. What is unusual about penguin giantism is the speed that it occurred, with multiple giant forms arising in a relatively short space of time. The driver for large penguins has been hypothesised to be a combination of better thermoregulation, making it easier to dive into the colder depths, and radiating to fill the niches left by the extinction of Mesozoic marine reptiles. Giant penguins survived until the Late Oligocene, however it is believed that with the evolution of toothed whales and pinnipeds, they found themselves outcompeted for resources. Despite this, some modern penguins, such as the emperor penguin, do still reach impressive sizes today.

trait.name: Ossified Tendons
entries: Lambeosaurus has Advantage on Strength saving throws.

trait.name: Observant Prey Animal
entries: Lambeosaurus has Expertise in passive {@skill Perception} (included above). If three or more Lambeosaurus are within 50 ft. of each other, they all gain Advantage on {@skill Perception} checks.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, you do not need to change Lambeosaurus' CR.

trait.name: Thumbs Up (3/Day)
entries: As a Bonus Action, Lambeosaurus can give itself or an ally within 60 ft. a "thumbs up" using its head crest. Once within the next 10 minutes, that creature can add a {@dice 1d6} die roll to any one skill check, attack roll, or saving throw it makes (declared before rolling).. A creature may only benefit from one additional die from Thumbs Up at a time.
Additionally, if a creature rolls a 6 on this extra die and the skill check, attack roll, or saving throw is successful, it is then treated as though it were a critical hit/success.

action.name: Rearing Stomp
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, Reach 5 ft., up to two targets. {@h}14 ({@damage 2d10 + 3}) Bludgeoning damage.
In order for Lambeosaurus to target two creatures with this attack, they must be within 10 ft. of each other and within Lambeosaurus' reach.
If Lambeosaurus didn't move this turn and it uses this attack, the damage of this attack is increased by {@dice 1d10} and Lambeosaurus' speed becomes 0 until the end of its turn.

action.name: Raucous Call
entries: Each non-Lambeosaurus creature within 15 ft. of Lambeosaurus must succeed a {@dc 13} Constitution saving throw or take {@dice 1d8} Thunder damage. They take half as much on a success.
All other Lambeosaurus within 500 ft. are alerted to the fact that this Lambeosaurus is in danger.
"LAM-BEE-OH-SORE-US"
{@b (LAMBE'S REPTILE)}

At the right times of year, evening walks through the Cretaceous greenery are accompanied by strange, long, bellowing hoots in the distance. These are the mating calls of Lambeosaurus and are, surprisingly, quite melodic. Certainly pleasant additions to the evening chorus.

{@i Lambeosaurus} is a lambeosaurine hadrosaur from the Late Cretaceous (77 million years ago) of Alberta, Canada. Like its close relative {@i Parasaurolophus} ({@b page 283}), it had a distinctive head crest.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Lambeosaurus} was a large hadrosaur, reaching 25 ft. long with a weight of more than 3 tonnes. It was a quadruped with tall hind legs, a thick tail, and gracile forelimbs. Its skull was somewhat horse-like, being long and tall at the back, but it also had a hard keratinous beak. Its crest changed shape as the animal grew, starting out as a low notch at the top of the skull before becoming more elaborate as they matured. Adult crests varied a lot in their appearance between individuals of different sexes and ages, with the most common morphotypes being a tall forward pointing crest with a thin spike pointing behind, or a larger more rounded crest without the spike. Adult {@i Lambeosaurus} crests had passages linked to the nostrils that would have allowed its calls to resonate within the crest's cavities, amplifying them and extending their range. The distinctive appearance of the crest would also have been useful as a signalling device, especially during the mating season.

As with several other dinosaurs featured in this book, {@i Lambeosaurus} has been found in the Dinosaur Park Formation in southern Alberta, Canada. This exceptionally fossiliferous site has produced huge numbers of dinosaur fossils with five hadrosaur genera known. Their remains not only consist of body fossils but also include a handful of eggshells. This suggests that the area may have been used as a nesting site and raises the question of if the hadrosaurs were there permanently or seasonally.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Recent studies into their dietary preferences suggest that {@i Lambeosaurus} was a generalist herbivore, hoovering up any plant material it could, regardless of quality. This had several advantages as it did not have to spend large portions of the day in search of food and, while it took in relatively low-quality food, the sheer volume it ate in a day would more than satisfy its needs.

We suggest playing {@i Lambeosaurus} as an animal that lives in large, generally single-sex, herds. They should spend most of their time wandering lazily through sparse forests or open plains, calmly grazing on anything edible within reach. While most feed, there should always be one or two individuals taking a break to glance around them for potential danger. In the breeding season, males should produce loud, low, resonating mating cries that can be heard for miles. Females will then respond if they are receptive and, upon meeting, males should perform elaborate displays using their head crests to entice the female and threaten rival males. {@i Lambeosaurus} should generally treat humanoids with caution, giving them a wide berth and fleeing from fights unless defending offspring.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Lambeosaurines were a highly successful group of hadrosaurs that appeared in the Cretaceous 86 million years ago and quickly became widespread. The group Lambeosaurini itself first appeared in the fossil record 77 million years ago in North America, but within 5 million years had spread to both Europe and Asia. Some lambeosaurines grew to giant sizes with {@i Magnapaulia} weighing more than 10 tonnes, making it one of the biggest hadrosaurs known. As with many Cretaceous dinosaur groups, they died out in the end-Cretaceous extinction event.

monster.name: Langstonia (Magical Variant)

trait.name: Crocodile Resilience
entries: Langstonia has Resistance to Poison damage and Immunity to the {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned} condition.

trait.name: Tenacious Predator
entries: Langstonia was a major predator of its environment. It has Immunity to the {@condition frightened|XPHB|Frightened} condition and has Advantage on Wisdom saving throws.

trait.name: Blood Follower
entries: Langstonia has Advantage on Survival and {@skill Perception} checks to track creatures that are currently under the effect of Minor Tear or another bleeding condition.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Langstonia's CR to 2 and increase its XP to 450 accordingly.

trait.name: Blood Soaker
entries: The damage caused by Langstonia's Minor Tear is increased to {@dice 1d6}. Whenever a creature is damaged by Minor Tear and is within 100 ft. of Langstonia, Langstonia gains Temporary Hit Points equal to the damage dealt.

action.name: Tearing Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}5 ({@damage 1d6 + 2}) Piercing damage.
A creature hit by this attack begins to bleed. It gains the Minor Tear condition described below.

action.name: Minor Tear
entries: This creature is bleeding from a minor wound. At the start of its turn in combat or every minute outside of combat, the creature takes {@dice 1d4} Slashing damage. This effect persists until one of the following occurs (removing all stacks):

- The creature is healed by at least 5 Hit Points. - The creature finishes a Short or Long Rest (do not take damage while resting). - A {@dc 10} {@skill Medicine} check is passed on the creature. - It dies.
This effect can stack up to three times for a maximum of {@dice 3d4} Slashing damage.

legendary.name: Snapping Step Back
entries: Langstonia may make a Tearing Bite attack, then Disengages and must move 5 ft. directly away from the creature it made the Tearing Bite attack against.

legendary.name: Mammal Crushing Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}6 ({@damage 1d8 + 2}) Piercing damage.
A mammal (including mammalian humanoids) hit by this attack has its speed reduced by 10 ft. for 1 minute (non-cumulative).

legendaryHeader: Langstonia can take 1 Legendary Action. Only one legendary option can be used at a time and only at the end of another creature's turn. Langstonia regains spent Legendary Actions at the start of its turn.

entries: {@i "LANG-STONE-EE-AH"} {@b (NAMED FOR PALAEONTOLOGIST WANN LANGSTON JR.)}

Many adventurers presume that the younger periods of our history are much less dangerous than the more ancient ones. While this is generally true, one should still not lower one's guard, as, in some regions, the "Age of Reptiles" still very much persists.
Adventuring humans, elves, dwarves, halflings, and gnomes may find themselves particularly prone to attack by specialist mammal hunting crocodylomorphs.

{@i Langstonia} is a sebecosuchid crocodylomorph from the Middle Miocene (13 million years ago) of Colombia. One of the last sebecosuchids, {@i Langstonia} is thought to have been one of the top terrestrial predators in an environment where, despite its recent age, reptiles remained the dominant fauna.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Langstonia} was one of the largest sebecosuchids, and is estimated to have reached 8 to 13 ft. long and weighed up to 820 lb. It had long legs and stood with an erect gait, with a powerfully built body and a long tail held erect behind it. While the skulls of crocodiles are generally quite low and flat, {@i Langstonia}'s was very thin and tall. Its jaws were deep with serrated, interlocking teeth more like that of a theropod dinosaur than a crocodile's, and large muscles gave it a very powerful bite. It is thought to have had a specialised bone-crushing bite to bring down big mammalian prey.

{@i Langstonia} was discovered in the Villavieja Formation in the Hualia region of Colombia. This was deposited in a well-vegetated floodplain situated between several river tributaries in a warm, but not tropical, climate. The fossils found in the Villavieja Formation include a range of animals that are either unique to South America (which was an isolated continent for much of its existence) or they were the last surviving members of their families. Familiar groups like armadillos, opossums, bats, anteaters, sloths, and manatees lived alongside much more bizarre animals like the almost elephant-like astrapotherians and the hornless rhino-like toxodonts. Although marsupialforme carnivores were present (most being small, excluding {@i Dukecynus}), the arch predators were giant crocodylomorphs, like the huge gharial {@i Gryposuchus} (that was likely piscivorous) and the 20 ft. long sebecosuchid {@i Barinasuchus}.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Langstonia} was one of the main terrestrial predators in its region, specialising in medium-to-large sized prey and only directly competing with {@i Dukecynus} and the much larger {@i Barinasuchus}. It is thought to have been an ambush hunter, capable of chasing prey for short distances and using its powerful jaws to either disable them or open large wounds. It may then have backed off and waited for its victim to die of either blood loss or shock.

We suggest playing {@i Langstonia} as a typical reptilian terrestrial predator. It should spend most of its time either basking in the sun or searching for prey and be largely solitary. It may tolerate other {@i Langstonia}, so long as they give each other a respectful distance. Hunts are generally solo affairs, but once prey has been brought down, the carcass might be swarmed by multiple {@i Langstonia} in a violent feeding frenzy. Humanoids are not a primary food source, but a hungry {@i Langstonia} should not turn its nose up at what appears to be an easy meal.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Langstonia} is a member of the Sebicidae. This is a group of sebocosuchians that first appeared in the Late Cretaceous (68 million years ago) in Spain. Following the extinction of the non-avian dinosaurs, they experienced a major diversification event and evolved into a wide variety of forms. While their palaeogeographic record is incomplete, we know that by the end of the Eocene they had populations in Europe, Africa, and especially South America, where most of the species are found. Here, they faced limited competition from the local marsupialforme carnivores (which tended to be smaller) and quickly established themselves as arch predators. The last sebicids died out around 4 million years ago in the Early Pliocene, with researchers suggesting that the influx of placental mammals following the creation of the American land bridge led to them undergoing sudden competition pressure from animals like {@i Smilodon} ({@b page 105}), which ultimately outcompeted them.
