trait.name: Fossorial Adaptations
entries: Leptoceratops has a burrow speed of 5 ft. and a Darkvision of 10 ft. (included above).

trait.name: Blocking Head
entries: Leptoceratops may stand in its burrow with its head blocking the entrance. If it does, it gains the benefits of Three-quarters Cover (+5 to AC), prevents other creatures from entering the burrow, and it may still attack creatures that are within 5 ft. of the entrance to the burrow.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Leptoceratops' CR to 1/2 and increase its XP to 100 accordingly.

trait.name: Gravel Spray
entries: Ranged Weapon Attack: +3 to hit, Range 15 ft., one target. Hit: 6 ({@dice 2d4 + 1}) Bludgeoning damage.

The area between Leptoceratops and the target of this attack is flushed with dust and dirt in a 15 ft. cone from Leptoceratops. That area and creatures within it are heavily obscured until the start of Leptoceratops' next turn.

action.name: Plant-Shearing Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}5 ({@damage 1d8 + 1}) Piercing damage.
This attack deals an additional {@dice 1d10} Piercing damage to plant-based creatures, creatures composed of plants, and wooden objects.
"LEP-TOE-SER-AH-TOPS"
{@b (SMALL HORNED FACE)}

Records of burrowing dinosaurs are relatively sparse. However, one small ceratopsian, Leptoceratops, is thought to have dug living chambers in soft sediments. We searched for this animal for several days to confirm this hypothesis and were delighted to stumble across of a creche of them with their heads curiously poking out of their burrows. Be wary of stepping back into the range of snapping jaws though, as they tend to charge out from hidden holes to see off intruders.

{@i Leptoceratops} was a small ceratopsian from the Late Cretaceous (67 million years ago) of Alberta and Montana, North America. While a member of the famous horned dinosaurs, it was from a different subgroup than animals like {@i Triceratops} ({@b page 324}) and did not possess any horns itself.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Leptoceratops} was a small ceratopsian, reaching only about 6 to 7 ft. in length. It had a stout body, a short tail, five fingered hands with large claws on the first three digits, and relatively long hind legs. Its skull was large and robust, with a deep jaw, a hard beak, and a small flat frill along the back of its head. It had a strong bite, allowing it to feed on a wide variety of plants with little difficulty. Most unusually, while all ceratopsians were capable of a vertical chewing motion, {@i Leptoceratops} was able to rotate its jaw like a mammal, making it even more efficient at processing plants than other dinosaurs. Traditionally, it has been seen as facultatively quadrupedal (being able to switch between four and two legs), with it taking a bipedal stance when running. However, a recent study into the gait of basal ceratopsians suggests that it was in fact almost always quadrupedal and while it may have been able to stand on just two legs for a short period of time, this was probably just to feed on taller shrubbery, rather than for running.

{@i Leptoceratops} has been found in several Late Cretaceous formations in North America, but is most well-known from the famous Hell Creek Formation of Montana. This is an exceptionally rich unit that has produced many fossils including those of some of the most famous dinosaurs. The formation was deposited on a floodplain in a forested subtropical environment rich in plant life. This habitat was able to support a wide variety of animals including other marginocephalians (like the well-known {@i Triceratops}), tyrannosaurs, several small theropods, and hadrosaurs. Non-dinosaur fossils include fish, crocodylomorphs, pterosaurs, turtles, mammals, and a wide variety of plants.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Several {@i Leptoceratops} fossils have been found buried together. This was originally interpreted as them being caught in a mudslide or landslide, but more recent studies suggest that {@i Leptoceratops} was fossorial. This means it frequently dug and spent time in burrows. Anatomical evidence supports this, with its large forelimb claws and its fused neck vertebrae being adaptations for digging. The latter would not only help support its large head but also allow it to use its head as a shovel to help clear out tunnels. This lifestyle came with several advantages, including being able to lay eggs in a more protected space and have somewhere to flee to if pursued by predators. They may also have been multigenerational, with adults, sub-adults, and juveniles sharing the burrows for extended periods of time.

We suggest playing {@i Leptoceratops} as a skittish browser. It should spend much of its time in its burrow, carefully checking its environment for threats before venturing out. While foraging, it should always try to stay within running distance of its home and should be quick to flee to the safety of its burrow if threatened. If approached while within the burrow, an adult may block the entrance with its large head and snap at anyone trying to enter. However, if pressured enough, it may be forced to abandon the burrow, as well as any infants or juveniles within.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Leptoceratops} is the namesake of the Leptoceratopsidae. This is the sister group to the Coronosauria, the group that includes the true horned dinosaurs like {@i Triceratops}. The leptoceratopsids were relatively widespread and first evolved in Asia in the Late Cretaceous, around 83 million years ago. They then later migrated to North America and Europe. Like so many other dinosaurs, the leptoceratopsids met their end in the end-Cretaceous extinction.
Leptocertops tail fossil.

trait.name: Heavyset Body & Pillar Limbs
entries: Lisowicia has Advantage on Strength checks, Strength saving throws, and any saving throw to avoid being knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.

trait.name: Possibly Latrinic
entries: Lisowicia has Vulnerability to Poison damage (included above).

trait.name: Badlands Survivor
entries: Lisowicia only needs to drink water once a week and has Resistance to Radiant damage (included above).

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, you do not need to change Lisowicia's CR.

trait.name: Randomise Survival
entries: Replace Lisowicia's Poison Vulnerability and Radiant Resistance with new random damage types by rolling on the table below. First replace the Vulnerability, then the Resistance, rerolling the Resistance if it is the same result as the Vulnerability. Lisowicia's hide flickers/bubbles with energies of the damage type that it has Resistance to.
{@b {@i 1d8 - D}}{@b {@i amage}} {@b {@i type}} {@i 1 - Acid 5 - Lightning 2 - Cold 6 - Necrotic 3 - Fire 7 - Psychic 4 - Force 8 - Thunder}

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Lisowicia chooses the Attack action, it may make one Beaked Crunch attack and one Pillar Stomp attack.

action.name: Beaked Crunch
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 7} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}14 ({@damage 2d8 + 5}) Piercing damage.

action.name: Pillar Stomp
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 7} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}18 ({@damage 2d10 + 7}) Bludgeoning damage.
Lisowicia may only use this attack against a creature that is smaller than itself.
"LEES-OH-VEE-CHIA"
{@b (NAMED FOR THE TOWN OF LISOWICE)}

The sight of a Lisowicia calf gambolling along the side of a river is enough to melt the heart of even the hardiest adventurer, but only the very foolish would try to approach it. The adults are fiercely protective and will use their immense size to crush any would-be harasser.

{@i Lisowicia} is a dicynodont from the Late Triassic (210 million years ago) of Lisowice, Poland. One of the first truly giant tetrapods in the fossil record, this elephant-sized synapsid was a close relative of both {@i Placerias} ({@b page 286}) and {@i Woznikella} ({@b page 122}).

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Lisowicia} was the largest dicynodont known, reaching 15 ft. long and weighing 5 to 7 tonnes. It had a heavyset body with a short tail and powerful pillar-like legs that ended in plantigrade (flat-footed) feet. Its front and hind feet were held erect beneath its body, which is very unusual for a dicynodont, as most had sprawling forelimbs. This is likely an adaptation to support its great size. Its head was massive with an elongated snout, large beak, and horn-like projections jutting out of its cheeks. It was completely toothless and, instead, chewed up plants using triangular projections of its jaw bone.

{@i Lisowicia} was found in the Lipie Śląskie clay pits in Southern Poland. These were laid down in the floodplain of a river running through an arid environment and, while not exceptionally fossiliferous, they have produced a reasonable diversity of animals. Several fish species including freshwater coelacanths and sharks lived in the river system, alongside some temnospondyl amphibians. Synapsids like dicynodonts or the proto-mammal {@i Hallautherium} were the most common large animals, but big archosaurs like the carnivorous {@i Smok} were also present.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Lisowicia} was originally described as a high browser, taking advantage of its size to avoid competition with other dicynodonts. However, a recent study argued that it instead spent most of its life with its head down, feeding on low-lying vegetation. Evidence for communal latrines in related animals (see {@i Woznikella} {@b page 122}) suggest that these animals moved in sizable herds and infants likely stayed with their parents for an extended period. As they were so massive, an adult {@i Lisowicia} had few predators. However, tooth marks on juvenile remains show that the 20 ft. long archosaur {@i Smok} predated upon them.

We suggest playing {@i Lisowicia} as a communal animal, travelling in herds of a dozen or so individuals. They should constantly be on the move, searching for food and migrating between water sources. As the adults graze, the youngsters will often be found at play with each other. If they sense a threat to their young, the adults will form a barrier round them. This can quickly be followed by a charge where they will either snap with their powerful jaws or simply crush attackers with their weight.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Lisowicia} is a member of the Stahleckeriidae. This is a group of Triassic dicynodonts that included {@i Woznikella} and {@i Placerias}. The first definitive stahleckeriids came from the Early Triassic (246 million years ago) of Africa before they eventually migrated into what would later become the Americas, Asia, and Europe. Stahleckerids were generally large-bodied dicynodonts weighing a tonne or more. They were one of the only dicynodont groups to survive the Permo-Triassic extinction and became highly successful for most of the Triassic. Eventually, increasingly arid conditions caused their numbers to plummet, with only a handful of species like {@i Lisowicia} surviving until the Triassic-Jurassic boundary where they finally died out.

Sulej, T. 2020. The herd instinct goes back before mammals. {@i ACADEMIA. The magazine of the Polish Academy of Sciences}, pp.8-10.
Sulej, T. 2024. Osteology and relationships of the Late Triassic giant dicynodont {@i Lisowicia}. {@i Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society}, {@b 202 (1)}, pp.zlae085.

monster.name: Livyatan (Magical Variant)

legendaryHeader: Livyatan can take 2 Legendary Actions, choosing from the options below. Only one legendary option can be used at a time and only at the end of another creature's turn. Livyatan regains spent Legendary Actions at the start of its turn.

entries: {@i "LIV-E-AH-TAN"} {@b (NAMED FOR THE ORIGINAL HEBREW WORD FOR THE BIBLICAL LEVIATHAN)}

The sailors often tell tall tales of great sea beasts - krakens and leviathans that devour ships whole. Although such creatures are reported in wizarding academic studies, they are exceptionally rare and not of particular concern. What are much more common, however, are large aquatic predators. Typically, these animals are only threats to very small ships and swimmers. Nevertheless, there is one, Livyatan, that is far more dangerous. We witnessed firsthand two of these titanic predators work in unison to capsize a ship and devour its stock & crew. I strongly recommend avoiding their migration routes wherever possible.

{@i Livyatan} was a large carnivorous whale found in the Late Miocene Pisco Formation (10 to 5 million years ago) of Peru. A distant relative of the modern sperm whale, it is thought to have been a specialist hunter of large aquatic animals, including other whales.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: Although {@i Livyatan} is currently known only from its skull and isolated teeth, comparisons with more completely known relatives allow us to estimate that it was between 44 and 57 ft. long and weighed perhaps 57 tonnes. It resembled a modern sperm whale in appearance, with an elongate body, long fluked tail, and a very large rectangular head. Like sperm whales, its forehead housed a spermaceti organ, a large structure containing a waxy fluid that enables powerful echolocation and may have been used for ramming other whales (a behaviour seen in some sperm whales). {@i Livyatan} differs from modern whales in the structure of its jaws and teeth. Its jaws were shorter, more robust, and much stronger than those of sperm whales. Its teeth were extremely large, with some reaching 14 in. long. Some of these teeth show damage and wear facets indicative of predation upon particularly large prey (macroraptorial).

The holotype (original specimen) for {@i Livyatan} is from the Pisco Formation, Peru, although evidence for {@i Livyatan} (or closely related animals) has also been found in the Americas, South Africa, and Australia. The Pisco Formation was deposited in a near-shore oceanic environment with some lagoonal influence. The formation is a famous site of exceptional preservation (Lagerstätten) with an extremely rich fossil fauna. This includes a variety of fish, whales, seals, sharks (including {@i Megalodon}), rays, and even the semi-aquatic sloth {@i Thalassocnus} ({@b page 314}). Many of these would have easily fallen within the feeding range of {@i Livyatan} and, along with {@i Megalodon}, it was likely an arch predator for the region.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: While modern sperm whales are famous for their deep-diving abilities, the association of {@i Livyatan} fossils with shallow water deposits, combined with their adaptations for hunting large fish and mammals, suggests that {@i Livyatan} would have stayed relatively close to the surface. A common hunting tactic for oceanic predators is to charge smaller prey from underneath, ambushing and stunning them. {@i Livyatan} likely used this tactic as its large size would have made it less agile relative to its prey, so the element of surprise would have been vital. While it occupies a similar niche to orcas, it would have been able to hunt much larger prey alone and has been suggested to be a solitary animal. That being said, {@i Livyatan} was likely an intelligent animal with at least some notable social behaviour and it's unlikely they remained in total isolation, perhaps living in small family pods of one or two adults and their recent young.

We suggest playing {@i Livyatan} as a patient patroller of the ocean, with a preference to hunting along well used migration paths. It should be an extremely dangerous animal to fight - intelligent, cunning, and powerful. Any object of significant size might be considered potential prey, and {@i Livyatan} should show at least curiosity towards large ships, as well as the ability to learn how to capsize them. Parties travelling through their hunting ground should watch the waters below in case a hungry {@i Livyatan} charges their vessel from beneath. A {@i Livyatan} should be cautious and potentially aggressive to other large oceanic predators, so much so that it could be dissuaded from attacking a party by redirecting its focus to potential competitors.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Livyatan} is arguably the largest member of the Physteroidea. This group of odontocetes (toothed whales) first appeared in the Oligocene, 25 million years ago, and includes modern animals like sperm whales and their smaller cousins the kogiads. Raptorial sperm whales like {@i Livyatan} were one of the dominant predators in the Miocene Ocean and were successful enough to have had a global range. Interestingly, the oceans these predators lived in had a much greater number of medium to large sized carnivores than we find today. Their extinction has been linked to climate change in the Pliocene that led to the disappearance of many small to medium sized whales that they preyed upon, followed by the rise of the truly giant baleen whales. These huge whales would have required very different hunting strategies and the macroraptorial sperm whales may have struggled to adapt fast enough. It has also been suggested that the evolution of competing orcas during this time may have increased pressure on sperm whale populations, resulting in an evolutionary bottleneck, where only the smaller kogiads and specialised deep-diving sperm whales survived.

"MEH-GAH-LOH-SIR-US"
{@b (GREAT HORN)}

Deer always held an air of mystery to me, but none so much so as the Megaloceros. This enormous titan strides the wilds with the utmost confidence. Few predators could dare challenge its might during mating season, and those that do don't often live to regret it. A majestic and dangerous animal.

{@i Megaloceros} is an extinct deer from the Pleistocene (450,000 years ago) from Northern Eurasia. Colloquially known as the Irish Elk, it became famous not only for its great size but also its impressive antlers.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Megaloceros} is among the largest deer in the fossil record. The biggest individuals reached 6 to 7 ft. tall and might have weighed up to 1500 lb. It was a very powerfully built animal, with thick bones and a reinforced skull. It also had a fatty hump between its shoulders that served as a food store during leaner months. Cave paintings show it was a pale brown with light fur on its neck, dark fur around its shoulders, and a distinctive diagonal stripe on its flanks. Its antlers were enormous and, in some males, had a span of nearly 12 ft. Their morphology is similar to the antlers of fallow deer, being flat and broad with the margins made of upward pointing prongs. Like modern deer, these grew seasonally, increasing in size each year, and were shed in early March. {@i Megaloceros} has been found in numerous Pleistocene and Holocene locations across Eurasia but, given its common name, it should be no surprise that the most numerous and best-preserved fossils were found in Ireland. The Irish material is around 13,000 years old and is often found in peatland. Based on the morphology of its teeth, {@i Megaloceros} was both a grazer and a browser, although which it preferred varied from place to place. Irish and German {@i Megaloceros} primarily fed on grass and flowers, while British animals ate a much higher number of leaves.

{@i Megaloceros} was well-adapted to live in open grasslands or shrublands and shared its ecosystem with a rich mammalian megafaunal assemblage. Fossils show it not only lived alongside exotic species like the woolly mammoth and cave hyena, but also more mundane animals like wolves, bears, horses, and boars.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Megaloceros} was a herd animal, with fossils discovered near Dublin, Ireland indicating that males and females lived alongside each other from spring to autumn, with males being segregated from the main herd in winter. This separation supports the idea of seasonal rutting and an annual breeding season. Analyses of the antler's resistances show that, while they were capable of interlocking and engaging in fights, they were less resistant to continuous stress than red or fallow deer antlers. As such, in rutting they were likely first used for a threatening display, then swept from side to side in fighting, rather than locked with other antlers and pushed as a last resort.

We suggest playing {@i Megaloceros} as an analogue for modern deer. It should be found grazing in herds within open fields or along the borders of dense forests. It will be an alert animal with some individuals always on the look out for danger. When startled, the herd should default to fleeing unless it is mating season. In mating season, rutting stags may meet threats directly, first swinging their antlers, then charging and bludgeoning or stabbing threats that don't quickly retreat. Two or more rutting males may prioritise fighting each other first, forcing the rest of the herd to flee from the threat.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Megaloceros} is a member of the Cervidae, although where it falls within deer phylogeny has been the subject of debate. The morphology of its antlers are similar to that of {@i Dama}, the living fallow deer, and it was for a long time taken as a sign of a close relationship. However, in the 2000s, a study using molecular phylogeny argued that genetically {@i Megaloceros} was more closely related to {@i Cervus}, the red deer. In fact, they suggested synonymising {@i Megaloceros} with {@i Cervus} and speculated that they likely interbred. This study fell under heavy scrutiny, and it is now thought that their results were actually due to contaminated samples. Later molecular phylogenies strongly indicate a relationship to fallow deer.

{@i Megaloceros} went extinct relatively recently, surviving until approximately 8000 years ago. Historically, it was hypothesised they went extinct due to the ever-increasing size of their antlers, which would have been difficult to support and may have gotten trapped in foliage. Today, this idea is considered poorly supported and instead it is thought that {@i Megaloceros} was hit heavily by climatic changes that not only resulted in a shift between glacial and postglacial conditions but also changed the open grasslands into more dense forest. Human hunting may also have been a contributing factor, with the last, small relic populations in Russia possibly hunted to extinction.

A creature hit by this attack that is smaller than Meganeura is {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} and {@condition restrained|XPHB|Restrained} (escape {@dc 8}).
"MEG-AH-NUR-AH"
{@b (LARGE VEIN)}

Trudging through the Carboniferous swamps can be a noisy affair, with all manner of chittering insects and splashing amphibians darting from our presence. However, at particular times of year, the overwhelming thudding of dozens of Meganeura carpets the riverways. These enormous dragonfly-like insects flit around constantly, performing intricate territorial dances and snatching up small prey. I'm very glad that our party didn't have a fairy member, or we may have had a serious issue on our hands.

{@i Meganeura} is a meganisopteran ("griffenfly") insect from the Late Carboniferous (300 million years ago) of Commentry, France. With an enormous wingspan for an insect, this dragonfly-like animal is one of the largest and most famous insects in the fossil record.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Meganeura} was a giant amongst insects, with a wingspan of 2.5 ft. and weighing up to 150 grams (50 times that of its living relatives). It had four wings, six barbed legs, and an elongated thorax tipped with small leaf-like extensions. Its head was armed with vicious mouth parts and huge eyes that took up most of the upper portion of the head. This gave it excellent vision and, based on comparisons with dragonflies, allowed it to track the movements of flying prey from far away without them blending into their surroundings.

{@i Meganeura} has only been found in the French Commentry Coal Measures. These are coal-rich strata laid down in very swampy densely vegetated environments that had abundant wildlife. Alongside {@i Meganeura} were numerous other arthropods like other primitive insects (for example, the six-winged Palaeodictyoptera that were some of the first herbivores, and primitive cockroaches and mantises), arachnids like scorpions, and aquatic arthropods like eurypterids. The swamps were also inhabited by temnospondyl amphibians like {@i Branchiosaurus} that preyed upon the many invertebrates.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Like dragonflies, {@i Meganeura} was a carnivorous aerial hunter and would have been the arch flying predator of its day. It flew over waterways, using its excellent vision to scan for prey. Once spotted, it would snatch targets out of the air or off of the ground with its barbed limbs and immediately begin consuming them. Due to its size, it was not able to beat its wings at the same frequency as dragonflies, which would have made them "thud" rather than "buzz", and also made it slightly less agile (although still remarkably adept at flying). This means {@i Meganeura} would have specialised in hunting larger, slower-moving prey. {@i Meganeura} required fresh water for reproduction, as its nymph (juvenile) stages were fully aquatic, and would spend most of its time near water. Rarely, adults may venture away from water bodies and into jungles or forests, but will always return to water during the breeding season (if they live long enough). {@i Meganeura} nymphs were also voracious predators and would have hunted anything that they could, but would have themselves been predated on by other aquatic organisms.

We suggest playing {@i Meganeura} as an agile aerial predator that patrols riverways and swamps. For brief periods during the mating season, they should be a very common sight, and otherwise may rarely be spotted in forests or jungles. They should respond quickly to any movement, whether by diving towards potential prey or darting away in fear. While too small to see most humanoids as prey, {@i Meganeura} would have been capable of giving a rather nasty bite if caught and would certainly predate upon familiars and tiny party companions.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Meganeura} belongs to the Meganisoptera, commonly known as the griffinflies. This is a group of palaeopterans (dragonflies and damselflies (Odonata), mayflies (Ephemeropteroidea), and other closely related extinct four-winged insects) that first appeared in the Late Carboniferous 317 million years ago and have been found in formations across North America and Europe. While most are comparable to modern insects in terms of size, some animals like {@i Meganeura} and the Late Permian surviving {@i Meganeuropsis} grew to truly enormous proportions. For many years, scientists argued that the high oxygen content in the Carboniferous was the reason griffinflies reached such huge sizes, but their survival throughout the Permian when oxygen levels were much lower challenges this. Another possible explanation is the relatively low number of aerial predators, allowing them to occupy an arch predator role without competition. Regardless of the cause, griffinflies failed to survive the end Permian extinction, with the last species disappearing around 255 to 250 million years ago.

Every other creature within 5 ft. of it must succeed a {@dc 11} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}. Moganopterus then begins to fly and must fly 20 ft. in a straight line (either horizontally, or vertically up). Moganopterus can only begin flying by using this ability, or if it is falling.

entries: {@i "MOH-GAN-OP-TER-US"} {@b (NAME DERIVED FROM GAN JIANG AND MO YE, LEGENDARY SWORDSMITHS IN CHINESE FOLKLORE)}

My colleague and friend, Reginald Dhrolin, frequently tells of his adventures in our past, usually while indulging in a flagon of ale as I partake in some wine. Despite our differences, I find his accounts most informative. Among his description of the Yixian Formation and battling tyrannosauroids atop a frozen peak, he shared tales of strange filter-feeding pterosaurs on the same mountain. As his party rested, they observed these animals drinking at the water's edge, picking up mouthfuls of minnow-like fish. I must say that I long to see these animals in the flesh, although their aggressive predatory neighbours have deterred me from travelling there myself.

{@i Moganopterus} is a ctenochasmatid pterosaur from the Early Cretaceous (124 million years ago) of China. A strange pterosaur with a very elongated skull, it is the largest ctenochasmatid in the fossil record.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Moganopterus} is known only from a complete skull (measuring 3 ft. long) and some neck vertebrae. The rest of the body may be unknown, but based on the size of the skull, the original description estimated its wingspan to be about 23 ft. However, a more recent study re-evaluated the holotype and scaled the animal down to 11 ft. Its head had bizarre proportions, with extremely long and thin jaws and a short pointed head crest at the back of its skull. It also had a second small round crest at the tip of the upper jaw and its teeth were conical and needle-like, forming an overlapping mesh that could be closed to potentially filter-feed.

{@i Moganopterus} was from the Yixian Formation in Liaoning Province, China. This was a cold, high-altitude, volcanic area that we described in detail as a holistic environment in {@i Dr Dhrolin's Dictionary of Dinosaurs} ({@b pages 38-41 in DDDD}). As we discuss there, it is a site of exceptional preservation that has produced fossils of a wide variety of taxa such as therizinosaurs, tyrannosauroids, sauropods, and ceratopsians. Many of these are so well preserved that they retain soft tissues like skin or feathers.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: As mentioned above, {@i Moganopterus} was a filter-feeding pterosaur. It waded into shallow waters and fed by pushing water through its interlocking teeth. As the water passed through, any animals too big to fit through the gaps in the teeth would be trapped and swallowed whole. An analysis of the tooth wear patterns in a related pterosaur suggests that {@i Moganopterus} wasn't simply passively filtering and may have been more active in finding its prey, perhaps digging through sediment or snapping at schools of small fish.

We suggest playing {@i Moganopterus} as a common sight along the banks of rivers or mountain lakes. Flocks of them should be seen wading through the shallows in search of food, or standing on riverbanks. They should have no qualms about searching for food in cold waters or at high altitude. During the breeding season, they should build their nests in elevated soil not too far from a nearby water source and a mated pair should be fiercely territorial. If a predator or curious humanoid approaches, any nearby {@i Moganopterus} should take flight and try to drive them away. They will mob the intruder, flying past and battering them with their wings or snapping at them with their needle-like teeth until the harassment forces them to flee.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Moganopterus} is a member of the Ctenochasmatidae. The oldest ctenochasmatids first appeared in the fossil record 160 to 150 million years ago in China and South America, but the most-well known examples come from fossil lagerstätten (sites of exceptional preservation) in Germany. Ctenochasmatids were all filter-feeding pterosaurs with a variety of tooth morphologies, ranging from the simple conical needles of {@i Moganopterus} to the extremely long and thin tight meshes of {@i Pterodaustro} ({@b page 162 in DDDD}). Ctenochasmatids died out 105 million years ago, not long before the transition from the Early to Late Cretaceous.

trait.name: Ramming Fighter
entries: Pachycephalosaurus has Resistance to Bludgeoning damage (included above).

trait.name: Alert Animal

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Pachycephalosaurus' CR to 5 and increase its XP to 1800 accordingly.

trait.name: Wolf in Sheep's Clothing
entries: Pachycephalosaurus is secretly a carnivorous predator that appears to be a herbivore. It gains the following attack that it can use as a Bonus Action against creatures that are lying {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.

trait.name: Devour Flesh
entries: Melee Weapon Attack: +5 to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. Hit: 12 ({@dice 2d8 + 3}) Piercing damage plus 3 ({@dice 1d6}) Slashing damage.
Pachycephalosaurus gains Temporary Hit Points equal to the total damage this attack deals.

The first time a humanoid sees this, they must succeed a {@dc 12} Wisdom saving throw or be {@condition frightened|XPHB|Frightened} of Pachycephalosaurus for the next minute (they may repeat the save at the end of each of their turns).

action.name: Skull Ram
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}8 ({@damage 1d10 + 3}) Bludgeoning damage plus 7 ({@damage 1d8 + 3}) Piercing damage.
A Large or smaller creature hit by this attack is pushed 5 ft. backwards and knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.
Additionally, if Pachycephalosaurus moved at least 15 ft. this turn, a creature that is hit by this attack has its movement speed reduced by 15 ft. for 2 rounds (to a minimum of 0 ft., cumulative).

action.name: Goring Head Crush
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}19 ({@damage 3d10 + 3}) Bludgeoning damage plus 12 ({@damage 2d8 + 3}) Piercing damage.
Pachycephalosaurus may only use this attack against a creature that is lying {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.
{@i "PACK-E-KEF-AH-LOW-SORE-US"} {@b (THICK HEADED REPTILE)}

Have you ever watched a ram or goat charge and knock over an unsuspecting person, pushing them to the ground and nudging at their rear end? It is quite comical really. It is not, however, quite so comical when the animal doing so is a half-tonne armoured dinosaur. Even the most heavily equipped Fighters may find themselves knocked around endlessly by several of these ill-tempered creatures.

{@i Pachycephalosaurus} was a bipedal marginocephalian dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of the western United States (70 million years ago). A close relative of the horned ceratopsians, it is most famous for its robust domed skull.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: While it is a well-known dinosaur, the remains of {@i Pachycephalosaurus} are surprisingly sparse. It is known only from skull material, but full body reconstructions have been made using other, more complete, closely related pachycephalosaurs. Using these relations, it has been estimated that {@i Pachycephalosaurus} likely reached somewhere in the range of 15 ft. long and weighed up to half a tonne. Pachycephalosaurs were relatively stocky bipeds, with short forelimbs and thick tails. They had a relatively long snout, a narrow jaw tipped with a hard beak, and small leaf-shaped teeth with well-developed dental ridges. The top of the snout was covered in small knobs and horns running backwards up the skull, which then expanded into a huge, solid, bony dome, surrounded by a ring of small blunted horns. {@i Pachycephalosaurus} has long been regarded as a herbivore that likely browsed on hard ferns. However, a jaw fossil studied in 2018 showed that in the front of its jaws it had pointed,

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: We recommend running Pachycephalosaurus in small herds. Having one player character knocked around while each Pachycephalosaurus backs off to charge again is particularly "fun".

almost blade-like teeth, comparable to those found in theropods. This has led several researchers to speculate that {@i Pachycephalosaurus} may have been omnivorous, supplementing its diet by scavenging or hunting. While there are very few animals that are 100% herbivorous (many will eat eggs, insects, small vertebrates, or bone to gain valuable nutrients), these teeth alone are insufficient evidence for hunting behaviour and may have instead had a social function.

{@i Pachycephalosaurus} is known from two formations; the Hell Creek Formation and the Lance Formation, both extending over several states in western North America. These were laid down in rivers and deltas along the edge of the Western Interior Seaway, a massive body of water that covered much of the North American continent during the Cretaceous. These formations are very fossil rich and show that {@i Pachycephalosaurus} lived alongside numerous other animals ranging from pterosaurs to small mammals, to superstar dinosaurs like {@i Triceratops} ({@b page 324}) and {@i Tyrannosaurus} ({@b page 192 in DDDD}).

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: When we discuss the behaviour of {@i Pachycephalosaurus}, we must inevitably turn our attention to its domed skull. This bizarre structure's function has been debated since the animal's discovery, and several hypotheses have been proposed. However, the most commonly proposed and well-supported function is the use of the dome for intraspecific (within the same species) headbutting. Surprisingly, the idea first appeared in popular science books and science fiction short stories, before being published on by research scientists in the 1970s. Strong evidence for the headbutting behaviour can be found in the thickness of the skull, the bone seemingly being capable of healing quickly, the presence of healed impact wounds, and the reinforced structure of the spine and hips.

We suggest playing {@i Pachycephalosaurus} as a highly social, alert animal living in small herds. In these groups, young animals should be seen play-fighting often, while adults should be very vocal, engaging in quick scuffles and grooming each other with their front teeth. Head-butting should be something seen all the time, but it should be at its most intense during the mating season between competing males and from unreceptive females being bothered by amorous males. Humanoids should be seen as an intruding threat, and disturbed herds should be jumpy and quick to anger. When attacking, {@i Pachycephalosaurus} should be keen to gang up, repeatedly headbutting foes to knock them over, much like rams do.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Pachycephalosaurus} is thought to be the largest member of the Pachycephalosauria. This was a group of bipedal dinosaurs found in Asia and North America and were the sister-group to the ceratopsians. Together, they make up the Marginocephalia or margin head dinosaurs.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: We have provided the British pronunciation of this dinosaur's name.

Pachycephalosauria first appears in the fossil record in the Late Cretaceous of China 92 million years ago. The group proved relatively successful and spread across much of Asia before migrating to North America. While the body-plan of pachycephalosaurs was conservative, it has been noted that the earlier basal forms did not have the fully formed domed skull. Instead, they had much lower and flatter skulls and, based on comparisons with the later more derived animals, did not engage in head-butting behaviour in the same manner as {@i Pachycephalosaurus}. The group went extinct alongside all non-avian dinosaurs during the end-Cretaceous mass extinction event.

trait.name: Giant Columnar Limbs
entries: Paraceratherium has Resistance to Bludgeoning, Piercing, and Slashing damage (included above), and has Advantage on any saving throw to resist being knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.

trait.name: Migratory
entries: Paraceratherium is experienced with many environments. It is not slowed by natural Difficult Terrain.

trait.name: Sexually Dimorphic
entries: Only male Paraceratherium have tusks. When this Paraceratherium is first encountered, choose or randomly determine (DM's choice) whether it is male or female. If it is female, it cannot make an Incisor Gore attack.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Paraceratherium's CR to 9 and increase its XP to 5000 accordingly.

trait.name: Spirit of the Forest
entries: Some Paraceratherium that spend enough time deep within forests transform into mythical spirit-like entities that embody nature itself. They become guardians of the forest and wander it silently at night, with an eerie magical glow emanating from them.
Paraceratherium gains Immunity to all damage from a non-magical source and its attacks deal Force damage instead of their usual damage type.

trait.name: Spiritual Shift (3/Day)
entries: As a Bonus Action, Paraceratherium may become one with the forest and appear partially translucent. If it does so, melee and ranged attacks against it are made at Disadvantage until the start of its next turn. Additionally, if it is damaged by an attack, it may choose to teleport up to 30 ft. to an unoccupied space that it can see.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Paraceratherium chooses the Attack action, it may make two Three-Toed Stomp attacks and one Incisor Gore attack (see Sexually Dimorphic).

action.name: Three-Toed Stomp
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 9} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}19 ({@damage 2d12 + 6}) Bludgeoning damage.
A creature hit by this attack that is Large or smaller must succeed a {@dc 17} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.

action.name: Incisor Gore
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 9} to hit, Reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}9 ({@damage 1d6 + 6}) Piercing damage.
A Medium or smaller creature hit by this attack is thrown up to 10 ft. by Paraceratherium in a direction of its choosing.
{@i "PAR-AH-SER-AH-THER-EE-UM"} {@b (NEAR HORNLESS BEAST)}

On rare occasions, the trembling ground reveals the coming of a herd of gigantic Paraceratherium. These enormous animals tower above the plains, migrating in large herds composed of (largely) peaceful giants. The handful of infants, which are still horse-sized, gleefully play amongst their kin. Thankfully, they pay little mind to humanoids like us and we can observe them in relative safety.
{@i Paraceratherium} is a rhinocerotoid from the Oligocene (34 million years ago) of Europe and Asia. A hornless relative of modern rhinos, it was among the largest land mammals to walk the Earth.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Paraceratherium} is an unusual animal that looked like a cross between a rhino and a giraffe. It grew at least 15 ft. tall and may have weighed between 12 and 17 tonnes (possibly even as much as 20). It stood on four pillar-like legs, with its tall forelimbs giving it a sloping back. Its neck was thick and elongated, held aloft like a giraffe's. Its head was rectangular and horse-like, lacking the horns seen in many rhinos. Some authors have suggested that it may have had a small tapir-like trunk, although this is still speculative. {@i Paraceratherium}'s teeth were unique in that it lost its canines and most of its incisors. It retained only a single pair on the bottom and top, modified into large cones, with the upper pair pointing down and the lower pair angled forward. This may have been a sexually dimorphic trait, with some individuals interpreted as males having more tusk-like teeth.

{@i Paraceratherium} has been found in a number of formations across Eurasia and was adaptive enough to survive in a variety of environments. It lived near the margins of arid deserts, near dense shrublands, in steppe forests, and in subtropical woodlands. Across its habitats it co-existed with a huge variety of animals including wolves, horses, nimvarid cats, and multiple other species of rhinocerotoids.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: With its massive size and tall neck, {@i Paraceratherium} avoided competition by browsing higher in the trees than other herbivores. Fossils indicate that it probably lived in large herds and its wide distribution suggests that these herds were likely migratory. An adult {@i Paraceratherium} dwarfed any carnivore that it may have encountered and it would have been mostly immune to predation (although bite marks from crocodiles left on bones show they were almost certainly scavenged). Young animals, however, would have been much easier targets, relying on the larger adults to protect them for a decade or more until they were large enough to defend themselves.

We suggest playing {@i Paraceratherium} as an animal constantly on the move, with herds following seasonal rains in a constant search for food. Calves should be playful creatures, often seen chasing each other or investigating anything novel they come across. Adults should be largely fearless, towering over most threats and usually only attacking in defence of their young. The only time they should be more prone to violence should be the mating season, when rutting males gore each other with their incisors or rear up to crush opponents beneath their feet. Anyone who, either by choice or poor timing, finds themselves in the middle of a fight risks being crushed by duelling angry giants.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Paraceratherium} is the most well-known member of the Paraceratheriidae. This is a group of rhinocerotoids that first appeared in Asia in the Eocene (47 million years ago) and quickly spread across all of Asia, before reaching Eastern Europe around 30 million years ago. While some species were no bigger than a horse, others grew to exceptional sizes with the heaviest animals ({@i Paraceratherium} and {@i Dzungariotherium}) approaching almost 20 tonnes. By 23 million years ago, the paraceratheriids fell into rapid decline before becoming extinct. What caused this remains a mystery, although some authors have argued that they were affected by climate change while others have suggested that they were outcompeted by other large herbivores like proboscideans (elephants and their kin).

trait.name: Deep Sea Animal
entries: Parapuzosia can only breathe in water and has Resistance to Cold and Thunder damage (included above).

trait.name: Chambered Phragmocone

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, you do not need to change Parapuzosia's CR.

trait.name: Biostratigraphic Index Animal
entries: Parapuzosia's remains are magically enchanted with fossils. Their carcasses glow with a cracked glass effect, hinting that there may be treasures hidden within their coiled shells. Upon death, Parapuzosia's shell may be cracked open ({@dc 10} Strength check) to reveal Poor Quality Fossiliferous Strata (page 51) hidden within.

If three Parapuzosia carcasses are within 10 ft. of each other, they instead magically combine to form a single Moderate Quality Fossiliferous Strata (page 51). If six Parapuzosia carcasses are within 15 ft. of each other, they instead magically combine to form a single Exceptional Quality Fossiliferous Strata (page 51).
Parapuzosia's remains float in water for up to a month before they start to decay and sink to the ocean floor.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Parapuzosia chooses the Attack action, it may make one Gripping Tentacles attack and one Snipping Beak attack.

action.name: Gripping Tentacles
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}5 ({@damage 1d6 + 2}) Bludgeoning damage.
A Medium or smaller creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} and {@condition restrained|XPHB|Restrained} (escape {@dc 12}).

action.name: Snipping Beak
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}9 ({@damage 2d6 + 2}) Piercing damage.
Parapuzosia may only use this attack against a creature that it is currently Grappling.

bonus.name: Ink Squirt
entries: As a Bonus Action, Parapuzosia can release a jet of ink. It may select a point within 5 ft. of itself. All water in a 5 ft. diameter sphere from that point becomes filled with black ink, rendering it opaque and obscuring line of sight into and through the water (creatures inside the ink are {@condition blinded|XPHB|Blinded} and have Total Cover until they leave it). This effect persists for 30 seconds, unless a particularly strong current disperses the water.
"PAR-AH-PU-ZO-SEE-AH"
{@b (BESIDE SNAIL AXIS)}

Ammonites and their drifting shells are exceptionally common on the ancient oceans. Some of these can reach preposterous sizes, with the largest I've observed being about 6 ft. in diameter. These belonged to monstrous cephalopods that can occasionally be seen looming in the depths below.

{@i Parapuzosia} was a giant ammonite from Early Cretaceous (lower Campanian) of Europe and North America. The biggest ammonite in the fossil record, it had a tightly coiled 6 ft. wide shell divided into multiple chambers. Only the head, with its long tentacles and hooked beak, were exposed to the outside. Unlike the benthic {@i Diplomoceras} ({@b page 210}), {@i Parapuzosia} spent its days rising and falling through the water column as it hunted plankton, larval fish, and tiny invertebrates.

There is a lot of biological and ecological overlap between {@i Parapuzosia} and {@i Diplomoceras} ({@b page 210}) so, instead of just restating ourselves, we've decided to instead look at one of the most important roles ammonites have in palaeontology: helping us date rocks through biostratigraphy.

entries.name: Ammonites in Biostratigraphy
entries: One of the many challenges in palaeontology is effectively identifying the age of strata (layers of rock). Geochronological techniques like radiometric dating can give us well supported absolute timings, but require specific types of rocks (usually volcanic rocks) that aren't present everywhere or at all times. To fill in the gaps left by their absence, we use a field of science called Biostratigraphy ({@b page 21, Chapter 1}) for which ammonites are a key group.

Biostratigraphy is the assigning of relative ages to strata based on the fossils found within them. Even if two sedimentary layers look very different, if they preserve the same species, we can be reasonably certain they were probably deposited at around the same time. For example, if we find a collection of identical fossils in a stratum in Mexico and in Britain, we can deduce that they should be about the same age. Similarly, if we have two strata from Mexico that look very similar but one has {@i Parapuzosia} in it and one has the middle Campanian ammonite {@i Bevahites} in it, we can say the {@i Parapuzosia} layer must have been deposited first. Biostratigraphy is an exceptionally powerful tool as it allows us to quickly and easily date the rocks we are working on and without the use of complex laboratory equipment, as well as build a detailed record of the relative ages of rocks around the world. Importantly, we usually don't use single taxa to identify these intervals and instead use multiple taxa that are present at varying overlapping time periods. This means that we can determine the rock's age by the combination of the presence/absence of several key fossil taxa.

entries.name: Biozones
entries: We can use biostratigraphy to divide strata into different intervals based on the fossils found within them. We refer to these divisions as "Biozones" and they can be defined by several different fossil compositions, such as the presence, absence, or change in abundance of one or more key taxa. We often use biozones to define particular Ages in the geological timescale ({@b page 18, Chapter 1}), although larger divisions of time (such as Epochs and Periods) are defined by other significant changes in global biology and/ or geology.

entries.name: Index Fossils
entries: If a particular fossil taxon defines a biozone, it is called an index or zone fossil. To be a good index fossil, it must meet several key criteria. First and foremost, it needs to be preserved in high numbers in a manner that is good enough for consistent identification. Secondly, the taxon should have a wide geographic distribution, allowing it to be found in multiple locations. Finally, it should be a relatively chronologically short-lived taxon, allowing for a higher degree of resolution for the biozone.

Ammonites tend to be excellent index fossils as they are found in large numbers in marine settings with excellent preservation potential, individual species often exist for a relatively short period of time, and they can be found in oceans across the world. It has also been suggested that their shells float for a very long time after death, allowing them to drift very far, even if the animals themselves only inhabited one specific region. In contrast, land vertebrates tend to make for very poor index fossils as they are usually found in relatively low numbers and terrestrial deposits have a much lower preservation potential than marine ones. One of the only major exceptions to this is {@i Psittacosaurus} ({@b page 52 in DDDD}), which occurs in such huge numbers with enough short-lived species in Asia to be a viable index fossil.
