trait.name: Wetland Wander
entries: Parasaurolophus is not slowed by muddy Difficult Terrain.

trait.name: Robust Quadruped
entries: So long as Parasaurolophus did not Dash on its previous turn, it has Advantage on any saving throw to avoid being knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone} and {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled}.

trait.name: Herd Instincts
entries: Parasaurolophus fervently defends its allies. Parasaurolophus has Advantage on attacks if another allied creature is below half Hit Points and is within 5 ft. of it.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, you do not need to change Parasaurolophus' CR.

trait.name: Snorkel
entries: Parasaurolophus can breathe through its head crest, allowing it to hide its body entirely submerged in water, with only a small apple-sized protrusion revealing its presence. While submerged in water, Parasaurolophus has a swim speed of 30 ft. and Advantage on {@skill Stealth} checks.

trait.name: Fires of Creation (3/Day)
entries: As an Action, Parasaurolophus can exhale a wave of fire. Each creature within a 15 ft. cone in front of Parasaurolophus must make a {@dc 13} Dexterity saving throw. Each creature takes 17 ({@dice 4d6 + 3}) Fire damage on a failed save, or half as much damage on a successful one.

action.name: Shoulder Crush
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 6} to hit, Reach 5 ft., up to two targets. {@h}27 ({@damage 4d10 + 5}) Bludgeoning damage.

In order for Parasaurolophus to target two creatures with this attack, they must be within 5 ft. of each other and within Parasaurolophus' reach. When Parasaurolophus hits with this attack, it inflicts {@dice 2d4} Bludgeoning damage to itself.

action.name: Complex Cacophonous Honk
entries: Each non-Parasaurolophus creature within 20 ft. of Parasaurolophus must succeed a {@dc 14} Constitution saving throw or take {@dice 2d8} Thunder damage. They take half as much on a success. All other Parasaurolophus within 1000 ft. are alerted to the fact that this Parasaurolophus is in danger. This honk may also communicate complex information to any other Parasaurolophus that hears it, such as the type of creatures it is fighting or where they are.
"PAH-RAH-SORE-OH-LOW-FUS'"
{@b (BESIDE CRESTED REPTILE)}
Hadrosaurs are among my favourite group of dinosaurs, largely because of their interesting vocalisations and (relatively)

docile nature. They have a... cow-like quality to them. Of the hadrosaurs, Parasaurolophus is the most fantastically vocal, calling in deep bellows that can be heard for miles. Their chorus is truly a beautiful sound to behold and many an evening did we make rest to their song.

{@i Parasaurolophus} was a medium to large sized hadrosaurid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous (76 to 66 million years ago) of North America. One of the most famous herbivorous dinosaurs, it is most well-known for possessing a long, curved tubular crest projecting out of the back of its skull.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Parasaurolophus} grew to between 25 to 30 ft. long and may have weighed between 3 and 5 tonnes. Like other hadrosaurs, it had large hindlimbs and smaller, more delicate forelimbs. This has been interpreted as evidence for facultative bipedalism (able to shift from 4 to 2 legs). However, more recent research has argued that, due to limitations in the range of motion in its shoulders, elbows, and hands as well as the structure of its muscles, hadrosaurs were likely fully quadrupedal animals. This seems to be supported by evidence that the middle 3 digits of the 5 fingered hand would have been a single unit when the animal was alive, forming a fleshy pad, with the nails fusing together into a single large hoof. {@i Parasaurolophus'} most distinctive feature was its long tubular crest that extended out of the back of its skull, and is made up of a long and convoluted hollow tube linked to the nostrils. The size and shape of this crest varied with age, species, and probably sex, but in the largest animals it could reach up to 6.5 ft. in length. The function of this crest is discussed below in "Crest Interpretation".

{@i Parasaurolophus} appears to have largely inhabited humid environments including jungles, swamps, marshy deltas, and the coastlines of the Western Interior Seaway (a large body of water that divided North America in two). It shared its environment with a wide variety of other animals including other dinosaurs like other hadrosaurs, tyrannosaurs, ceratopsians, ankylosaurs, and ornithomimids.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Like all hadrosaurs, {@i Parasaurolophus} was a herbivore with teeth adapted for chewing tough plant material. It also possessed a specialised bone at the front of its jaw called the predentary, which is also found in other herbivorous dinosaur groups (like the stegosaurs and ceratopsians). This supported a narrow beak and, combined with a mouth downturned at the sides, gave {@i Parasaurolophus} the duck-billed appearance that many hadrosaurs are known for. As its beak was rather thin, it is thought to have been a selective feeder on conifers, able to pick out and process nutritious, but tough, leaves by plucking then grinding them.

We suggest playing {@i Parasaurolophus} as a highly vocal browser, moving in small groups of no more than half a dozen or so, with the individuals widely spread out as they move about. They should be constantly calling to reassure each other of their positions and to warn of danger. They should be alert and reactive animals that may show curiosity, fear, or aggression in equal measure when faced with something new. This makes them very unpredictable and adventurers may find that spooking one animal triggers a stampede.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Multiple species of {@i Parasaurolophus} have been found in several Late Cretaceous formations across North America, suggesting that it was both quite common and successful. It is a member of the Lambeosaurinae, which are a group of primarily medium- to large-sized hadrosaurs from North America and Eurasia (although there is some evidence of dwarfism in European taxa). This highly diverse group first appeared 86 million years ago and survived up until the end Cretaceous extinction. One of their most distinctive common features was the presence of elaborate bony crests. These structures were found in numerous lambeosaurs and had a variety of morphologies. The exact function of the crests has been one of the primary points of research for the group, so much so we discuss it in some detail in its own section here.

entries.name: Crest Interpretation
entries: One of the most detailed areas of study for {@i Parasaurolophus} and its relatives is the function of their unusual crests. These structures range in shape from semi-circular ridges to short prongs, to elaborate forked structures. Early research produced some truly wild suggestions. One study argued that these crests could perhaps be used like a snorkel, allowing {@i Parasaurolophus} to remain submerged for long periods of time. However, since there was no exit at the end of the crest to allow air in or out, this is impossible. Another suggestion was that the crest could be rested against a notch in the vertebrae and used to deflect branches as the animal moved through wooded regions.

However, this notch was actually a misinterpreted pathological (injury) feature. Some authors have suggested that the crest was used to improve the animal's sense of smell. Again, this was not supported by other anatomy and research shows that the olfactory (scent) region of the nose is outside the spaces in the crest, also ruling this out.

Disregarding these unsupported speculations, the most well-supported hypothesis is that the hollow crest helped amplify hadrosaurs' calls. Hadrosaurs had excellent hearing and would have been able to hear low frequency sounds from miles away. By moving air and vibrations through the crest, they could amplify their calls, making them travel much further. The shape of the crest may also have altered the sound of the call, making the cries of different hadrosaurs more distinct. Similarly, having such wildly different crest shapes would have made the heads of each species quite distinct and made it easier for individuals to identify their own species and function as elaborate sexual signalling devices. This is supported by the fact that the crests seem to form when the animals were relatively young, but only become much more prominent when they reached sexual maturity rather than when they reached somatic (physical) maturity.

entries.name: References
entries: Evans, D.C. 2006. Nasal cavity homologies and cranial crest function in lambeosaurine dinosaurs. {@i Paleobiology}, {@b 32 (1)}, pp.109-125.
Hamilton, S.M, 2022. {@i Inferred musculature and kinematics of the forelimb in a lambeosaurine hadrosaurid dinosaur.} Unpublished Masters Thesis, University of Alberta.
Hone, D.W., Naish, D. and Cuthill, I.C. 2012. Does mutual sexual selection explain the evolution of head crests in pterosaurs and dinosaurs?. {@i Lethaia}, {@b 45 (2)}, pp.139-156.
Mallon, J.C. and Anderson, J.S. 2013. Skull ecomorphology of megaherbivorous dinosaurs from the Dinosaur Park Formation (upper Campanian) of Alberta, Canada. {@i PLoS One}, {@b 8 (7)}, pp.e67182.

trait.name: Broad Tenacious Herbivore
entries: Placerias has Advantage on Strength and Wisdom saving throws.

trait.name: Sexual Dimorphism
entries: Only male Placerias may make Cheek
Gore attacks. Female Placerias gain {@dice 2d10 + 4} Temporary Hit Points after completing a Long Rest.

trait.name: Badlands Herds
entries: Placerias has Resistance to Radiant damage (included above) and can survive for up to a week without water. Additionally, if Placerias is within 30 ft. of at least four other Placerias, increase its passive Perception from 11 to 13.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Placerias' CR to 3 and increase its XP to 700 accordingly.

trait.name: Sunstricken Undead
entries: Placerias has spent months wandering the deserts in search of water, perishing in the desiccating heat. Animated by a desperate desire for water, it now wanders the wastes looking for any moisture... even if it is tied up in another creature. Apply the following changes to Placerias:

- Change Placerias' creature type to Undead. It does not require sleep and will endlessly search for a source of fresh water or blood to ease its unquenchable thirst, aggressively attacking any non-Undead creature.

- Its body appears desiccated, thin, and skeletal. - It has Immunity to Poison, Necrotic, and Radiant damage. - Its Body Crush attacks deal an additional {@dice 1d12} Necrotic damage. - If it is able to drink a gallon or more of water or kills another creature with its Body Crush attack, Placerias dies and its body disintegrates (it does not grant XP if it dies in this manner).

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Placerias chooses the Attack action, it may make one Body Crush attack and (if it is male) one Cheek Gore attack.

action.name: Body Crush
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}11 ({@damage 2d8 + 2}) Bludgeoning damage.

action.name: Cheek Gore
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}9 ({@damage 2d6 + 2}) Piercing damage.
"PLAH-SER-EE-AS"
{@b (BROAD BODY)}

As we cleared the top ridgeline of a Triassic cuesta, we could see the sprawling plains below and our goal - a small encampment in an open fern plain. I must admit, however, that we weren't expecting to see near enough a thousand large and squat animals browsing on the plains around it. The vast herd, that was not here two days ago, now surrounded the small encampment where, I imagine, the guards stood watch nervously. We opted to spend a night on the ridge and hope that they'd moved on by the next morning.
{@i Placerias} is a large dicynodont from the Late Triassic (230 million years ago) of Arizona, USA. One of the last dicynodonts, it is thought to have lived in large migratory herds.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Placerias} was a large dicynodont, reaching 10 ft. long and weighing up to 2 tonnes. It was a stocky animal with a thick neck, a round body with wide ribs and a short tail. Its hind legs were positioned under its body, giving its rear an erect stance, but its forelimbs sprawled out to the sides. Its skull had a wide back and a set of powerful toothless jaws tipped by a sharp beak. The bones in its cheeks were modified to have long triangular horn-like projections with keratinous sheaths. These horns came in two forms, either long and forward facing (thought to be the male morph) or short and pointing to the sides (probably the female).

{@i Placerias} was found in the Chinle Formation, not far from the {@condition petrified|XPHB|Petrified} Forest National Park, Arizona, USA. This was deposited in a sub-tropical equatorial floodplain near the western sea, and experienced a range of humidities, resulting in palustrine (swampy freshwater) and eolian (dry wind-blown) deposits. It has yielded a wide variety of fossil groups, including freshwater coelacanths and lungfish, several species of shark, huge crocodile-like phytosaurs, bizarre ankylosaur-like aetosaur pseudosuchians, and the arch predator pseudosuchian {@i Postosuchus}. There were also several species of archosaurs, most notably some early pterosaurs and theropods like {@i Coelophysis}.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Placerias} was a low-browsing herbivore that specialised in robust plants like conifers and cycads. At a well-known site nicknamed "the {@i Placerias} Quarry", palaeontologists discovered the remains of at least 40 individuals that died in a mass mortality event. Evidence suggests that the quarry experienced seasonal flooding but, based on the weathering of the bones, rather than being drowned the {@i Placerias} seemed to have died during a drought.

It is possible that they lived in large herds and migrated between water sources, running the risk of dying of dehydration while travelling between water sources during particularly harsh dry periods.

We suggest playing {@i Placerias} as an animal akin to modern wildebeest, that is, a large herbivore that travels in huge herds following seasonal rains. As they travel, the herds will be followed by predators waiting to pick off the young or weak. This means that individuals towards the edge of the herd should be much more wary and reactive if approached.
As they are too slow to effectively flee from threats, a frightened {@i Placerias} will almost always turn and fight.
They can defend themselves either by using their weight or, in the case of the males, trying to gore an attacker with their cheek horns.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Placerias} was a late surviving stahleckeriid dicynodont related to both {@i Lisowicia} ({@b page 261}) and {@i Woznikella} ({@b page 122}). This was a subgroup of Kannemeyeriiformes, a highly diverse group of Triassic dicynodonts closely related to the more well-known lystrosaurids. They first appeared in China before spreading throughout Pangaea. They were large terrestrial herbivores that some have argued were competitors with early sauropodomorph dinosaurs, and the extinction of the Kannemeyeriiformes may have paved the way for dinosaurs to rapidly evolve into large herbivores.

entries.name: References
entries: Fiorillo, A.R., Padian, K. and Musikasinthorn, C. 2000. Taphonomy and depositional setting of the {@i Placerias} Quarry (Chinle Formation: Late Triassic, Arizona). {@i Palaios}, {@b 15 (5)}, pp.373-386.
Lucas, S.G. and Heckert, A.B. 2002. Skull of the dicynodont {@i Placerias} from the Upper Triassic of Arizona. {@i New Mexico Mus Nat Hist Sci Bull}, {@b 21}, pp.127-130.

Pinto, J.L., Marshall, C.R., Nesbitt, S.J. and Varajão de Latorre, D. 2024. Quantitative evidence for dimorphism suggests sexual selection in the maxillary caniniform process of {@i Placerias hesternus}. {@i Plos one}, {@b 19 (5)}, pp.e0297894.
Rowe, T. 1979. {@i Placerias}, an unusual reptile from the Chinle Formation. {@i Plateau}, {@b 51 (4)}, pp.30-32.

trait.name: Prosauropod
entries: Plateosaurus has Advantage on checks and saving throws to avoid being Shoved or knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.

trait.name: Overview
entries: Plateosaurus has Advantage on {@skill Perception} checks that involve sight.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Plateosaurus' CR to 7 and increase its XP to 2900 accordingly.

trait.name: Plate-O-Saurus
entries: Plateosaurus is covered in naturally occurring metallic armoured plate. Its AC is 18 and a Fortress Plate Amenity can be recovered from it when slain (see Howdahs, page 235 in DDDD).

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Plateosaurus chooses the Attack action, it may make one Grasping Claws attack and one Huge Tail attack.

action.name: Grasping Claws
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 7} to hit, Reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}15 ({@damage 2d10 + 4}) Slashing damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 15} Strength saving throw or drop an item it is wielding.

action.name: Huge Tail
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 7} to hit, Reach 15 ft., one target. {@h}10 ({@damage 1d12 + 4}) Bludgeoning damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 15} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.

bonus.name: Claw Ground
entries: Plateosaurus scrapes at the ground with its massive, clawed hands, similar to a bull preparing to charge. It performs an {@skill Intimidation} check at Advantage against all non-Plateosaurus creatures within 60 ft. that can see it.

reaction.name: Turning Tail Defence
entries: When Plateosaurus is hit by a melee attack, it may use its Reaction to make a Huge Tail attack at the creature that hit it.
"PLAH-TAE-OH-SORE-US"
{@b (BROAD REPTILE)}

We sometimes assume that giant dinosaurs were restricted to the Jurassic and Cretaceous. However, the Triassic gave rise to some animals that were indeed gigantic. In the woody central scrublands, thundering footsteps can herald the arrival of a Plateosaurus. This predecessor to the titanic sauropods was already enormous and best given space, lest it crush you under its bulk.

{@i Plateosaurus} is an early sauropodomorph from the Late Triassic (220 to 204 million years ago) of Europe. The most well-known member of the group Plateosauridae (sometimes called the prosauropods), it is one of the first truly large dinosaurs to appear in the fossil record.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Plateosaurus} is a very well-known animal, with more than 100 well-preserved skeletons discovered. Adults could grow more than 30 ft. long and weigh up to 4 tonnes, although interestingly there is strong evidence that they were variable in size as adults, with some weighing as little as half a tonne. They were bipedal, with long forelimbs ending in five fingered hands. The three largest digits bore prominent claws adapted for grasping. Like their giant descendants, they had an elongate neck and a proportionally small skull. Their teeth were flat and leaf-shaped, with strong crenulations (ridges) along their edges.

{@i Plateosaurus} has been found in several formations in Germany (particularly the Trossington Formation), and has also been found in Norway. These sites were deposited in either watering holes or mud traps (muddy ground that can fatally capture animals) in a semi-arid environment. It shared its environment with a variety of other animals, including multiple other sauropodomorphs, several species of theropod, and other reptiles and amphibians.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Plateosaurus'} teeth are similar to those of modern plant-eating lizards, strongly suggesting that it was a herbivore, although it may have supplemented its diet with eggs and small animals in the same manner as deer and cows. It likely used its large claws to grasp branches and pull them down to feed on. Previous studies suggested that {@i Plateosaurus} swallowed gastroliths (small stones) to help grind tough plant matter in its stomach, but this is now thought to have been a misinterpretation. Given its large size and the lack of giant theropods in the Triassic, adult {@i Plateosaurus} likely had few predators, but may have still formed herds for defence. However, evidence for this behaviour was based on large assemblages of adults found in mud traps, and this association has since been proposed to be coincidental, casting doubt on their herding behaviour. Therefore, we currently have no strong evidence for how social {@i Plateosaurus} was.

We suggest playing {@i Plateosaurus} as a large, slow-moving browser. It should move from tree to tree as it feeds, with the air of confidence found in large animals with few threats. It may be played as a solitary animal, or in small herds. If startled or threatened by a party, it should first attempt to frighten them away with a display of aggression, perhaps clawing at the ground and performing mock charges. An attack will most likely only come if the target of its ire refuses to back away.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Plateosaurus} is a plateosaurid, a group that first arose approximately 225 million years ago in the central portion of the supercontinent Pangea (which later became modern Europe, Asia, Africa, and Greenland). This herbivorous group was originally quite small with later animals growing to be giants of their time and developing the sauropod-like traits of smaller heads, longer necks, and robust limbs. While successful during the Late Triassic, the plateosaurids would be one of a number of terrestrial (on land) vertebrate groups that did not survive the Triassic-Jurassic extinction event, which killed off approximately 76% of all life.

entries.name: References
entries: Button, D.J., Barrett, P.M. and Rayfield, E.J. 2016. Comparative cranial myology and biomechanics of {@i Plateosaurus} and {@i Camarasaurus} and evolution of the sauropod feeding apparatus. {@i Palaeontology}, {@b 59 (6)}, pp.887-913.
Chapelle, K.E., Botha, J. and Choiniere, J.N. 2021. Extreme growth plasticity in the early branching sauropodomorph {@i Massospondylus} carinatus. {@i Biology Letters}, {@b 17 (5)}, pp.20200843.
Sander, P.M. 1992. The Norian {@i Plateosaurus} bonebeds of central Europe and their taphonomy. {@i Palaeogeography, Palaeoclimatology, Palaeoecology}, {@b 93 (3-4)}, pp.255-299.

trait.name: Tiny Spike
entries: If a creature hits Plectronoceras with a melee attack, that creature takes 1 Piercing damage.

trait.name: Aquatic
entries: Plectronoceras can only breathe while in water.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, Plectronoceras becomes an unbalanced "gag" creature. We suggest treating it as a CR 10 creature (5900 XP), although its capacity to both deal damage and survive attacks are wildly unfair.

trait.name: Evasive Casting
entries: Plectronoceras can take up to three Reactions per round of combat.
If it would be hit by a melee attack, it may use a Reaction to cast Misty Step without using a spell slot to move to another location and avoid the attack.
If it would be hit by a ranged attack, it may use a Reaction to snare the projectile, reducing the damage to 0.
If it would be targeted or hit by a spell, it may use a Reaction to cast Reflect without using a spell slot.

trait.name: Awful Enemy
entries: Plectronoceras' Intelligence score is increased to 10. It can understand all languages but cannot speak. Plectronoceras does not roll for initiative. Instead, it always takes its turn at initiative 20 in combat.
Once per day, if Plectronoceras would be reduced to 0 Hit Points from a spell or attack, it may instead remain at 1 Hit Point.

action.name: Slime
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 0} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}0 (0) Acid damage.
"PLEK-TRON-OH-SEAR-AS"
{@b (SPUR-LIKE HORN)}

Long before creatures walked the world, some tiny things swam and slimed across the ocean floor and in the shallow pools of desolate rocky coasts. Such creatures share a primordial bond with the world that is beyond description and are intertwined with the fundamental forces of our planet. One such creature seems able to harness the powers of the weave with devastating results and is properly "dressed" to do so. I suggest avoiding it - Plectronoceras, the First Wizard.

{@i Plectronoceras} is a strange benthic (bottom-dwelling) mollusc from the Late Cambrian (501 million years ago) of the Liaotung region in Northeastern China. Known only from its shell, it is the oldest member of the cephalopods (octopuses and their relatives) to appear in the fossil record.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Plectronoceras} is only known from incomplete remains but, based on what has been discovered, the shell was measured only between 0.8-1.5 in. long. Compared to later cephalopods like ammonites, its shell was simple and unornamented. It was compressed laterally, meaning it had shallow sides and would have looked quite thin from a front-facing view. The shell was endogastric, meaning it curved backwards away from the head, giving it the appearance of a long, curved, pointed hat. Inside the shell was a section called a phragmacone, which is a cavity divided into chambers by walls termed septae.

Each chamber was connected by a barrier called a siphuncle, which was a soft-tissue structure that linked each chamber and allowed them to be filled or emptied with water. This would have let {@i Plectronoceras} control its buoyancy and it either made small "hops" along the seafloor to move or pushed itself into the substrate to stay in place. Unlike many of its later relatives, it could not shoot out a jet of water to move quickly, so it likely lived at a rather slow pace. No soft tissue is known from it, however it likely had simple tentacles based on its relatives. As it was a benthic (sea floor-dwelling) animal, it may have modified much of its body into a snail-like foot that allowed it to crawl along the seafloor.

{@i Plectronoceras} is a rare fossil within the Fengshan Formation of the Wuhutsui Basin, Liaotung, China. This formation is made up of shelly mudstones mixed with shale and limestone. It seems to have been deposited on a shallow ocean ramp that transitioned into a deeper ocean shelf over time. The Fengshan fauna contained a variety of animals including early jellyfish, molluscs, and trilobites. {@i Ellisella coral} While {@i Plectronoceras} would have been incapable of hunting adults of these animals, it would have likely fed on their eggs or dead remains that settled on the seafloor.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: As a benthic animal, {@i Plectronoceras} would have been a detritivore (feeds on detritus). This means it fed primarily by moving over the seafloor looking for organic debris that had become mixed in with sand particles, including small animal eggs, carcasses, faeces, and other organic matter. This lifestyle did not require a great deal of advanced behaviour, but one interesting question regarding {@i Plectronoceras} is how intelligent it may have been. Derived cephalopods like octopuses are highly intelligent, perhaps comparable to a 3-year-old child. {@i Plectronoceras} on the other hand, is a member of the nautiloids, an early branching group generally considered to be much less advanced. Recent studies into the modern nautilus, however, suggest that it is more intelligent than previously believed and may have some advanced learning or information retention skills.

We suggest playing {@i Plectronoceras} as a peaceful creature, moving along the bottom of the seafloor (perhaps even in shallows) largely uninterested in the comings and goings of humanoids. Its main reaction should be to make small "hops" to avoid being stepped on or to dodge benthic predators. However, perhaps this small creature is not as dull as it appears, possibly concealing a hidden intelligence. Perhaps even it might know something of the magical arts. After all, its shell does look remarkably similar to a wizard's hat...

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Plectronoceras} is the oldest known member of the Nautiloidea. Nautiloids first appeared in the Late Cambrian (501 million years ago) and initially were extremely successful with a global distribution. However, like most groups alive at the time, they were severely impacted by the Permian extinction event with only a few members surviving into the Mesozoic. Of these, only a handful of lineages established themselves and remained successful right up until the Miocene/Pliocene cooling event (23 to 5.3 million years ago), where they became much more restricted. Today, only two genera and six species of nautiloid remain, restricted to select parts of the Indo-Pacific region.

Kobayashi, T. 1987. The Ancestory of the Cephalopoda From {@i Helcionell}a to {@i Plectronoceras}. {@i Proceedings of the Japan Academy, Series B}, {@b 63 (5)}, pp.135-138.

spellcasting.name: The First Wizard
headerEntries: Plectronoceras is a 15th level spellcaster. Its spell attack modifier is +10 and its spell save DC is 18 (not based on a specific stat) and it never requires verbal or material components to cast spells. It knows the following spells:

trait.name: Macroraptorial Crocodylomorph
entries: Plesiosuchus has Advantage on attacks against Large and Huge creatures. It also has Resistance to Poison damage (included above) and Advantage on any check or saving throw to prevent or end the {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned} condition.

trait.name: Pursuit Swimmer
entries: Plesiosuchus has Advantage on {@skill Survival} checks to track prey. It also has Advantage
on {@skill Athletics} checks and may swim for up to 8 hours continuously without requiring rest.

trait.name: Aquatic Ectotherm
entries: Plesiosuchus can hold its breath for 10 minutes. However, it has Vulnerability to Cold damage (included above).

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Plesiosuchus' CR to 5 and increase its XP to 1800 accordingly.

trait.name: Reef Ripper
entries: Plesiosuchus' back is covered in rocky corals and vivid sea anemones. Increase Plesiosuchus' AC to 16. If a creature hits it with a melee attack, that creature takes {@dice 2d4} Poison damage (no save allowed).

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Plesiosuchus chooses the Attack action, it may make any combination of two Winding Bite or Gripping Bite attacks.

action.name: Winding Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}13 ({@damage 3d6 + 3}) Piercing damage.

A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 13} Constitution saving throw or be winded, forcing it to gasp for air. If the creature is submerged in water and unable to breathe in water, it will immediately begin to suffocate.

action.name: Gripping Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}13 ({@damage 3d6 + 3}) Piercing damage.
A Large or smaller creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} (escape {@dc 13}).
"PLEE-ZEE-OH-SOO-KUS"
{@b (NEAR CROCODILE)}

Tropical seas bear numerous threats, particularly stinging animals like jellyfish and cone snails that can catch adventurers off-guard. However, in the Mesozoic, one of the largest threats among tropical island seas are the large, hostile, and exceedingly persistent Plesiosuchus. These fully aquatic crocodiles are dangerous predators that do not easily abandon a hunt once they've identified you as prey.
{@i Plesiosuchus} is a metriorhynchid crocodylomorph from the Late Jurassic (154 million years ago) of England. A fully oceanic animal, it specialised in hunting other large marine reptiles.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Plesiosuchus} was the largest metriorhynchid and it grew up to 22 ft. long and weighed up to 1 tonne. It was so heavily adapted for a life at sea, that it lost the ability to move on land. Its body was more tube-like than normal crocodylomorphs, with smooth skin lacking any dermal armour. Its legs were adapted into paddles and it had a mosasaur-like tail fluke, with the vertebrae extending into the lower half. Its jaws were robust with a wide gape, giving it a quick and powerful bite. Its teeth were numerous, large, and serrated, clearly identifying it as a predator.

{@i Plesiosuchus} is found in the Kimmeridge Clay Formation of Dorset, England. This is one of the most famous Jurassic formations in the world and was deposited in a shallow tropical sea. It is highly fossiliferous and heavily studied, yielding hundreds of high-quality vertebrate fossils, including marine and terrestrial animals. These include numerous dinosaurs, pterosaurs and, most relevant here, more than a dozen species of marine reptiles. While most of these would have been either prey or rivals for {@i Plesiosuchus}, the giant pliosaur {@i Pliosaurus} was a potential predator.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Plesiosuchus} was more robust than most marine crocodiles and, based on analyses of the morphology of its skull, it is thought to have been macroraptorial. This means that it preferentially hunted large prey, with much of its diet made up of other marine reptiles. Studies into its braincase anatomy suggest it was well adapted to be a pursuit predator and may have hunted by chasing its prey until they were too exhausted to fight back. Being fully aquatic, {@i Plesiosuchus} could not come on land and the anatomy of infant {@i Plesiosuchus}, combined with an unusually large pelvic opening for a reptile, suggests it likely gave birth to liveyoung. This is a trait unique within Archosauria.

We suggest playing {@i Plesiosuchus} as an arch predator, cruising near the surface of the ocean in search of prey. Once spotted, it should rush in and either try to immediately inflict a crippling wound or chase their prey to the point of exhaustion. As the tired animal attempts to surface to breathe, the {@i Plesiosuchus} should force them under water to try and drown them. Once a year, females will move into shallower water to give birth in relative safety. Their pups are semi-independent at birth, but the mother will stay near for several months as an extra line of defence. While a passing boat or ship is too large and strange to be seen as prey, anything that comes too close to a nursery could be quickly swarmed by angry parents defending their young. Swimming humanoids should be seen as easy prey in any setting.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Plesiosuchus} is a member of the Metriorhynchidae. Along with the more terrestrial Teleosauridae, they make up the group Thalattosuchia. These were marine adapted crocodylomorphs that first appeared 190 million years ago in what is now the United Kingdom. By 160 million years ago, they had spread into the rest of Laurasia (North America and Eurasia) and to western Gondwana (South America). While the teleosaurs retained their ability to walk on land, the metriorhynchids became fully aquatic. Despite this adaptation, they seemed to have remained exothermic ("cold-blooded"), whereas most marine reptiles developed endothermy ("hot-blooded"). This may have contributed to their extinction as they would have been more sensitive to climatic changes such as the cooling effect seen at the end of the Jurassic. While metriorhynchids survived into the Early Cretaceous, this seems limited to warmer tropical seas and by 120 million years ago, the Thalattosuchia had completely disappeared.

trait.name: Otter-like Adaptations
entries: While in water, Potamotherium has a Blindsight of 10 ft. (included above). Potamotherium can also hold its breath for up to 10 minutes.

trait.name: Weasel-like Wriggle
entries: When making a Dexterity saving throw to take half damage from an attack, spell, or effect, Potamotherium instead takes no damage if the saving throw is succeeded.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, you do not need to change Potamotherium's CR.

trait.name: Riverbeast
entries: Potamotherium knows the Shape Water cantrip. If Potamotherium are present in a riverless environment for a prolonged period of time (weeks to months), their presence will eventually stimulate the formation of a river.

action.name: Wriggling Nip
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}4 ({@damage 1d4 + 2}) Piercing damage.
If this attack misses, Potamotherium may use its Reaction to attempt the attack again against the same creature.
"POH-TAH-MOH-THER-EH-UM"
{@b (RIVER BEAST)}

In wetlands and along rivers, you may encounter the adorable Potamotherium. This otter-like animal is actually an early relative of seals and an excellent example of convergent evolution. Perhaps we will see the opposite one day, with the oceans full of seal-like otters. An interesting hypothesis to muse upon and a perfect excuse to spend a few hours observing these beautiful little creatures.

{@i Potamotherium} is a semantorid from the very Late Oligocene to Late Miocene (23 to 11 million years ago) of Europe, as well as the northwestern USA. It bears a striking resemblance to a modern otter but, after several decades of analysis, we now think it is actually a form of early seal.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Potamotherium} was a medium-sized semi-aquatic carnivore that was, in many ways, very similar to an otter. It grew to about 5 ft. long and weighed up to 30 lb. It had an elongate body with short legs, each ending in webbed feet bearing sharp claws. While its tail was somewhat flattened, it was not to the same degree as an otter. Its spine was highly flexible, allowing it to twist and turn in the water. It had a boxy head with sharp teeth and a quick, but relatively weak, bite. Studies into its brain morphology strongly suggest it had well-developed whiskers which would have allowed it to find its way through murky water.

{@i Potamotherium} has been found in several latest Oligocene to Late Miocene formations across Europe as well as several locations in North America. These formations were deposited in both lacustrine (lake) and fluvial (river) environments. These habitats are rich in a variety of different fauna, but it is notable that {@i Potamotherium} is often found in very carnivore-rich locations. One site in Hungary produced only a small handful of carnivore fossils, but included {@i Potamotherium} alongside multiple species of mustelids and amphicynodonts, a basal semi-aquatic carnivore group thought to be related to either seals or bears. This faunal diversity suggests that these freshwater habitats were rich enough in resources to support multiple competing species.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: There have been several studies into the ecomorphology (the relationship between an animals physical features and its environment) of {@i Potamotherium} that suggest it was extremely otter-like in its behaviour. It was an excellent swimmer that would have spent most of its time in the water, using its sensitive whiskers to find its way around. Studies of its forearms reveal that it wasn't as dextrous with its paws as some specialist shellfish eating otters, meaning it was not built to manipulate prey like bivalves. Instead its jaws were much more like fish-eating otters, lacking a powerful bite but strong enough to grab and tear at less-protected prey.

We suggest playing {@i Potamotherium} as an analogue for the modern otter. It should be a speedy, active predator that is frequently seen chasing fish in rivers or streams. When not hunting, it should be found either in a riverside burrow (similar to an otter's holt) or reclining on the bank. It can be a highly curious and vocal animal, often seen playing with other {@i Potamotherium} or easily distracted by novel experiences. They may even be found sliding down muddy slopes or rolling in grass while cheerfully chirping to themselves. While highly aggressive if threatened, a quiet and patient adventurer resting at the riverside may find themselves approached by a curious {@i Potamotherium}, eager to see what potential treats they have in their pockets.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: The phylogenetic affinities of {@i Potamotherium} have been the subject of considerable debate. When first discovered in the 1800s, it was identified as a basal lutrine mustelid (the otter family), however as early as the 1930s some researchers noted that its dentition was more primitive than other mustelids and more like that of seals (which are their sister group). As time went on, research into their neurology also showed that their brains were more seal-like than otter-like. In the 2010s, new phylogenies placed {@i Potomatherium} as a basal Semantoridae, a group of otter-like carnivores that are now thought to be some of the earliest basal pinnipeds (seals) and represent transitional forms between the groups fully terrestrial ancestors and their aquatic (and eventually marine) descendants. Their resemblance to otters was superficial and a result of convergent evolution due to them sharing similar environmental niches. In this case, semantorids appeared in the Late Oligocene (24 million years ago) and became successful freshwater predators. Lutrines appeared later in the Miocene (approximately 11 million years ago) and developed a similar body type. As such, it's possible that the newly arrived lutrines competed directly with the semantorids and, in combination with environmental changes, may have been responsible for the latter group's extinction.

trait.name: Fleshy Crest Display
entries: Prosaurolophus can communicate with other Prosaurolophus silently, so long as they can see it. Prosaurolophus has Advantage on {@skill Intimidation} checks.

trait.name: Migratory
entries: Prosaurolophus is experienced with many environments. It is not slowed by natural Difficult Terrain.

trait.name: Robust Herbivore
entries: So long as Prosaurolophus did not Dash on its previous turn, it has Advantage on any saving throw to avoid being knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone} or {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled}.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Prosaurolophus' CR to 5 and increase its XP to 1800 accordingly.

trait.name: Devil's Crest
entries: The fleshy head crest on Prosaurolophus' head reveals its true nature - protruding into pair jutting devil's horns.
Prosaurolophus' creature type becomes Devil, its alignment becomes Chaotic Evil, it gains Immunity to Fire damage and Resistance to Bludgeoning, Piercing, and Slashing damage.
Additionally, each of Prosaurolophus' attacks deal an additional {@dice 1d6} Fire damage.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Prosaurolophus chooses the Attack action, it may make two Plodding Trample attacks.

action.name: Plodding Trample
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}14 ({@damage 2d10 + 3}) Bludgeoning damage.
If Prosaurolophus moved at least 10 ft. this turn, a creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 13} Strength saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.
"PRO-SORE-OL-OH-FUS"
{@b (BEFORE REPTILE CREST)}

Migrating mega-herds of Prosaurolophus are a seasonal event across many regions of the Cretaceous and are an absolute treat to observe. As the wet season begins and arid badlands transform into verdant shrublands, these animals travel in their thousands to take advantage of the bounty. It is a stunning event to behold.

{@i Prosaurolophus} was a hadrosaur from the Late Cretaceous (75 million years ago) of North America. Despite its name, it belongs to a different branch of the hadrosaur family than {@i Parasaurolophus} ({@b page 283}).

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Prosaurolophus} was a reasonably large hadrosaur, reaching 28 ft. in length and weighing about 3 tonnes. In terms of its overall morphology, it was a fairly typical looking hadrosaur being quadrupedal with a thick tail, low shoulders, elongated skull, a keratinous beak, and a tight battery of hundreds of teeth that allowed it to chew food effectively. Based on its dental wear patterns, it may have been a higher browser than other competing hadrosaurs. Between its eyes it had a short triangular crest rising above the top of its skull, with a concave depression on each side. Interestingly, unlike {@i Parasaurolophus} and other large-crested hadrosaurs, the crest underwent isometric growth. This means that the shape of the crest did not change greatly as the animal grew. It has been suggested that, as the crest may have been too small to be useful for display, {@i Prosaurolophus} may have had some kind of soft tissue structures running from the nose and anchoring to the crest. This is supported by evidence for fleshy nostrils and crests in other hadrosaurs. If present, these may have been brightly coloured or been able to inflate, either of which would have been useful in communication.

{@i Prosaurolophus} has been found in both the Two Medicine and Dinosaur Park Formations, which crop out in Alberta, Canada, and Montana, USA, respectively. The Dinosaur Park Formation was laid down in a floodplain near the margin of the Western Interior Seaway. The Two Medicine Formation was formed further inland in a drier, more elevated environment. It co-existed with numerous other taxa including multiple species of hadrosaurs, ceratopsians, ankylosaurs, dromaeosaurs, and several species of tyrannosaur.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: In the Dinosaur Park Formation, {@i Prosaurolophus} has been found within same-species bonebeds, amalgamations of fossils from dozens of individuals of the same taxon. This has been taken as evidence that it was a herding animal, with some speculation that it may have lived in smaller groups for some of the year, then gathered into larger herds seasonally.

We suggest playing {@i Prosaurolophus} as a migratory animal. In the dry season, they should be found in small family groups made up of females and their young, with males living more isolated lives. They should eke out a living by browsing on tough plants like conifers. Once the wet season begins, families should migrate great distances to gather in newly formed verdant wetlands and fern savannahs. These families will amalgamate together to form larger herds, and it is here that animals will mate and reproduce over several months. During this period, {@i Prosaurolophus} should be at its most dangerous, with the males fighting for the right to mate and females aggressively defending their families.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Prosaurolophus} is a member of Saurolophinae. This is a subgroup of hadrosaurs that first appeared approximately 86 million years ago and includes the largest hadrosaurs in the fossil record. Saurolophines were very successful, with fossils showing that they were able to populate North America, South America, Russia, and China. The largest saurolophines are the only other dinosaurs to reach similar sizes to big sauropods, with the biggest reaching nearly 20 tonnes. Their success meant that several species survived up to the end Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary where, like so many others, they died out in the end Cretaceous extinction event.

trait.name: Aquatic Organism
entries: Pterygotus can only breathe while underwater.

trait.name: Paddle-like Appendages
entries: If Pterygotus takes the Dash action, triple its swim speed instead of doubling it.

trait.name: Compound Eyes & Ocelli
entries: Pterygotus has a passive Perception of 14, +4 to {@skill Perception} checks, and cannot be surprised in the first round of combat.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Pterygotus' CR to 2 and increase its XP to 450 accordingly.

trait.name: Sky Scorpion
entries: Pterygotus has large insectoid wings, gaining a fly speed of 25 ft. and can breathe both air and water. Pterygotus gains the following attack:

trait.name: Scorpion Tail
entries: Melee Weapon Attack: +4 to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. Hit: 7 ({@dice 2d4 + 2}) Piercing damage plus 3 ({@dice 1d6}) Poison damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 12} Constitution saving throw or become {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned} for 1 minute.

action.name: Cheliceral Claws
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}7 ({@damage 2d4 + 2}) Piercing damage.
A creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} and {@condition restrained|XPHB|Restrained} (escape {@dc 12}).

If a creature starts its turn {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} by Pterygotus in this manner, that creature takes {@dice 1d4 + 2} Piercing damage and Pterygotus recovers lost Hit Points equal to the same amount of damage as it picks bits off to devour.
While Pterygotus is grappling a creature with this attack, it may only attack the {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} creature.
"TER-E-GO-TUS"
{@b (WINGED ONE)}

Many of us have observed crabs picking at food while waiting in a dockyard or walking the coast - pulling off bits with their claws and nibbling them. An interesting behaviour, and one shared by many prehistoric aquatic arthropods. One animal though, Pterygotus, turns this simple act into a horror show. This predatory "sea scorpion" is so large that it could easily grab a grown adult and begin the same process... perhaps even while they're alive.

{@i Pterygotus} is a giant aquatic arthropod that was found globally during the Middle Silurian to Late Devonian (428-372 million years ago). While it is also called a sea scorpion, it is not a true arachnid (spiders, scorpions, mites, and their kin), belonging instead to an extinct sibling group called the eurypterids.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: Depending on the species, {@i Pterygotus} varied a lot in size. The smallest specimens were as little as 20 in. long while the largest individuals could reach 6 ft. in length. Most of its body was made up of flat overlapping plates, the surface of which had a raised keel towards the back end. It had a semi-circular head with two large compound eyes on the upper surface. Most of its limbs were small and skinny, unable to bear its weight out of the water, although one leg on each side of the head was modified into a flat paddle it used for swimming. Held in front of the mouth were two more appendages called chelicerae. These long and paired graspers ended in large, almost crab-like, pincers lined with sharp teeth along their inside edge. The shape of the teeth in the claws were highly distinctive and can be used to identify different species.

{@i Pterygotus} has been found in geological formations across the world and likely had a global distribution. They have been found in most aquatic environments from freshwater rivers and lakes to deep marine oceans, and they shared these ecosystems with a wide variety of animals. {@i Pterygotus} have been found in formations containing jawless agnathan fish, armoured placoderm fish (like {@i Dunkleosteus} ({@b page 216})), trilobites ({@b page 328}), graptolites, bivalves, gastropods, and other eurypterids. It was clearly a highly adaptive and highly successful animal.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Pterygotus}' large grasping chelicerae were highly flexible, capable of grabbing and tearing food apart before bringing it to the mouth. Based on fossil evidence showing that some fish bear puncture marks very similar to the teeth within the claws, these were likely opportunistic hunters that could strike quickly. This, combined with their ability to freely swim in the water column, means that they may have been active predators, opportunistically chasing down anything that came into range, grabbing and holding it with their piercing claws while it struggled to escape.

We suggest playing {@i Pterygotus} as a fast-swimming, reactive animal that is prone to attacking anything of the right size to be potential prey. As it might grow to over 6 ft. long, this naturally includes Small humanoids, while larger players may find themselves under instinctive attack even if a single {@i Pterygotus} may struggle against them. Once triggered, an attack should be extremely fast with the chelicerae lashing out to grab hold of the prey and attempt to tear them apart without necessarily waiting for them to die. While {@i Pterygotus} may potentially be found in any body of water, the largest and most dangerous specimens should be found in marine settings. The worst-case scenario for anyone unlucky enough to fall into the water is the risk of being swarmed by several {@i Pterygotus} at once, as, by attacking together, they pose much more of a risk to larger humanoid species.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Pterygotus} is one of the largest members of the Eurypteridae. This group of arthropods first appeared in the Ordovician (467 million years ago) and survived all the way up to the Late Permian (250 million years ago). They are thought to have first evolved in North America, before migrating to Eurasia. Very few eurypterids seem to have established themselves outside this range, with {@i Pterygotus} being one of the few cosmopolitan species. Eurypterids were broadly divided into free-swimming eurypterines and benthic (bottom dwelling) stylonurians. Eurypterids survived to the end of the Permian but were one of the many groups to die out during the Permo-Triassic extinction. This was the largest extinction event in history and wiped out nearly 60% of all families of living organisms, including about 80% of all marine life.

monster.name: Shonisaurus (Magical Variant)

trait.name: Ocean Titan
entries: Shonisaurus has Resistance to Bludgeoning, Piercing, and Slashing damage, and Immunity to Cold and Thunder damage (all included above). Shonisaurus can hold its breath for up to 2 hours and cannot be knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone} while in water.

trait.name: Enormous Eyes
entries: Shonisaurus has Expertise in Perception and a Darkvision of 120 ft. (included above).

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, you do not need to change Shonisaurus' CR.

trait.name: Living Submarine
entries: Shonisaurus can breathe in water as well as air.

Shonisaurus can transport up to six Medium or smaller creatures in a magical extradimensional space found within its stomach. This space is approximately 30 cubic ft. and, while in this extradimensional space, creatures can move and breathe as normal.
Other extradimensional spaces (such as open bags of holding) entering this space function normally, are not destroyed, and do not open a gate to the Astral Plane.

As an Action, Shonisaurus may attempt to swallow a Medium or smaller creature within 5 ft. of it, moving them into its extradimensional space. An unwilling creature must make a {@dc 17} Dexterity saving throw to avoid being swallowed.

As an Action, Shonisaurus may regurgitate any creature from this extradimensional space, causing them to appear within 5 ft. of its mouth. Creatures inside the space may also attempt a {@dc 22} Strength check to force regurgitation. If Shonisaurus dies, all creatures that are currently swallowed in its extradimensional space are regurgitated.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Shonisaurus chooses the Attack action, it may make two Ichthyosaur Maw attacks and one
Tail Crash attack. Alternatively, it may make three Tail Crash attacks.

action.name: Ichthyosaur Maw
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 14} to hit, Reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}21 ({@damage 2d12 + 8}) Piercing damage.

action.name: Tail Crash
entries: Each other creature within a 10 ft. radius of Shonisaurus must make a {@dc 22} Constitution saving throw, taking {@dice 2d6} Thunder damage and {@dice 3d6} Bludgeoning damage on a failed save, or half as much on a successful save.

legendary.name: Reposition
entries: Shonisaurus Disengages and swims up to 25 ft.

legendary.name: Swimming Charge
entries: Shonisaurus swims up to 25 ft., then may make a single Ichthyosaur Maw attack. If Shonisaurus swam at least 20 ft. in a straight line immediately before making this attack, it deals an additional {@dice 1d12} Piercing damage on a hit.

legendaryHeader: Shonisaurus can take 2 Legendary Actions, choosing from the options below. Only one legendary option can be used at a time and only at the end of another creature's turn. Shonisaurus regains spent Legendary Actions at the start of its turn.

entries: {@i "SHO-NEE-SORE-US"} {@b (REPTILE FROM THE SHOSHONE MOUNTAINS)}

While voyaging in the deep ocean, you may glimpse an enormous ichthyosaur surfacing for air. Out there, those giants are seen as a bad omen by sailors - indicative of a bad catch (likely from spooking away fish schools!). They can, more conspicuously, also be seasonally found in coastal coves where mothers birth their young. Here, their reputation as a problem creature is more literal, as the females are exceptionally aggressive during that time of year.

{@i Shonisaurus} is a large ichthyosaur from the Late Triassic (227 million years ago) of Nevada, USA. One of the biggest predators of the Triassic seas, some individuals may have grown to the same length as the largest modern whales.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: There is some debate about how big {@i Shonisaurus} could grow. Most adult fossils suggest it grew to about 49 ft. long and weighed around 30 tonnes, although one contested specimen suggests that the largest individuals may have grown to as big as 69 ft. long. It had long pointed jaws with large conical teeth, and preserved stomach contents show that, unlike many other ichthyosaurs which feed primarily on cephalopods, {@i Shonisaurus} was a more generalist predator, feeding on fish. Its eyes were large and rounded, suggesting excellent vision, including in low-light conditions. It had a deep ribcage with a large body that tapered towards the tail, topped with a fleshy dorsal fin. Its limbs were large and paddle-like, and its tail ended in a crescent moon fluke, with the tail vertebrae curved downwards into the lower fluke The majority of {@i Shonisaurus} fossils were collected from the Luning Formation in West Union Canyon, Nevada, USA. This is a marine deposit and was laid down in shallow waters along a continental shelf that transitioned into a low-energy deep water environment. This formation does not have a diverse vertebrate assemblage, consisting mainly of {@i Shonisaurus} fossils alongside some indeterminate fish, although it has a more diverse and abundant invertebrate fauna, including numerous corals, ammonites, and shellfish. This suggests that {@i Shonisaurus} filled the role of a macro-predator that fed on much smaller prey, or that they were gathering in this food-poor location for a reason other than hunger.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: The Liuning Formation is an ichthyosaur Lagerstätte (site of exceptional preservation) and it has allowed insights into the behaviour of {@i Shonisaurus}. Fossils from large individuals are unusually abundant and, while there are the remains of newborns, there are no fossils from intermediate sized juveniles or subadults. It has been proposed that this disparity, combined with the unusually low vertebrate species diversity, is evidence that {@i Shonisaurus} were gathering here to raise newborns and possibly conceive next year's offspring. Individuals would migrate to this location and gather in large single-sex groups. Females could then birth live young, and potentially come into season shortly afterwards. Such a congregation of adults would help deter predators from attacking the infants, in a similar manner to modern whales.

We suggest playing {@i Shonisaurus} as a deep-sea animal, spending much of its life in the open ocean. Males should be solitary while females may be accompanied by one or two offspring. They should most often be seen at the surface of the water, charging into shoals of fish to snap up prey. While humanoids may not be a preferred meal for them, they may feel threatened if boats or ships approach too closely, which could cause them to lash out. Each year, pregnant females should travel along the coast looking for protected inlets and bays to give birth in and raise young. This is when they should be at their most dangerous, and sailors or fishermen who enter these bays may find themselves set upon by several angry mothers.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Shonisaurus} is a member of the Shastosauridae. This is a group of ichthyosaurs from the Late Triassic with the oldest species dating back to 235 million years ago from China, although the group was present across the northern hemisphere. Shastosaurids appear to have been exclusively large-bodied animals, with even the smallest being over 20 ft. long. Gut contents suggests that they were major oceanic predators with a generalist diet. The youngest remains have been found near the Triassic-Jurassic boundary, and it is thought that the group went extinct during the End-Triassic extinction event.

trait.name: Sweeping Rear Defences
entries: A creature attacking Stegosaurus does not gain Advantage for any ability or effect that would grant them Advantage on attacks for outnumbering or flanking Stegosaurus.

trait.name: Intimidating Plates
entries: Stegosaurus always appears to be a well-defended Huge creature to other Beasts, regardless of its size. Other Beasts will avoid attacking Stegosaurus, unless they are Huge or larger in size, or are particularly desperate. Stegosaurus has +10 to {@skill Intimidation} checks (included above).

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Stegosaurus' CR to 7 and increase its XP to 2900 accordingly

trait.name: Secondary Tail Brain
entries: Increase Stegosaurus' Intelligence score to 5. If a creature comes within 10 ft. of Stegosaurus, it may use its Reaction to make a Tailsweep attack against that creature (and may choose to also target up to two other creatures within range).

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Stegosaurus chooses the Attack action, it may make two Thagomise attacks, or a single Tailsweep attack.

action.name: Thagomise
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 8} to hit, Reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}18 ({@damage 2d12 + 5}) Piercing damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 16} Constitution saving throw or it gain the "Pierced" condition (see below). Creatures that are Huge or larger make this save at Disadvantage.
This attack is made at advantage against Neanderthal player characters and Neanderthal NPCs.

action.name: Tailsweep
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 8} to hit, Reach 10 ft., up to three targets. {@h}11 ({@damage 1d12 + 5}) Piercing damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 16} Constitution saving throw or it gain the "Pierced" condition (see below).

action.name: Condition: Pierced
entries: A creature that is Pierced has been impaled by several large horns or thagomisers.

This creatures' speed is reduced by 15 ft. (to a minimum of 5 ft.) and, at the start of its turn in combat or every minute outside of combat, the creature takes {@dice 1d12} Piercing damage (no save allowed).

This effect persists until the creature completes a Long or Short Rest (no damage during the rest), until it receives a Lesser Restoration effect, or it falls {@condition unconscious|XPHB|Unconscious}. Multiple instances of this condition do not stack.
"STEG-OH-SORE-US"
{@b (ROOF REPTILE)}

I have read many papers and research scrolls on the biology and ecology of Stegosaurus. This extremely large and dangerous herbivore is heavily armed and armoured - a veritable powerhouse of bony defence and offence. One particularly prolific researcher, Professor Thag Simmons, met his untimely end during a research excursion into Stegosaurus behaviour - don't take these animals lightly!

{@i Stegosaurus} is a stegosaur from the Late Jurassic (155 million years ago) of North America and Europe. One of the many dinosaurs discovered during the infamous American Bone Wars of the 1800s, it has become one of the most well-known of all dinosaurs.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Stegosaurus} was the largest stegosaur, reaching up to 27 ft. long and weighing between 3 to 7 tonnes. It had very long hindlegs and relatively short forelegs, which gave it a tall, forward sloping back. Its neck was held in a relatively low position and it had a long, narrow head on a long neck. While many herbivorous dinosaurs had a beak-tipped snout, {@i Stegosaurus}' beak extended over much of the length of its jaws. It had small, leaf-shaped triangular teeth. {@i Stegosaurus}' most distinctive feature were its three types of bony osteoderms. It had small, pebble-like bones covering the underside of its neck, four large pointed spikes at the tip of its tail, and a double row of huge diamond-shaped plates running along its back.

{@i Stegosaurus} has been found in both North America and Portugal, but it is most well-known from the Morrison Formation of Colorado, Utah, and Wyoming, USA. This was laid down in a warm semi-arid environment with seasonal rains that fed numerous rivers and lakes in the area. The Morrison Formation is arguably the most famous dinosaur yielding unit from the Jurassic and has a diverse fauna with multiple species of sauropods (most notably {@i Diplodocus, Apatosaurus}, and {@i Brachiosaurus}), ankylosaurs, and stegosaurs, as well as several famous theropods such as {@i Ceratosaurus}, {@i Allosaurus} ({@b page 196 in DDDD}), and {@i Torvosaurus} ({@b page 321}).

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: The most prominent question about {@i Stegosaurus} was the function of its osteoderms, particularly its back plates. Many hypotheses have been put forward, but the most popular are thermoregulation, defence, and sexual display.

Thermoregulation has been suggested based on their surface large area and heavy vascularisation, which might have allowed them to efficiently dissipate heat. Recent analyses have questioned this as most other large dinosaurs appear to be able to thermoregulate effectively without plates. Defensively, the throat armour may have been valuable, but the back plates left its flanks unprotected. Sexual display seems the most probable primary function, particularly since the plates have positive allometry (rapid growth relative to the rest of the body), a feature common for sexual display structures. The tail spikes are much less controversial, as there is strong evidence that they functioned as weapons. {@i Allosaurus} vertebrae have been found with a distinct puncture hole matching the shape of a stegosaur spike.
We suggest playing {@i Stegosaurus} as an animal living in small herds of females and their young. They should be slow movers with a generally unhurried air about them.

During the mating season, lone males will travel dozens of miles to find and display to fertile females. They should stand with their sides facing a potential mate, showing off the size and the colour of their plates. If two males vie for the same female, they should begin circling each other before swiping at each other with their tails. When faced with an enemy who is undeterred by a threat display, a {@i Stegosaurus} will spin around to keep its tail facing the foe and strike when they approach too close.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Stegosaurus} is the largest member of the Stegosauridae. This group of armoured thyreophorans first arose 169 million years ago in China before spreading to North America, Europe, Africa, and South America. Most stegosaurs have a combination of spikes and plates running down the midline of their back, with many also having a pair of large shoulder spines, like {@i Kentrosaurus} ({@b page 138 in DDDD}). Interestingly, this is a trait that {@i Stegosaurus} itself lacks. While common up until the end of the Jurassic, stegosaurs went into sharp decline in the Early Cretaceous, with the last known species disappearing in China approximately 110 million years ago.

entries.name: References
entries: Carpenter, K., Sanders, F., McWhinney, L.A. and Wood, L. 2005. Chapter 17. Evidence for predator-prey relationships: examples for {@i Allosaurus} and {@i Stegosaurus}. In. Carpenter, K. (Ed.) {@i The carnivorous dinosaurs}, pp.325-350.

Hayashi, S., Carpenter, K. and Suzuki, D. 2009. Different growth patterns between the skeleton and osteoderms of {@i Stegosaurus} (Ornithischia: Thyreophora). {@i Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology}, {@b 29 (1)}, pp.123-131.

Maidment, S.C., Norman, D.B., Barrett, P.M. and Upchurch, P. 2008. Systematics and phylogeny of Stegosauria (Dinosauria: Ornithischia). {@i Journal of Systematic Palaeontology}, {@b 6 (4)}, pp.367-407.

Saitta, E.T., Bonhomme, V., Lukens, M., Vidal, D., Longrich, N.R., Richmond, D.R. and Stockdale, M.T. 2025. The function and Evolution of Stegosaur Osteoderms and Hypothesized Sexual Dimorphism in {@i Hesperosaurus. bioRxiv}, {@b 2025.04.10.648273}, pp.1-48.

trait.name: Ambush Hunter
entries: Teleocrater has Advantage on {@skill Stealth} checks.

trait.name: Feeding Frenzy
entries: If another creature is reduced to 0 Hit Points or dies within 50 ft. of Teleocrater, it goes into a feeding frenzy. It gains Resistance to Bludgeoning, Piercing, and Slashing damage until the end of combat.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, you do not need to change Teleocrater's CR.

trait.name: Aura of the Ancestor
entries: Teleocrater is one of the early ancestors of all dinosaurs and pterosaurs. It can project an aura that makes its descendants recognise that and they see it as a close relative.
Dinosaurs and pterosaurs within 100 ft. of Teleocrater treat it as an ally and will defend it with their lives.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Teleocrater chooses the Attack action, it may make two Razor-Toothed Bite attacks.

action.name: Razor-Toothed Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}4 ({@damage 1d6 + 1}) Piercing damage.
"TEE-LEE-OH-CRAY-TEAR"
{@b (COMPLETED BASIN)}

Upon stumbling past a recent carcass, we were privy to the feeding habits of several Teleocrater. This low-standing four-legged reptile looks slow at first glance, however I can assure you that the motion in that utter feeding frenzy was anything but. We know now that, should one of us become injured, we should not take time to recuperate steadily, and instead immediately turn to healing magic or potions, lest we suffer the same fate.

{@i Teleocrater} is a quadrupedal archosaur from the Middle Triassic (247 million years ago) of Tanzania, Africa. It was one of the earliest members of the Avemetatarsalia, the line of archosaurs that includes both dinosaurs and pterosaurs.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Teleocrater} was a relatively large predator for its time, measuring between 7-10 ft. long and weighing up to 65 lb. Based on its bone histology (internal bone structure), {@i Teleocrater} grew rapidly in comparison to other archosaurs, although slower than its more derived relatives. It had a proportionally long neck that ended with a small rectangular head. Only one tooth has been found, but it shows that {@i Teleocrater} was a carnivore as the tooth is curved and serrated. It was quadrupedal, with the hindlimbs being noticeably longer than the front. Unlike some later avemetatarsalians, it was an obligate quadruped (had to walk on all four limbs) and was unable to run on its hind legs alone.

While the origin of the holotype specimen was not certain when it was originally described, later material showed that {@i Teleocrater} was found in the Manda Formation from the Ruhuhu Basin in Tanzania. This was deposited on a floodplain that experienced seasonal rains and hosted a series of semi-permanent waterbodies. This would have allowed for a rich vegetation and a diverse animal assemblage. {@i Teleocrater} lived alongside animals such as synapsids, like the herbivorous dicynodonts, and carnivores like {@i Cynognathus}, as well as a wide variety of other archosaurs, such as the herbivorous {@i Asilisaurus} and the predatory pseudosuchian {@i Nundasuchus}.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Teleocrater} had a more primitive foot structure compared to later avemetatarsalians and it is thought to have been a relatively slow runner with a semi-erect gait, although their bone histology indicates it was not a sluggish animal. It likely hunted by stalking prey until it was as close as possible before rushing them, attempting to bring them down quickly and avoid an energetic chase.

We suggest playing {@i Teleocrater} as a stealthy predator, moving through the undergrowth to quietly stalk its prey. Once close enough to an animal, it should charge suddenly and attempt to kill its prey as quickly as possible. If their intended target avoids the first strike, they should only be willing to chase them for a short distance before giving up. Large carcasses may be swarmed by a mob of {@i Teleocrater}, each one vying for a position during a feeding frenzy. Infighting should be common and approaching them in this frenzied state is the easiest way to trigger an attack.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Teleocrater} is one of the most, if not the most, basal avemetatarsalians in the fossil record. Avemetatarsalia is a diverse group of archosaurs that first appeared 247 million years ago. It is often defined by the structure of the ankle joint and most members of the group have a mesotarsal joint. This means that the ankle joint is formed in such a way that it works along a simple hinge, allowing greater forward and backwards motion but less rotation. {@i Teleocrater,} as the most basal member, retains the crurotarsal joint. This allowed for greater flexibility and rotation of the joint and is associated with animals that have a sprawling or semi-erect stance. Avemetatarsalians were hugely successful, and have survived into the modern day in the form of birds. The derived avemetatarsalians eventually replaced more basal animals like {@i Teleocrater}, which is thought to have died out approximately 242 million years ago.

entries: Marsà, J.A.G., Agnolín, F.L. and Novas, F.E. 2020. Comparative bone microstructure of three archosauromorphs from the Carnian, Late Triassic Chañares Formation of Argentina. {@i Acta Palaeontologica Polonica}, {@b 65 (2)}, pp.387-398.

Nesbitt, S.J., Butler, R.J., Ezcurra, M.D., Barrett, P.M., Stocker, M.R., Angielczyk, K.D., Smith, R.M., Sidor, C.A., Niedźwiedzki, G., Sennikov, A.G. and Charig, A.J. 2017. The earliest bird-line archosaurs and the assembly of the dinosaur body plan. {@i Nature}, {@b 544 (7651)}, pp.484-487.
