trait.name: Benthic Walker
entries: Rather than swimming well, Thalassocnus sinks and walks along the bottom. If it is at the bottom of a body of water and is fully submerged, it can walk along it at a speed of 30 ft.
Thalassocnus can hold its breath for up to 1 hour.

trait.name: Sloth
entries: Thalassocnus cannot use its Wisdom bonus for {@skill Perception} checks or for its passive Perception, but may use its Wisdom bonus for {@skill Stealth} checks (all included above).
While outside of water, Thalassocnus has Disadvantage on Dexterity saving throws.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Thalassocnus' CR to 1 and increase its XP to 200 accordingly.

trait.name: Manatee Mind or Hippo Heart
entries: When Thalassocnus is first encountered, roll {@dice 1d6} to determine if its behaviour is more like that of a manatee or a hippo.
On a 1-3, it is like a manatee and is a peaceful, curious creature - only attacking to defend itself or its kin. Its alignment becomes Lawful Good and its AC is increased to 13.

On a 4-6, it is like a hippo and is a violent and aggressive animal, trying to kill anything that comes close enough for it to attack. Its alignment becomes Chaotic Evil (just like all real hippos) and its Powerful Bite attack deals an extra {@dice 1d6} Force damage.

action.name: Root-pulling Claw
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 4} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}7 ({@damage 2d4 + 2}) Slashing damage.

A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 12} Strength saving throw. On a failed save, the hit creature either drops an object that it is wielding or is {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} (DM's choice, escape {@dc 12}).

action.name: Powerful Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 6} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}11 ({@damage 2d8 + 2}) Piercing damage.
Thalassocnus may only use this attack against a creature that it is Grappling.
{@i "THA-LASS-OCK-NUS"} {@b (SEA OCNUS, THE GREEK GOD OF SLOTHFULNESS)}

The descriptions of a large, lanky beast that wallows in coastal shallows did not adequately prepare me for meeting a real-life Thalassocnus. This particularly bizarre mammal strides slowly across the water's bottom with slow-motion movements.
Although relatively docile, I would rather not find out how powerful its formidable-looking claws actually are.

{@i Thalassocnus} is a medium-sized ground sloth from the Miocene and Pliocene (7-3 million years ago) of South America. {@i Thalassocnus} is a highly unusual member of its family as, rather than being a terrestrial browser, it was an aquatic grazer that lived its life in the shallow ocean near the shoreline.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Thalassocnus} grew to between 8 to 11 ft. long and weighed between 200 and 400 lb. Its body was squat with a short tail and four long limbs. Its neck tilted downwards, presumably to allow for more easy grazing. Its front legs were robust, each one tipped with five sharp claws, whereas its hind legs were stocky and relatively short, with plantigrade feet (flat feet). These feet functioned as simple paddles and allowed {@i Thalassocnus} to move through the water. Its skull had elongated jaws with strong biting muscles and well-developed lips, possibly even extending into a short trunk in a similar manner to modern elephant seals. While {@i Thalassocnus} was certainly at least a partially aquatic animal, with later species likely almost never coming onto land, it is not thought to have been a particularly good swimmer. Like hippos, it had dense bones that gave it negative buoyancy (making it sink rather than float) and would have walked along the seafloor rather than actually swimming.

{@i Thalassocnus} has been found in several formations in South American countries such as Chile, Argentina, and Peru. With one notable exception (see below), it has been recovered from warm near-shore marine environments that would have been rich in seagrass. It shared this environment with a wide variety of marine mammals and fish, some of the most notable being large predatory sperm whales like {@i Livyatan} ({@b page 264}) and the infamous giant shark {@i Otodus megalodon}. While these giants were likely too large to come close enough to the shore to habitually prey on {@i Thalassocnus}, other smaller whales and sharks would have been prominent predators within its habitat.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Thalassocnus} was a specialist grazer. It is thought to have fed by diving to the seafloor and using its powerful claws to dig up seagrass by the roots. It may have lived in small family groups consisting of a few females and their calves. Calves may have been born into shallow water creches where the mothers could care for them in relative safety.

We suggest playing {@i Thalassocnus} as an ancient analogue of the manatee. For much of the day it should be found in warm bays and shallow seas, grazing along the sea floor. When at rest, you are more likely to come across them half asleep in pools only deep enough to cover their bodies. If threatened at sea, a {@i Thalassocnus} will likely break for the shallows in the hopes that its pursuer is reliant on deeper water. If cornered close to shore, or if it feels its young are threatened, it will lash out with its claws or attempt to bite with its powerful jaws, but a party that flees to the shore will be able to easily out-manoeuvre its attacks.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Thalassocnus} is a bizarre member of the Nothrotheriidae. These are large sloths that first appeared in the fossil record approximately 17.5 million years ago. The vast majority were terrestrial browsers. However, {@i Thalassocnus} is the one taxon believed to have fully migrated to a marine environment. According to recently described fossil evidence, the earliest {@i Thalassocnus} were much more terrestrial, being semi-aquatic animals that lived more inland. They later migrated to the coast where it is thought that they primarily fed on seagrass along the shoreline before transitioning into fully marine grazers. The driving force for this adaptation to an aquatic lifestyle is thought to have been related to the spread of deserts in South America, which drove animals to find novel means of survival. {@i Thalassocnus} died out approximately 3 million years ago in an extinction event tied to the reduction in the number of seagrasses caused by the closing of the Central American Seaway and the subsequent cooling of the oceans. {@i Thalassocnus} was unable to survive without abundant seagrass and was poorly adapted to cooler waters.

trait.name: Slow Metabolism
entries: Therizinosaurus has Advantage on saving throws to prevent the {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned} condition. However, if it does become {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned}, the duration of that condition is doubled.

trait.name: Stand Ground
entries: Therizinosaurus isn't typically able to flee from large predators. Instead, it has adapted to stand its ground and scare off threats with its claws. It has
Advantage on Wisdom saving throws and {@skill Intimidation} checks. It will never attempt to flee.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, you may wish to increase Therizinosaurus' CR. However, how much this increases by will depend on the weapon properties that you give to its Meter-Long Saber-Claws attack. We suggest that you consider increasing Therizinosaurus' to CR 5 (1800 XP) or CR 6 (2300 XP).

{@b {@i Sabers of Legend}}{@i. Therizinosaurus' Meter-Long Saber-Claws attack gains the effects and bonuses of a magic sword weapon of the DM's choice. This includes any magic bonus to the to hit and damage rolls, as well as any other effect the magic weapon would have if used to attack.}

Additionally, Therizinosaurus' Meter-Long Saber-Claws damage is considered magical and it deals Slashing damage or another damage type that the selected weapon would deal. These claws lose these magical properties if they are harvested from Therizinosaurus.

trait.name: Blade Fighter
entries: Therizinosaurus has Resistance to Slashing damage.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Therizinosaurus chooses the Attack action, it may make two Metre-Long Saber-Claws attacks.

action.name: Meter-Long Saber-Claws
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, Reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}9 ({@damage 1d12 + 3}) Slashing damage.
A creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 16} Constitution saving throw or take {@dice 3d12} additional Slashing damage.

action.name: Threaten
entries: Therizinosaurus spreads and waves its metre-long claws, displaying its horrific weapons. Any creature within 50 ft. that is engaged in combat with Therizinosaurus must succeed a {@dc 14} Wisdom saving throw or be {@condition frightened|XPHB|Frightened} of Therizinosaurus for 1 minute. At the end of its turn, that creature may repeat the saving throw, ending the effect on a success.
"THER-IH-ZEE-NO-SORE-US"
{@b (SCYTHE REPTILE)}

My research into herbivorous dinosaurs led us to track down a particularly unusual animal. This enormous, feathered, sloth-like beast could be found sitting squatly in the forests, pulling at branches and grazing at its leisure. Despite its small head and docile appearance, its scything talons suggested a more sinister nature. However, we were utterly unprepared for its savagery once we got too close. Our recklessness cost our paladin his favourite breastplate and at least two pints of his blood. He's lucky to be alive.

{@i Therizinosaurus} was a large, bizarre looking theropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous (around 70 million years ago) Gobi Desert of Mongolia. A more derived relative of {@i Beipiaosaurus} ({@b page 45 in DDDD}), it gets its name from its enormous claws.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Therizinosaurus} was a very large theropod, around 30 ft. in length and weighing up to 6 tonnes. While it is only known from incomplete material, based on other related animals, it probably stood in a more upright position than other theropods with its neck held aloft. This would have given it a sloping back which was offset by it having a sizable potbelly. Its legs were robust, ending in flat-footed (plantigrade) four-toed feet. It had a long neck but probably had a relatively short tail. This neck supported a very small head with jaws lined by leaf-shaped teeth that transitioned into a keratinous beak towards the snout. Most strikingly it had huge arms, estimated to be 7 ft. long, ending in three-fingered hands, with each finger supporting an enormous, elongated sabered claw. These claws were over 3 ft. long, made of bone, and would have been covered in a keratinous sheath in life, making them the largest claws of any animal known.

{@i Therizinosaurus} is found in the Late Cretaceous Nemegt Formation, which was laid down in a forested floodplain environment, with associated streams, lakes, and further nearby forests. This resulted in a rich environment able to support a wide variety of animals, including mammals, fish, and a diverse array of dinosaurs. {@i Therizinosaurus} lived alongside several species of ankylosaurs, pachycephalosaurs, sauropods, hadrosaurs, and a large number of theropods. Amongst these were multiple species of tyrannosaurs like {@i Tarbosaurus}, which was likely the only predator large enough to threaten an adult {@i Therizinosaurus}.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Despite being a very big theropod, the small head combined with its leaf-shaped teeth and large gut found in therizinosaurians identifies them as herbivorous. These animals likely spent much of their days lazily browsing high foliage and resting to allow digestion. This naturally raises the question as to why such an animal would have such prodigious claws?

Several functions have been proposed, including defence against predators, pulling branches, digging, or display. One study in 2014 argued that the claws were relatively weak and therefore may not have been suitable for combat or digging. While still useful as a last line of defence, the author argued that they were most likely used to grip or pull-down foliage with display as a major secondary function. A more comprehensive study in 2023 argued that {@i Therizinosaurus'}
claws would not have stood up to the stresses involved in grabbing foliage and instead proposed that they were purely for display.

While it is not surprising that such long, thin structures are relatively weak, it must be noted that a 2018 research exercise found that {@i Therizinosaurus} had quite strong arms that could tolerate significant strain. Given the length and strength of its arms, {@i Therizinosaurus} was certainly using them extensively. Perhaps, as is often the case, the most probable answer is that they were multifunctional, playing a role in both display and some mechanical functions, whether feeding, grooming, competing for a mate, or a slashing panicked defence.

We suggest playing {@i Therizinosaurus} as an animal that tends to live life in the slow lane. It should spend much of its day feeding, whether alone or in a small group, or resting in the shade as it takes time to digest. This should create the image of an almost laid-back placid animal uninterested in those around it. However, if approached without caution, it should rise up and display its claws as a threat. If a party is not quick to retreat it should take the initiative and move to attack.
Examples of historic swords

entries.name: References Phylogeny
entries: {@i Therizinosaurus} is the largest member of the Therizinosauria, a group of highly derived theropods that arose in the Middle to Late Jurassic and persisted right up until the end Cretaceous extinction event. Their origins are not yet resolved, as the most basal member, {@i Falcarius,} is from the Early Cretaceous Cedar Mountains of North America, yet the oldest animals are from Chinese deposits. Given that the vast majority of therizinosaurs are from Chinese or Mongolian deposits, it is likely that the group originated in Asia before migrating to North America. Interestingly, not only were basal animals present in the American assemblage, but also the much more derived therizinosaurids. This may suggest that early members of the lineage migrated over in the Early Cretaceous and then a second transition of derived forms followed later.

Lautenschlager, S. 2014. Morphological and functional diversity in therizinosaur claws and the implications for theropod claw evolution. {@i Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences}, {@b 281} ({@b 1785}), pp.20140497.

monster.name: Torvosaurus (Magical Variant)

trait.name: Tactical Legendary Resistance (1/Day)
entries: If Torvosaurus fails a saving throw, it may choose to succeed instead. However, it can use 1 fewer Legendary Actions this round if it does so and it cannot use this Legendary Resistance if it has no more Legendary Actions available to use this round.

trait.name: Arch Predator
entries: Torvosaurus cannot be easily swayed from the hunt. It has Advantage on Wisdom saving throws.

trait.name: Floodland Hunter
entries: Torvosaurus is not slowed by muddy Difficult Terrain.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Torvosaurus' CR to 8 and increase its XP to 3900 accordingly.

trait.name: From Freeze-out Hills
entries: Torvosaurus' body is encrusted with large ice crystals. It has Immunity to Cold damage, its AC is increased to 16, and its attacks deal an additional {@dice 1d8} Cold damage.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Torvosaurus chooses the Attack action, it may make two Savage Strike attacks.

action.name: Savage Strike
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 8} to hit, Reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}16 ({@damage 2d10 + 5}) (see below) damage.
Torvosaurus lashes out with one of its myriad attacks - headbutting, clawing, biting, or lashing with its tail. When making a Savage Strike, you can select either
Bludgeoning, Piercing, or Slashing as the damage type.

A creature hit by this attack is either knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}, is {@condition frightened|XPHB|Frightened} of Torvosaurus for two rounds, or is {@condition blinded|XPHB|Blinded} for one round (DM's choice).

legendary.name: Strike and Tear
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 8} to hit, Reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}8 ({@damage 1d6 + 5}) Piercing damage.
After making this attack, Torvosaurus may move up to 10 ft. A creature hit by this attack begins to bleed, gaining the "Moderate Tear" Condition described below.

legendary.name: Condition: Moderate Tear
entries: This creature is bleeding from a torn wound. At the start of its turn in combat or every minute outside of combat while not resting, the creature takes {@dice 1d6} Slashing damage (no save allowed).
This effect persists until one of the following occurs:
- The creature is healed by at least 8 Hit Points (cumulative). - The creature completes a Short or Long Rest. - A {@dc 12} {@skill Medicine} check is passed on the creature. - It dies.
Multiple instances of Moderate Tear do not stack, but do reset the amount of healing required.

legendaryHeader: Torvosaurus can take 1 Legendary Action. Only one legendary option can be used at a time and only at the end of another creature's turn. Torvosaurus regains spent Legendary Actions at the start of its turn.

entries: "TOR-VOH-SORE-US"
{@b (SAVAGE REPTILE)}

Few regions in the Jurassic are free of the threat of a Torvosaurus. These large predatory theropod dinosaurs are remarkably widespread and more than once our party outpaced one that had been stalking us, only to move into the territory of another a day or so later. Rest assured that an animal of this size being commonplace does not make it any less dangerous.

{@i Torvosaurus} was a large megalosaurid theropod dinosaur from the Jurassic (165 to 148 million years ago) of North America and Europe (with some evidence that it may also have been present in Africa). A robust and powerful animal, it is one of the biggest carnivores known from the Jurassic.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Torvosaurus} was enormous for a Jurassic theropod, with the European species growing as large as 33 ft. long and weighing between 3 to 4 tonnes. The American species was slightly smaller at 30 ft. long and 2 to 3 tonnes. It had an elongate boxy skull, with an indentation along the upper jaw that gave it a "kink" when seen from the side. Its teeth were large, curved, and serrated, with the front three teeth in the upper jaw before the kink tightly compressed and partially overlapped. While its arms were relatively short for its size (although not as exetreme as tyrannosaurs or abelisaurs), they were very muscular and ended in three large, clawed fingers.

{@i Torvosaurus} has been found in several formations in America (the Morrison Formation) and Europe (the Lourinhã Formation), with potential material also being recovered from Tanzania. These formations were laid down in a combination of floodplains and lake environments, suggesting that it was an adaptable animal that migrated into several different habitats in search of food. {@i Torvosaurus} has been found alongside a variety of other dinosaurs such as stegosaurs, sauropods, and other large carnivores, like {@i Ceratosaurus} and {@i Allosaurus} ({@b page 196 in DDDD}). These large carnivores may have avoided competing with {@i Torvosaurus} by specialising in hunting specific animal groups or within specific habitats that {@i Torvosaurus} infrequently visited.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Given its large size and powerful build, {@i Torvosaurus} has been suggested to have specialised in hunting sauropods. This proposal has some support in the fossil record, as several sauropod fossils have been found with teeth marks attributed to {@i Torvosaurus}. While these may have been caused by the animal scavenging a carcass, it has broadly been assumed that {@i Torvosaurus} was capable of hunting at least immature sauropods. One method it may have used is known as the "strike and tear" model (biting and ripping chunks off of the body, letting trauma and blood loss kill the prey). While we have little information regarding their social behaviour, we have found a nest containing {@i Torvosaurus} eggs which may indicate some level of parental care.

We suggest playing {@i Torvosaurus} as a solitary predator, one that follows sauropod herds along migration routes. Social interactions between {@i Torvosaurus} should be rare and cautious, with smaller individuals retreating and similarly sized animals attempting to intimidate each other with displays. A female {@i Torvosaurus} should bury her eggs in the rich soil found near rivers, and remain in the general area - responding aggressively to those who come too close to the nest.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Torvosaurus} is a member of the Megalosauridae. This is a group of medium to large-sized theropods that first appeared in the Middle Jurassic, approximately 170 million years ago. Named for their most famous member {@i Megalosaurus} ({@b page 148 in DDDD}), these were among the first theropods to start reaching sizes that we consider "giant". The group appears to have originated in Europe before expanding to a global distribution. Despite their overall success, the group appears to have died out during the end-Jurassic extinction event 143 million years ago, but left a significant legacy in their descendents the Spinosauridae.

trait.name: Enormous Frill
entries: If Triceratops is facing the direction that an attack originated from, increase Triceratops' AC by 3 against that attack.
Creatures that benefit from half or three-quarters cover by being behind Triceratops gain an additional +1 to their AC from that cover.

trait.name: Thrashing Tenacious Herbivore
entries: Triceratops has Advantage on {@skill Intimidation} checks and Wisdom saving throws.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change Triceratops' CR to 8 and increase its XP to 3900 accordingly.

trait.name: West Indian Lilac Vulnerability
entries: If Triceratops becomes {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned} from, or takes Poison damage from, the effects of a plant or attacks/abilities from a plant-based creature, it also becomes {@condition stunned|XPHB|Stunned} for 1 minute.

trait.name: Horns of the Magi
entries: Triceratops' horns together function in the same manner as Staff of the Magi (Retributive Strike occurs if something or over-absorbing breaks its horns, but it can't break them itself intentionally). Its spellcasting ability is Constitution (spell save {@dc 14}, +6 to hit with spell attacks). It may use all of the abilities and effects of a Staff of the Magi but can only cast spells up to level 5 (e.g. expending 7 charges to cast Fireball at 5th-level).

Additionally, Horns of the Magi allow Triceratops to cast: Greater Restoration (7 charges), Healing Word (2nd-level, 2 charges), Mass Cure Wounds (5th-level, 7 charges), Revivify (3 charges), Shield of Faith (1 charge), and Gust of Wind (2 charges).

action.name: Colossal Horn Skewer
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 9} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}25 ({@damage 3d12 + 6}) Piercing damage.

action.name: Piercing Charge
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 9} to hit, Reach 5 ft., up to two targets. {@h}25 ({@damage 3d12 + 6}) Piercing damage plus 12 ({@damage 1d12 + 6}) Bludgeoning damage.
Triceratops can only make this attack if it moved at least 30 ft. in a straight line this turn.

reaction.name: Horned Re-pose
entries: If an enemy fails to hit Triceratops with a melee attack while within 10 ft. of it, it may use its Reaction to make a Colossal Horn Skewer attack back at them.
"TRY-SEH-RUH-TOPS"
{@b (THREE HORNED FACE)}

Among the most famous of dinosaurs is the Triceratops. This titanic horned ceratopsian, with its elaborate headgear, is awe-inspiring to observe. It is probably the third most requested animal to track and view when we lead a prehistoric expedition and, despite how many warnings we give, there is always at least one adventurer who approaches it too closely - quickly drawing the ire of this titanic herbivore.
{@i Triceratops} is a large ceratopsian from the Late Cretaceous (68 million years ago) of western North America. Since its discovery in the 1880s, it has become a true dinosaur superstar.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Triceratops} was a giant animal, growing to about 30 ft. long and weighing 6 to 10 tonnes. It was quadrupedal with surprisingly delicate wrists, slightly rotated inwards with only the first three toes touching the ground. Its body was round with an arching back, short tail, and thick muscular neck. As with all ceratopsians, the most distinctive feature was its enormous skull that could make up a third of its total length. It was robust with an elongated snout and beaked jaws lined with rows of packed teeth (dental batteries). Its solid head frill was broad and fan-shaped, curving round at the sides to shield much of the neck. Along the margins of the frill were epioccipitals, ornamental bones that in most ceratopsians tended to be quite elaborate but in {@i Triceratops} were relatively small and triangular. The jugal (cheek bones) extended outwards into sideways pointing projections.

Lastly, it had three horns, one on its nose and two above its brows. The nose horn was smaller and pointed forward. The enormous brow horns were long and curved, reaching 3 to 4 ft in length, and would have been extended much further by a keratin sheath in life. The exact function of the horns and frill, as we discuss later, has historically been one of the major points of debate about this animal.

{@i Triceratops} has been found in multiple formations across western North America, most famously the Hell Creek Formation, which was deposited in a forested floodplain. {@i Triceratops} is the most common dinosaur within the formation with several bonebeds containing the remains of hundreds of individuals. While this could be taken as evidence that they were highly social, and indeed they are usually portrayed as gregarious herd animals in a similar vein to {@i Centrosaurus} ({@b page 116 in DDDD}), these are not the result of some tragic mass death event. Instead, they were individuals dying in isolation in the same region over many years. In fact there is very little evidence for adult {@i Triceratops} living in herds and they may have spent much of the year alone, only gathering together to breed.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Triceratops} was a herbivore that fed on ground plants such as ferns, palms, and various trees like cypress and hazels. It would use its toothless beak to shear off large volumes of plant material, then chew it using its tightly packed dental batteries.

We suggest playing {@i Triceratops} as a largely solitary animal, although young siblings may remain together for safety until they are old enough to defend themselves. During the breeding season, {@i Triceratops} should gather in groups where both sexes fight for mating rights. These battles can be fierce, with injuries like broken horns and damaged frills being commonplace. An adult {@i Triceratops} should be too large and well defended for most predators to tackle, with only the likes of a particularly hungry {@i Tyrannosaurus} being a major threat. If attacked, a {@i Triceratops} should take an aggressive stance, bellowing and shaking its head in an intimidation display. If this doesn't cause the aggressor to back down, its horns and wide frill make for a powerful offensive/defensive combination. {@i Triceratops} are well-travelled animals with overlapping home ranges. They can also be surprisingly altruistic and, if a passing bull stumbles upon another {@i Triceratops} under attack, it may quickly charge in to help. {@i Triceratops}' horns are a tempting target for trophy hunters and those that have survived attacks react aggressively upon seeing a humanoid. Individuals that have never been hunted are more relaxed and even curious about the habits of these strange little creatures.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Triceratops} is the most well-known member of the Triceratopsini. This is a somewhat controversial group of large Late Cretaceous ceratopsians that first appeared in the fossil record 75 million years ago and survived up until the end Cretaceous extinction. While it initially seems to be quite a diverse group, there has been a lot of debate as to which taxa are valid with five of the eight members sometimes synonymised with {@i Triceratops} in different studies. The most famous example of this is {@i Torosaurus}, a ceratopsian with an exceptionally long frill that was argued to be an older morph of {@i Triceratops} in the 2010s. This interpretation eventually fell out of favour, with a 2022 study identifying sub-adult examples, however the validity of the other controversial triceratopsines is still debated and they are sometimes lumped in as aberrant or juvenile examples of {@i Triceratops}.

entries.name: Horn and Frill Function
entries: There is no image more classically prehistoric than that of {@i Triceratops} locked in life-or-death combat with {@i Tyrannosaurus}. To say it is ingrained in our cultural memory would be an understatement. Yet, even as the media continues to push their rivalry in new shows like the reboot of {@i Walking With Dinosaurs}, scientists have for many years debated the function of {@i Triceratops'} horns. While bite marks show that adult {@i Triceratops} were certainly fed upon by {@i Tyrannosaurus} and associated fossils like the famous "Dueling Dinosaurs" may suggest that younger animals were potentially vulnerable to smaller predators like {@i Nanotyrannus}, there is strong evidence that {@i Triceratops}' horns may have been used far more against members of its own species.

It is often proposed that the frills and horns were for species distinction. In areas where multiple ceratopsian species overlapped, distinctive head ornamentation would have allowed animals to easily spot members of their own species. However, studies show that this is unlikely as we do not see an increase in variation in sites like Hell Creek where several ceratopsian species overlap, or a decrease where species are found in isolation. Instead, the most recent research argues that the horns and frills were sexually selected. These structures would have evolved as a means of improving the reproductive success of the animal. Sexually selected structures usually undergo positive allometry (growing faster than the rest of the body) which we see in {@i Triceratops}, where the frill and horns go from tiny in infants to enormous and exaggerated in adults. The frills of adults would have been excellent for signalling vigour to both mates and rivals, particularly if brightly coloured. The horns, meanwhile, also had the dual function of signalling and combat. When brought together, they interlock for head-to-head wrestling, a behaviour seen in many horned/antlered animals. To reduce the chance of being fatally wounded in a fight, the jugal projection and frill acted as extra protection for vulnerable spots like the neck and eyes. In several fossils, both of these show evidence of damage and healing that corresponds well to wounds inflicted by the horns of another {@i Triceratops}. Usually, sexually selected structures like this are also sexually dimorphic, generally exaggerated in males.

However, the large horns and frills of {@i Triceratops} are present in both sexes and this suggests that both sexes had to compete for the right to reproduce, whether that be an eager bull displaying its frill to a group of females, or two cows fighting for the attention of an interested male.

Nevertheless, {@i Triceratops'} horns and frill were undoubtedly useful for defence. In modern horned animals, while they certainly are primarily used for intraspecific (within the same species) conflict, they are equally useful in driving away predators. African buffalo are especially well-documented using their horns to gore lions or toss them violently into the air. An adult {@i Triceratops} facing off against a {@i Tyrannosaurus} would certainly have employed any weapon it had in self-defence, whether that be stabbing with its horns or intimidating with its frill. However, the infamous clash of giants was probably a fairly rare occurrence in the lives of either animal, as predators will almost always target easier prey where possible. Day-to-day, you would have been much more likely to see these incredible animals using their horns socially, rather than impaling an attacking {@i Tyrannosaurus}.

trait.name: Swarm
entries: The Trilobite Swarm can occupy another creature's space and vice versa, and it can move through any opening large enough for a Tiny beast. The swarm can't regain Hit Points or gain Temporary Hit Points, and has Immunity to the {@condition charmed|XPHB|Charmed}, {@condition frightened|XPHB|Frightened}, {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled}, {@condition paralyzed|XPHB|Paralyzed}, {@condition petrified|XPHB|Petrified}, {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}, {@condition restrained|XPHB|Restrained}, and {@condition stunned|XPHB|Stunned} conditions (included above).

trait.name: Hidden Gills
entries: The Trilobite Swarm can breathe in water. Additionally, it may breathe for up to an hour after leaving the water, then must return to water or begin to suffocate.

trait.name: Complex Eyes
entries: The Trilobite Swarm has Darkvision 10 ft. and Expertise in {@skill Perception} (both included above).

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, you do not need to change Trilobite Swarm's CR.

trait.name: Fossil Herald
entries: Upon defeating the Trilobite Swarm, the creature that dealt the killing blow gains an innate knowledge of the local palaeontology.

{@i For the next 48 hours their chances of discovering valuable fossils increases and the next time that creature rolls on a Strata table (}{@b {@i pages 52-54}}{@i ), they may instead roll twice and choose one result to keep, discarding the other.}

action.name: Swarming Consumption
entries: The Trilobite Swarm scurries over a creature within 5 ft. That creature must succeed a {@dc 6} Dexterity saving throw or lose {@dice 1d4 + 1} days' worth of rations.

action.name: Tickling Spikey Feet
entries: The Trilobite Swarm crawls all over a Small or Medium sized creature that it is within 5 ft. of.
That creature must succeed a {@dc 8} Constitution saving throw or be knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}, drop an item they are wielding, and take 1 point of Piercing damage.
{@i "TRY-LOW-BITE"} {@b (THREE LOBES)}

For much of our history, you can find small unfamiliar shells washed up on the shores of ancient beaches. The strange, segmented remains are of the abundant trilobites that inhabit all manner of ocean environments. From shallow rock pools to the crushing depths, these little creatures scuttling around in search of food. For experienced adventurers, these shells are a stark reminder to not leave rations unattended near the sea, lest they be unwantedly devoured.

Trilobita (more commonly known as trilobites) are one of the most well-known non-dinosaurian fossil groups. These arthropods first appeared in the fossil record in the Cambrian (520 million years ago) and became a global phenomenon, surviving until their extinction in the Permian (252 million years ago). They were an incredibly diverse group with thousands of research papers dedicated to their study. Here, we have opted to discuss them as a group, rather than picking a single genus to focus on.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: Trilobites range widely in length, from as small as 1 mm to as big as 2 ft. As their name suggests, their body can be divided into three sections: the cephalon (head), thorax (body) and pygidium (tail). These sections are subdivided into multiple segments and can have a lot of variation in ornamentation. Several groups developed large spines along the length of their body, while others grew elaborate "horns" similar to those found on some beetles.

Thanks to exceptionally preserved specimens, we know they had sensory antennae attached to the ventral side of the cephalon. Each segment had a pair of legs, with the cephalon having 4 to 5 pairs of endoprites (walking legs) that also supported exopodites (gills) to keep the animal oxygenated. Trilobites had complex compound eyes with calcite lenses. These eyes varied widely in morphology and number of lenses, with some relatively flat against the body, others huge and bulb-like protruding from the sides of their cephalons, and others still standing erect on stalks with overhanging "shades". While early trilobites likely only had relatively simple vision, more derived forms would have had very advanced vision and were probably able to clearly see objects and judge distance.

Trilobites were exclusively marine organisms, being either benthic (seafloor) walkers or pelagic (open ocean) swimmers. With their long history, they shared their habitats with a vast array of different organisms, from the predatory Cambrian giant {@i Anomalocaris} ({@b page 169}) to the Devonian armoured fish like {@i Dunkleosteus} ({@b page 216}). They are also commonly found alongside more other long surviving animals like corals, shelly fauna like brachiopods, and crinoids (sea lilies).

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: The behaviour of trilobites was as variable as their morphology but broadly speaking they had three main feeding strategies. Some were active predators with large mouths and hooked raspers to scrape off flesh. These hunters tended to feed on benthic worms, large plankton, or other trilobites. Others were scavengers, moving along the seafloor and sifting through sediment with wing-like limbs in search of organic detritus. Finally, the pelagic trilobites tended to be filter feeders, possessing a chamber under their exoskeleton that helped filter plankton out of the surrounding water.

We suggest playing trilobites as a common sight in the ocean, whether you are swimming close to shore or diving in the deep, oxygen-poor depths. Trilobites should not pay much attention to other organisms unless they are small enough to eat or they are perceived as approaching to attack. If startled, they should roll up into a ball to protect their soft underbelly, similar to a Woodlouse (Oniscidea). A single trilobite is not a threat to a humanoid of any size, however large numbers of trilobites can swarm inactive or unsuspecting humanoids. While not particularly dangerous, they can certainly be a nuisance and consume or soil food supplies.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Trilobites are the most well-known members of the Artiopoda. This extinct group of arthropods first evolved in the Early Cambrian 520 million years ago in what is now China. Most are not well known outside of fossil lagerstätten (sites of exceptional preservation) due to most of their bodies being composed of non-mineralised tissues. Trilobites, with their hard mineralised exoskeleton, are an exception to this and have the highest preservation potential within the group, allowing them to be preserved in many deposits. After enjoying success in the Cambrian, trilobite diversity went into sharp decline in the Middle Devonian due to the group being heavily impacted by several extinction events. Only one family, the Proetida, survived into the Permian. However, the group as a whole never recovered and died out 252 million years ago in the Permo-Triassic Extinction.

trait.name: Clumsy Glider
entries: While falling and not {@condition incapacitated|XPHB|Incapacitated}, Yi can glide (albeit not particularly well). While doing so it may move 5 ft. horizontally for every 5 ft. it descends. If it moves in this manner, Yi takes no damage from falling this turn.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, you do not need to change Yi's CR.

trait.name: Familiar
entries: Yi may be used as a familiar via the Find Familiar spell or any similar effect.

trait.name: Miniature Wyvern
entries: In a fantasy setting, Yi's morphology emulates that of a Wyvern, including a Wyvern's venom.
If a creature is hit by Yi's Downturned Nip attack, it must succeed a {@dc 8} Constitution saving throw or take 1 Poison damage and be {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned} for 1 minute.
As an Action, Yi may force a creature within 5 ft. of it to make this saving throw (even if it is a Familiar).

action.name: Downturned Nip
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 2} to hit, Reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}1 ({@damage 1d2}) Piercing damage.
{@i "EE"} {@b (MANDARIN FOR WING)}

The coniferous canopy above us was alive with a cacophony of alert calls. These strange bat-like dinosaurs sailed clumsily between the branches, following our party and making sure everything in the forest knew we were there. Despite the frustration caused by their alert calls, they were nonetheless adorable travelling companions. When we settled for the rest for the night, I was able to hand feed three of them!
{@i Yi} is a small theropod dinosaur from the Jurassic (164-159 million years ago) of Hebei, China. It is unusual in several ways, not least because its forelimbs were modified into bat-like wings.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Yi} is a small dinosaur known from a single exceptionally well-preserved specimen. It weighed only about 13 oz. and stood about 1 ft. tall. Its skull was quite short and squat, with a downturned lower jaw towards the end. It only had teeth in the front of its jaw, which were long, straight, and forward pointing. Its arms were enormous for its size with a total span just shy of 2 ft. Its fingers were long with curved claws. It also had an unusual rod-like structure projecting backwards from its wrist, called a styliform element, which supported a membranous wing. This wing was functional but, due to the lack of strong chest muscles, it's unlikely {@i Yi} was a powerful flyer. Studies suggest it may have been a somewhat awkward glider that moved through the air with limited control, perhaps similar to {@i Microraptor} ({@b page 50 of DDDD}).

{@i Yi}'s diet has been subject to debate, due to its unusual skull and reduced number of teeth compared to most other small theropods. Studies into the structure of the skull, as well as possible stomach contents from related animals, suggests that it ate mostly plants and insects. {@i Yi} was discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation in the Hebei province in North China. The formation was laid down in a subtropical environment and, based on the large number and variety of terrestrial plants, was likely a forested area.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: The lifestyle of {@i Yi} and its relatives has been the subject to much research over the years. Evidence such as its hallux (first toe) being reversed which allowed the feet to grip or perch, the elongated fingers with claws, and the gliding membrane has led scientists to consider {@i Yi} to be an arboreal animal, climbing through the treetops and using its wings to glide from tree to tree. It may have done this in search of food or to escape predators. Unlike most modern arboreal birds, it would have relied on all four limbs to climb.

We suggest playing {@i Yi} as an agile (albeit slightly clumsy) animal, flitting between branches as it moves through the canopy. Individuals should make trilling calls to communicate throughout the forest and a party might expect to be greeted by the warning shrieks of {@i Yi} jumping between the treetops once they have been spotted. Like many arboreal animals, they should be willing to come down to the ground in search of food and may find themselves drawn to a campsite if there is the chance of an easy meal. This could be just the opening to try and tame this otherwise cautious animal.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Yi} is a member of the Scansoriopterygidae. This is a group of small theropod dinosaurs with some members showing adaptations for climbing or gliding. The group has an extremely restricted range, known only from the Middle-Late Jurassic Tiaojishan Formation of China. The reason for this very limited fossil record has been considered by several authors, with some hypothesising that they were outcompeted by more efficient dinosaurs. Their membranous wings were less efficient and harder to control than feathered wings, so animals like {@i Microraptor} and birds may have outcompeted {@i Yi} for food. The Scansoriopterygidae seem to have been an evolutionary lineage with limited success that couldn't compete with other airborne archosaurs.

trait.name: Stiffened Sinews
entries: Tenontosaurus has Advantage on Strength saving throws and Strength checks.

trait.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, you do not need to change Tenontosaurus' CR. However, please note that using these rules adds three extra CR 3 creatures to the combat.

trait.name: Spectral Survivalism
entries: Tenontosaurus is haunted by spiritual manifestations of its primary predator, Deinonychus, that can manifest when it is stressed. The first time Tenontosaurus becomes Bloodied (falls below half its maximum Hit Points) each day, three Spectral Deinonychus appear within 30 ft. of it. They are hostile to everything except each other.

trait.name: Spectral Tail
entries: To combat the spectral predators that torment Tenontosaurus, it has gained an unusual magical adaptation. Its tail is sheathed in spiritual energy, giving it an ethereal prehensile extension.

Tenontosaurus' Powerful Tail attacks deal an additional {@dice 1d4} Necrotic damage. Additionally, a creature hit by Tenontosaurus' Powerful Tail attack may be {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} (escape {@dc 16}) instead of being knocked away.
At the start of each of Tenontosaurus' turns, any creature that it is currently Grappling takes {@dice 2d10} Necrotic damage.

action.name: Multiattack
entries: If Tenontosaurus chooses the Attack action, it may make up to two Powerful Tail attacks.

action.name: Powerful Tail
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 5} to hit, Reach 10 ft., one target. {@h}8 ({@damage 1d10 + 3}) Bludgeoning damage.
A Medium or smaller creature hit by this attack must succeed a {@dc 13} Strength saving throw or be pushed directly backwards 10 ft. and knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.
Chosen by Kevin LauCK
{@i "TEN-ON-TOH-SORE-US"} {@b (SINEW REPTILE)}

Great nesting herds of Tenontosaurus gather annually in open fern plains and sparse forests to reproduce. While magnificent to behold, these animals are fiercely territorial during nesting season and are best avoided. Unfortunately, this often results in a detour of several hours of walking, as the nest grounds can stretch for miles upon miles.

{@i Tenonotosaurus} is an iguanodontian ornithopod from the Early Cretaceous (115 million years ago) of North America. An earlier evolutionary branch of its relatives {@i Iguanodon} ({@b page 134 in DDDD}) and {@i Parasaurolophus} ({@b page 283}), it is famous for how often its remains are found alongside those of multiple individuals of the dromaeosaurid {@i Deinonychus}.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Tenontosaurus} was a medium-sized ornithopod, growing up to 23 ft. long and weighing about 1 tonne. It had a standard ornithopod body, with large hind legs and more lightly built forelimbs. Its tail was broad and long, making up nearly half the animal's total length. Its head was elongate and horse-like, tipped with a keratinous beak. This narrow beak, combined with its posture, suggests that {@i Tenontosaurus} was a browser that specialised in eating low growing ferns, cycads, and ginkgo trees. Based on research into the structure of its legs and wrists, {@i Tenontosaurus} is thought to have been able to rear up and walk on two legs (facultatively bipedal), although one study suggested that, based on its mass, it would have been preferentially quadrupedal. It is possible that younger animals were more prone to moving bipedally while the bigger adults spent most of their time on all fours.

{@i Tenontosaurus} has been found in several formations across the USA, such as the Cedar Mountain, Cloverly, and Antlers formations, some of which are extensive and span multiple states. These formations were deposited in environments rich in rivers and lakes that supported a wide diversity of overlapping dinosaur fauna, including multiple ornithopod species, late surviving brachiosaurid sauropods, small ceratopsians, nodosaurid ankylosaurs, and theropods like the small tyrannosauroid {@i Moros}, early therizinosaurs like {@i Falcarius}, the giant carcharodontosaurid {@i Acrocanthosaurus,} and the dromaeosaurid {@i Deinonychus}. The latter is especially noteworthy due to its frequent association with {@i Tenontosaurus} fossils (see below).

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: There is evidence that {@i Tenontosaurus} was gregarious for at least part of its life, as fossil deposits have been found containing the remains of multiple juveniles that died together. These may represent fully precocious (independent) infants that grouped together for protection until they were old enough to defend themselves, or maybe these juveniles were still cared for by their parents, whether as part of a herd or in a creche with a small number of guardian adults. {@i Tenontosaurus}' young would have taken several years to grow to maturity, as studies of bone histology (internal structure) show that they were slower to grow than their larger cousins and took more time to reach their adult size. Despite this, we know that they were capable of breeding before reaching physical maturity as remains have been found from animals estimated to be about 8 years old that were still growing but had medullary bone (bone used for forming eggshells).

We suggest playing {@i Tenontosaurus} as an animal that comes together annually at communal nesting sites where many females build their nests. They should be very territorial of the area surrounding their nests, threatening or attacking any animal that approaches too close. After the eggs hatch, the mothers should spend several weeks feeding their young but once they are large enough, many of the adults should abandon the nests. A few younger males and females should remain to act as guardians to the now largely independent offspring, but eventually they too should move on. Once on their own, the youngsters should divide into multiple small herds and may stay together for years before eventually joining larger herds or striking out independently. If attacked by a predator, {@i Tenontosaurus} should either flee or use its powerful tail as a weapon, striking with enough force to knock a humanoid-sized creature flying. The greatest danger, however, may not be the animal itself, but rather the predators that accompany it. Many {@i Tenontosaurus} herds are followed by predatory mobs of {@i Deinonychus} waiting for an opportunity to strike and are not particularly picky about whetting their appetite on any unsuspecting passing prey first.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Tenontosaurus} was an early branching iguanodontian, currently found within the Rhabdodontomorpha. The exact content of this group is currently in flux as it was originally thought to include animals from America, Europe, and Australia, but recently some of the Australian species have been moved to a separate clade. Most rhabdodontomorphs were small-to-medium sized, with {@i Tenontosaurus} being one of the largest members. While {@i Tenontosaurus} itself appears to have died out approximately 108 million years ago, the rhabdodontomorphs survived right up to the end Cretaceous extinction.

entries.name: Pack Hunting Raptors
entries: One of the most famous concepts in palaeontology is that of the pack-hunting dromaeosaur. While popularised through {@i Jurassic Park}, the original hypothesis came from studies of the remains of {@i Tenontosaurus}, which were frequently found in association with multiple individuals of {@i Deinonychus}. Analyses of tooth marks strongly suggests that {@i Deinonychus} not only hunted {@i Tenontosaurus}, but that it was amongst their preferred prey. {@i Deinonychus} weighed approximately 200 lb. and was dwarfed by even a sub-adult {@i Tenontosaurus,} so these {@i Deinonychus} likely had to work together if they were to bring this large prey down.

However, this presumption was challenged in the 2000s by a study that looked at the taphonomy of {@i Deinonychus} bones and gregarious behaviour in modern archosaurs like raptorial birds and crocodiles. They argued that the {@i Deinonychus} remains showed strong evidence of both in-fighting and cannibalism, which is evidence against organised pack hunting. They also noted that modern archosaurs and lizards do not show co-operative hunting and instead gather at kill sites simply to take advantage of an abundant food source, frequently fighting and may cannibalise younger animals, which aligns with many of the cannibalised {@i Deinonychus} remains being sub-adults.

Later research challenged this position too, highlighting that social predators can also be highly aggressive and cannibalistic at kill sites. Others noted that crocodiles, while not strictly pack hunters, frequently live in large groups and have been seen co-operatively hunting. While tightknit wolf-like predators working in-sync to bring down a {@i Tenontosaurus} may be more fantasy than fact, perhaps {@i Deinonychus} was socially complex enough to work together when needed as long as the reward provided a banquet for all.

A Tiny or Small creature hit by this attack is {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} (escape {@dc 7}).

{@i "TROW-OH-DON"} {@b (WOUNDING TOOTH)}

Night watches in the Cretaceous are often eerie affairs. None so much so, however, as a night where a flock of Troodon take interest in the campsite. These nocturnal animals will sit motionless in the undergrowth, watching with shimmering, forward-facing eyes that reflect firelight and moonlight alike. While not particularly bothersome when faced alone, they usually move in flocks of 6 to 10 animals, making them bolder and much more formidable - particularly so when most of the party are still asleep.

{@i Troodon} is a troodontid theropod from the Late Cretaceous (77 million years ago) of North America, whose taxonomic validity has been debated repeatedly. As of 2026, the most recent study argues that newly described material from Montana should be the new neotype (new name holder), along with material currently assigned to {@i Stenonychosaurus}. As this is the most recent publication, we follow its recommendations and use {@i Stenonychosaurus} as our reference for {@i Troodon} biology and ecology.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Troodon} was a small theropod, growing to about 8 ft. long and weighing 60 to 80 lb. While similar in size to dromaeosaurs like {@i Deinonychus} (and also having a retractable sickle-shaped claw on each foot), it was a more lightly built animal. Its legs were longer and thinner, its torso more gracile, it had smaller hands, and it had a shorter tail. {@i Troodon}'s skull was thin and pointed, with very large and slightly forward-facing eyes. This not only gave it good binocular vision, but may have allowed it to see more clearly at night. {@i Troodon} may have been an omnivore that fed on a fairly large amount of plant matter, based on its prominent teeth serrations and stress-resistant jaw tips.

Material that has been assigned to either {@i Troodon} or {@i Stenonychosaurus} has been found in several exceptionally well-known fossil locations in the USA, such as the Judith River Formation in Montana and the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, Canada. These were deposited in forested floodplains positioned not too far from the coast of an inland sea. They are extremely fossil rich locales that have produced a wide variety of dinosaur taxa, including ceratopsians (the most common), ankylosaurs, and ornithopods, as well as multiple theropod lineages like ornithomimids, oviraptorsaurs, maniraptorans, and several tyrannosaurs. Freshwater plesiosaurs and azhdarchid pterosaurs are also present in much smaller numbers, alongside various non-dinosaurian reptiles. Of relevance for {@i Troodon}, the Dinosaur Park Formation contains several lineages of mammals which likely made up a significant proportion of their diet.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Several nests containing more than 20 eggs have been attributed to a troodontid. While this is impressive, recent research suggests that female {@i Troodon} were only capable of laying 4 to 6 eggs at a time. As such, the nests are thought to be communal, with several females using a single nest like rheas or ostriches, and {@i Troodon} may have lived in sizable flocks or gathered seasonally to lay. It also has interesting implications for their parenting behaviour, as communal nests are usually overseen by a dominant male and female who share the brooding and parenting duties for all the eggs and chicks. It is possible that {@i Troodon} behaved similarly and may have had quite complicated social behaviour.

We suggest playing {@i Troodon} as a curious animal, prone to investigating anything new that appears in its environment. They should frequently be found foraging for fruit or chasing down small mammals, pinning them with their sickle claws before swallowing them whole. They should also be common scavengers, picking at carcasses until chased off by a larger carnivore. {@i Troodon} nests and young should be fiercely guarded by the dominant male and female, who may lead a flock of other adults and semi-adults. {@i Troodon} should be curious of humanoids, but keep their distance unless defending a nest.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Troodon} is a member of the Troodontidae, a large group of small theropods best known for their distinctive serrated teeth. The oldest confidently identified troodontid first appeared in the Late Jurassic (156 to 146 million years ago) in North America, but the majority are known from Cretaceous formations. They were a reasonably successful group, found across much of North America, Europe, and China. They were also able to successfully migrate into more extreme climates, as several large troodontid fossils have been found in the polar Prince Creek Formation. While {@i Troodon} itself is not known past 76 million years ago, the troodontids would remain part of the dinosaurian fauna of the Northern Hemisphere up until the end Cretaceous extinction.

entries.name: Identity Crisis
entries: The first {@i Troodon} fossil was found in Montana in 1855, a single tooth with large distinctive serrations. This isolated tooth was named {@i Troodon} and became its holotype (name-bearer). This may not seem like best practice to us today, as no other characteristics of the animal can be used in its description, but this was not uncommon in the early days of palaeontology. Later 1930s expeditions found skeletons with identical teeth in Alberta, Canada, which were named {@i Stenonychosaurus.} By the 1950s, many other Troodontid genera had been described, but these were synonymised together as {@i Troodon} in the 1980s. However, in the 1990s, it was argued that the lack of characteristics in {@i Troodon}'s original description should render it taxonomically invalid as a {@i nomen dubium} (dubious name), with {@i Stenonychosaurus} being the valid name. This was supported by more in-depth research published in 2011. However, a 2025 study argued that {@i Troodon} and {@i Stenonychosaurus} were synonymous with {@i Troodon} bearing seniority. They suggested that material from the Two Medicine Formation be designated as the {@i Troodon} neotype (a new specimen to be the representative of the species). At the time of writing, those authors are preparing a submission to the ICZN ({@b page 10}) to request the erection of the neotype, but this may be rejected or another team may publish a counter argument in the future. All of this highlights that palaeontology is a dynamic science, with new studies constantly challenging older consensus.
