legendaryGroup.name: Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted
lairActions: Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted inhabits foggy, moist swamp environments. She strides amongst the murk, squelching wet mud underfoot.

While in her swamp, on initiative count 20 (losing initiative ties), Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted takes a Lair Action to cause one of the following effects; Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted cannot use the same Lair Action two rounds in a row:

Toxic fumes bubble from the marshy swamp. Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted selects a point within 100 ft. of her that she can see. Each creature within 20 ft. of that point must make a {@dc 18} Constitution saving throw, taking {@dice 6d6} Poison damage on a failed save, or half as much on a successful save.

Water sloshes around the swamp, making the mud saturated and difficult to walk through. Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted selects a point within 100 ft. of her that she can see. The ground within 20 ft. of that point becomes muddy Difficult Terrain.

Magically enhanced rotten remains fuel rapid plant and fungal growth. Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted selects a point within 100 ft. of her that she can see. The ground within 20 ft. of that point becomes filled with new plant and fungal growth. Each creature in that area that is an ally of Dreadfoot, Protector of the Hunted (including herself) regains {@dice 3d10} lost Hit Points.

legendaryGroup.name: Nessie, Spirit of the Loch
lairActions: Nessie, Spirit of the Loch inhabits the deep dark waters of a mysterious fog-covered loch. She dwells within caverns, underwater caves, and shipwrecks in the shadowy depths.

While in her Loch, on initiative count 20 (losing initiative ties), Nessie, Spirit of the Loch takes a Lair Action to cause one of the following effects; she cannot use the same Lair Action two rounds in a row:
A deep, thick fog emanates from the loch's waters, encompassing the entire surface of the loch and up to 20 ft. in height. Visibility within the fog is reduced to 15 ft.
The fog persists for 1 hour or can be dispersed by strong winds.

A large pocket of air trapped on the loch's bottom bubbles to the surface. Select a point within 50 ft. of Nessie, Spirit of the Loch that is within water. A column of bubbles appears at that point that occupies a 10 ft. wide cylinder from the water's bottom to its surface. Any creature that is within the column must succeed a {@dc 12} Strength saving throw or be pulled up to 60 ft. to the water's surface.
If the creature has a swim speed, it makes this saving throw at Advantage.
A mysterious creature-like shape moves across the Loch. Creatures within 100 ft. that observe the shape must succeed a {@dc 16} Wisdom saving throw to determine that it is an illusion.
The illusion persists for up to 1 hour (Nessie, Spirit of the Loch's choosing). Attacks and spells against the illusion automatically fail, but do not reveal that it is an illusion.

legendaryGroup.name: Skeletal Tyrannosaurus
lairActions: While in its museum (or other lair), on initiative count 20 (losing initiative ties), Skeletal Tyrannosaurus takes a Lair Action to cause one of the following effects; it cannot use the same Lair Action two rounds in a row:
A ghostly bellow echoes through the museum/lair. All non-magical candles, fire, lanterns, and torches etc. are snuffed out.

A single display up to Medium in size within the museum/lair becomes animated as though the spell Animate Objects were cast on it (cannot be countered, lasts 1 minute). It will patrol the museum and is hostile to all creatures except for Skeletal Tyrannosaurus.

entries.name: Creature Type
entries: You are a humanoid. You are considered a dinosaur for any prerequisite or effect that requires you to be a dinosaur.

entries.name: Size
entries: Your size is Medium.

entries.name: Speed
entries: 30 ft.

entries.name: Age
entries: Laramidians live for between 50 to 80 years and mature at 15 to 18 years old.

entries.name: Musclebound
entries: You count as a Large creature for determining your carrying capacity and the weight you can manoeuvre.

entries.name: Bonecrusher
entries: You possess some of the strongest jaws in the animal kingdom. You can use these to make Unarmed Strikes, dealing {@dice 1d6} + Strength modifier Piercing damage, instead of the Bludgeoning damage you would normally deal for an unarmed strike. At level 10, the damage die is increased to {@dice 1d8}.

entries.name: Stalker
entries: Your powerful sense of smell allows you to track animals over long distances, particularly if they are bleeding. You have Advantage on Survival and {@skill Perception} checks to track or find creatures that are below their maximum Hit Points.

entries.name: Aura of the Apex
entries: You have Advantage on saving throws to avoid the {@condition frightened|XPHB|Frightened} condition and you have Proficiency in {@skill Intimidation} checks. {@i Elephant molar}

entries.name: Custom Lineage
entries: Adventurers are, by their very nature, exceptional. When playing a Laramidian character, you may replace the Species Traits {@i Bonecrusher} and {@i Aura of the Apex} with a single feat. We advise agreeing this with your Dungeon Master before doing so.

entries.name: Languages
entries: You know Archosauric, Common, and another language of your choice in addition to any other languages you know.

entries.name: Ability Score Improvement
entries: If you have not already selected ability score improvements earlier in character creation, you may increase your Strength by 1, Constitution by 1, and Charisma by 1. Alternatively, you may increase one ability score by 2 and another one by 1, or you may increase three different ability scores by 1

entries.name: Creature Type
entries: You are a humanoid. You are considered a human for any prerequisite or effect that requires you to be a human.

entries.name: Size
entries: Your size is Medium.

entries.name: Speed
entries: 30 ft.

entries.name: Age
entries: Neanderthals have similar life spans to humans. They would have lived for between 30 to 80 years, depending on their diet and access to medical care, and mature at 10 to 12 years old.

entries.name: True Human Variant
entries: You may select a single feat and gain the abilities of that feat. If your game limits the level in which certain feats can be taken, you can select from any feats that would normally be available to you as though you were level 4.

entries.name: Hardy Hunter
entries: You are a hardy hunter, capable of following prey for days at a time. When calculating your travel pace, your distance travelled is one stage faster than the pace you are travelling at (i.e. if you're travelling at a slow pace, your travel distance is that of a normal pace). You also have Advantage on {@skill Survival} checks to track creatures while in snowy or icy environments.

entries.name: Ice Age Adaptations
entries: You have Resistance to Cold damage and are not slowed by Difficult Terrain caused by ice or snow. Additionally, you have Darkvision up to 15 ft.

entries.name: Languages
entries: You know Archosauric and Common in addition to any other languages you know.

entries.name: Ability Score Improvement
entries: If you have not already selected ability score improvements earlier in character creation, you may increase all of your ability scores by 1. Alternatively, you may increase one ability score by 2 and another one by 1, or you may increase three different ability scores by 1.

entries.name: Creature Type
entries: You are a humanoid. You are considered a trilobite for any prerequisite or effect that requires you to be a trilobite.

entries.name: Size
entries: Your size is Medium.

entries.name: Speed
entries: 30 ft.

entries.name: Age
entries: Phacopsians typically live for between 1200 and 1400 years and mature at 100 to 200 years old.

entries.name: Detritivore
entries: You can consume any rotting organic matter for sustenance and have Immunity to the {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned} condition.

entries.name: Panoramic Vision
entries: You can see in every direction around you. Creatures attacking you do not gain Advantage on attacks from any ability or effect that would grant them Advantage from outnumbering or flanking you.

entries.name: Mineralised Exoskeleton
entries: You have Resistance to Slashing and Piercing damage, but have Vulnerability to Bludgeoning damage.

entries.name: Deep Sea Inhabitant
entries: You have a swim speed of 30 ft., Darkvision up to 30 ft., and can breathe both in and out of water.

entries.name: Custom Lineage
entries: Adventurers are, by their very nature, exceptional. When playing a Phacopsian character, you may replace the Species Traits {@i Detritivore}, {@i Panoramic Vision}, and {@i Mineralised Exoskeleton} with a single feat of your choice. We advise agreeing this with your Dungeon Master before doing so.

entries.name: Languages
entries: You know Aquan, Archosauric, Common, and one other language of your choice in addition to any other languages you know.

entries.name: Ability Score Improvement
entries: If you have not already selected ability score improvements earlier in character creation, you may increase your Wisdom by 2 and Constitution by 1.
Alternatively, you may increase one ability score by 2 and another one by 1, or you may increase three different ability scores by 1.

entries.name: Creature Type
entries: You are a humanoid. You are considered a dinosaur and pterosaur for any prerequisite or effect that requires you to be a dinosaur or pterosaur.

entries.name: Size
entries: Your size is Small.

entries.name: Speed
entries: 30 ft.

entries.name: Age
entries: Rhynchie typically live for between 42 and 55 years and mature at 8 to 10 years old.

entries.name: Diving Flyer
entries: You have a fly speed of 30 ft. and a swim speed of 20 ft. Both of these speeds are reduced by 10 ft. if you are wearing medium or heavy armour.

entries.name: Snatcher
entries: You do not provoke Opportunity Attacks when moving out of an enemy's reach and have Proficiency in {@skill Sleight of Hand} checks.

entries.name: Custom Lineage
entries: Adventurers are, by their very nature, exceptional. When playing a Rhynchie character, you may replace the Species Trait {@i Snatcher} with a single feat of your choice. We advise agreeing this with your Dungeon Master before doing so.

entries.name: Languages
entries: You know Archosauric, Common, and one other language of your choice in addition to any other languages you know.

entries.name: Ability Score Improvement
entries: If you have not already selected ability score improvements earlier in character creation, you may increase your Dexterity by 3. Alternatively, you may increase one ability score by 2 and another one by 1, or you may increase three different ability scores by 1.

entries.name: Creature Type
entries: You are a humanoid. You are considered a dinosaur for any prerequisite or effect that requires you to be a dinosaur.

entries.name: Size
entries: Your size is Medium.

entries.name: Speed
entries: 30 ft.

entries.name: Age
entries: Sauropans typically live for between 300 to 380 years and mature at 35 to 40 years old.

entries.name: Overview
entries: You have a higher viewpoint than other Medium humanoids. Double your Proficiency Bonus for determining your passive Perception.

entries.name: Caravan Carrier
entries: You count as a Large creature for determining your carrying capacity and the weight you can manoeuvre.

entries.name: Desert Migrant
entries: You have Resistance to Radiant damage, can survive for up to a week without drinking water, and can navigate sand dunes and desolate deserts as though they were normal terrain.

entries.name: Columnar Limbs
entries: You have Advantage on any saving throw to avoid being knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone}.

entries.name: Custom Lineage
entries: Adventurers are, by their very nature, exceptional. When playing a Sauropan character, you may replace the Species Traits {@i Caravan Carrier} and {@i Desert Migrant} with a single feat of your choice. We advise agreeing this with your Dungeon Master before doing so.

entries.name: Languages
entries: You know Archosauric, Common, and one other language of your choice in addition to any other languages you know.

entries.name: Ability Score Improvement
entries: If you have not already selected ability score improvements earlier in character creation, you may increase your Strength by 1, your Constitution by 1, and your Wisdom by 1. Alternatively, you may increase one ability score by 2 and another one by 1, or you may increase three different ability scores by 1.

entries.name: Creature Type
entries: You are a humanoid. You are considered a cat for any prerequisite or effect that requires you to be a cat.

entries.name: Size
entries: Your size is Medium.

entries.name: Speed
entries: 30 ft.

entries.name: Age
entries: Machaerans live for between 80 to 110 years and mature at 18 to 20 years old.

entries.name: Hunter's Eyes
entries: You have Darkvision up to 60 ft.

entries.name: Terrifying Roar
entries: As an Action, you can let out a terrifying roar, baring your massive saber-teeth. Each enemy within 100 ft. that can see and hear you must succeed a Charisma saving throw with a DC equal to 8 + your Proficiency Bonus + your Charisma modifier or be {@condition frightened|XPHB|Frightened} of you for 1 minute. At the end of its turn, a creature may attempt this save again, ending the effect on a success. You may use this ability a number of times equal to your Proficiency Bonus, then must complete a Long Rest to regain all expent uses.

entries.name: Killing Bite
entries: Your sabered teeth are specifically adapted to deal the finishing blow to downed prey. If a Medium or Small creature within 5 ft. of you is lying {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone} and {@condition restrained|XPHB|Restrained}, {@condition incapacitated|XPHB|Incapacitated}, or {@condition unconscious|XPHB|Unconscious}, you may use your Action to attempt to deal them a killing bite. You deal {@dice 4d6} + your Strength modifier Piercing damage to them.
Alternatively, the DM may decide that they die instantly.

entries.name: Custom Lineage
entries: Adventurers are, by their very nature, exceptional. When playing a Machaeran character, you may replace the Species Traits {@i Terrifying Roar} and {@i Killing Bite} with a single feat of your choice. We advise agreeing this with your Dungeon Master before doing so.

entries.name: Languages
entries: You know Archosauric, Common, and one other language of your choice in addition to any other languages you know.

entries.name: Ability Score Improvement
entries: If you have not already selected ability score improvements earlier in character creation, you may increase your Strength by 1 and your Charisma by 2. Alternatively, you may increase one ability score by 2 and another one by 1, or you may increase three different ability scores by 1.

entries.name: Physical Description
entries: Laramidians are tall and powerfully built saurians with short but stocky arms, three fingered hands and a long, powerful tail. Their most distinctive trait is their large, deep-jawed head with tiny horns above their eyebrows. They have rows of thick, spike-like teeth, although these are rarely seen outside of combat due to Laramidian culture.

entries.name: Background
entries: Laramidians are based on tyrannosaurid dinosaurs like {@i Daspletosaurus}, a medium sized relative of {@i Tyrannosaurus}. The name "Laramidians" comes from the name of the ancient Late Cretaceous island continent Laramidia (now western North America). It was inhabited by several tyrannosaur species and was formed when the interior of North America was flooded by a large inland sea. Laramidians evolved as a violent, predatory species, but later developed into a calmer and more peaceful society through an extreme doctrine of self-control. Violence is abhorred as a sign of weakness, predation or the eating of meat is seen as a sin, and the ruling elite ingrain in their people a strong sense of public service to others. Individualism is seen as a pathway towards aggression and the Laramidians have a strong societal pressure to put the well-being of the group above that of the individual. As with any strict regime, a growing but as yet splintered underground rebellious element exists that preaches the virtue of a return to the Laramidians' former violent ways.

entries.name: Reproduction and Child-rearing
entries: Laramidians are born from clutches of 2 to 4 eggs. Children are highly distinctive, being much more lightly built than their parents, with long pointed snouts and awkward skinny legs. Laramidian families are very tight-knit, and children are raised with great care by their parents. Laramidian society encourages the father to be the primary carer of the young, while the mother is typically a strict educator, but this is not a hard edict, and it is not uncommon to find a family where the roles have been switched. Rather than meat, children are fed foods like bird's eggs, soybeans, and insects. They will not taste flesh until after their 18th birthday, where they will eat meat as part of a maturation ceremony. This formal event may be delayed if the parents feel their child is lacking in maturity or self-control. Even as adults, Laramidians tend to have strong familial bonds, with grown children frequently remaining in contact with, and caring for, their elderly parents.

entries.name: The Culture of Abulys
entries: The Laramidian settlement of Abulys takes its name from {@i Abulysodon}, an early synonym for {@i Tyrannosaurus}. It is a wealthy city built in the centre of an isolated floodplain, surrounded by farms and villages. Abulys is the central hub for Laramidian society and politics. It is from here that the key doctrine of self-denial is enforced. Laramidians are raised from birth to repress any violent tendencies, with the only form of aggression permitted being social facial biting. Adults bite the muzzle of their friends or family hard enough to leave scars. These scars are revered as proof of strong personal ties, and they are usually only absent in young children or those who have been ostracised. The consumption of meat is forbidden within Laramidian society outside of major ceremonies or events. The punishment for the majority of the populace if discovered eating meat can vary considerably depending on the perpetrators age and social status, ranging from heavy fines, to prison time, to exile.

The Laramidian doctrine places great value upon working in the service of others, whether a more highly ranked Laramidian or an employer who belongs to a species the Laramidians once preyed upon. Many Laramidians work in public service roles such as shopkeeping, farming, or law enforcement. Life can sometimes be difficult as other species still fear the Laramidians due to their intimidating appearance, which often leads to them being prone to mistreatment.

The Laramidian doctrines are enforced by a small group of families, said to be the direct descendants of the first migrants to settle Abulys. While they impose rigid standards on the masses, many rumours exist that they are much more lenient on their inner circles, with stories abounding of meat laden feasts, ritualistic combat, and secret hunting trips. These tales are perhaps why there is growing rebellious sentiment amongst young Laramidians. Many believe that extreme self-control is ultimately harmful to the individual and argue for temperance over abstinence. They believe Laramidians should be free to hunt non-sentient species while also learning the discipline needed to live peacefully alongside their non-Laramidian neighbours. These Laramidians are the most likely to become adventurers who, through either frustration or exile, find themselves searching for a new way of life.

There is also the small but extremist cult of the tyrannosaur demigod Kyae-no-Limos, The Blue Death that live in the shadows of Laramidian society. They frequently engage in the murder and the consumption of non-Laramidians, as well as ritualistic cannibalism. The cult exists as largely independent cells but all fall under the leadership of a single powerful warlock.

entries.name: History and Religion
entries: Laramidian history is a tale of extremes. They were once a violent and aggressive culture that hunted other sentient species for food. Eventually, their prey banded together and drove them back, reducing the Laramidian population by more than half in a bloody war. The eldest of the survivors led their people away from their traditional hunting grounds to safety in an isolated river valley. In an attempt to preserve the few remaining Laramidians, their leaders banned all forms of conflict within their society or with other cultures. Within two generations, this edict became an unbreakable and unforgiving doctrine that was vigorously enforced. The descendants of the original elders would use this philosophy as a means of retaining political power under a few key families. Eventually, their numbers had grown enough to sustain a large population centre and the city of Abulys was built.

While religion is not taboo in Laramidian society, its potential for division or conflict means public practice is discouraged. Laramidians who practice their faith usually do so in small private ceremonies and the most commonly worshipped gods are those that preach temperance or uphold rationality. More diverse worship is usually found either in the rebellious youths, who tend to follow gods of a good but chaotic nature that encourage self-fulfilment, or dark cults that worship beings of violence and bloodshed.

entries.name: Names
entries: The naming conventions of Laramidians varies greatly, but many parents try to convey calming themes in their children's given names, hoping that this will aid them in their journey of pacifism and acceptance in other societies. If these names are in Archosauric, much of their meaning can be lost in translation, and they may sound like typical Archosauric names to a non-speaker. However, if given in Common, they may have names like Gentlebreeze, Sunshine, Lavendar, and Softspeak.

raceFluff.name: Neanderthal
entries: Whereas our other playable species are pure fantasy, here we present one based on a real lineage of people, the Neanderthals ({@i Homo neanderthalensis}) that existed 450,000 to 40,000 years ago. As our primary goal when writing this book is to educate, we have decided to take a slightly different approach by presenting an overview of their ecology and culture, followed by a fictionalised account of our take on them as a humanoid species within a fantasy setting. This way we can not only inform, but clearly separate fact from fiction.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: Neanderthals were shorter than modern humans, averaging between 5 to 5.5 ft. tall. They were stocky, with broad shoulders, heavy muscles, and relatively short limbs. Their skulls were low and sloping, and their eyes were larger than ours, mantled by a thick unified brow ridge. These would have given them relatively good low-light vision, meaning they may have been most active during dawn and dusk. Neanderthals had large, powerful jaws, but a surprisingly small chin. Their build made them much stronger than a common modern human of the same size, with excellent stamina for long journeys. This stocky build is believed to be at least in part an adaptation for heat retention, allowing them to thrive in colder biomes.

entries.name: Biogeography
entries: Neanderthals were first discovered in the Neander Valley in Germany, which is where their name is derived from. Subsequent finds have extended their range across much of Europe and adjacent areas of western and southwestern Asia. Their current eastern-most occurrence is within the Altai Mountains in Mongolia. While they were well-adapted to cold environments, fossil evidence suggests they were a highly adaptable species and were comfortable living in a variety of climates, including warmer temperate forests and even in hot southern beaches during interglacial periods.

entries.name: Neanderthal Society
entries: While frequently portrayed in the media as dim-witted, Neanderthals were, in fact, a highly intelligent and capable species. Fossil evidence supports a capacity for advanced language, complex emotions, and abstract thinking. They were a hunter-gatherer species, specialising in large megafaunal prey like horses, deer, mammoths, and even hibernating cave bears. They were nomadic, living in bands of up to 25 or more individuals, and often found shelter in caves, establishing an exterior hearth which likely formed a community centre for social interactions. Numerous artefacts such as tools, bone jewellery, scraped hides, cave art, and perhaps even a simple flute suggests that they engaged with their world in much the same way that we did. While we can only speculate on their spiritual beliefs (some hypotheses propose that they formed cults worshipping eagles and cave bears), we know that they buried their dead. The graves of children found alongside isolated tools or animal bones indicate that Neanderthals laid their loved ones to rest using ceremonial rites.

entries.name: Phylogeny and Extinction
entries: When Neanderthals first deviated from other hominids is still a topic of debate, but it certainly occurred less than 1 million years ago. Neanderthals were similar enough to us to interbreed and produce fertile offspring, with up to 4% of the modern human genome made up of Neanderthal DNA. Neanderthals disappeared approximately 40,000 to 35,000 years ago and the cause of their extinction is contentious. Some argue that they were driven to extinction by climatic factors and a reduction in the number of megafaunal prey. This hypothesis is supported by them being a sparsely populated species, with no more than 12,000 reproductive adults estimated to be present at any one time spread across Eurasia, making them especially susceptible to environmental change. Another major hypothesis is competition with our species, where we may have outcompeted them for resources or, through interbreeding, reduced the number of non-hybrid Neanderthals to unsustainable levels. Perhaps, like many other cases, it was a combination of factors rather than any single one that drove them to extinction. Ultimately, the loss of Neanderthals is a sobering thought. To study Neanderthals is to understand that the human experience was not exclusively ours, that we were not the first to look to the sky and ponder existence. That we {@i Homo sapien}s are not unique or special. Neanderthals danced, sang, feared, loved, and mourned, just like us.

entries.name: Fantasy Information
entries: The following account of Neanderthal society is fantasy, but it is informed by real-world science where possible. For instance, the Elder Druid as a societal leader is purely fictional but based on the real importance of understanding nature as a hunter-gatherer species. Similarly, their approach to child rearing is taken from the importance of communal child-rearing in many human societies. How they interact with strangers or how bands intermingle is based on real fossil evidence and research into several modern cultures. For consistency with our other playable species, all information is given in the present tense.

entries.name: Neanderthal Fantasy Society
entries: Neanderthal culture is based around a strong sense of tradition, meaning that, outside of a few outliers that settle in the towns and cities of other species, most live a traditional nomadic existence. They travel in bands of up to 25 individuals, usually led by an Elder Druid. These bands follow animal herds throughout their yearly migrations, striking up temporary camps where resources are plentiful, but rarely staying in one place for more than a few weeks. These camps usually consist of a cave with a circular tent set up in front of it. The first night in a cave is typically spent painting protective symbols and glyphs on the walls, using a specialised ochre dye made from clay. After this, the hearth is set up, forming the centre of the band's small insular society. Here stories are told, pelts are scraped, food is prepared, and lessons are taught. Each early morning, hunters set out to stalk deer, mammoths, or other large game, while the remaining adults butcher kills from the day before, tend to the children, craft objects, and forage for edible plants nearby. Neanderthals are a highly creative people, and many use traditional stone or bone tools to prepare beautiful home-made jewellery or craft specialist objects.
Neanderthals are generally polygamous, although monogamous bonds are perfectly acceptable within their culture. Children grow faster than modern humans, reaching puberty around 10 years old.

Neanderthals are strongly communal and, once weaned at around 2 years old, children are cared for by the entire band, rather than just their mothers. Few, if any, children know who their biological father is. All adults are expected to teach, play with, and care for any child in their band.
Any dereliction of this group parenting duty is a serious offence and may lead to the Elder Druid imposing a temporary banishment.

entries.name: Sparse Wandering Nomads
entries: Where Neanderthals first evolved has long been lost to the annals of history, but today they are most frequently found in subarctic forests and tundra. Very rarely, bands will move towards warmer climates in search of exotic resources, with a tiny number becoming coastal hunters, specialising in hunting dolphins, walruses, and other great beasts of the sea. Neanderthals are usually quite few in number compared to other humanoid species, spread thinly across a continent. While this allows them to avoid competition, it also means that many can go months or years without seeing a stranger. As such, many bands find their numbers dwindling over time. To avoid bands dying out, several Elder Druids routinely arrange for their bands to meet up once every few years to intermingle, trade, and allow youngsters to socialise. Here, alliances are forged and individuals can move from one band to another as they choose, or peel off with several others to form a new small band. This not only brings fresh blood to the families, but also new skills and experiences that can enrich both bands.

Neanderthals are cautious people who, while not automatically distrusting of strangers, believe that one must prove their worth before they are treated as an equal. This applies to any humanoid species they encounter, and many have found a group of Neanderthals seemingly unwelcoming at first. However, if a stranger tells a great story, trades with honesty, or hunts with skill, they will quickly find that the band will welcome them joyously, and many are soon weighed down by gifts after only a short meeting.

entries.name: Fantasy Religion
entries: Neanderthal religion is varied, with each band worshiping a particular god or spirit, usually one connected in some way to nature, animals, or hunting. While they lack many of the more formal rituals you find with other species, they see their Elder Druid as their connection to their deities and look to them as conduits of the gods' desires. Many also see certain animals, particularly eagles and bears, as symbolic beings. Eagles are seen as fierce hunters that provide for their family and are associated with life, resulting in eagle bones being frequently used as personal protection talismans. Bears are seen as dangerous arch predators and a common rite of passage for a group of young hunters is to slay one during its hibernation. Even a hibernating bear is dangerous when awoken, but if killed, each hunter is given one of its claws as a pendant. The Elder Druid will then carve their name into the claw, forever denoting them as worthy warriors.

entries.name: Names
entries: Neanderthals are as advanced as common modern humans in terms of their ability to vocalise, so their naming conventions are likewise just as variable, although they tend to avoid names with short vowel sounds as their anatomy would have made these difficult to pronounce. We suggest that, when creating a Neanderthal character, you pick a name that you feel is appropriate for your setting but try to exclude "i" and "e" sounds.

entries.name: References
entries: King, W. 1864. The reputed fossil man of the Neanderthal. {@i Quarterly Journal of Science}, {@b 1 (11)}, 88-97.
Sykes, R.W. 2020. {@i Kindred: Neanderthal life, love, death and art}. Bloomsbury Sigma, London, pp. 400.

entries.name: Physical Description
entries: Phacopsians have dark armoured exoskeletons, two primary arms and two primary legs, with about ten pairs of smaller appendages running down their fronts that are typically kept tucked against their bodies unless swimming. One of their more prominent features are their large, (sometimes stalked) compound eyes that allow for panoramic vision.

entries.name: Background
entries: Phacopsians are arthropod-humanoids based on the trilobite genus {@i Phacops}. They thrive in deep, dark, marine settings and often live extremely sedate, slow lives in the crushing depths. Phacopsians have the unusual ability to eat any decaying organic matter and so do not have the usual requirements for a functioning society. Food production and cooking are unnecessary within Phacopsian communities, so they tend to instead focus on shared protection and companionship. Food management is only a concern for particularly large communities that cannot be supported by the environment's normal detritus. In those cases, deep sea sponges are cultivated in marine "fields".

entries.name: Reproduction and Gender
entries: Phacopsians are a spawning species and are extremely un-attentive parents. Every century or so, they return to deep water to complete a mass spawning ceremony. This is a time of grand celebration for all Phacopsians and culminates in the release of thousands of fertilised eggs into deep open water. Offspring then develop as planktonic (free-floating) fauna, before entering a benthic (bottom-dwelling) stage of immaturity. It usually takes 100-200 years before offspring reach a stage of maturity where they can stand on their hind legs and join Phacopsian society.

Due to this method of reproduction and lifecycle, sexual intercourse and gender identities are somewhat alien to the Phacopsians. Older and well-travelled Phacopsians eventually grasp these concepts, but it takes time and patience for them to do so.

entries.name: Phacopsians of Voidwallow Trench
entries: The Phacopsians of Voidwallow Trench are arguably the most well-organised and well-structured community of Phacopsians. This is largely due to a singular historic event within living memory of most Phacopsians, simply known as "Incursion Day". Approximately 800 years ago, a series of portals appeared unexpectedly within the depths of Voidwallow Trench, and disgorged hordes of demons enchanted with water breathing. This force was, apparently, targeting the region as an undefended entry point to prepare for a full-scale conquering of the material plane. Little did the invaders know that the region was in fact heavily populated by Phacopsians living in disorganised communes.

The abrupt and imminent threat caused the otherwise docile and disjunct communities to band together against a common foe. Practically overnight, armies of tens of thousands flocked to the portals, battling back the intruders. After weeks of bloody fighting, the demonic forces were driven back and the portals sealed. In their place, massive fortifications were erected lest others attempt to encroach on the Phacopsians' waters, and the Kingdom of Voidwallow was formally founded.

entries.name: History and Religion
entries: After a millennium of a peaceful and quiet existence, the events of Incursion Day fundamentally changed the dynamic of Phacopsian society. Although many in the surrounding regions still live hermit-style lives of detritus feeding, those that experienced the invasion firsthand subsequently unified under a single kingdom with the ruling monarch being the eldest surviving member of the fighting force. The Kingdom rapidly became a fortified state of castles, bastions, and outposts, all accompanied by subterranean hot vent forges and blacksmiths that produced abundant armaments for the militarised population. Centuries later, the kingdom remains ready for any threat and particularly restless Phacopsians have begun to venture out into other oceans and even onto the land.

Due to the inherent lack of traceable heritage among Phacopsians, the throne is passed from eldest to next eldest individual. This leads to relatively short reigns for monarchs as they are usually on their deathbed when crowned and rule for decades rather than centuries. As such, much of the kingdom's day-to-day rule is handled by a council of younger elders. The council is secular and the worship of any deity is allowed, but generally frowned upon. This is due to the history of relatively solitary communities not interacting enough with other humanoids to generate cohesive religions. However, in recent years this has changed due to more Phacopsians venturing past Voidwallow Trench's borders.

entries.name: Names
entries: Phacopsian names in their native Aquan are usually indistinguishable from bubbling and frothing to non-Aquan speakers. To Aquan speakers, this is an extremely ancient dialect and difficult, but not impossible, to understand. Translated into Common, these names sound very unusual, with lots of onomatopoeic popping sounds. Examples include: Bupopquip, Loploplip, Pipipop. Due to this difficulty in pronunciation, some Phacopsians elect to adopt a generic Common name as well.

entries.name: Physical Description
entries: These pterosaurfolk are small and skinny, with their most prominent feature being their large heads with protruding conical teeth that come together to form an interlocking grin. Their forelimbs are dexterous, with an elongated last finger that connects a sturdy membrane to their sides, forming a long and narrow foldable wing. They are covered in a soft downy fuzz, possess long mobile tails tipped with a diamond-shaped flared end, and have stubby, short legs.

entries.name: Background
entries: The Rhynchie are a small, but raucous people that inhabit coastlines and port cities around the globe. Based on the piscivorous pterosaur {@i Rhamphorhynchus}, they evolved from species that filled a gull-like niche of coastal life, intimately associating them with water and naughty behaviour. We envision the Rhynchie as highly individualistic and the personal culture of each will vary dramatically depending on their individual ideologies.

entries.name: Reproduction and Child-rearing
entries: The Rhynchie are an egg laying species but differ from other peoples in that they are highly secretive with their eggs, protecting them from danger and harsh weather by hiding them away in secluded crevices along rocky coastal cliffs. These locations prevent all ground-dwelling individuals from finding them and shelter them from the worst storms. Females lay a single egg annually and a mated pair of Rhynchie will take it in turns to slink away from their town or village to check on their hidden egg. They favour this method of incubation as the small size of Rhynchie eggs can cause them to be easily mistaken for common cooking ingredients in bustling towns. Once an egg hatches, their young will be brought to their local settlement and raised in the same manner as any of the other local children.

entries.name: Rhynchie of the Bone Coast
entries: The Bone Coast is a stretch of coastline along the southernmost edge of the largest continent. It is a harsh region with sharp jagged cliffs and strong seasonality, with a wet season of battering storms and a dry season of scorching sunshine. This harsh duality comes with its upsides; an exceptionally rich and abundant ocean that is well-stocked with fish. Combined, these make for an environment ideal for the Rhynchie and dozens of major Rhynchie settlements with countless hideouts can be found along the Bone Coast. In this region, the Rhynchie typically fill one of two roles: fishermen or pirates. Those inclined to a life of peace fish the bountiful waters all year round, feeding themselves and their communities with plenty, then exporting their excess catch to regions further inland. Those inclined to a life of mischief harass and raid passing ships for their goods, attacking from both their own small boats and on-the-wing. This combined approach makes the Rhynchie very formidable opponents, so long as enough can be convinced to work together.

As such, the treacherous weather and ever-present threat of piracy makes the Bone Coast a particularly dangerous stretch of water and warrants its eerie name. Several major pirate factions vie for control over sections of the Bone Coast, including (but not limited to) the Black-Tooths, the Snatchers, the Freewings, and the Blaggard Beaks. The region is littered with shipwrecks and boasts a treasure trove of sunken loot ripe for the taking for those foolish enough to brave the waters.

entries.name: History and Religion
entries: The Bone Coast has a bloody history of conflict between the warring pirate factions. Over the centuries since its settlement, hundreds of factions have risen and fallen with equal vigour, usually tied to a particular Rhynchie captain with an especially charismatic personality. From these, six primary ports have been founded along fortifiable inlets, coves, and spits. These are: Gâteau de Pierre, Daggerspire, Merchant's Cove, Maw's Cave, Fort Ricketywood, and Maiden's Rest. These are surrounded by at least thirty more moderately sized coastal towns, usually at the mouth of a river, and countless smugglers' dens. Hidden passageways and secret caves are commonplace among the jagged stone and pebble beaches, masking the presence of all but the most gaudy of pirate groups.

Every few months, fierce cannonball and ballista fire is exchanged between skirmishing fleets and the next morning a new flag may fly over the nearest port. In each case, the ports themselves are rarely ransacked, as a change in "governance" is so common that they would be abandoned if the inhabitants couldn't persist there.

The Rhynchie of the Bone Coast are generally superstitious and invariably worship gods that represent warfare, honour, thievery, commerce, fishing, weather, and, of course, the sea. These factors are so prevalent in the lives of most Bone Coast Rhynchie that little else matters in their day-to-day affairs. They tend not to have formal places of worship and instead visit soothsayers or wisemen who proclaim (sometimes dishonestly) to have some divine connection to the gods.

entries.name: Names
entries: Rhynchie tend to have long, dragging names that can be easily heard over the intermittent sound of crashing water. Volume is a key factor to a name's pronunciation and a Rhynchie unfamiliar with other cultures will not recognise a name unless it is spoken at a sufficient volume.
Typical Rhynchie names include: Kroo-oohkee, Ver-reenkk, or Eee-lee-baan.

entries.name: Physical Description
entries: Sauropans are heavily built reptilian humanoids with columnar limbs, long tails, and extremely long necks topped with small heads. The shortest of these peoples are usually 8 ft. tall, and they tower over most of their companions. They have thick leathery scaly skin.

entries.name: Background
entries: Sauropans are based on {@i Spinophorosaurus nigerensis}, an unusual sauropod found from the Middle Jurassic of central Niger. Its name originated from a pair of twin broken elements found near the pelvic region which were originally identified as a pair of stegosaur-like tail spikes. However, these have since been re-interpreted as mis-identified clavicles. We envision this race of people as nomadic desert wanderers, similar to modern African elephants, travelling from water source to water source in search of fresh plant growth.

entries.name: Reproduction and Gender
entries: Sauropans are an egg-laying species that reproduce slowly. Females may lay a single very large egg once every 3 to 4 years, and the egg is incubated in an open nest for approximately 2 years before hatching. These eggs require high temperatures and are typically left exposed to the harsh desert sun or kept by lit fires at night. In nomadic groups of Sauropans, the eggs are transported in specialised open caravan trains that are padded with dried plants. This leads to Sauropan caravans being prime targets for egg-stealing predators and has made them a very wary people.

Sauropans do not differ particularly from other species with regards to their gender identities. However, unlike mammalian humanoids and archosaurian humanoids that have plumage or other ornamentation, they lack prominent sexually dimorphc features and they also lack obvious vocal identifiers. As such, non-Sauropans sometimes find it very difficult to determine the genders of Sauropans that they are interacting with.
If you would rather not have characters be misgendered in your campaign, you can simply ignore this last paragraph.

entries.name: The Caravans of Yashi Masu Tafiya
entries: "Yashi masu tafiya" means "sand walkers" in Hausa, the Chadic language spoken in Niger. The name is taken to evoke images of a nomadic desert wandering sauropod-people. The Yashi Masu Tafiya Caravans comprise a series of about 50 travelling groups of Sauropans who traverse the central desert regions of their home continent in convoys of wooden carts and caravans. Caravans vary dramatically in size and range from 10-20 individuals with a handful of carts to huge beast-drawn trains with thousands of members. Individual caravans may have a single dedicated purpose with specific routes or be generalist wanderers. They can act as guides for travellers of the arid regions, ferry trade goods, or may be the envoys of a particular religion. In any case, most Yashi Masu Tafiya Caravans are seen as highly useful to surrounding nations and strict prohibitions outlaw attacking them. As such, the caravans generally only have to contend with bandits and wild animals. The most high-value caravans are often escorted by guards of other nations, such as mobile Ankylier ({@b page 249 in DDDD}) garrisons or Jeholrak ({@b page 246 in DDDD}) dinosaur-mounted cavalry.

entries.name: History and Religion
entries: The Yashi Masu Tafiya Caravans have a long and peaceful history, only marred by the occasional trade dispute or colossal beast attack. They keep a written history in the form of collections of scrolls that are either housed in fixed sacred locations or transported in specialist relic-museum caravan carts. The most ancient of historical records are engraved in stone pillars that are arranged in large circles around key oases. These are cherished spiritual places to the Sauropans and are highly respected as open-air temples. Their maintenance not only denotes their cultural significance, but also their practical importance as sources of water in particularly harsh desert environments.

In Sauropan society, each caravan is guided by an individual nominated to be the leader, which may be an elected official, matriarch, spiritual visionary, or elder. Once every decade or so, caravan leaders meet at an oasis-temple to discuss Yashi Masu Tafiya matters moving forward for the next decade. This is the closest thing to a formal government that the Sauropans have and determines which caravans have access to specific trade routes or guide contracts.

As a well-travelled people, the Sauropans are exposed to many religions and cults from different societies. This has led to a broad acceptance of any and all ideologies among Sauropan society, and no individual is penalised for their personal belief. In some instances, this has led to caravans becoming entirely dedicated to the preaching or spreading of a particular religion. However, this usually only lasts as long as that caravan's leader remains dedicated to the cause.

entries.name: Names
entries: Most Sauropan names are spoken in a bass-heavy dialect of Archosauric that is difficult for many to understand. This is because the sub-language is meant to be communicated through ground vibrations, rather than the air, and is most easily understood by those with large columnar limbs. For smaller light-weight peoples, much of the subtleties of the dialect is lost. To non-Archosauric speakers and in Common translations, the names are long and hyphenated with rolling o's, ah's, and m's. Examples include: Furr-grooo, Remm-nemm, and Raahh-gaahh-jarr.

entries.name: Physical Description
entries: Machaerans are tall and muscular hairy cat-humanoids. Their upper bodies are well-built and powerful, while their legs are thinner and well suited for running. Their most prominent feature is their stocky faces with furry beards (on males) and huge protruding saber-like fangs. Sharp-clawed hands and feet are adorned with soft-bean pads, giving a high contrast between their soft, fuzzy appearance and their potential for powerful violence.

entries.name: Background
entries: Machaerans are based on the saber-toothed cat {@i Homotherium latidens,} a smaller and more lightly built relative of {@i Smilodon} ({@b page 105}) that occupied a wide variety of environments including the cold Mammoth Steppes of Eurasia. Their name is taken from the Latin word "{@i Machera}" for "saber" or "sword". Rather than have the Machaerans exist in a quintessential ice age "cave-man"-esque community, we have decided to invert the typical aesthetic and base the Machaerans around pre-industrial London during the frigid winter. Consequently, their society is that of a strictly tiered class system, with a bustling working class, thriving middle class, and opulent upper class.

entries.name: Reproduction and Gender
entries: Machaerans are mammals and therefore birth live young, then nurse them on lactated milk. Females deliver litters of 3 to 4 kittens and nurse them for 4 to 6 months after birth, but may not directly care for them after that, depending on their class within Machaerans society. Middle and Upper class families may have a nanny undertake the majority of the childcare. However, in almost all cases, Machaerans are loving and caring parents, a trait common among mammals.

entries.name: City: Ciudad Pegajosa
entries: Ciudad Pegajosa takes its name from the Spanish for "sticky city", in tribute to the Spanish-named La Brea pits of Los Angeles. It is a fitting name for the oil-slicked icy cobblestone streets that are flanked by whirling steam-punk machines and smothered by thick smog. Founded in a region rich in natural oil, the city rapidly grew and flourished with the abundant access to this new fuel, despite the frigid surrounding environment.

Ciudad Pegajosa rests on the verge of industrial revolution, with an underlying shifting power struggle between the societal classes. The thriving middle-class is growing steadily as technological advancement rapidly expands industry, which presses further on the already struggling working-class. Throughout this, the upper-class shelters themselves from the growing unrest within opulent palaces, masquerade balls, and social parties.

entries.name: History and Religion
entries: Ciudad Pegajosa's history is relatively short, but no less dynamic than other societies. In its brief 80-year history, it has seen dramatic change, with a vast area of desolate tundra transformed into a bustling metropolis of industry, trade, and wealth. However, this is not distributed evenly among the peoples of Ciudad Pegajosa and financial inequalities stir conflict within the city. Its initial founding was marked by a land lordship deal between prospectors and the native population of farmers and hunters inhabiting the tundra. A levy on all future commerce taking place on the utilised land was agreed to be paid to the initial inhabitants, which resulted in them being catapulted into elite aristocracy upon the city's rapid expansion, founding the Upper Class. The prospecting companies then established a firm Middle Class of industrial and proactive individuals. Those who flocked to the city's wealth in the latter years found themselves sorely disappointed by the lack of remaining opportunity and those who chose to stay congregated into the labourer-heavy Working Class.

Given its explosive expansion in wealth, the primary religion of Ciudad Pegajosa is the worship of deities representing trade, commerce, greed, and wealth itself. In fact, the Upper Class has, in recent years, imposed strict sanctions on the worship of deities not directly tied to these aspects. As such, Ciudad Pegajosa technically has a formal state religion, in so much so that the worshipped deity must be one of a small number of specific gods. This is, of course, not reflected in the hearts and minds of the Working Class, who instead follow their own religious ideologies, but often project a farcical public compliance.

entries.name: Names
entries: The naming conventions of Machaerans within Ciudad Pegajosa has changed rapidly in recent years, and most individuals are named in a convention in accordance with their social status. Those in the Working Class maintain traditional shorthand names with common role-based surnames shared among many families, such as John Smith, Beth Butcher, or Nate Carpenter. Those who form the Middle Class usually use similar given names, albeit typically with the longer version of the name, and then a surname that are more indicative of a location that their family moved from, such as Jonathan Woodling, Bethany Appleton, or Nathan Riverwell.

Upper Class names are similar to those of the Middle Class, however they are often adorned with ostentatious titles and unequivocally include the hyphenated "-Foundling" as in indication of the family's history of land ownership within Ciudad Pegajosa, such as Sir Jonathan Woodling-Foundling, Lady Grace Bethany Appleton-Foundling, or Lord Nathanel Riverwell-Foundling the 3rd.

subclassFeature.name: Knowledge Is Power
entries: When you join the College of Education at 3rd level, any creature that rolls a Bardic Inspiration die from you may also add your Intelligence modifier to that roll. Additionally, you may use your Bardic Inspiration a number of times equal to your Intelligence modifier or your Charisma modifier (whichever is higher, minimum of once).
You may use your Intelligence modifier instead of your Charisma modifier for determining your to hit bonus and spell save DCs for your Bard spells.

subclassFeature.name: Attention Class!
entries: You know the {@spell Thaumaturgy} cantrip.

subclassFeature.name: Reading Around
entries: You gain Proficiency in one skill from History, Nature, or Religion.

subclassFeature.name: College of Education
entries: A College of Education Bard is one who uses their powers of inspiration to inform and educate others. Through inspiring words, music, and energetic mannerisms, they teach those around them how best to complete tasks and use weapons (whether they're willing or not!). They also have a knack for learning on the fly themselves and are exceptionally good at copying spells.

subclassFeature.name: Those Who Can't Do, Teach
entries: When an ally within 60 ft. of you who can hear and understand you attempts a skill check, you may use your Reaction to instruct them with that check (after they've rolled). They may add your Intelligence modifier to the roll for that skill check. You may do this a number of times equal to your Intelligence modifier or your Charisma modifier (whichever is higher, minimum of once), then must finish a Long Rest before you regain all expended uses of this trait.

Additionally, you know the {@spell Martial Instruction|ProfessorPrimulasPortfolioofPalaeontology} spell. This spell is always prepared for you and does not count against the number of Bard spells you can prepare.

subclassFeature.name: Life Is a Lesson
entries: If you observe a spell being cast (i.e. you can hear/see the verbal/somatic components) within 60 ft. of you and that is of a level that you have spell slots for, you can expend one use of your Bardic Inspiration to temporarily learn that spell until you finish your next Long Rest. You may cast it as though it were a Bard spell.

subclassFeature.name: Excellent Educator
entries: Over the course of a Long Rest, you may educate an accompanying creature that is resting at the same time as you. Until that creature's next Long Rest, they have Proficiency in one skill that you are also proficient in. The creature does not have to be willing to receive this benefit, as you drone on at them until they listen.

subclassFeature.name: Precocious
entries: The spells you learn from Life is a Lesson do not fade from your knowledge over a Long Rest. The maximum number of spells you can learn from that ability is 5. If you already know 5 spells from Life is a Lesson and try to learn another, you must first choose to forget one of those spells to replace it with the new spell.

subclassFeature.name: Magnum Opus
entries: Your study of music, dance, education, and inspiration has inspired you to write your magnum opus. When you use your Bardic Inspiration, you may replace your regular Bardic Inspiration die with a {@dice d100}. If the inspiration die rolls a 90 or above, you and all friendly creatures who can hear you also gain Heroic Inspiration. If the inspiration die rolls a 10 or below, your performance is woefully underwhelming for your best work, and you gain a level of Exhaustion. If the inspiration die rolls a 1, it is such a letdown that you are consumed by shame and fall {@condition unconscious||Unconscious} for {@dice 1d4} hours.
You may do this once, then must wait 30 days before you can do so again as it takes considerable time for you to recover to the peak of your abilities.

subclassFeature.name: Dinosaurian Presence
entries: You radiate carnivorous predatory energy. You know the {@spell Thaumaturgy} cantrip and may cast it even if you are raging. Strength is your spellcasting ability for this spell.
When you make an {@skill Intimidation} check, you have Advantage on that check if you are the same size category as, or larger than, the target.

subclassFeature.name: Combat Maw
entries: You can wield specialist maw weapons (see below), leaving your hands free. You gain training (Proficiency) with this new weapon type and a mundane maw weapon (either a {@item Razormaw|ProfessorPrimulasPortfolioofPalaeontology} or {@item Greatmaw|ProfessorPrimulasPortfolioofPalaeontology}, your choice) magically appears in your inventory, gifted to you by a mysterious tyrannosaur deity.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: As with any weapons, these items can be found as magical variants (+1, +2, +3) or with additional enchantments. Please see page 420 for examples of such magical maw weapons. The two basic mundane maw weapons are outlined here.

subclassFeature.name: Grappling Bite
entries: When you hit a creature with an attack using a maw weapon, you can use your Bonus Action to attempt to Grapple that creature with your maw weapon. If the creature is your size category or smaller, it is automatically {@condition grappled||Grappled} and has Disadvantage on any roll to escape from the Grapple. If the creature is larger than you, you must make a contested {@skill Athletics} check (vs {@skill Athletics} or Acrobatics, target's choice), as per the normal rules for Grappling.

If you use your Bonus Action to go into a rage, then subsequently hit with an attack using your maw weapon on the same turn, you may attempt to Grapple the hit creature as part of that attack. While you have a creature {@condition grappled||Grappled} with a maw weapon, you can't attack a different creature with your maw weapon until the Grapple ends.

subclassFeature.name: Drag Prey
entries: While Grappling a creature, or multiple creatures, and while your maw weapon is equipped, your speed isn't halved when you move with those creatures.

subclassFeature.name: Path of the Tyrannosaur
entries: A Path of the Tyrannosaur Barbarian is a fearsome foe. They venerate these great predators and emulate their hunting style, channelling their strength into colossal jaw attacks with specialised maw weapons. This mouth-focused combat gives them unnatural powers to grip and consume their foes in a predatory haze.

subclassFeature.name: Tyrant's Presence
entries: You take on the presence of an enormous predatory dinosaur to bolster your own ferocity. When you start to rage, you may also increase your size. If your current size category is Medium or larger, you increase in size by one category. If your current size is Small or smaller, you increase in size by two categories.

subclassFeature.name: Improved Drag Prey
entries: Once on each of your turns, when you move a creature while Grappling it by dragging it, you may select an additional effect from the list below:

items.name: Debilitating Drag
items.entry: Until the start of your next turn, the {@condition grappled||Grappled} creature's speed is reduced by the same amount you move it this turn (to a minimum of 0).

items.name: Drag & Shake
items.entry: The creature must succeed a Constitution saving throw with a DC equal to 8 plus your Strength Modifier and your Proficiency Bonus. On a failed save, they drop an item of your choice that they are wielding. It is dropped at a point of your choosing during the move.

items.name: Opportunistic Drag
items.entry: You leave your prey open to attack. When you drag a creature within the melee reach of an ally, they may use their Reaction to make one Opportunity Attack against the dragged creature. Only one creature can benefit from this in a single turn.

subclassFeature.name: Predatory Instincts
entries: The scent of blood and weakened prey awakens your carnivorous predatory instincts. Creatures that are at or below half of their maximum Hit Points gain a -3 penalty to their rolls to avoid or end your Grapple.

subclassFeature.name: Precognitive Predation
entries: Your predatory instincts allow you to sense when a creature is trying to use magic to escape. If a creature within your maw weapon's reach attempts to teleport (e.g. they cast {@spell Misty Step} or {@spell Dimension Door}), you may use your Reaction to make an Opportunity Attack against that creature before they teleport. On a hit, the creature is {@condition grappled||Grappled}, and their resource is expended but they don't teleport.

subclassFeature.name: Titanic Predator
entries: You radiate the ferocious aura of a titanic arch predatory dinosaur. When you start to rage, you may also increase your size. If your current size category is Medium or larger, you increase in size by one or two categories (your choice). If your current size is Small or smaller, you increase your size by two or three categories (your choice). This size increase replaces the size increase granted by Tyrant's Presence.

While Grappling a creature with your maw weapon, you may attack another creature and attacking in this manner does not break your initial Grapple. Additionally, you may Grapple a second creature if you are already Grappling one and have another hand free. While Grappling two creatures in this manner, when you hit one of them with an attack with your maw weapon, the other takes Piercing damage equal to your Strength modifier plus Proficiency Bonus.

subclassFeature.name: Devour Whole
entries: When you take the Attack action on your turn, you can replace one of your attacks with an attempt to devour a creature that you are Grappling in a gory frenzy. Make a contested {@skill Athletics} check against that creature. If you are larger than the {@condition grappled||Grappled} creature, it makes its {@skill Athletics} check at Disadvantage.

On a success, if the creature has 100 Hit Points or fewer, it dies as it is devoured whole and you regain {@dice 4d10} lost Hit Points. If the creature has more than 100 Hit Points, it takes {@dice 7d10} piercing damage as you bite a huge chunk out of it and you regain lost Hit Points equal to half the damage dealt. On a failure, the creature takes half that much damage, and you regain lost Hit Points equal to half the damage dealt.
Once you use this trait, you can't use it again until you finish a Short or Long Rest.

subclassFeature.name: Tyrant King
entries: While you are Grappling one or more creatures with your maw weapon, they are also {@condition restrained||Restrained}. Additionally, while raging, your speed is increased by 30 ft.

If the creature has more than 100 Hit Points, it takes {@dice 7d10} piercing damage as you bite a huge chunk out of it and you regain lost Hit Points equal to half the damage dealt. On a failure, the creature takes half that much damage, and you regain lost Hit Points equal to half the damage dealt.
Once you use this trait, you can't use it again until you finish a Short or Long Rest.

subclassFeature.name: Tyrant King
entries: While you are Grappling one or more creatures with your maw weapon, they are also {@condition restrained||Restrained}. Additionally, while raging, your speed is increased by 30 ft.

subclassFeature.name: Expanded Spell List
entries: The Ancient Beast lets you choose from an expanded list of spells when you learn a Warlock spell. The following spells are added to the Warlock spell list for you.

entries.caption: Ancient Beast Expanded Spells
rows: {@spell animal friendship}, {@spell speak with animals}, {@spell disguise self}

entries: *When randomly determining the species that a creature Reincarnates as, instead of rolling a {@dice d100} and consulting the normal table of results, instead roll either a {@dice d6} or a {@dice d12} if you also have access to Dr Dhrolin's Dictionary of Dinosaurs and use the following corresponding result: (1) {@race Neanderthal|ProfessorPrimulasPortfolioofPalaeontology}, (2) {@race Phacopsian|ProfessorPrimulasPortfolioofPalaeontology}, (3) {@race Rhynchie|ProfessorPrimulasPortfolioofPalaeontology}, (4) {@race Sauropan|ProfessorPrimulasPortfolioofPalaeontology}, (5) {@race Machaeran|ProfessorPrimulasPortfolioofPalaeontology}, (6) {@race Laramidian|ProfessorPrimulasPortfolioofPalaeontology}, (7) {@race Pluvenn|DrDhrolinsDictionaryofDinosaurs}, (8) {@race Manyhorn|DrDhrolinsDictionaryofDinosaurs}, (9) {@race Limukin|DrDhrolinsDictionaryofDinosaurs}, (10) {@race Children of Seth|DrDhrolinsDictionaryofDinosaurs}, (11) {@race Ankylier|DrDhrolinsDictionaryofDinosaurs}, (12) {@race Jeholrak|DrDhrolinsDictionaryofDinosaurs}.

subclassFeature.name: Bestial Snarl
entries: You have Advantage on {@skill Intimidation} checks.

subclassFeature.name: Ancient Beast Patron
entries: An Ancient Beast Warlock is someone who has made a pact with a mighty ancient beast spirit from deep in their world's past. The spirit may be a benevolent, noble creature seeking to protect the weak and innocent (such as Greathorn, the Indomitable, page 40), or it may be malevolent (such as Kyae-no-Limos, The Blue Death, page 41), seeing other creatures as prey and seeking the thrill of the hunt through them. Whatever the spirit's motives, it finds the modern world to be alien and grants their Warlock the power to reshape themselves and their allies into more familiar ancient forms.

subclassFeature.name: Bestial Enhancements
entries: Through occult magic or forbidden alchemy, your patron has taught you how to unlock primal power within your allies, reshaping them and unleashing the bestial traits of their forebearers. As an Action, you can enhance up to two friendly creature within 60 ft. of you that you can see (which can include yourself). Select an enhancement from the list below and both creatures gain the associated benefit for 10 minutes.

entries.caption: Bestial Enhancements
rows: The creature grows bony osteoderms or chitinous plates.
Increase the creature's AC by 2. If you are level 10 or higher, instead increase the creature's AC by 3.
The creature grows large bony spines out of its body.
When the creature is hit by a melee attack, it may use its Reaction to inflict {@dice 1d6} + its Strength modifier Piercing damage to the attacker.
The creature becomes covered in a dense woolly coat of coarse fur.
The creature gains Resistance to Cold damage.
The creature becomes covered in a thick waxy layer of scales.
The creature gains Resistance to Fire damage.
The creature's nails or claws extend into vicious barbed claws.
The creature's unarmed and natural weapon attacks deal additional damage equal to your Charisma modifier.
The creature gains a climb speed equal to its speed and gains Resistance to falling damage.
The creature's eyes turn a solid black, as their pupils grow.
The creature's limbs begin to twitch, as its nervous system speeds up.
The creature can add your Charisma modifier to its Dexterity saving throws.
The creature's eyes enlarge and become more forward facing, making them better at judging distances.
The creature gains +1 to hit with ranged attacks (including ranged spell attacks), or +2 if you are level 6 or higher, or +3 if you are level 14 or higher.
The creature is able to stretch its joints further than normal, making its attacks more agile.

The creature gains +1 to hit with melee attacks (including melee spell attacks), or +2 if you are level 6 or higher, or +3 if you are level 14 or higher. The creature also increases the Reach of its melee attacks by 5 ft.

entries: At higher levels, you can enhance more creatures at once and each creature may have a different enhancement. You can enhance up to three creatures at level 6, up to four creatures at level 10, and up to six creatures at level 14.

You may use this trait a number of times equal to your Charisma modifier, then must finish a Long Rest before you regain all expended uses. Creatures may only benefit from a single Bestial Enhancement at a time, replacing their current one if a new one is applied.

subclassFeature.name: Pact of the Ancient Beast
entries: Your patron shares a lineage with you, either through distant kinship or as a deity that intervened in your species' evolution. This allows their power to manifest directly from within your being, channelling their magic through you as a vessel.

entries.name: Pact Boon
entries: You may choose to take on the appearance of your patron in subtle ways, with either sharpened claws, snake-like eyes, enlarged canine teeth, or woolly fur. As a Bonus Action, you may dismiss or hide these cosmetic features, but they reappear if you fall {@condition unconscious||Unconscious} or choose to show them again.

subclassFeature.name: Adaptive Bestial Enhancements
entries: As a Bonus Action, you may adapt a Bestial Enhancement to a new form. Select one creature within 60 ft. of you that has an active Bestial Enhancement. Change that Bestial Enhancement to a different one. This change does not count towards the total number of Bestial Enhancements you can do before requiring a rest and does not extend the duration of the enhancement.

subclassFeature.name: Improved Bestial Enhancements
entries: When a creature receives one of your Bestial Enhancements (excluding a changed enhancement from Adaptive Bestial Enhancements), it also gains Temporary Hit Points equal to your Charisma modifier.

subclassFeature.name: Pack Hunter
entries: Whenever a creature is hit by one of your cantrips, it is magically marked as prey for your enhanced companions. The next attack against the marked creature by a creature with one of your active Bestial Enhancements is made at Advantage.

subclassFeature.name: Pack Leader
entries: Each time you use your Bestial Enhancement, one of the creatures you select may gain two enhancements instead of one. This overrides the usual limitation of a creature having only one active enhancement.

subclassFeature.name: Supreme Enhancement
entries: You may cast the spell {@spell Polymorph} at 4th level without requiring material components and without using a spell slot. You may do this once, then must finish a Long Rest before you can do so again. Additionally, when you cast Polymorph using this feature, if you polymorph a creature into a dinosaur (or other prehistoric animal), you do not need to maintain concentration for the spells' effect to persist.

entries.caption: Ancient Beast Spells
rows: {@spell animal friendship|XPHB}, {@spell speak with animals|XPHB}, {@spell disguise self|XPHB}, {@spell Evolution/Devolution|DrDhrolinsDictionaryofDinosaurs}, {@spell enhance ability|XPHB}

subclassFeature.name: Naturalism
entries: Beginning when you select this school at 2nd level, you may choose up to six spells from the Druid spell list. These spells are Wizard spells for you and can be learned and prepared in the same manner as a Wizard spell.

Additionally, you know the spell {@spell Evolution/Devolution|DrDhrolinsDictionaryofDinosaurs}, which is always prepared for you and does not count towards the number of spells you can prepare each day.

subclassFeature.name: School of Taxonomy
entries: A School of Taxonomy Wizard focuses their study on the categorisation and classification of living creatures, particularly beasts, often recording detailed information about each creature they encounter within their spellbooks. This grants them a particular knowledge of the attributes, mannerisms, and weaknesses of creatures they encounter, as well as how to use the Weave to reshape those characteristics to create new weaknesses.

subclassFeature.name: Cladistic Chaos
entries: You are able to tap into the magic that ties creatures to their ancestry. You know the {@spell Cladistic Chaos|ProfessorPrimulasPortfolioofPalaeontology} spell, which is always prepared for you and does not count towards the number of spells you can prepare.

subclassFeature.name: Phylogenetics
entries: You can cross reference previous research of related creatures to better understand your foe. As a Bonus Action, you can determine the damage Immunities, Resistances, and Vulnerabilities of a non-undead, non-construct creature that you can see and that is within 100 ft. of you. You may do this once, then must finish a Short or Long Rest before you can do so again.

subclassFeature.name: Improved Cladistic Chaos
entries: Once per turn, if a creature succeeds on its Wisdom saving throw against your Cladistic Chaos spell, you may attempt to redirect that magic to another creature. Select another non-undead, non-construct creature that is within 60 ft. of you and within 20 ft. of the initial target. You repeat your cast of Cladistic Chaos (without using an additional spell slot), targeting the selected creature instead.

subclassFeature.name: Cladistic Reinterpretation
entries: Once per turn, when you roll on the Cladistic Chaos Vulnerability table, you may choose to reroll the result. If you do so, you must use the second rolled result.

subclassFeature.name: Informative Anatomical Exploitation
entries: You are able to provide simplistic guidance to your allies about how best to exploit a creature's anatomy. The first time an ally deals damage to a creature that is under the effects of your Cladistic Chaos spell each turn, their attack or spell deals an additional {@dice 1d6} damage (of its usual damage type).

subclassFeature.name: Masterful Anatomical Exploitation
entries: You have an intimate knowledge of living creatures, allowing you to exploit their anatomic weaknesses. When determining the damage dealt by your spells, non-undead, non-construct creatures with Immunity to any of the spell's damage instead count as Resistance to that damage, and non-undead, non-construct creatures with Resistance to any of the spell's damage types instead take damage as though they had no Resistance to it.

subclassFeature.name: Quick Reference
entries: You may cast Cladistic Chaos as a Bonus Action. You can do this once, then must finish a Short Rest before you can do so again.

subclassFeature.name: Phylogenetic Master
entries: When you cast Cladistic Chaos, you may select one result from the {@dice d20} Vulnerability table instead of rolling, excluding "Extremely Weak" (if you are rolling multiple dice, roll the others normally).
You can do this once, then must finish a Long Rest before you can do so again.

subclassFeature.name: Naturalist Savant
entries: Choose two Druid spells, each of which must be no higher than level 2 and add them to your spellbook for free. Whenever you gain access to a new level of spell slot in this class, you can add one Druid spell to your spellbook for free. The chosen spell must be of a level for which you have spell slots. Additionally, you know the spell {@spell Evolution/Devolution|DrDhrolinsDictionaryofDinosaurs}, which is always prepared for you and does not count towards the number of spells you can prepare after each Long Rest.
