spell.name: Martial Instruction
entries: {@i Target: One willing creature within 60 ft. who can hear and understand you, or self.}

Choose a type of weapon. You magically instruct the target in the proper use of that weapon type. For the next minute, the target creature gains training (Proficiency) with that weapon if they were not already proficient with it and can use the Weapon Mastery associated with that weapon (or increase the damage that weapon deals by 2 if you are not using Weapon Mastery rules).
After 10 minutes, bad habits creep back into the creature's technique and posture, rendering their attacks less effective and this effect ends.

entriesHigherLevel.name: At Higher Levels
entries: When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 2nd level or higher, you can target one additional creature for each slot level above 1st.

spell.name: Cladistic Chaos
entries: {@i Target: One non-undead, non-construct creature within range that you can see.}

You attempt to magically manipulate the anatomy of a creature, creating weaknesses that it didn't possess before. The target must succeed on a Wisdom saving throw against your spell save DC or gain a random set of Vulnerabilities from the {@dice d20} table below. If the creature has Immunity or Resistance to one or more of the damage types, it instead loses its Immunity or Resistance to those damage types. Additionally, if the creature failed its Wisdom saving throw by 5 or more, you may also roll on the {@dice d12} Visual Change table below. The creature loses its current creature type and gains the rolled type instead.

entries.caption: Cladistic Chaos Visual Change
rows: The creature sprouts small wriggling tentacles.
The creature becomes covered in thick dense fur or feathers.
The creature radiates a soft glowing yellow light.
The creature sprouts bony scales and ridges along its head and back.
The creature becomes semi-transparent and has a brightly coloured body.
The creature is vividly coloured and gives off a pink mist as it moves.
The creature sprouts protruding horns on its head and its flesh becomes a deep red colour.
The creature becomes noticeably taller but does not increase in size category.
The creature rears backwards and walks on two legs, sprouting those legs if it didn't already have them.
The creature sprouts an extra set of non-functional limbs.
The creature's body becomes soft and doughy.
The creature sprouts woody twigs and leaves.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: We think that it's pretty funny for the verbal component of this spell to be loudly shouting "I cast", followed by the rolled Vulnerability's name.

entriesHigherLevel.name: At Higher Levels
entries: When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 3rd level or higher, you can target one additional creature for each slot level above 2nd. If more than one creature is targeted by this spell, roll for each creature separately. Alternatively, when you cast this spell using a spell slot of 5th level or higher, if you only target a single creature, you can instead roll an additional d20 for each slot level above 2nd to determine which damage types, selecting a single result from all of the dice you roll.

optionalfeature.name: Bestial Pounce
entries: When you cast a cantrip, you can immediately leap up to 10 ft. before casting it. Moving in this manner does not provoke Opportunity Attacks. You may do this a number of times equal to your Charisma modifier, then must complete a Short or Long Rest to regain all expended uses.

optionalfeature.name: Fighting Instinct
entries: When making a ranged attack or ranged spell attack while within 5 ft. of an enemy, you do not gain Disadvantage on that attack for being within 5 ft. of that creature.

otherSummary.entry: Level 5+ (or Level 3+ for an Ancient Beast Patron)
otherSummary.entrySummary: Level 5+ (or Level 3+ for an Ancient Beast Patron)

optionalfeature.name: Predatory Focus
entries: You can cast spells as though you were holding a spell focus, even if you are holding something else, and may ignore the somatic components of spells.

optionalfeature.name: Animalistic Movement
entries: Select one of the following movement options. So long as you are not wearing medium or heavy armour, you can use that movement option.

items: You may Dash as a Bonus Action.
You gain a swim speed equal to your walking speed.
You gain a climb speed equal to your walking speed.

You can glide 1 ft. horizontally for every 1 ft. you descend while falling (without using any of your movement) and have Immunity to falling damage, so long as your are not {@condition incapacitated||Incapacitated}.
You gain a 5 ft. burrow speed and can only burrow through soft soil/mud/dirt.

entries.name: Repeatable
entries: You can gain this invocation more than once. Each time you do so, choose a different movement option.

item.name: Razormaw
entries: This spiked weapon is made from the jaws of either a medium-sized predatory creature, the sharp beak or tusked skull of a medium-sized herbivorous creature, or a constructed row of spikes, attached to the wearer's jawline.
{@i Melee weapon (martial, maw).} May only be wielded by a Path of the Tyrannosaur Barbarian (or similarly themed class/NPC). Does not require the use of hands to wield.
This weapon counts as a light weapon even though it is not held in your hands. You may make an attack following the usual light weapon Bonus Action rules with another weapon that you are wielding.

item.name: Greatmaw
entries: This spiked weapon is made from the jaws of either a large or larger-sized predatory creature, the monstrous beak or tusked bones of a large or larger-sized herbivorous creature, or a constructed row of brutal spikes, attached to the wearer's head, neck, and jawline.
{@i Melee weapon (martial, maw).} May only be wielded by a Path of the Tyrannosaur Barbarian (or similarly themed class/NPC). Does not require the use of hands to wield.

item.name: Skulking Plate
entries: {@i Breastplate, Half Plate, or Full Plate}

This heavy armour is padded by thick downy feathers that prevents its metal plates from touching each other. The wearer of this armour does not have Disadvantage on {@skill Stealth} checks as a penalty for wearing heavy armour, however, while attempting to move stealthily, their speed is reduced by 5 ft.

item.name: Osteodermal Absorbing Mail
entries: {@i Ring Mail, Chain Mail, or Scale Mail (uncommon/rare/very rare/legendary)}

The wearer may use their Reaction to reduce incoming Bludgeoning, Piercing, or Slashing damage. When hit by an attack, or when failing a saving throw, the wearer may use their Reaction to reduce the total damage received from the attack/effect by {@dice 1d4}/1d8/1d12/1d20. The armour can absorb a total of 100/200/300/400 damage before it becomes ineffective and loses this feature, becoming mundane armour.

item.name: Quillback Armour
entries: When hit by a melee attack by an enemy that is within 5 ft. of the wearer, the wearer may use their Reaction to inflict {@dice 1d6} Piercing damage to the attacking creature (no save allowed).

item.name: Survivalist's Clothes
entries: This khaki jacket and legging set is covered in pockets. When reaching into these pockets, the wearer will always be able to retrieve a useful mundane survivalist trinket attached to the clothing by string, such as a compass, whistle, sextant, spyglass, etc. While attuned to this item, the wearer has Advantage on {@skill Survival} checks. If one of these trinkets is forcibly removed from the clothing, the trinket disintegrates into dust, and then reappears in one of the pockets, reattached to the clothing.

item.name: Helm of Bestial Thought
entries: While attuned to this item, the wearer may use their Action to probe the mind of a beast that they can see within 100 ft. They can determine how the beast is feeling and its immediate intentions. The wearer may use this ability a number of times equal to their Proficiency Bonus, then must finish a Long Rest to regain all expended uses.

item.name: Henodus Shield
entries: This +1/+2/+3 shield can be attached to the wielder's back while in water to provide magical propulsion and protection. While attuned to this item, the wielder gains a swim speed of 30 ft.

item.name: Sauropan Sunblocker
entries: This tall glass-like shield is tinted with a deep blue colour. While attuned, the wielder has Immunity to Radiant damage and Resistance to Fire damage. They are also unaffected by temperatures as high as 40°C (104°F) that originate from sunny weather.

item.name: Regal Jacket
entries: This set of Machaeran formal clothes gives the wearer an aura of authority that assists them in formal discussions. The wearer has Expertise on Charisma checks when talking to a humanoid that understands them, excluding {@skill Persuasion} checks to haggle prices. When they attempt a {@skill Persuasion} check to haggle prices, they instead do so at Disadvantage.

item.name: Picker's Gloves
entries: These fine cloth gloves are studded with small metal beads on the palms and insides of the fingers. They allow the wearer to pick parts off of plants without the worry of being pricked by thorns or stung by hidden insects. A creature wearing these gloves has Advantage on {@skill Survival} or {@skill Nature} checks to harvest components of plants.

item.name: Towering Beast Feller
entries: {@i Handaxe, Axe, or Greataxe (uncommon/rare/very rare)}
This mundane/+1/+2 axe grants the wielder Advantage on attacks against beasts with the Sauropod or Proboscidean subtypes.

item.name: Missionary's Will
entries: This shining chrome weapon shimmers with subtle radiant energies that coat incantations with healing magic. While attuned to this item, if the wielder casts a spell of level 2 or higher that has a verbal component, they may also heal a creature within 20 ft. of them that they can see for {@dice 1d4} Hit Points. In addition to this, while attuned the wielder also knows the Guidance cantrip.

item.name: Flesh-Reaper
entries: This weapon deals an additional {@dice 1d4} Slashing damage to Beasts hit by an attack from it. Additionally, you may use this weapon to help you harvest resources from a slain beast, increasing the amount normally gathered by 20%.

item.name: Earthen Mind Wand
entries: This wand is a +1 spell focus. While attuned to this item, the wielder has an additional +2 modifier to any Constitution saving throw to resist losing Concentration.

item.name: Saber-Toothed Mawhelm
entries: This barbaric maw weapon also incorporates a saber-toothed cat's skull into its construction, worn as a helm. When a creature is hit by a critical attack from this weapon, it suffers an additional {@dice 2d4} Piercing damage (don't double these extra dice).

item.name: Helicoprion Buzzmaw
entries: This +1 magical maw weapon suspends a spinning {@i Helicoprion} jaw in front of the wearer's jaw. When a creature is hit by an attack from this weapon, it deals the usual damage for a +1 Greatmaw Maw Weapon. Then, the wielder rolls successive 1d4s until a 1 is rolled. The hit creature takes an additional 2 Slashing damage for each die rolled in this way. This effect may only be used once per turn and has a maximum bonus damage of 24.

item.name: Amphibious Blade
entries: This fine and light blade can be wielded with ease both on land and underwater. A creature attacking with this weapon while in water does not have Disadvantage imposed on its attacks for not having a swim speed and for not dealing Piercing damage.

item.name: Tyrant's Toofs
entries: This enormous maw weapon is constructed from a {@i Tyrannosaurus} jaw. The wielder may opt to unleash the full power of this weapon in their attacks, dealing an extra {@dice 1d4} Piercing damage and {@dice 1d4} Bludgeoning damage, in addition to the normal {@dice 1d12} Piercing damage for this weapon type. After this weapon is used to attack in this manner, the wielder's speed is reduced by 10 ft. for each attack made in this way (to a minimum of 5 ft.) until the start of their next turn.

item.name: Ankylomaul
entries: This magical weapon is crafted from the tail of an {@i Ankylosaurus}. It is a +2 Maul and any creature hit by an attack from this weapon must succeed a Constitution saving throw with a DC equal to 8 + your Strength modifier + your Proficiency Bonus. On a failed save, the hit creature suffers from a Shattering Blow, lowering its movement speed(s) by 10 ft. (to a minimum of 5 ft.). Multiple instances of this Shattering Blow effect are cumulative and all stacks can be removed by a Lesser Restoration spell, equivalent effect, or Long Rest.

item.name: Causality's Consequence
entries: An ornate wooden staff topped with the visage of a colourful butterfly, this staff may be used as a +2 quarterstaff or a +2 spell focus and allows the wielder to meddle with the subtleties of causality. When the wielder finishes a Long Rest, roll a {@dice d20}. Until their next Long Rest, they can replace a single attack roll, saving throw, or ability check made by them or a creature that they can see with that roll. If unused, this roll is discarded when they begin a Long Rest.

Additionally, if the DM is rolling on the {@i Time Travel Minor Effects} table or {@i Time Travel Major Effects} table ({@b pages 75-77}) for an effect that would affect the attuned creature, the DM does so at Disadvantage. Alternatively, a creature attuned to this weapon has a {@i Chrono-consequence Value} 20 less than it normally would.

item.name: Memorial Pearl
entries: This inch-diameter pearl is delicately carved with a magical script describing the victory of Phacopsian culture's "Incursion Day". It can be attached to a staff or wand, or be held. Demons and Devils have Disadvantage on saving throws against spells cast by the wielder of this spell focus.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: We recommend increasing the rarity of Memorial Pearl to Very Rare if you are running a particularly demon or devil heavy campaign.

item.name: Potion of Fossiling
entries: This thick lime-green potion has small shards of rock floating in it. Drinking this potion grants a creature +5 to their passive Perception to spot Fossiliferous Strata ({@b page 51}), as well as Advantage on all Investigation, Nature, or {@skill Perception} checks to search for Fossiliferous Strata, for the next 24 hours.

item.name: Crystal of Amplification
entries: This small, fragile iridescent crystal carries volatile magic. A creature can crush this crystal while attempting to cast a spell, destroying the crystal. If they do so, that spell is cast at one level higher than it was originally cast at, without the need to expend a higher-level spell slot. However, this effect fails if the level of the spell would exceed the highest-level spell slot that creature has (spent or unspent).

item.name: Potion/Great Potion of Ankylosaur Hide
entries: If a creature drinks this oily purple potion, rock-like bony osteoderms appear all over their body. Consuming this potion provides a +2/+3 bonus to the consumer's AC for the next hour. This effect is not cumulative if multiple potions are consumed.

item.name: Vial of Tar
entries: This vial contains sticky tar that, when covering a creature, prevents them from taking Reactions and slows their walking speed by 5 ft. The vial can be thrown at a creature, which must make a Dexterity saving throw with a DC equal to 8 + your Dexterity modifier + your Proficiency Bonus. The effect persists for 10 minutes, before the tar begins to dry and can be scraped away.

item.name: Absorbing Crystal
entries: This large, beautiful crystal radiates protective magical energies. While attuned to this item, at dawn each day, the bearer selects one element type from Acid, Cold, Fire, Force, Lightning, Necrotic, Poison, Psychic, Radiant, or Thunder. The first time the attuned creature would take damage of that type that day, the damage is instead redirected into the crystal. The crystal can absorb up to 100 points of damage (cumulative across multiple days) before it cracks and loses its magical properties.

item.name: Neandertools
entries: This small collection of simple tools have multipurpose heads that allow them to be used for a variety of functions. These tools count as Thieves' Tools, Cobbler's Tools, Leatherworker's Tools, and Woodcarver's Tools. This tool set can also be wielded as a mundane Dagger, but the tools cannot be used for other purposes while doing so.

item.name: Child's Enchanted Plushie
entries: This magical soft toy is crafted in the shape of a purple dinosaur or another ancient creature and occasionally whispers "I love you" (although it can only be heard by the creature attuned to it). Each plushie has a magical keyword (learnt when attuned) which, when spoken by the attuned creature, transforms the toy into a real version of the creature that the plushie looks like. The creature is friendly to whomever said the keyword, but otherwise is a wild animal, and repeating the word transforms the creature back into its toy.

This item is typically found in the care of a young child, whose insatiable desire for a dinosaur friend conjured the toy into existence. If the creature that the plushie turns into is slain, the item is destroyed.

item.name: Spirit of the Ice Forest
entries: This fist-sized gemstone mounted on a silver chain harbours the soul of an ice elemental and is often found at the heart of frozen ice forests. It radiates cold magical energies. While attuned to this item, the bearer has Immunity to Cold damage and can comfortably tolerate freezing temperatures.

item.name: Bottled Feat
entries: This six-inch glass bottle contains a shrunken severed humanoid foot immersed in a dull green liquid, with a sticker that reads "Do not drink". The first time a creature attunes to this item, they may select an origin feat (or other feat available at 1st level). The Bottled Feat then grants the attuned creature that feat, so long as they remain attuned to it. If another creature attunes to the Bottled Feat, it retains the feat that was originally selected and cannot be changed.

Vendors may sell Bottled Feats that already have an assigned feat. If the liquid is drunk, the drinker is {@condition poisoned||Poisoned} for 48 hours (no save allowed) and the Bottled Feat is rendered a magic-less mundane bottle.

item.name: Laramidian Peace Bracelet
entries: This simple bracelet or circlet of fresh flowers conveys an air of calm and relaxation upon the wearer. A creature wearing this item gains +1 to Wisdom and Charisma saving throws. However, once equipped, the effects of this item begin to diminish as the flowers slowly wilt and are lost after six hours. The effects of multiple Laramidian Peace Bracelets are not cumulative.

items.name: Trodden Path:
entries: You have Proficiency in Survival checks when tracking a creature, or Expertise if you already had Proficiency.

items.name: Wildfeast:
entries: When foraging for food in a wild environment, you find twice as much as you normally would.

items.name: Bush Medicine:
entries: You have Proficiency in Medicine checks when in a wild environment that you are familiar with.

items.name: Back Alley Barter:
entries: You have Expertise in Persuasion checks when bartering with another non-Lawful individual.

items.name: Covert Connections:
entries: The first time you are caught committing (or accused of committing) wrongdoings by guards while in a town or city, you can utilise your covert connections to have a more lenient punishment/ fine (if any at all). You may only use this ability once in each town or city you visit.

items.name: Appraise:
entries: If you spend 1 minute examining any medium or smaller object, you can determine its exact value.

items.name: Legitimate Connections:
entries: You can sell your goods in cities and major towns at prices 10-20% more expensive than you normally would be able to (at DM's discretion).

items.name: Ability Score Increase:
entries: Increase your Strength or Dexterity score by 1, to a maximum of 20.

items.name: Weak Spot:
entries: When attacking a dinosaur (Beasts with the subtype Dinosaur, Marginocephalian, Ornithopod, Sauropod, Theropod, or Thyreophoran (or any Beast with no listed subtype that you're pretty sure is a dinosaur, including birds)) with a ranged, melee, or spell attack, your attacks critically hit on a roll one lower than they normally would (i.e. a roll of 19 if you normally only critically hit on a 20).

items.name: Dino-Hunt:
entries: You have Advantage on Survival checks to track dinosaurs (as described above).

items.name: Ability Score Increase:
entries: Increase your Wisdom or Intelligence score by 1, to a maximum of 20.

items.name: Preserve:
entries: If you spend at least 1 hour attending to a carcass or perishable goods, you can halt the processes of decay on that carcass or perishable goods for the next week.

Food altered in this way remains edible for one week. Carcasses altered in this way are treated as though they died less than one minute ago for the next week. Once an object or carcass has been preserved in this manner, it cannot be preserved again using this ability and will deteriorate as normal after the week passes.

items.name: Ability Score Increase:
entries: Increase your Intelligence or Wisdom score by 1, to a maximum of 20.

items.name: Arcane Examination:
entries: You can spend 10 minutes intensely studying an object or person that is within 30 ft. of you in an arcane ritual. If you do so, you then gain Truesight 30 ft. for 1 minute for the purposes of examining that object or person, revealing any hidden visual details (you cannot see through darkness or into the ethereal plane and you see everything else as you normally would with your regular sight).

items.name: Arcane Recall:
entries: You have Advantage on History checks to recall information. Additionally, your encyclopaedic knowledge of creatures allows you to write exceptionally detailed information for your museum displays, making them remarkably accurate and informative. If you assist in the creation of displays within a museum, they generate 10% additional revenue (cumulative with other bonuses).

items.name: Ability Score Increase:
entries: Increase your Strength or Dexterity score by 1, to a maximum of 20.

items.name: Whipmaster:
entries: If you did not already have it, you gain training (Proficiency) with whips. The damage dice for attacks you make with whips increases from 1d4 to 1d8 and the Reach bonus of your whip attacks is increased from 5 ft. to 10 ft. (giving a total Reach of 15 ft.)

Additionally, when you hit a creature with an attack from your whip, you may use your Bonus Action to attempt to Grapple that creature. It must make a Strength saving throw with a DC equal to 8 plus your Strength bonus and your Proficiency Bonus, and is Grappled on a failed save. While you have a creature Grappled in this manner, you cannot attack with your whip or with any other two-handed weapon.

items.name: Ability Score Increase:
entries: Increase your Constitution, Intelligence, or Wisdom score by 1, to a maximum of 20.

items.name: Resistance to Chrono-Consequences:
entries: When you or your party triggers a roll on the Major/Minor Effect Tables ({@b page 75 to 77}), you may make a DC 10 Constitution saving throw. On a success, the result of that roll is reduced by two stages.

Alternatively, if your party has a Chrono-Consequence Value ({@b page 78}), each time this value would increase, you may make a DC 10 Constitution saving throw. On a success, the Chrono-Consequence Value that you would gain is reduced by 5 to a minimum of 0.

items.name: Ability Score Increase:
entries: Increase your Charisma, Intelligence, or Wisdom score by 1, to a maximum of 20.

items.name: Masterful Museum:
entries: You're able to both market your museum better and have a keen eye for creating amazing looking museum displays. Your museum is far more popular than those of your peers. It generates 50% more revenue than it normally would (cumulative with other bonuses, but may be capped by the DM, {@b see page 62}).

background.name: Curator
entries: A curator is someone who has spent a considerable portion of their life as a professional procurer, storer, displayer, and maintainer of precious artefacts, fossils, and/or minerals. They have a keen eye for value and a delicate touch.

items.name: Skill Proficiencies:
items.entry: {@skill History}, {@skill Sleight of Hand}

items.name: Tool Proficiencies:
items.entry: Analysis Tools and Jeweller's Tools

items.name: Languages:
items.entry: One language of your choice

items.name: Equipment:
items.entry: Choose A or B: (A) Analysis Tools, Backpack, Fine Clothes, Glass Bottle (5), Pouch; or (B) 50 gp.

entries.name: 5.5 Edition Character Creation
entries: If you use your background to determine your ability score improvements and provide a starting feat, we recommend the following:

items.name: Feat:
items.entry: {@feat Auctioneer|ProfessorPrimulasPortfolioofPalaeontology} or {@feat Backalley Trader|ProfessorPrimulasPortfolioofPalaeontology}

items.name: Ability Scores:
items.entry: Intelligence, Wisdom, Charisma

items.name: Gentle Touch:
items.entry: You have Advantage on rolls to extract fossils and minerals without damaging them, and Advantage on any roll to pick up a fragile object without damaging it.

items.name: Curate:
items.entry: Over the course of a Short or Long Rest, you can attempt to repair a damaged tiny object (such as a handheld artifact or fossil), so long as you have appropriate tools. You may roll a {@skill Sleight of Hand} check with a DC determined by the object's value (DM's discretion). On a success, the object is repaired.

entries.name: Suggested Tools: Analysis Tools
entries: {@i Common, 10 gp., 1 lb.} These tools provide a +2 to any skill check where you are examining an object small enough to fit into your hand, regardless of the skill you are using.

entries.caption: Curation Specialism
rows: You curate and collect ancient, rare, and unusual coins. For every 200 gp. you acquire, you can identify one rare 1 gp. coin worth {@dice 1d10} gp. to specific collectors.
Ancient weapons are your specialist interest. When examining damage or a wound, whether it was inflicted by a weapon, you can tell what type of weapon caused it.
You love fossils. You can identify the remains of beasts from small components of their bodies.
You curate and collect vibrant gemstones. You know the value of any gemstone at a glance.
You curate samples of rocks. You know the value of any non-gemstone mineral or crystal at a glance and know where best to sell it.
You curate ancient scrolls and texts. You can determine the author of any scroll or book and its potential value.

You curate ancient rings, necklaces, bracelets, and other jewellery. Over the course of a Long or Short rest, you can polish a jewellery item to increase its value by 10%. You may only do this once per item.
You love to collect unusual insects from different environments and keep small vials on you to collect new samples. You're aware of which insects give a nasty bite or sting.

entries.caption: Personality Traits
rows: I demand that people handle every ancient artifact carefully - they're fragile!
I'm enthusiastic and excited to show off these ancient artifacts.
I like to give stoic and monotone informative lectures about the items I find.
I love to dress in the style of a specific ancient civilisation.
My clothes are scruffy and dusty because I am constantly handling dirty old objects.
I obsessively clean my hands in case I have to handle something precious.
I wear the jewellery of a specific ancient civilisation.
I fill my pockets with small shards of history - pebbles, coins, and broken pottery.

entries.caption: Ideals
rows: I wish to collect all of the artefacts that I can from a specific region.
I wish to collect all of the artefacts that I can from a specific time period.
I wish to share my passion with as many people as possible.
I'm looking to make as much coin as I can using my profession.
I'm hoping to restore the history of a civilisation for its descendants.
I want to preserve our past so that we don't lose it.

entries.caption: Bonds
rows: I mistakenly sold a fake artefact to a collector, and they are out for vengeance.
I'm seeking the descendants of a specific historic person to ask about their family history.
I accidentally broke an important cultural artefact. I'm well known to and disliked by people of that culture.
I have a special artefact gift that I want to give to a specific person I love.
I mistakenly bought a fake artefact from a dodgy deal, and want to track them down to get even.
I idolise a specific person from history.

entries.caption: Flaws
rows: I have no qualms about graverobbing and don't care about where the objects I curate were sourced from.
I'm wanted by guards of a specific country/region for smuggling artefacts (even if I thought it was the right thing to do).
I get angry when unqualified people touch an artefact - they might damage it!
I will study and ponder any artefact that I find for hours if left to my own devices.
I'm extremely fussy about sourcing artefacts ethically, and will accuse those of graverobbing if they don't have extensive documentation of their collection's origin.
I'm naive about the dangers outside of my museum/collection.

background.name: Archaeologist
entries: From whip-wielding tomb raiders, to dusty lecture-hall educators, archaeologists are those who are fascinated with ancient civilisations. They want to learn as much as they can about past societies by examining ancient texts and excavating ruins.

items.name: Skill Proficiencies:
items.entry: {@skill History}, {@skill Religion}

items.name: Tool Proficiencies:
items.entry: {@item Excavator's Tools|DrDhrolinsDictionaryofDinosaurs}, Cartographer's Tools, and {@item Research Scrolls|DrDhrolinsDictionaryofDinosaurs} (page 290 in DDDD)

items.name: Languages:
items.entry: One language of your choice

items.name: Equipment:
items.entry: Choose A or B: (A) Excavator's Tools, Explorer's Pack, Map, Traveler's Clothes, Shovel, Whip, 28 gp.; or (B) 50 gp.

entries.name: 5.5 Edition Character Creation
entries: If you use your background to determine your ability score improvements and provide a starting feat, we recommend the following:

items.name: Feat:
items.entry: {@feat Wildswalker|ProfessorPrimulasPortfolioofPalaeontology} or {@feat Backalley Trader|ProfessorPrimulasPortfolioofPalaeontology}

items.name: Ability Scores:
items.entry: Intelligence, Wisdom, Strength

items.name: It Belongs in a Museum:
items.entry: You have Advantage on {@skill Persuasion} checks when confronted about carrying an object (excluding remains of humanoids).

items.name: Raider of Tombs:
items.entry: You have Proficiency in any check or saving throw to spot traps and avoid the effects of traps.

entries.name: Suggested Tools: Excavator's Tools
entries: {@i Common, 5 gp., 8 lb.} These tools are used to carefully extract fossils or minerals from rock/mud/dirt. They cause your harvested gemstones to be 10% more valuable and harvested fossils to be 25% more valuable.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: We designed the Excavator's Tools in Dr Dhrolin's Dictionary of Dinosaurs (page 288 in DDDD) long before we came up with the fossil hunting rules in this book. In that book, it provides a 100% increase to the price of fossils extracted. That would be very over-powered with our new system, so this version of the tool only provides an increase of 25%. If you are not using our fossil hunting system, then this tool can revert back to a 100% increase.

entries.caption: Archaeologist Type
rows: You prefer to study periods of history that have written records. You know much of your region's history very well.
You source your best artefacts from, and learn the most from, tombs and burial grounds. You can vaguely understand Thieves' Cant, but can't speak it.
You study shipwrecks and sunken hulls in search of long lost cargo. You're a good swimmer and can hold your breath for twice as long as normal.
You prefer to study periods of history that have no written records. While exploring a cave or tunnel, you can easily recall which direction leads to the entrance.

You like to re-enact the roles of people in past societies, either partaking in mock battles or living as a person of a specific time for a few weeks. With preparation, you can convincingly act as someone from a different period in history.
Great works of art - sculpture, paintings, and music are your primary interest. You may have one instrument Proficiency, or Proficiency with Painter's Tools.
You work with local governments to ensure historic sites are not destroyed by develop-ments. Guards are much more lenient with you if caught carrying contraband artefacts.
You often work as a teacher or give public talks on your area of expertise. You can talk clearly and loudly, even to large noisy crowds.

entries.caption: Personality Traits
rows: I often look down at the path I'm walking on, hoping to spot fragments of our past.
I fancy myself as a rugged adventuring type.
I have a phobia of snakes.
I use phrases and sayings from ancient societies that don't make much sense in modern language.
I keep the first ancient coin I ever found with me at all times.
I see myself as a stuffy and formal academic.
I demand that people handle every ancient artefact carefully - they're fragile!
I'm enthusiastic and excited to show off these ancient artefacts.

entries.caption: Ideals
rows: I seek to preserve as much history as I can.
I'm seeking fame for finding a legendary artefact or lost civilisation.
Establishing a flourishing museum is my dream goal.
There is a specific artefact that I'm hoping to return to its homeland.
There is a specific artefact that I'm hoping to curate in our national museum.
I'm hoping to build my own private collection of artefacts.

entries.caption: Bonds
rows: My former mentor expects great things from me.
I have several disgruntled students who dislike me.
I seized/stole an artefact from a group of dangerous people who are out to get me.
I have a great fondness for a specific historical culture and its descendants.
In every major city I have an ex-partner who I have a dicey relationship with.
I'm competing with a rival archaeologist to find the best artefacts.

entries.caption: Flaws
rows: I don't care how an artefact is sourced, so long as it ends up in a museum.
I'm a bit of a maverick - always seeking dangerous adventure.
I'm jaded from the study of gory history.
I'm snobby about other's lack of knowledge about the past.
I don't care who buys my artefacts, so long as I get paid.
I value important artefacts more than people.

background.name: Field Guide
entries: Field Guides are intimately familiar with a specific environment type and spend a large portion of their lives as guides for travellers through that environment. They are used to "roughing it" in the wilds and find great fulfilment in observing nature and the natural world.

items.name: Skill Proficiencies:
items.entry: {@skill Nature}, {@skill Survival}

items.name: Tool Proficiencies:
items.entry: Cartographer's Tools, Navigator's Tools, and a Musical Instrument of your choice.

items.name: Languages:
items.entry: One language of your choice

items.name: Equipment:
items.entry: Choose A or B: (A) Bell, Explorer's Pack, Iron Pot, Map, Tent, Traveler's Clothes, Musical Instrument (your choice); or (B) 45 gp. In addition to A or B, you also have Cartographer's Tools.

entries.name: 5.5 Edition Character Creation
entries: If you use your background to determine your ability score improvements and provide a starting feat, we recommend the following:

items.name: Feat:
items.entry: {@feat Wildswalker|ProfessorPrimulasPortfolioofPalaeontology} or {@feat Tough|XPHB}

items.name: Ability Scores:
items.entry: Strength, Constitution, Wisdom

items.name: Mind for Maps:
items.entry: You cannot get lost in the environment of your Field Guide type and are always able to retrace your steps.

items.name: Familiar Terrain:
items.entry: You can easily recognise whether an area of your Field Guide environment type has been unnaturally altered in any way (i.e. by the prolonged presence of a dragon).

entries.caption: Field Guide Type
rows: You guide people through deserts. You're unbothered by extreme heat from the sun.
You guide people through caves. You can tell which way looks safe to delve.
You guide people through dense jungles. You can determine whether there are dangerous venomous beasts in the area or not.
You guide people over mountains. You can tell when the cliffs are becoming unstable a full round before a rockfall/avalanche.
You guide people through swamps. You can determine the depth of even the murkiest swamp water and can find shallow routes through it.
You guide people through frozen wastes. You're unbothered by extreme cold from wind and snow.
You guide people through wild forests. You can move through a forest without making a loud noise.
You guide people across open water. You're a strong swimmer and can navigate open water using the stars. Swap your Cartographer's Tools for Navigator's Tools.

entries.caption: Personality Traits
rows: I like to kick pebbles and stones as I walk.
I constantly look back at whoever I'm walking with to ensure they're keeping up.
I like to frequently climb trees or high rocks to view the horizon.
I love to explore new regions and quickly learn new routes.
I prefer to tread paths I've walked before, stepping in my own worn footprints.
I get easily distracted by a new trail, following it wherever it leads.
Animal tracks are a specific interest of mine.
I pride myself on being prepared for every survival situation.

entries.caption: Ideals
rows: I'm eager to help guide people who are lost.
I value my knowledge and know to charge people for guidance.
I lost a loved one to the wilderness and I'll never let that happen again.
There are such amazing hidden views that I can't wait to show people.
I'm hoping to find a grand hidden treasure on my treks.

entries.caption: Bonds
rows: I must preserve my preferred environment. Threats to it matter to me.
I want to help educate people about my preferred environment.
I once misled and ditched a group of bandits in the wilds that were forcing me to guide them. They'll want to get even if they ever find me.
I'm familiar with some of the wild beasts of my environment. They know I'm a friendly face.
I'm part of a Field Guide guild and have several rivals.
I lost a loved one in the wilds as a child. I still hope that they're out there somewhere.

entries.caption: Flaws
rows: I dislike the bustle of settlements and am uncomfortable in towns and cities.
I am very offended when people don't respect local customs.
I generally don't respect local customs and always do things my own way.
I've had some pretty bad encounters with monsters in the wilds. I'm fearful of creatures much larger than myself.
I don't sleep well outside of my chosen environment.
I go at my own pace. If you're not fast enough to keep up, you'll be left behind.

data.name: Introduction

entries.name: Foreword
entries: Welcome adventurer and thank you sincerely for supporting us. We are delighted that you've chosen to include even more palaeontological elements into your games and we hope that you enjoy using these rules and artwork as much as we enjoyed creating them.

We are PalaeoGames, a team of palaeontology research scientists and artists who have a passion for tabletop roleplaying games. {@i Professor Primula's Portfolio of Palaeontology} is our second major palaeontological outreach project, and we are immensely thankful to the wonderful backers who have helped make this dream a reality.

entries.name: What's in This Book?
entries: {@i Professor Primula's Portfolio of Palaeontology} contains homebrew rules for including a variety of scientifically credible prehistoric elements in your DnD 5e and 5.5e tabletop roleplaying games. This book is the sequel to {@i Dr Dhrolin's Dictionary of Dinosaurs}, but does not require that book to be used.

With the exception of some original monsters, every creature, plant, and environment in this book is based on real, up-to-date science which can be used to both entertain and educate. We've also included a variety of fantasy rules, such as playable humanoid species, subclasses, items, backgrounds, etc., all of which can be used together to form a cohesive prehistoric campaign (doubly-so if combined with other prehistoric content from {@i Dr Dhrolin's Dictionary of Dinosaurs}). However, {@i Professor Primula's Portfolio of Palaeontology} is a "{@i splashbook",} meaning that any component from this book can be splashed into an existing setting to add deep history or prehistoric shenanigans, without requiring the other content from the book. For example, you can simply add an animal like {@i Smilodon} ({@b page 105}) into your existing game world, or take one of our systems, like our fossil hunting and museum system ({@b pages 50-69}), to add in an extra layer of gameplay.

entries.name: Design Philosophy
entries: Like in Dr Dhrolin's Dictionary of Dinosaurs, we've taken a different approach to creature design than the official DnD books. Life is diverse and we believe that the current 5E and 5.5E systems of normal, proficiency, and expertise for calculations based on one chosen ability score is insufficient to express that diversity. To give us more granularity in our designs and to better represent what we think these animals were like in real life, we have disregarded some aspects of this system, allowing us to increase/ decrease the offensive/defensive capabilities of our creature designs without over-inflating/deflating their ability scores.

{@b {@i For example, we may think that a particular}} {@b {@i dinosaur should be low CR, but have a very high}} {@b {@i Survival skill. Rather than massively over-inflating}} {@b {@i its Wisdom ability score, we've just given it a higher}} {@b {@i Survival skill bonus. This prevents it from having}} {@b {@i an over-inflated Wisdom saving throw bonus.}}

However, we have reviewed the feedback for Dr Dhrolin's and have limited this approach largely (but not entirely) to skill bonuses and saving throws for animals in this book and have tried to leave Hit Point calculations and Proficiency Bonuses untouched, apart from where it's particularly important. In most cases, we have opted not to add bespoke traits to each creature explaining those choices to save space in the book and to simplify stat blocks.

We've also added names to the armour class of each of our creatures, describing their defensive integument (skin/fur/feathers). This is purely to give DMs and players the opportunity to better visualise and describe combat, and because we think that having every stat block say "Natural Armour" would be boring!

If you wish, you may recalculate any of these creatures' saving throws, skill bonuses, attacks or abilities, using their ability scores and the proficiency bonus for their CR, applying proficiency and expertise where you see fit. You may also rename their armour to "Natural Armour". Remember - this is homebrew and you can rebrew it however you like!
Historic reconstruction of Ceratosaurus.

In addition to these gaming elements, we've included two sections addressing further aspects of palaeontology and geology that weren't included in {@i Dr Dhrolin's Dictionary of Dinosaurs}. These help players and DMs better understand the terminology used in our books, as well as provide context for some of our design choices. In {@i Dr Dhrolin's Dictionary of Dinosaurs}, you will find sections explaining the basics of what palaeontology actually is, what's involved in being a palaeontologist, career options, and different types of fossils, along with brief introductions to geological time, evolution, and the origins of life on Earth. In {@i Professor Primula's Portfolio of Palaeontology}, we've provided more detailed explanations of geological time and the concept of deep-time, as well as an introduction into phylogenetics - the science of the organisation of life. We hope that you find these sections accessible and informative to read.

entries.name: Providing Education Through Gaming
entries: PalaeoGames' core objective is to provide both entertaining and informative TTRPG content. While we feel that we achieve this quite well with our creature stat blocks, there are some associated fields of science that need to be explained in greater detail than our creature profiles and game systems allow. In {@i Dr Dhrolin's Dictionary of Dinosaurs}, we introduced palaeontology as a whole (including career paths, types of fossils, how we interpret fossils, and how we reconstruct extinct organisms), a brief description of geological time, an introduction to evolution, and how life formed on Earth. In this book, we're taking a deep-dive into two other topics in greater detail: Systematics and Deep Time. Understanding both of these will clarify some of the terms that are presented in our animal profiles.

entries.name: Systematics Taxonomy and Phylogenetics
entries: The keen eyed of you will have noticed that many of our creatures in this book (and our other books) include creature subtypes that aren't used elsewhere in TTRPGs. The reason why we have done this is to provide a bit more information about the evolutionary relationships between different creatures, AKA the discipline of Systematics and its sub-disciplines Phylogenetics and Taxonomy. However, without a proper explanation, this information can seem confusing and daunting.

Historically, we categorised organisms based on their physical traits, although now many scientists supplement or replace this with genetic information (DNA and RNA) where possible (called {@b Molecular Systematics}). In palaeontology, because of the nature of the material available to us, we mostly use physical characters while still sometimes referring to modern molecular systematic studies of related animals to help inform our understanding.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: {@i Lots of people think that getting DNA matches between organisms must offer a perfect answer to their evolutionary relationships. However, it's important to note that Molecular Systematics isn't flawless and suffers from some of the same issues as regular systematics, like} {@b {@i Convergent}} {@b {@i Evolution}}{@i, for example. Some lineages of organisms independently evolve the same physical traits and it's possible, although rare, that multiple lineages also independently evolve the same DNA sequences to adapt to similar situations.}

entries.name: Taxonomy and Naming Life
entries: Taxonomy is a field of science that can be summarised as the naming, describing, and classification of living organisms. Its goal is to organise biodiversity in a manner that reflects real relationships between organisms. While many systems have been used over the years, modern taxonomy is usually thought of as first established by Carl Linnaeus (the "father of taxonomy") in 1735. Linnaean taxonomy is a hierarchical system that separates organisms into groups called Taxa (plural, Taxon as singular), and successively smaller, ranked, subgroups within those groups. The classical hierarchical groups are: {@b Domain}, {@b Kingdom}, {@b Phylum}, {@b Class}, {@b Order}, {@b Family}, {@b Genus}, and {@b Species}. However, this simplistic system doesn't reflect the complexity of life and the diversity of each tier is inconsistent between different lineages. For example, the order Coleoptera (Beetles) has >400,000 described species and contains far more diversity than an equivalently-tiered order of mammals, like Primates, that has somewhere between 300-500 described species. Moreover, the Linnean system was conceived before we had any real notion of evolution and how things are related to one another so, apart from genus and species, which are still used today, the other ranks have become largely obsolete outside of the pre-university Biology classroom.

The Linnaean hierarchical groups were originally intended to be equal across different lineages. However, our understanding of evolution disrupts this by revealing that some groups that were previously described as a high rank actually sit within a lower rank. One of the most prominent examples of this is {@b Class Aves} (birds) being revealed to sit inside of the dinosaur {@b Family Deinonychosauria} (dromaeosaurs and their kin), which itself sits in {@b Class Reptilia} (reptiles)! As such, taxonomists have largely abandoned the Linnaean rankings and in doing so also removed the requirement to label new groupings as sub-ranks within Linnaean's system (i.e. subfamily, infraorder, subclass, etc.). Once we establish that an organism belongs to a specific category (e.g. Reptilia), all of its descendants are considered part of that group and are organised into lower level subgroups. In essence, the taxonomic organisation is still hierarchical, but their ranks are not fixed.

When we erect a new grouping of organisms, regardless of if it was within the Linnaean hierarchy or not, that group must have a specific set of characteristics that an organism should meet in order to be placed within it. For example, {@b Animalia} (animals) are defined as multicellular organisms that consume organic material, breathe oxygen, have myocytes (muscle cells) allowing them to move, can reproduce sexually, and grow from a hollow sphere of cells (the blastula) during embryonic development. This is where taxonomy can become very difficult, as some of these characters might be lost by a lineage over time as organisms evolve and change, potentially losing some of the original traits as they adapt to an ever changing environment. The loss of a character may be so distinctive that it becomes a defining feature of a new subgrouping. This is why using multiple characteristics is so important, as it lets us recognise relationships in even very distantly related organisms like humans and fish.

entries.name: When and Why We Name New Organisms & Taxonomic Groups
entries: When and why we name new organisms and/or erect new groupings for them to reside within is an important component of taxonomy.

The reason for naming a new organism is rather simple really: the discovered organism is morphologically different enough to warrant its own species. This is different from the public's common perception of what a "species" is. Most laypersons think of Ernst Mayr's biological species definition when describing a species, which was established in 1942 and focuses on {@b reproductive isolation}. Reproductive isolation is when a population of organisms are only able to successfully interbreed within their population, isolating them genetically from other closely related animals. This definition comes with several problems and isn't the method we actually use for determining new species. Firstly, it isn't possible to test for reproductive isolation in fossils and is unethical as well as impractical to do so for modern animals. Secondly, reproductive isolation is a result of speciation, not the cause of it. Finally, the realities of nature are not so binary - many species can have partial success in breeding with other species, creating viable hybrids.

In palaeontology, we label an organism as a new species when we think that it is sufficiently morphologically different enough to represent a different population of animals (which are also probably largely genetically isolated). We call this a {@b morphospecies}. This does, however, mean that there is a level of personal interpretation by the author when determining whether their discovery meets the criteria, as well as from the scientists who review the paper. This ambiguity can lead to disagreements about whether or not an organism is distinctive enough to be labelled as a new species - with there being nicknames for scientists that lean into extreme interpretations - "{@b Lumpers}" and "{@b Splitters}". These names are self-explanatory, with Lumpers frequently lumping any new discoveries into an existing taxon and are often criticised for artificially reducing the diversity of groups they study. Splitters are the opposite, splitting many new specimens into separate taxa, artificially inflating the taxonomic diversity. Splitters tend to be more common (as describing new taxa is broadly beneficial to an author's professional portfolio) but arguably, both practices are equally unhelpful. Erroneously erected taxa by Splitters may be formally noted as doubtful ({@i nomen dubia}), insufficiently erected ({@i nomen nudum}), or invalidly erected ({@i nomen invalidum}).

The standards for erecting a new non-species phylogenetic group are somewhat different. Instead of being based just on our interpretation of when groups differ in morphology, there can be a more substantial mathematical origin by coming from a proper phylogenetic analysis (see the page opposite). Sometimes, these studies will rearrange different groups of organisms in a new configuration that has not previously been named. For example, if we have three organisms A, B, and C; and our analysis highlights that organism A is closer to organism B than organism C, then there should be a taxonomic name that encompasses A+B, but not C. If this name doesn't already exist, we can erect a new one that represents this relationship. However, due to the constantly changing nature of phylogenetics, these phylogenetic group names can quickly become obsolete and we try to appropriately maintain or revise them where possible.

entries.name: What's in a Name?
entries: Above, we've described how we name new species and other taxonomic groupings, but choosing what those names are is another topic entirely. It's important to note that there are rules and regulations for erecting scientific names, and the standardised international guidance for naming organisms is governed by the {@b International Code of Zoological Nomenclature (ICZN)} for animals, and the {@b International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants (ICN)} for algae, fungi, and plants. These systems ensure that scientific names are created, formatted, and published appropriately and consistently, avoiding confusion and duplication.

When we name something new, we usually give it a genus {@b and} species name, unless it is likely to be very closely related to an existing genus. The genus and species together form the scientific name (binomial nomenclature) of an organism. This name should always be written in italics, with the genus having a capital first letter. These names are generally combinations of Latin or Greek words (though now it's common for these to be in any non-English language) that highlight some aspect of the organism, its habitat, or honour people or places.
For example, {@i Homo sapiens} is the genus and species name for modern humans and means "wise human"
or "discerning man" ({@i Homo} meaning "man" as a non-gendered term, and {@i sapiens} meaning "knowledgeable/ wise/discerning").

Most modern animals have colloquial/common names that are not linked to their scientific name (like the Red Fox ({@i Vulpes vulpes}) or Feral Pigeons ({@i Columba livia})). However, some animals have common names that are derived from their scientific name (like Gorillas ({@i Gorilla gorilla}) or the Boa constrictor ({@i Boa constrictor})).

Common names are usually not used for prehistoric animals (although there are exceptions like dire wolves or cave lions). Instead, they are often referred to by their genus name in common usage (e.g., Velociraptor for †{@i Velociraptor mongoliensis}); a dagger (†) may be used to indicate extinction in technical contexts. One well-known exception in popular media is the use of {@i T. rex}, an abbreviation of {@i Tyrannosaurus rex}, instead of just {@i Tyrannosaurus}. This convention of abbreviating full binomials is typically used in research papers when referencing the same taxon multiple times in a single document but "{@i T. rex}" is the exception in having widespread usage.

entries.name: Phylogenetics
entries: Phylogenetics is the science behind how we determine how closely related organisms are to each other. This is a complex field that includes a lot of mathematics that many laypersons and scientists alike find intimidating, although simple analyses can be undertaken that may still be effective. We'll summarise only the basics here.

Phylogenetics allows us to visualise and interpret the relationship between animals using a {@b Phylogenetic Tree}, essentially a single branch of the "tree of life", which is a representation of the interconnected lineages that links all life on Earth together to a single starting organism that first originated on the early Earth ({@b see The Origin of Life of Earth, page 17 in DDDD}). On such a tree, each connecting point between branches represents the last common ancestor of the two deviating lineages. Each such point represents a {@b Clade}, that is a group of organisms that includes an {@b ancestor} and {@b all of its descendants}.

Ideally, all of the taxonomic hierarchical groups we describe would be inclusive clades with every organism descended from a single taxon, making them {@b Monophyletic}. However, sometimes we can erect groups that include organisms that do not share the group's defining common ancestor, making them {@b Polyphyletic}. An extreme example of how this could occur would be if you only classified Mammals as "things with hair that produce milk", {@i Charles Darwin's first illustration of a phylogenetic tree from 1837.}
then mistakenly included coconuts in the group. How we determine which groups are mono/polyphyletic is described later when we discuss evaluating a phylogenetic tree.

entries.name: Measuring Characters
entries: Before constructing a phylogenetic tree, a scientist must first analyse their specimens. To do this, they must establish a series of {@b Characteristics/Characters} that they will measure from the organisms, as well as how many specimens will be included (usually, including multiple examples of each described species means greater accuracy).

Choosing how many characters to measure, which characters to measure, and how they're measured is both the most difficult and most important part of performing a phylogenetic analysis. Characters are either morphological (physical traits like bone structure) or molecular (genetic data, such as DNA or protein sequences) and are usually provided as binary answers ({@b states}), sometimes with the option for "no result" or "unknown" (to allow incomplete specimens to be included).

Morphological characters can be simple absence/ presence questions, like "{@i does the organism have limbs?}" or can be more sophisticated questions about the ratios/ sizes of structures that we know all of the organisms included have, like "{@i is the femur greater than twelve times longer than it is wide?}". Having lots of sophisticated characters like this allows you to take into account many different aspects of an organism's anatomy while avoiding using fixed measurement values that would cause different sized individuals of the same species to potentially show up as unrelated species.

Having lots of characters is important, so long as the same thing isn't being measured multiple times and the number of characters doesn't reach an impractical size that hinders the research (it's not much use trying to code for a million characters for a hundred thousand specimens if you only have a week to do it!). The same is true for the number of specimens - having more is almost always better, but if you include a large number of highly fragmentary remains that don't demonstrate your characters, they will create confusing and uninformative results.
Once the characters for all of the specimens have been measured, a {@b Data Matrix} is created. Below is a simplified example, with each character presented as "C#".

entries.name: Matrix
entries: {@b C1 C2 C3 C4 C5 C6 Specimen #1} 1 0 1 1 ?
1 {@b Specimen #2} 0 1 0 1 1 0 {@b Specimen #3} 0 1 1 1 1 0 {@b Specimen #4} ?

1 1 0 1 0 Finally, a scientist may wish to add {@b Weighting} to some of their characters. This amplifies the result of that character in the analysis and is reserved for specific characters that are known to be very important in the analysis to prevent them from being "flooded out" by multiple less-important characters. One example might be the character "{@i does the organism have limbs?}" if you are running the analysis on a group of snakes that are all known to be limbless.

entries.name: Producing a Tree
entries: After assembling your data matrix and determining any character weighting, you can begin constructing a phylogenetic tree. There are several different mathematical ways to do this, but the two most popular are {@b Maximum Parsimony} and {@b Bayesian Inference}.

A tree constructed using Maximum Parsimony is built by calculating the fewest possible evolutionary changes needed to explain all of the character occurrences, minimising the number of times that a character evolved independently (called a {@b homoplasy}). In essence, it follows the logic of Occam's Razor: that the simplest answer is often the most probable and the best.

Bayesian Inference is a more complex mathematical approach, which allows for the use of incomplete data (like the question marks in our example table from fragmentary specimens). It estimates the likelihood of multiple trees and produces a {@b posterior probability distribution}, which is a collection of different trees (potentially thousands) and their associated probabilities. From these, it generates a {@b consensus tree} that incorporates the most common and likely relationships between the specimens. This consensus tree is more mathematically robust than a tree generated by Maximum Parsimony. Thankfully, all of the complex mathematics involved can be handled by specialist software.

entries.name: Evaluating a Tree
entries: Simply producing a tree via one of these methods is often not sufficient to satisfy scrutiny from other scientists. The tree must be statistically evaluated to determine how confident we can be in its various branches. To do this, we use a method called {@b Bootstrap Resampling}, which is a repeated re-analysis of subsets of the original data matrix. This allows us to see how often specific groupings re-occur (although we can already see this for Bayesian Inference trees by reviewing the probabilities of each branch from their posterior probability trees).

Ideally, your tree will achieve a high support value as close to 100% bootstrap for Maximum Parsimony and 1.0 posterior probability for Bayesian Inference. The higher your support value is, the more confident you can be that each branch on your tree represents a real clade (a {@b Monophyletic Clade}) and isn't an "inaccurate" clade that contains organisms that actually sit on a different branch in life (referred to as {@b Polyphyletic Clades} when identified). Once you have satisfactory confidence in your tree, it can be published in a scientific journal, either as its own paper or as part of a wider analysis which may even require a new clade name for any newly identified confident monophyletic clade. In the same manner as describing organism names, there is an international body Apomorphy Ancestral trait Derived trait Homoplasy Synapomorphy Plesiomorphy Autapomorphy {@i Diagram showing types of character traits in relation to being ancestral or derived. Adapted from:} Page, R.D.M and Holmes, E.C. 2009. {@i Molecular Evolution: A Phylogenetic Approach}. Wiley-Blackwell, pp. 352.
that provides standardised guidance for clade names, called the {@b International Society for Phylogenetic Nomenclature (ISPN)}.

As with all things in science, new data, specimens, or different interpretations of the same material can provide new trees that challenge the previous consensus, and heated debates may rage regarding which tree is most reflective of real life.

entries.name: Interpreting the Tree
entries: A well-supported phylogenetic tree not only reveals the likely relationships between organisms, but also highlights points where those lineages branched away from each other (called {@b Nodes}). As outlined earlier, each of these nodes represents a clade, and highlights where a change in the measured characters occurs. Each of the characters can then be labelled with an appropriate term for each organism that describes whether the character is {@b Ancestral} or {@b Derived} and how it relates to the rest of the tree.

items: {@b Plesiomorphies} are ancestral characters that are present in multiple taxa (sometimes all) in the tree and that originate from a common ancestor, so aren't particularly useful to determine relationships within the tree.
{@b Apomorphies} are the opposite of this, they are new characters that evolved from a plesiomorphic character and are useful to help group organisms.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: We don't just discard polyphyletic clades as discussing them can be useful and, in some cases, a clade can be identified as polyphyletic, but the monophyletic alternative(s) may remain unresolved.

items: {@b Synapomorphies} are apomorphies that can be shown to have evolved from a common ancestor within the tree and are present in their descendants.
{@b Autapomorphies} are completely new characters that only occur in one taxon within the tree.
Finally, {@b Homoplasies} are traits that occur in some of the taxa in the tree independently and are not connected by a common ancestor, usually caused by convergent evolution.

entries: These terms can be better visualised in the diagram above.

We can then use the characters that we've identified as synapomorphies and autapomorphies to be the defining characteristics for any new clade. This provides us with concise and clear definitions of what characteristics categorise an organism into a particular clade and these are often a combination of several characters. For example, Tyrannosauridae (the clade that includes {@i Tyrannosaurus}) has a series of defining characters that describe the skull and pelvis shape and was coined in 1906 by Sir Henry Fairfield Osborn.

entries.name: Our Current Understanding of the
Tree of Life
entries: Each phylogenetic investigation represents the exploration of a single small branch of the vast interconnected tree of life. Since the development of this field of science, humanity has calculated billions, if not trillions, of phylogenetic trees exploring these relationships.

{@b Marsupialia Mammalia Afrotheria Placentalia Boreoeutheria Euarchontoglires} There is still a huge amount of work to do and new data/interpretations constantly up-end our existing understanding, but we nonetheless have some pretty firm conclusions regarding the relationships of many organisms. When looking at trees like these, it's important to remember that any node can be rotated to allow for re-visualisation of the same information. For example, the diagram above represents the same information displayed in two different ways that might make some aspects of it easier to understand.

How precisely each tree resolves the relationships of the organisms included in it (i.e. whether it just looks at high-level relationships, or goes all the way down to species-level) will depend on the goals of the scientist(s) that created it and how broad it is in its overall scope. More restricted studies of smaller clades tend to resolve relationships more precisely. This is usually because studies restricted to specific groups have characters measured that are relevant and may be unique to those groups (e.g. choosing characters to measure dozens of bone lengths to precisely resolve animal relationships is a bit silly if your study also includes boneless arthropods).

We can also use these trees to determine other useful information. For example, branch length can be plotted against time to form a {@b geochronological plot} of the tree's evolution, allowing us to better understand when groups originated, diversified, and went extinct.

entries.name: Concluding Remarks
entries: Systematics is complex and includes an array of unintuitive terms from both statistics and biology that can be quite overwhelming. If you've gotten this far and feel like you're starting to vaguely understand it, then you've done excellently - well done! If not, don't worry. It takes years to master these subjects, and this is just a brief discussion in a TTRPG book after all!

In that vein, you can always play around with designing your own phylogenetic trees for the fantasy creatures in your game worlds to get to grips with these concepts better. These can include nodes where deities or other supernatural forces interfere with a creature's lineage, creating a magical synapomorphy and giving rise to a new clade. This is particularly fun to do with dragons, which can have a wide variety of morphologies, colours, and origins.

Whether you're looking at real species or dreaming up fictional lineages, in order to discuss their systematics and evolutionary history, the depth of time required for that creature to evolve must also be considered. In the next section we look at the concept of Deep Time and the Geological Timescale.

entries.name: Deep Time and the Geological Timescale
entries: The Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago. It's fair to call it old. Very old... very, {@i very} old. We casually throw around terms referring to millions and billions of years, but these are such truly vast amounts of time that we struggle to understand the enormity of what they actually represent. Even our powerful sapien imaginations cannot truly fathom them, despite what we try to tell ourselves. Our lives and memories are simply too limited to fully grasp how much change occurs over these time periods - both to the landscape and to the organisms that inhabit it. We use the term {@b Deep Time} to signify this difference in understanding when discussing timeframes of millions of years or more. This is a term also used by cosmologists, who apply it to even longer periods of time!
To tackle this problem, geologists have developed the {@b Geological Timescale}, which breaks down this enormous timeframe into successively smaller, slightly less enormous, intervals..

entries.name: Geologic Time Scale
entries: The printed book reproduces the Geological Society of America's Geologic Time Scale chart on page 20 (used with permission). The chart is not reproduced in this conversion; see Walker, J.D., and Geissman, J.W., compilers, 2022, Geologic Time Scale v. 6.0: Geological Society of America, {@link https://doi.org/10.1130/2022.CTS006C|https://doi.org/10.1130/2022.CTS006C}.
Example images of how an environment can change over geological time. The images show the following ages:

items: 1. Proterozoic.
2. Cambrian.
3. Ordovician.
4. Carboniferous (specifically Pennsylvanian).
5. Permian.
6. Pleistocene.

entries.name: Divisions of Time
entries: The geological timescale uses internationally-recognised standardised units of time that are determined and maintained by the {@b International Commission on Stratigraphy (ICS)}. These units are broken down into further subunits in a (usually) hierarchical sequence as follows:

items: An {@b Eon} is the largest unit, ranging from about 2 billion years to several hundred million years in duration.

entries: There are four eons: the Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic, and Phanerozoic. Eons are characterised by planetary-scale fundamental changes in geology.

items: An {@b Era} is the second largest unit, ranging from hundreds of millions of years to tens of millions of years. Eras are characterised by planetary-scale major changes in geology and the composition of life on Earth.
A {@b Period} ranges from tens of millions of years to millions of years. Periods are characterised by wide-scale changes in geology and the composition of life on Earth.
An {@b Epoch} is the second smallest unit, ranging from millions of years to hundreds of thousands of years.

entries: Epochs are generally characterised by large scale changes in geology.

items: An {@b Age} is the smallest unit, ranging from millions of years to thousands of years. Ages are generally characterised by smaller scale changes in geology.
A {@b Chron} is a non-specified unit of time that can be used to describe certain phenomena that don't align with other geological divisions of time.

entries: When plotted together against age, these units form the Geological Timescale, as shown on the next page.

How the boundaries for these timescales are defined depends on several geological and biological factors, however Eons, Eras, and Periods can generally be attributed to major changes in global geology and/ or biology. For example, from the geological side, the Hadean Eon represents a period of Earth's history just after its formation where its surface was still molten in many places. The transition from the Hadean to the Archean represents the stabilisation of that outer crust. For biological examples, the end of the Ordovician, Permian, Triassic, and Cretaceous periods are all marked by major global mass extinction events. Both of these types of factors act as biostratigraphic markers and allow us to better define the boundaries between major intervals with most boundaries including both geological and biological factors. After all, most global events that cause an extinction also affect the planet's geology.

Occasionally, we're able to internationally agree on a very specific layer that denotes the transition between one division of time to another. When a firm consensus is reached, we may declare a {@b Golden Spike} (or {@b Global Boundary Stratotype Section and Point (GSSP)}) layer at a specific locality that denotes the exact point in Earth's record of the boundary.

In addition to understanding how we divide up Earth's deep history, as well as how those divisions are determined, it is also important to understand how we interpret the age of the rocks that we are studying. This is a field of science called {@b Geochronology}.

entries.name: Geochronology
entries: The scientific study of how we determine/estimate the age of rocks and sediments is called Geochronology, which itself is composed of several other subfields of science. The goal of this field is to provide, where possible, absolute ages (or at least accurate ranges of ages) for events and rock layers. There are several ways in which these ages can be determined, depending on the type of rocks you're dealing with.

entries.name: Radiometric Dating
entries: The most reliable method of geochronology is radiometric dating. This methodology uses the {@b decay of radioactive isotopes} (unstable elements that give off radiation, changing into a more stable new element/isotope) to determine the age of rock. In essence, each type of radioactive isotope decays at a known rate (called its {@b half-life}), and we can therefore mathematically determine when the rock was formed by the ratio of unstable radioactive isotopes to its decayed stable isotopes/elements.

Different radioactive isotopes are useful in different situations, depending on the types of rock available, but also the sorts of age ranges that are being explored. {@b Uranium to Lead (U-Pb)} dating is suitable for very old igneous rocks that contain the mineral Zircon, as Uranium has a very long half-life. {@b Potassium to Argon (K-Ar)} dating is much more suitable for palaeontological dating in sedimentary rocks, as it is formed in volcanic events, allowing it to be deposited in sedimentary rocks by ash falls. Finally, {@b Carbon-14 to Carbon-13 (C14-C13)} dating is suitable for archaeology and recent palaeontology, as Carbon-14 has a short half-life (only usable up to about 50,000 years ago) and can be found in organic remains.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: It's worth pointing out that, whichever isotope is used, the media tends to report it all as "Carbon Dating", despite carbon only being suitable for relatively young material.

Importantly, not every type of rock or fossil can be subject to radiometric dating and most rocks that we perform appropriate radiometric dating on (like volcanic rocks) don't preserve fossils. Instead, they offer snapshots in a rock sequence that allows us to determine the age of specific layers, which we can then use to help estimate the ages of other layers. There are several ways in which we do this, outlined below.

entries.name: Biostratigraphy
entries: One of the most important uses of fossils, outside of improving our understanding of life on Earth, is for {@b biostratigraphy}. This field of science uses fossils to determine the {@b relative ages} of rocks, particularly those in different locations that share the same fossil taxa.

Importantly, it uses {@b fossil assemblages}, rather than singular taxa, but assigns certain taxa as {@b Index Fossils}. These are taxa (usually a genus or species-level) that were widespread, but only existed for a short period of geological time. Generally, marine animals like ammonites Index Fossil A {@b A A + B Fossil Assemblage A + B + C B + C B + C + D B None} and graptolites, which continued to evolve quickly and had a wide geographical distribution, are ideal candidates to be index fossils.

With a collection of many index fossils that overlap in their occurrence, it is possible to determine with remarkable specificity the relative age of a layer of sediment, as particular combinations of those index fossils only occurred for brief intervals. This allows sediments that lack suitable isotopes for radiometric dating to be correlated with those that can be dated radiometrically, even if they are on opposite sides of the world. The diagrams below and on the next page provide simplified examples of how this works.

entries.name: Palaeomagnetism
entries: In a similar approach to biostratigraphy, another method can be used to determine the relative ages of rocks from different locations - this time, using the magnetic alignment of the minerals in those rocks in the field of science called {@b Palaeomagnetism}. When volcanic rocks cool and sediments settle, magnetic minerals within them align with the Earth's magnetic field. However, over Earth's long history, its magnetic field has reversed in polarity many times, called {@b geomagnetic reversals}.

As Earth's magnetic field is ubiquitous across the entire planet, geologists can use the pattern of these reversals to correlate rocks from different locations, with varying reversal thicknesses functioning like a barcode. Again, this allows us to correlate rocks in areas where 1m Index Fossil B 2m Index Fossil C 3m {@b Rock Age} 4m Index Fossil D 5m 6m 7m {@i A diagram showing how the overlap of different index fossil occurrences allows us to use the overall fossil assemblage as a unique identifier for a particular age of rock.}

Note how some assemblages are missing in some locations, revealing that there was a period of erosion that removed those layers of rock in those locations!}

radiometric dating isn't possible with those in areas where it is. However, as rates of sediment deposition are not consistent everywhere and may vary over time, correlation can be difficult. Nevertheless, paleomagnetism remains a useful extra option for dating rocks, especially when looking at very long periods of time.

entries.name: Planetary Cycles
