entries: Finally, sometimes it is possible to attribute changes to layers in sediment deposition to {@b planetary cycles}, allowing geologists to simply count the layers of rock. The Earth's climate is influenced by astronomical cycles, called {@b Milankovitch Cycles,} that change the distribution of solar energy received from the Sun, resulting in consistent fluctuations in climate and therefore identifiable changes in sediment deposition.

There are three main cycles that are known to astrophysicists and that are observable in the sedimentary record. These are {@b eccentricity}, which is a variance in the shape of Earth's orbit around the sun occurring over approximately 100,000 years, {@b obliquity}, which is a variance in the tilt of Earth's axis occurring over approximately 41,000 years, and {@b precession}, which is the wobble of the Earth's axis occurring over approximately 26,000 years. Additionally, Earth's annual orbit around the Sun can also result in very fine-layered seasonal changes observable in some types of rock and is also technically a planetary cycle.

These predictable, consistent changes allow geologists to literally count layers of rock and, if they can be correlated to the correct cycle, assign ages to each layer from the nearest radiometric dating layer.

entries.name: Concluding Remarks
entries: Understanding deep time is not intuitive and, excluding radiometric dating, our knowledge is invariably informed by best-guess assessments and estimates. The complexities in the evolution and distribution of life on Earth creates limitations and uncertainties for biostratigraphy and changes in rates of sedimentation make interpreting paleomagnetism and some planetary cycles challenging. Nevertheless, the study of deep time, how it is divided up, and how we measure it is a well-established science and we have a high degree of confidence in our current understanding of the age of the Earth.

Now that we have covered some topics of real-world science, let's delve into how we bring components like these into our games to both entertain and educate our players. To begin with, we will tackle the means of introducing palaeontology, as a whole, into your game worlds through specific NPCs and plot hooks.

entries.name: Further Ideas for Introducing Palaeontology to your Campaign
entries: In our book {@i Dr Dhrolin's Dictionary of Dinosaurs}, we introduced a series of plot hooks and ideas for including palaeontology into your game world. These were Necromancer Island, which outlined a story idea for having re-animated prehistoric creatures in enclosures on an exotic island, The Ancient Plateau, where prehistoric lineages persisted to the modern day in an isolated high-altitude environment, The Mad Chronoficer, where time travel was used to bring prehistoric creatures to the present or plunge players into the past, and the Hollow World, where an ancient environment persisted deep underground towards the planet's core.. In {@i Professor Primula's Portfolio of Palaeontology}, we've decided to introduce several more plot hook ideas to assist DMs in bringing palaeontological elements into their campaigns. These are Dino-Planet, Nighttime at the Museum, The Waste Nexus, and Skull Island. For each of these, we provide a brief synopsis of the idea and how it can be used to introduce prehistoric creatures to your players. We have also elaborated significantly on Skull Island, dedicating an entire chapter to it later in the book. Each one of these could easily be used to construct an entire campaign around or can be splashed into an existing setting to flesh it out.

In addition to these story hooks, we have also created several game systems that compliment them. These systems will be introduced in later chapters. You can use any of these systems or ideas on their own, or all together to create a dynamic and varied prehistoric campaign.

To help flavour how all of these topics (and the creatures presented later) can be introduced, throughout the book we've also included "flavour text" in the form of Professor Primula's research notes and her opinions about creatures from her palaeontological portfolio. You can use these notes as inspiration for storytelling or as literal notes that players can find. Of course, to have her notes, we need to first introduce Professor Primula herself:
A skeleton of Allosaurus being erected at the American Museum of Natural History.

entries.name: Professor Primula, Palaeontologist
entries: Professor Elizabeth Primula is an elven scientist, senior research professor, and head of department at the University of Urgleshire. Her research topics are numerous, given her exceedingly long career (over 200 years), although she is currently most fascinated by how the functional morphology of vertebrates and arthropods impacts their behavioural tendencies.

Historically, Professor Primula has been a desk-based palaeontologist, preferring to scour literature and analyse museum-quality fossils in the comfort of her office or in archive rooms. Easy access to her personal library and other museum records have allowed her to undertake large-scale complex analyses with relative ease, and she has published numerous articles and books across all fields of palaeontology. Such prominent works include: "{@i The Ostracod Fauna of Urgleshire: A Comprehensive Review}", "{@i 'Will It Blend?' Helicoprion Feeding Mechanics}", and "{@i On The Origin of Dragons: Dinosaur Hybridisation?}". While Professor Primula has less practical fossil excavation experience than her colleagues, her extensive publication record renders her one of the most influential palaeontologists on the continent and certainly the senior-most palaeontologist at the University of Urgleshire.

"When establishing a research career, it is most important to ensure that you are well-read on a subject prior to publication. I suggest spending at least 10 years studying the literature before dabbling in any particular topic. At least, that is my "gold standard" and what I recommend to our students. The practical requirements of this can lead to an academic advantage for us longer-lived peoples, but also a much slower rate of publication."

Recently, the antics of her colleague Dr Dhrolin on his latest sabbatical highlighted that practical fieldwork beyond fossil collecting is entirely possible for palaeontology. Previous accounts of time travel and prehistoric creatures found hidden within secluded regions were dismissed as folklore, myth, and hoaxes. Professor Primula now has it on good authority that, under the right circumstances, it is actually possible to travel through, or observe creatures from, Deep Time. As such, the University of Urgleshire has granted Professor Primula summer leave to undertake a series of short field excursions between teaching terms, all fully funded by the university.
This book recounts both Professor Primula's notes from these field excursions and her notes from the background literature review she undertook prior to setting out.

"As the head of department, I do have some sway with university management. Dr Dhrolin, myself, and Master Marzogg put together a proposal to the university board to undertake a series of small research excursions. These will allow us to verify some of my hypotheses and, ultimately, to produce some truly groundbreaking research. The suggestion that this in turn might bring in a considerable number of large research grants in the future seemed to seal the deal. While I don't tend to dirty my hands with such fieldwork, I must admit that I am excited about the prospect of seeing some of these animals in the flesh."

entries.name: John Hammorc
entries: In our first book, {@i Dr Dhrolin's Dictionary of Dinosaurs}, we included a piece of artwork lovingly named "John Hammorc" by our community ({@b page 23 in DDDD}). By popular demand, we have created a stat block for John Hammorc and included him in this book. This NPC can either be used with the suggested "Necromancer Island" story hook ({@b also page 23 in DDDD}), or as a wealthy benefactor to hire a party to investigate "Skull Island" ({@b page 30-47}). Alternatively, you can use him in any other way you wish to help introduce prehistoric creatures into your campaigns.

entries.name: Story Hooks
entries: Now that these story hook NPCs have been introduced, we can outline some further ideas on how prehistoric elements can be introduced into your campaign. Here are some choice examples pulled from popular culture:

"I consider myself a relatively well-connected scientist, with contacts in other scientific fields, in governments, and with various organisations, as well as with entrepreneurs who may offer funding. Among those I've met, one individual stands out as particularly... eccentric. Mr John Hammorc is, by far, the most friendly and philanthropic person I have ever met and was exceptionally interested in the research notes of my peers and myself. He was keen to shower us with financial assistance in exchange for more details about our knowledge on time travel and prehistoric creatures. We, of course, complied with his generous offer. I am sure that other trained scientists could have deduced the same additional information from our published research, but I suppose he valued hearing it unfiltered from the original authors.
Nevertheless, I cannot shake this feeling that we may regret working with this unusual man."

entries.name: Dino-planet
entries: While DnD is traditionally a mediaeval inspired fantasy setting, there's nothing stopping you from sprinkling a little sci-fi into your games. Magical portals need not just lead to other planes of existence, they can also transport players across the universe/multiverse to other planets. One planet (or several planets) could be a prehistoric, primal Dino-World, where enormous beasts rule and players find themselves in a dire fight for survival in a primitive environment.

Portals are just one means to implement this idea. Magically enchanted spaceship-like vessels are already well-established in DnD, allowing for an alternative and more interactive means of transport to such worlds, perhaps forming a story arc in their own right.

Using this story hook allows you to build independent settings that can be populated with all manner of alien, futuristic, or prehistoric creatures (potentially intermingling all three) without having to directly impact your established game world. Unlike time travel, there is little potential for direct impact on your world's timeline from your player's actions (unless of course you want there to be!).

entries.name: Nighttime at the Museum
entries: Based on the modern classic family film of a very similar name, having your campaign focus on (or just include) a magically enchanted museum that animates its housed displays overnight allows for some epic and diverse storytelling in a confined space. Much like in the film, animated creatures can be "defeated" by completing specific tasks or in a traditional combat encounter - being either destroyed or magically returned to their displays when they are defeated. This story hook could also be combined with our new museum system ({@b pages 57-62}) that allows players to build up their own awesome museum, then ultimately be faced with surviving their creation in a cruel ironic twist - the better their museum is, the more dangerous it is.

This approach also allows you to include animals, plants, and peoples from vastly different periods of time or locations without any need for time travel shenanigans or other plot points. Their presence in the museum alone is reason enough to include them. The only challenge is determining the boundary of the museum, either in terms of duration of the animated effect or physical limits. We recommend the traditional story approach for this plot hook of sundown to sunrise and that the animated creatures are entirely restricted to the museum's grounds, unable to leave them on their own.

However you implement this idea, this approach can allow you to introduce all possible encounters long before the players actually face them, allowing for some seriously intimidating "Chekhov's gun" moments. Having your low-level party wandering around a museum, seeing the remains and displays of high-CR creatures, only to have that museum later come to life will make the players painfully aware of the dangers that await them. One of our highest-tier pledgers requested a creature design that is perfect for this story hook. On {@b pages 346-349}, you can find the Skeletal {@i Tyrannosaurus}, an ideal centrepiece for such a storyline.

entries.name: The Waste Nexus
entries: On the theme of portals and interdimensional magic, what happens when portals malfunction? Is there a demiplane or location where they divert to? Would this location be a nexus for the universe's waste and unwanted things? Such locations exist in many different fictional universes, often being timeless spaces that combine creatures, objects, and themes from a variety of times - from prehistoric, to mediaeval, to modern, to futuristic. In these locations, you can take creatures from all of history that are found in our books and lump them together in a chaotic mishmash of time periods, resulting in a particularly violent and chaotic environment.

Such locations are also excellent for recovering campaigns where the party has been defeated. A total party kill need not result in the players having to design new characters. Instead, they could find their characters awakening in this waste nexus world, greeted with the new challenge of clawing their way back into their original plane. In the same vein, this waste nexus can allow the introduction of a long-term villainous higher-power or pantheon that functions as a long-term (perhaps multi-campaign) BBEG. That is, the players are faced with the impossible task of killing a god and are immediately discarded into the waste nexus, where they work together with unlikely allies to escape and rally against the unkillable.

As part of our Time Travel Butterfly Effects ({@b pages 75-77}), we've introduced the Institution of Chronological Stability (ICS) ({@b pages 80-82}). This faction and its associated NPC stat blocks can be the perfect means to introduce the party to the concept of the waste nexus, and even send them there, should the party fall on their bad side.

entries.name: Skull Island
entries: Skull Island is a common feature in many fantasy and sci-fi settings. Originally featured in the 1932 novel and 1933 film both named {@i King Kong}, it has been a staple of speculative fiction ever since. The island generally takes its name from a large skull-shaped mountain found at its centre. Although this name and imagery has been repeated in dozens of unrelated stories since its inception, the original idea of it being an island of pure primal violence inhabited by strange often over-sized creatures and isolated tribal peoples ruled by the giant ape {@i Kong} remains consistent.

We love this setting. It allows you to include an isolated, totally outrageous environment of extremes. You can mix real prehistoric animals with wild creature designs, kaiju, and elemental magic to form this mythological setting. There is a vast array of options available to make the creatures on Skull Island unique and interesting in dramatic ways. So much so that we have opted to dedicate a significant portion of this book to suggesting how you might implement this idea. In the next section, we dive into far more detail about Skull Island and its monstrous inhabitants.

data.name: Skull Island
entries: Throughout my academic studies, I have heard mentioned several stories of an isolated island with unusually large creatures. While such rumours are rarely taken seriously by the research community (especially given the ambiguous information regarding the island's location), a recent artefact that crossed my path has given substance to them. Perhaps they warrant further investigation...

entries.name: A Brief Summary of This System

items: Skull Island is a mysterious place filled with strange and powerful creatures.
Use the Skull Island Effects table to empower creatures (either all creatures or a particular species).
Create massive demi-god kaiju using the Ultra-Gigantism rules that lord over the island.
Pit these monstrous creatures against each other or try to outmanoeuvre them.
These Ultra-Gigantism creatures can also be used as Patrons for your Ancient Beast Warlock and come with additional optional bonuses.

entries: Skull island takes inspiration from classic monster movies like {@i King Kong} and our favourite {@i strictly copyrighted gigantic nuclear-breathing reptile}. The core concept of this setting is that of an isolated, mysterious, and hostile island (usually only found by following a secret map or strange compass) that is inhabited by bizarre over-sized creatures, who themselves exist in the shadows of colossal monstrous kaiju. As such, the creatures of Skull Island can be separated into two categories: the {@b Skull Island Fauna} and creatures that have undergone {@b Ultra-Gigantism}. We think that these could make for a compelling palaeo-adjacent setting for your campaign and the concept is even more exciting if these creatures are prehistoric in origin or theme. As such, we have outlined rules for these two types of creatures:

entries.name: Skull Island Fauna
entries: In addition to the Ultra-Gigantism demi-gods, the "normal" creatures on Skull Island are also much more dangerous than their mainland/offshore counterparts. They are often enchanted or otherwise modified in some significant way, gaining unusual attributes and a changed appearance. To represent this, we have created the {@b Skull Island Effects} table opposite, which can be applied to a single creature species or every creature. You can use multiple Skull Island Effects applied to different creatures on the island to create a diverse array of unusual encounters. Multiple Skull Island Effects should not be applied to the same creature.

Applying a Skull Island Effect to a creature will significantly increase its combat potency, and the particulars of how much it does so will depend on the creature's initial stat block. However, we suggest as a rule of thumb to increase any creature's CR by 2 if it is modified in this way.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: If you're worried about balancing a specific creature, there are lots of online tools for calculating a creature's CR. You can enter in the details of the modified creature and re-calculate its CR.

entries.name: Skull Island Effects
entries: These powerful modified creatures are, however, mere inconveniences when compared to the colossal kaiju that have undergone {@b Ultra-Gigantism}. On the next few pages, we've outlined how to apply Ultra-Gigantism to any creature, provided some plot hook ideas for playing around them, and then provided lore for some examples from specific stat blocks:

rows: The creatures have Immunity to Fire damage, gain +1 AC, and their attacks deal an additional {@dice 1d8} Fire damage, or {@dice 1d4} each if they have Multiattack.
The creatures have a lava-like appearance, with glowing red flesh covered in glassy black rock.
The creatures have Resistance to Bludgeoning, Piercing, and Slashing damage, Advantage on Strength saving throws, and a climb speed equal to their speed.
The creatures are highly muscular and have strong forelimbs with fist-like hands.
The creatures have Resistance to all damage, and a +2 bonus to their AC.
The creatures are covered in thick bony, rocky, or sinewy armour that protects them from most harm.

The creatures have Immunity to Acid damage, increase the range of their ranged attacks by 10 ft., their melee attacks increase their reach by 5 ft., and their attacks deal an additional {@dice 1d8} Acid damage, or {@dice 1d4} each if they have Multiattack.
The creatures are extremely vividly coloured, with contrasting spots and stripes. Lethal toxins drip from their claws and maws.

The creatures are indistinguishable from plant life. They have Expertise in Stealth and are completely invisible if motionless in a plant-filled environment. Additionally, critical hits against them are resolved as though they were normal hits.
The creatures are covered in integument that looks like leaves and bark, with broad brightly-coloured crests that look like flowers.

The creatures have Immunity to Poison damage and a creature hit by any of their attacks must succeed on a Constitution saving throw with a DC equal to 8 + their CR, or be {@condition poisoned|XPHB|Poisoned} for 24 hours.
The creatures are covered in bulbous, pus-filled, cysts all over their hides. Their eyes are cloudy and milky in colour.

The creatures increase their speed by 10 ft., gain a +10 bonus to both {@skill Perception} checks and passive Perception, and they generally hunt at night. If they were herbivorous, they become omnivorous. Their attacks deal an additional {@dice 1d6} Piercing damage, or {@dice 1d4} each if they have Multiattack.
The creatures have a sleek, dark, and lean appearance, with large sensory organs on their heads and a twitchy disposition.

When an attacker hits one of the creatures with a melee attack, that attacker takes {@dice 1d6} Slashing damage. The creatures' attacks deal an additional {@dice 2d8} Slashing damage, or {@dice 2d4} each if they have Multiattack.
The creatures are bristling with blade-like protrusions, either in the form of osteoderms, or razor-edged hard feathers.

The creatures have Immunity to Slashing, Piercing, Fire, Cold, Lightning, Poison, Radiant, and Necrotic damage, but Vulnerability to Acid, Bludgeoning, and Thunder damage. Force and Psychic damage affect them normally.
The creatures are partially translucent and glass-like, with pulsing internal organs surrounded by shimmering magical energies.

Whenever the creature is first encountered or inflicts damage to a humanoid (including player characters), the damaged humanoid must make a {@dc 8} + the creature's CR Charisma saving throw or be {@condition frightened|XPHB|Frightened} of it for 1 minute. The humanoid can repeat this save at the end of each of their turns.
The creatures are terrifying in appearance, with torn scales, exposed flesh, and gruesome disfigurements.

entries.name: Ultra-gigantism
entries: A handful of specific creatures on Skull Island are regional demi-gods. When creating a creature with Ultra-Gigantism from an existing stat block, apply the following effects to their stat block:

items: Increase the creature's size (usually by two categories, to a maximum of Colossal and a minimum of Huge).
Increase the creature's Hit Points by 600.
Increase the creature's AC by 10.
Increase the creature's passive Perception by 10.
The creature gains Immunity to Bludgeoning, Piercing, and Slashing damage (and up to one other damage type that is appropriate).
Change the creature's CR to 30 (with 155,000 XP).
The creature's PB becomes +19.

entries: Ensure that you adjust any existing skill bonuses, saving throw bonuses, DC saves, and to hit attack modifiers accordingly (if you're unsure what the new number should be, simply increase them by 19 minus the creature's previous PB).

items: The creature gains the following Traits:

entries.name: Ultra-Gigantism
entries: The creature cannot be killed by any means other than an attack or ability from another creature with Ultra-Gigantism. If it is reduced to 0 Hit Points or otherwise defeated by any other means, it instead flees to its home to recover over 24 hours.
The creature can optionally speak, understand languages, and problem solve as though its Intelligence score was 10.

entries.name: Legendary Resistance (5/Day)
entries: If the creature fails a saving throw, it can choose to succeed instead.

items: The creature gains the following Actions:

entries.name: Multiattack
entries: When this creature chooses the Attack action, it may make three attacks of any combination with its Ultra Strike or Ultra Cleave.
{@b Ultra Strike}: Melee Weapon Attack: +24 to hit, reach 15 ft., one target. Hit: 54 ({@dice 8d10 + 10}) Force damage.

entries.name: Ultra Cleave
entries: Each creature within a 30 ft. cone in front of the Ultra-Gigantism creature must make a {@dc 32} Dexterity saving throw, taking 32 ({@dice 4d10 + 10}) Force damage on a failed save, or half as much damage on a successful save.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: We recommend re-flavouring the names and damage types of these attacks to fit the theme of the creature. You may also choose to remove any other attacks or actions if they are no longer relevant.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: Building creatures from scratch in DnD is quite complex, with specific calculations for Hit Points, skill check bonuses, saving throws, etc. based on the creature's ability scores, and Proficiency bonus (which is in turn a result of its CR). Rather than providing a step-by-step guide on how to do that, we've created this relatively simple system of additions to a stat block that allows you to re-design any creature to be a kaiju. That said, there may be some niche instances where these changes still allow players to easily overcome the creature. In those cases, we suggest that you use your own judgement on how to best address the situation, or rule that the players fail due to an unknown interfering attribute of the creature. In the same vein, some aspects of the Ultra-Gigantism creature may be overly powerful if the base creature already had powerful related abilities. In these cases, we again suggest that you use your own judgement to weaken the creature appropriately.

Creatures with Ultra-Gigantism are more like {@b demi-god manifestations of concepts}, rather than actual creatures. They encapsulate themes like violence, honour, hunger, human hubris in light of the power of nature, etc. The intended use for this ruleset is not for the players to directly fight the Ultra-Gigantism creature, but instead for them to facilitate a battle between two or more creatures modified in this way, or for the Ultra-Gigantism creatures to act as patrons/deities/environmental threats that the players work around.

When running multiple Ultra-Gigantism creatures fighting in a campaign, we suggest that only one should be player-friendly (or at least player-neutral) and the other(s) should be hostile - actively attacking the local inhabitants and chasing players (but rarely getting the opportunity to attack players directly). Alternatively, the players might be charged with incapacitating an Ultra-Gigantism creature and capturing it, only to find that it cannot be contained and breaks free (aka, the original {@i King Kong} storyline). The rules outlined above mean that players will typically have to enlist the help of another Ultra-Gigantism creature to subdue/slay their target.

Running creatures with Ultra-Gigantism does come with challenges and risks. Players invariably think that their characters can ultimately tackle and deal with any monster, so communicating to them in no uncertain terms that they cannot do that against this creature is a necessity. In the best cases, this stimulates out-of-the-box thinking and a less direct combat approach to those encounters. In the worst cases, you have to constantly tiptoe around TPKs. Consider using phrases like "{@i this creature is utterly beyond your capabilities}" or "{@i no matter how you look at it, this creature cannot be killed by you}" to clearly communicate your intent to your players.

Below, we've also included a list of encounter ideas to assist in this process, allowing you to guide the players through non-direct combat story lines. You could use one or more of these in the same campaign, picking or rolling for a result from the table below:

rows: Players must lure an Ultra-Gigantism creature into a confined area (i.e. a canyon or lagoon).
Players need to flee from an Ultra-Gigantism creature that is directly hunting them into a series of small caves or passages that it cannot enter.
Players need to initiate a fight between two Ultra-Gigantism creatures.
Players need to befriend an Ultra-Gigantism creature by feeding it, healing it, or providing an offering.
Players need to appease a cult that worships an Ultra-Gigantism creature as their god.
Players need to retrieve an object from deep within an Ultra-Gigantism creature's nest/lair.
Players need to navigate an environment with a patrolling Ultra-Gigantism creature, outmanoeuvring it where possible.
Players need to trick an Ultra-Gigantism creature into thinking that another is encroaching on its territory.
Players need to help overthrow an Ultra-Gigantism creature, to be replaced by another.
Players need to protect a city from an attack by an Ultra-Gigantism creature.

items: Top Left: Allosaurus foot.

entries: Right: Struthiomimus foot Bottom Left: Centrosaurus (formerly Monoclonius) foot.

entries.name: Examples of Ultra-gigantism Creatures
entries: We have designed several bespoke Ultra-Gigantism creatures below. These can be used directly in your campaigns, or act as points of inspiration to draw from for your own designs. Each is based on a specific creature's stat block, most of which are in this book (except for Ancient {@i Tyrannosaurus} ({@b page 195 in DDDD}) and the official Mammoth stat block). Additionally, {@b each of these has been fleshed out with fantasy lore to take on the role of demigods and as a patron for an Ancient Beast Warlock character (page 403),} providing a unique flavoured benefit for doing so.

entries.name: Mammugore
Alignment
entries: Chaotic Good Mammugore is a gigantic frozen mammoth carcass, encased in an enormous cubic block of ice. Only its icicle-covered tusks and enormous feet protrude from this block. The only signs of life are two glowing blue eyes within the ice and a steady, slow shuffle of its feet. The icy block itself radiates cold energy and steams constantly while exposed to the sun. It thunders titanically, albeit very slowly, across the landscape, as though it were a living mountain of ice.

Mammugore is an ill-tempered being, full of rage and quick to anger. It persists within the material plane, patrolling arctic deserts and frozen tundra in a never-ending battle to prevent the loss of those habitats. It is the embodiment of the planet's battle against humanoid-caused climate change, fighting both spiritually and physically to undo the damage created by humanoids. Wherever it travels, great blizzards follow in its wake, ensuring that the climate remains cold in that region for weeks afterwards.

Small humanoid settlements in these regions that Mammugore comes across are usually spared the worst of its anger and the freezing conditions that follow it, although it may become enraged if sources of heat, like campfires, aren't doused before its arrival. As such, most communities can simply wrap up warm and shelter as Mammugore passes by. However, pollution-heavy cities and careless expansion can result in months of howling frozen winds and heavy snowfall, or even outright attack from Mammugore.

Mammugore was once a normal woolly mammoth and was transformed over generations. Its original mammoth form died atop a glacier, becoming encased in a tomb of ice, freezing it, body and soul. While trapped, ongoing climate change caused the extinction of almost all animals it knew. Dozens of species died out and its soul watched in horror as its world morphed into an unfamiliar scorching habitat. As the climate warmed, its glacial prison shrank slowly. Hundreds of years later, the glacier's retreat finally reached the Mammoth carcass, releasing it. Centuries of built-up rage explosively transformed the carcass into Mammugore as it was freed, unleashing vengeance and pushing back the tide of climatic change.

If playing Mammugore as an Ultra-Gigantism creature, use the official Mammoth stat block as a base, then apply the Ultra-Gigantism rules. Its Ultra Strike and Ultra Cleave deal Cold damage and are called "Goring Strike" and "Goring Cleave" respectively.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: As an example of how to apply these changes to a creature's stat block, we've provided Mammugore's stat block as an adaptation of the official Mammoth stat block (page 365 in the 5.5e Monster Manual).

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: For each patron, we have provided two specific boons that give both mechanical and visual changes that you can apply to your Ancient Beast Warlock. We recommend that you ask your DM if they are happy for you to include these additional abilities.

entries.name: Mammugore as a Patron
entries: Mammugore is a being of rage, a manifestation of one aspect of nature's wrath. As such it will frequently grant power to mortals whose goals align with its thirst for vengeance against those who it perceives as atmospheric polluters, turning them into Ancient Beast Warlocks. Although Mammugore doesn't particularly care for its warlocks' wellbeing, it will support them however it can, to help further its own goals.
Specific boon: In addition to any other warlock boons, Mammugore grants you the following abilities:

entries.name: Fury of the Arctic (optional)
entries: When you are hit with an attack or fail a saving throw, you may expend a Warlock spell slot to give yourself Resistance to Cold damage until the end of the turn. You may use this ability once, then require a Short Rest before you may use it again. From level 6 onwards you may use this ability twice, then require a Short Rest before you regain all expent uses.

entries.name: Woolly Visage (optional)
entries: When you make an attack or cast a spell, you may momentarily take on the visage of a woolly beast. If you do, your body becomes covered in coarse fur, giving you the appearance of an arctic-adapted animal. This effect lasts for only 3 to 4 seconds before fading.

entries.name: Moutougezi
Alignment
entries: Chaotic Neutral Moutougezi is a shapeshifting demi-god that usually appears as a huge {@i Yi} with some attributes of other urban animals. They have racoon-like black markings across their eyes, mottled grey pigeon-like feathers on the body, and their long tail feathers are bushier than a normal {@i Yi} and coloured orange and white, similar to that of a fox.

Moutougezi is an ancient being, literally as old as civilisation itself. They take on many forms but in life they were a wild {@i Yi}, a small bat-winged dinosaur scurrying through the trees. When the very first ancient humanoids built the first simple encampments, Moutougezi was there to pick at the scraps and shelter in the shadows. In that period of worldly change, the gods watched their new humanoid creations with anticipation and Moutougezi's ingenuity in thriving within the settlement, along with their gift in providing intrigue and mischief for the humanoids, garnered the favour of several of these gods. Their collective blessing transformed Moutougezi from a simple animal into an intelligent, shapeshifting demi-god representation of this adaptable survivalist niche.

Industrialisation has an undeniable impact on the natural world, one of destruction and death. For many species, the loss of their natural habitats and disruption of their food chains has but one end: extinction. Yet, in this turmoil, there are those whose adaptability allows them to thrive, seeking out the bountiful resources a city can provide and living on the fringes of humanoid societies. In the real world, pigeons, foxes, rats, cockroaches, and many other opportunistic species coexist in our urban areas, albeit not always in a manner to our liking. Similar creatures capitalise on humanoid waste to thrive in Moutougezi's world and they are watched over by Moutougezi, the demigod of scavenging, opportunism, and co-survival with humanoids.

Moutougezi spends most of the time exploring the outer planes but also visits cities on the material plane at night. They will transform into an animal like a fox or cockroach to explore the city, looking for interesting trinkets or objects to take back with them. Occasionally, they will sneak into people's homes and scare them by suddenly transforming back into their true form. They delight in the panic such appearances cause and may spend many nights in one city until word of their presence spreads far and wide.

If playing Moutougezi as an Ultra-Gigantism creature, use the {@i Yi} ({@b page 332}) stat block as a base, then apply the Ultra-Gigantism rules. Its Ultra Strike and Ultra Cleave deal Poison damage and are called "Scavenger Strike" and "Scavenger Cleave" respectively.

entries.name: Moutougezi as a Patron
entries: Moutougezi's affections go beyond just urban animals, extending to humanoid underdogs and tricksters who thrive through cunning, rather than strength or knowledge. They will sometimes reach out to such individuals, to form a pact for those humanoids to become Ancient Beast Warlocks. Unlike most patrons, Moutougezi asks very little of its Warlocks; merely that they continue living by their own cunning and offer an interesting trinket from their adventures once in a while. Unfortunately, Moutougezi bores easily, and it is inevitable that they will eventually tire of their Warlock. When this happens, they usually wait until the most chaotic moment to strip the Warlock of their boons, giving Moutougezi one last moment of entertainment.
Specific boon: In addition to any other Warlock boons, Moutougezi grants you the following abilities:

entries.name: Hiding in Plain Sight (optional)
entries: You may cast the spell Disguise Self once without using a spell slot, then require a Short Rest before you may use it again. From level 6 onwards you may cast it twice without using a spell slot, then require a Short Rest before you regain all expent uses.

entries.name: Shifting Trickster (optional)
entries: When you make an attack or cast a spell, you may momentarily take on the superficial attributes of a local urban beast. This could be the chitinous antennae of a cockroach, the protruding incisors of a rat, or the flicking tail of a fox. This effect lasts for only 3 to 4 seconds before fading.

entries.name: Greathorn, the Indomitable
Alignment
entries: Lawful Good Greathorn, the Indomitable is an enormous gold-plated {@i Triceratops}. Its colossal body stands clad in shining metal and this form is a testimony to its unbreakable will. Its head is like a great helm, with dark eye sockets pierced by a noble light. Above its brow and nose are three blade-like horns. Its tough hide is replaced by thick overlapping sheets of golden armour. Greathorn, the Indomitable stands firm as a proud metallic behemoth.

Greathorn, the Indomitable is a stoic creature in both behaviour and name. It persists within the material plane and can be found either wandering great plains searching for those in need, or standing motionless atop a large cliff or in a wide clearing. Its presence often attracts humanoids, who may worship its motionless form as a great idol. It may remain still, ever watching, for decades and it is not unheard of for cities to be constructed around it. Over those years, those cities' citizens may mistake Greathorn, the Indomitable as some national monument, only realising that it is a living creature when it decides to move or intervenes to help defend the city.

Greathorn, the Indomitable is often seen as a manifestation of honour. Regardless of whether that is true, its actions are almost always honourable in nature. It favours protecting those in need and, when Greathorn, the Indomitable is not remaining motionless, it will actively seek out those in need, defending innocents wherever it can. In most small-scale cases, it will guide its followers to assist those in need, rather than acting itself. Only during large-scale conflicts does Greathorn, the Indomitable join the fray. Consequently, the plains that it inhabits can be very peaceful locations, as malicious invaders or raiders are quickly routed by the titanic creature.

Where Greathorn, the Indomitable originated from is ultimately unknown. Its mighty armoured form suggests that it was actively created, perhaps forged by the gods themselves. Unsurprisingly, this means many stories have arisen speculating as to its origins. The most widespread of these stories is that Greathorn, the Indomitable was once a mundane {@i Triceratops}, living as a powerful bull that always chose to intervene when its weaker kin were set upon. Perhaps some long-dead primal god witnessed the bravery and honour enacted by that {@i Triceratops} in its final moments and saw fit to reforge the beast into a demi-god. Or perhaps not. Ultimately, most in its territory care little for where Greathorn, the Indomitable comes from and are simply grateful to be under its protection.

If playing Greathorn, the Indomitable as an Ultra-Gigantism creature, use the {@i Triceratops} ({@b page 324}) stat block as a base, then apply the Ultra-Gigantism rules. Its Ultra Strike and Ultra Cleave deal Radiant damage and are called "Greathorn Strike" and "Greathorn Cleave" respectively.

entries.name: Greathorn, the Indomitable As a Patron
entries: Greathorn, the Indomitable will sometimes choose mortals that it deems worthy to receive its boons. Those lucky few become Ancient Beast Warlocks under Greathorn, the Indomitable and are charged with upholding peace and honour at all times. While Greathorn, the Indomitable is merciful, it will not tolerate its Warlocks committing acts that harm innocents, and will just as quickly strip away their boons.
Specific boon: In addition to any other Warlock boons, Greathorn, the Indomitable grants you the following abilities:

entries.name: Frill Shield (optional)
entries: If an ally within 5 ft. of you is hit by an attack, you may expend a Warlock spell slot to increase their AC by 2 until the end of the turn, potentially causing the attack to miss. You may do this once, then require a Short Rest before you can do so again. From level 6 onwards you may use this ability twice, then require a Short Rest before you regain all expent uses.

entries.name: Golden Form (optional)
entries: When you are struck by an attack, you may momentarily take on the visage of Greathorn, the Indomitable. If you do, your body becomes covered in golden metallic plates and jutting brass spikes, giving you the appearance of your patron. This effect lasts for only 3 to 4 seconds before fading.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: Kyae-no-Limos, The Blue Death's Gaping Maw (page opposite) ability is intentionally the most powerful of the extra abilities presented here. This is because of the drawback of Kyae-no-Limos, The Blue Death as a patron. The need to satisfy her cravings for slaughter can cause sticky roleplaying situations.

entries.name: Kyae-no-limos, the Blue Death
Alignment
entries: Chaotic Evil Kyae-no-Limos, The Blue Death is an enormous grey-blue {@i Tyrannosaurus} that has been twisted into a monstrous form. Her teeth have grown into protruding fangs that line a raw jaw with tattered skin. Her head is adorned by thick slabs of bone armour and her body has become huge and bloated. On her underbelly are dozens of painful, permanently weeping wounds that forever stain her skin with blood.

Kyae-no-Limos, The Blue Death was once a mundane {@i Tyrannosaurus}, although she stood out from her kin by reaching a size that no other could. She was the largest tyrannosaur in history and could only achieve this size through the excessive consumption of flesh. The bigger she became, the more her appetite grew. Despite being a masterful hunter, her great bulk forced her to seek larger prey and venture for years in search of more substantial food. Eventually, she found herself hunting the greatest prey of all, the mighty dragons. Their magical flesh was intoxicating and she soon fed on nothing else. However, the essence inherent in such beings tends to linger and may change those it resides within. Before long, she was warped into a grotesque creature whose hunger could no longer be satiated and whose lust for brutality was never-ending.

Through this process, Kyae-no-Limos, The Blue Death was born as a being of perpetual greed and hunger. She persists only to satisfy the endless void in her stomach and is a slave to her base instincts. She wants only to chase prey and then feel its life ebb in her teeth. Becoming a creature of such power and single-minded carnage does not go unnoticed. After decades of failed attempts to slay her, one brave Sauropan cleric sacrificed himself to shift the beast to the Lower Planes in a ritual banishment, trapping Kyae-no-Limos, The Blue Death within the abyss. Furious, she turned her wrath upon the demons and fiends that inhabit that realm, but their infernal nature prevented her from feeling the sensations she craved. Thus she shifted her attention to finding a way to breach the boundaries of reality that contain her.

The primary way in which Kyae-no-Limos, The Blue Death tries to escape the confines of the abyss is by forming pacts with those on the material plane. She whispers to depraved mortals with promises of satisfying their violent impulses, or tempts the greedy with power. How she snares them matters little, as the terms of the bond is always the same: Live your life as you see fit but once a week, you must commit a brutal act of bloodshed and consume the flesh of your slain prey. Fail to meet these terms, and your body and soul are forfeit, becoming food for her. Kyae-no-Limos, The Blue Death consumes the souls of those slain in this profane ritual and, on rare occasions, this grants her the power to temporarily escape her prison, returning to the material plane to gorge on the world again.

If playing Kyae-no-Limos, The Blue Death as an Ultra-Gigantism creature, use the Ancient {@i Tyrannosaurus} ({@b page 195 in DDDD}) stat block as a base, then apply the Ultra-Gigantism rules. Her Ultra Strike and Ultra Cleave deal Psychic or Piercing damage (your choice) and are called "Gorging Strike" and "Gorging Cleave" respectively.

entries.name: Kyae-no-limos, the Blue Death As a Patron
entries: Kyae-no-Limos, The Blue Death revels in carnage and destruction. She hungers for slaughter and little else. Those who pledge themselves to Kyae-no-Limos, The Blue Death become Ancient Beast Warlocks and are routinely goaded into taking the most violent path possible, although this does not mean that their actions need be evil. Nevertheless, Kyae-no-Limos, The Blue Death's Warlocks must routinely engage in violence, or risk being devoured themselves.
Specific boon: In addition to any other Warlock boons, Kyae-no-Limos, The Blue Death grants you the following abilities:

entries.name: Gaping Maw (optional)
entries: Calling on the spirit of Kyae-no-Limos, The Blue Death, a visage of its horrific maw covers your face. You may replace an Unarmed Strike attack you make with a Gaping Maw attack. When you hit with this attack, the strike deals {@dice 1d10} + your Charisma modifier Piercing damage, instead of the normal Bludgeoning damage for an Unarmed Strike. You may use this attack once, then require a Short Rest before you may use it again.
From level 6 onwards, if you reduce an enemy to 0 Hit Points with this attack, you regain an expended Warlock spell slot.

entries.name: Into the Jaws of Death (optional)
entries: When using Gaping Maw, a spectral visage of a {@i Tyrannosaurus} head will appear around your own, giving you the appearance of Kyae-no-Limos, The Blue Death as you attack with a vicious bite. This effect lasts for only 3 to 4 seconds before fading.

entries.name: Nemeg'o'tsk-ya
Alignment
entries: Lawful Evil The ghostly death-demigod Nemeg'o'tsk-ya is an enormous entity that drifts between the realms of the living and the dead. It appears as a jet-black translucent inky cloud-like {@i Therizinosaurus}, with huge corporeal bone scything talons and a bare-faced bony skull. It drifts effortlessly across the landscape, with its lower portions fading into transparency. As it does so, its colossal claws drag across the ground, carving gorges of jagged earth.

Nemeg'o'tsk-ya rarely intentionally interacts directly with living creatures, save for those who are on the brink of death. It only appears in the material plane in times of great dying, such as extinction events, or during the passing of a notable mortal whom it intends to observe. While in the material plane, it prefers to wander through misty hilly regions. During cataclysmic extinction events, Nemeg'o'tsk-ya will gorge itself on violence, slashing at the landscape, cutting through swathes of mortal beings in the moment before their inevitable demise. In this respect, it does not actively influence events, but rather seizes the opportunity to indulge in consequence-free carnage.

Like many representations of death, Nemeg'o'tsk-ya's primary purpose is to guide souls to different planes of existence. Its intimidating size and ferocity render it suitable only for cataclysmic extinction-level events, where large numbers of souls are suddenly requiring guidance, or when one particularly influential soul of its choosing does. When the latter occurs, it will often watch the passing from a great distance, peering over mountains and down valleys onto the mourning peoples below.

Nemeg'o'tsk-ya originates from the end-Cretaceous extinction event. The first creature to be slain in that event was a lonely {@i Therizinosaurus}, struck by a stray shard of the incoming asteroid and whose soul was the first among the tidal wave of death. Such a dramatic shift from life-to-death birthed this entity, with that {@i Therizinosaurus} acting as the focal point for its manifestation.

If playing Nemeg'o'tsk-ya as an Ultra-Gigantism creature, use the {@i Therizinosaurus} ({@b page 318}) stat block as a base, then apply the Ultra-Gigantism rules. Its Ultra Strike and Ultra Cleave deal Necrotic damage and are called "Reaping Strike" and "Reaping Cleave" respectively.

entries.name: Nemeg'o'tsk-ya as a Patron
entries: On rare occasions, Nemeg'o'tsk-ya will vicariously observe the small-scale lives and deaths of mortals through a specific person. It becomes their patron and they, in turn, become a Ancient Beast Warlock through their connection. Nemeg'o'tsk-ya is largely an uncaring deity, who favours experience and entertainment over other goals. Its demands may vary from person to person and could be to cause as much carnage as possible, to witness near-death experiences, or to assist in the passing of a specific person or beast.
Specific boon: In addition to any other Warlock boons, Nemeg'o'tsk-ya grants you the following abilities:

entries.name: Linked with Death (optional)
entries: You may use the Spare the Dying cantrip once, then require a Short Rest before you may use it again. From level 6 onwards, you may also replace the damage type of melee or ranged attacks with Necrotic damage.

entries.name: Deathly Visage (optional)
entries: When you make an attack or cast a spell, you may momentarily take on a deathly visage. If you do, the flesh on your face becomes translucent, giving your face the appearance of a skull and wafts of black mist drift from the remainder of your body. This effect lasts for 3 to 4 seconds before fading.

entries.name: Rutelunos, the Walking Canopy
Alignment
entries: True Neutral Few corporeal beings reach the colossal size of Rutelunos, The Walking Canopy. This titanic creature towers above even the other Ultra-Gigantism demi-gods described here. Rutelunos, The Walking Canopy is a long-necked sauropod that has the appearance of a living forest. Its body is covered in foliage, transitioning from fresh budding leaves on its head, to spring green growth down its neck, to golden autumnal brown on its body, and bare gnarled wooden spikes on its tail. Beneath this varied canopy, sickly stretched skin covers emaciated bones where mountainous flesh should be.

Rutelunos, The Walking Canopy was once an awakened {@i Dreadnoughtus}, given sapience by a Neanderthal Elder Druid. Throughout its life, it witnessed wildfires burn endless forest over and over, until it eventually starved to death. In its starving, desperate final moments, it pledged its soul to any deity that would prevent this suffering from happening to others. Several gods answered its plea, and their combined powers transformed the animal into Rutelunos, The Walking Canopy, granting it the means to enact this wish itself.

Rutelunos, The Walking Canopy appears in places where forests are destroyed by catastrophic events, and has done so for millennia. Once manifested, it will march across the landscape, crushing anything in its path. With each passing step, saplings sprout at unnatural speeds, until young trees stand in a burgeoning grove within its crater-like footprints. A few days after appearing and traversing the once ruined forest, now renewed, Rutelunos, The Walking Canopy will stop, let out a pained scream, then collapse onto the ground. As its spiritual essence leaves the material plane, its body transforms into dying leaves and twigs, blown away with the gentlest of breezes.

Rutelunos, The Walking Canopy's only goal is to restore forests where they once grew strong. In eons past, it was only seen after fires or natural disasters, rarely interacting with humanoids. However, the march of civilisation has sprawled towns and cities where there were once trees. Rutelunos, The Walking Canopy places no value on such "progress" and it may manifest within settlements where deforestation is too extensive. Once the march begins, it will leave destroyed buildings and broken bodies in its wake. If desperate townsfolk mount a defence, its passive walk will turn into a rage, lashing out with its branched tail and bringing its weight crashing down on its attackers.

If playing Rutelunos, The Walking Canopy as an Ultra-Gigantism creature, use the {@i Dreadnoughtus} ({@b page 213}) stat block as a base, then apply the Ultra-Gigantism rules. Its Ultra Strike and Ultra Cleave deal Thunder or Bludgeoning damage (your choice) and are called "Titanic Tail Strike" and "Titanic Stomp" respectively.

entries.name: Rutelunos, the Walking Canopy As a Patron
entries: People at risk of encountering Rutelunos, The Walking Canopy will frequently choose children to raise as potential Warlocks who can then attempt to bond with Rutelunos, The Walking Canopy in the hopes of protecting their homes. Rutelunos, The Walking Canopy may agree to become their patron, allowing them to become Ancient Beast Warlocks, and grant a settlement protection if certain conditions are met. These can vary from restoring lost woods to punishing those who fell trees for lumber. Faithful Warlocks may be rewarded with fertile land, whereas pact breakers draw titanic ire.
Specific boon: In addition to any other Warlock boons, Rutelunos, The Walking Canopy grants you the following abilities:

entries.name: Nature's Thorns (optional)
entries: You may cast the Entangle spell once without using a spell slot, then require a Short Rest before you may use it again. From level 6 onwards, you may also replace the damage type of melee or ranged attacks with Piercing or Poison damage.

entries.name: Soul of the Forest (optional)
entries: When you make an attack or cast a spell, you may choose to briefly alter your appearance. Your skin starts to harden, and any hair or feathers on your body momentarily transform into leaves. If you have been injured, instead of blood your wounds leak golden sap. This effect lasts for only 3 to 4 seconds before fading.

entries.name: Concluding Remarks
entries: The rules and creatures outlined above allow you to introduce prehistoric elements into your games in a truly fantastical way. Now let's take a look at some more grounded and realistic ways you can introduce prehistoric elements into your games, specifically palaeontology itself and fossil excavating. In the next section, we introduce a new system for finding, extracting, and displaying fossils in your games.

data.name: Fossil Hunting, Museums, and Burglaries
entries: In my many years, I have never taken the plunge to establish and run my own museum. Although I have desired to do so for over a century, the prospect of collecting, setting up, managing, and defending the artefacts on display renders the idea unpalatable. Thankfully, many adventuring parties take up these responsibilities, and I can simply enjoy their collections in exchange for a few gold coins. A price well worth it in my mind.

Adventurers travel the world, raid tombs, slay great monsters, and plunder dragon's hoards. Throughout this process, they acquire artefacts, objects of historical importance, and mighty trophies. Some players choose to sell these items for quick coin where, let's face it, they probably end up in the wrong hands. Others hoard their collection in their own dwellings or storage as a personal private stash of their accomplishments.

Many commonfolk and noblefolk alike see this behaviour as selfish. They long to learn of the deeds of local heroes and understand more about their region's history. The best means for player characters to fulfil this desire in our opinion, while also making a bit of coin, is to run their own museum. Below, we have designed several systems that allow players to gather fossils, artefacts, and trophies, then display them in their own museum and fend off burglars. These systems are quite complex, but allow for an in-depth museum experience in your campaign.

entries.name: Fossil Hunting
entries: Although fieldwork is not my forte, there remains a certain charm to dirtying one's own hands in the pursuit of specimens.

It is no surprise then, that fossil hunting is a common practice among adventuring parties that can spare the time and carrying capacity to do so. Those that do are often rewarded with valuable specimens, as few others can routinely venture into the wilds to fossil hunt, ensuring that most sites remain unpicked.

entries.name: Finding Fossils
entries: Investigation, Nature, or Perception. See the table opposite for details on the passive Perception and search DCs.

Player Characters and NPCs with the Geologist ({@b page 288 in DDDD}), Palaeontologist ({@b page 290 in DDDD}), or Field Guide ({@b page 414}) backgrounds automatically spot Fossiliferous Strata when they come within 30 ft. of it.

Once spotted, the size of the strata must then be determined. The DM may choose from or roll on the table opposite to determine the strata's size and how many times it can be harvested. Once harvested this number of times, it is then depleted until further rock is eroded, usually weeks or months later. Careless digging destroys fossils, so we recommend that players who try to forcibly expose more fossils only find broken fragments.

Any player characters or accompanying humanoid NPCs can attempt to harvest precious fossils or minerals from the Fossiliferous Strata using the described actions on the following page. Fossils and minerals can be found in the environment in rock layers called {@b Fossiliferous Strata}. These are patches of exposed rock that are typically 10x15 ft. in size (although they can be any size you wish) on a vertical cliff face or exposed ground. They come in three categories: {@b Poor, Moderate, and Exceptional}. The quality and value of fossils found in these different categories varies, and we recommend assigning them to low-level, mid-level, and high-level parties respectively. How difficult each strata type is to spot also differs, and players can either detect them through their passive Perception, or search for them using

entries.name: A Brief Summary of This System

items: Players passively spot or search for Fossiliferous Strata.
The DM determines the quality and quantity of fossils that can be harvested.
Players can spend 2 hours extracting a fossil or mineral with appropriate tools.
They perform {@dc 10} {@skill Sleight of Hand} or {@skill Nature} checks for the extraction.
The players or DM rolls for which fossil or mineral has been found from the appropriate table.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: The quality of fossiliferous strata that you may want your party to find will depend on how much gold value you're willing to potentially let them discover and subsequently earn in their museum. Given that there are several rounds of checks, and the potential for their fossils to be stolen later, we suggest being generous with this.

entries.name: Levels
entries: Poor 14 {@dc 10} Low (levels 1-6)
Moderate 16 {@dc 14} Mid (levels 7-14)
Exceptional 20 {@dc 18} High (levels 15-20)

entries.name: Recommended for Party Levels
entries: Small Exposure {@dice 1d4 + 1} Low (levels 1-6)
Medium Exposure {@dice 2d4 + 2} Mid (levels 7-14)
Large Exposure {@dice 3d6 + 4} High (levels 15-20)
Motherlode {@dice 4d8 + 8} Very High (18-20)

entries.name: Extracting Fossils
entries: If equipped with {@b appropriate equipment} (e.g. a hammer and chisel, a shovel, a pickaxe, Stonemason's tools, Smith's tools, or other tools at the DM's discretion), the player character/ NPC may spend {@b 2 hours} searching for and extracting a fossil or mineral from the strata. The harvesting player character/ NPC makes either a {@b Sleight of Hand} or {@b Nature check} (their choice) with the results described in the table to the right. Other player characters/NPCs can perform the Help action to assist them, granting them Advantage on the check, so long as they are not busy extracting their own fossil/mineral.
Player Characters and NPCs with the Curator ({@b page 410}) or Palaeontologist ({@b page 290 in DDDD}) background also make this roll at advantage.

entries.name: Extraction Outcome
entries: Critical Failure The fossil/mineral has been destroyed during extraction.
The fossil/mineral has been damaged heavily during extraction and is worth half its original value.
9 or lower 10 or higher The fossil/mineral has been extracted with minimal damage.
Critical Success The fossil/mineral has been extracted in a perfect manner, increasing its value by 50%

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: Make sure you let your players know if you're including this system beforehand so that they can prepare their equipment accordingly.

entries.name: Identifying Fossils
entries: Once a fossil has been successfully extracted, it can be immediately identified. The controlling player or DM (DM's choice) then rolls a {@dice d100} on the corresponding Fossiliferous Strata table below to determine what has been found. Alternatively, the DM may select a specific result from the appropriate table.

Each table outlines 20 possible finds with their corresponding rarities, market value, weight, and display size. Vertebrate fossils can be the DM's choice of whatever animal they think is appropriate. It could be a dinosaur like {@i Velociraptor} ({@b page 182 in DDDD}), a pterosaur like {@i Istiodactylus} ({@b page 154}), a marine reptile like {@i Eretmorhipis} ({@b page 220}), or even a mammal like {@i Smilodon} ({@b page 105}).

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: The display size corresponds to the space required in your museum to display the fossil, as discussed later. The fossils themselves do not have a size, as they may have been extracted in several parts, with their weight representing the total weight of all of the parts.
{@b poor Quality strata (passive perCeption 14, aCtive searCh dC 10)}

entries.name: Recommended for Low-level Parties (levels 1-6)
entries: {@b moderate Quality strata (passive perCeption 16, aCtive searCh dC 14)}
{@b exCeptional Quality strata (passive perCeption 20, aCtive searCh dC 18)}

entries.name: A Brief Summary of This System

items: The table on the next page provides a detailed list of artefacts that can be found in dungeons/ crypts/tombs.
Player characters and NPCs can search for artefacts over 2 hours.
They may do this twice per location.
The DM then rolls on a table to see what they have found.
They can apply a -7, -3, 0, or +3 modifier to the roll.
These objects can be displayed in museums for their cultural and historical significance.

entries: When exploring a dungeon, crypt, tomb, or other suitable locations that may house ancient artefacts (or even other museums!), player characters and NPCs can commit to searching for artefacts of cultural or historic importance to add to their collection.

If they spend {@b at least 2 hours searching}, each character may roll on the table on the next page, applying a -7, -3, 0, or +3 modifier at the DM's discretion as described, or the DM can select a result for them. Each player character can do this twice and any humanoid NPC can do it once, then the location has been exhausted of artefacts.
These artefacts are in addition to any other loot that would normally be available to players.

entries.name: Historic Artefacts
entries: {@b (modiFiers: starter party -7, low-level party -3, medium-level party 0, high-level party +3).}

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: We wanted to keep this roll to a single D20 table so there are extremes in value and the modifiers allow you to adapt it to your needs. Please also note that an average party of four characters will get to roll eight times on this table per dungeon, so this system can result in a significant increase in the party's wealth. If you do not want that, consider always keeping the modifier at -7 or -3.
available on the local black market for their Market Value (at DM's discretion), if players wish to purchase items for their museum.

entries.name: A Brief Summary of This System

items: When players slay a creature, they can recover the creature's body (or parts of it) to display in their museum.
They must be able to transport the carcass.
The creature's CR and several other factors determine its rarity.

entries: Slaying monsters is a staple of most TTRPGs. Some players (most players, in our experience) like to take trophies of their kills - usually a tooth, claw, or horn. However, the possibility of displaying an entire prepared creature skeleton or taxidermy in your own museum as a source of extra income is an exciting prospect. As such, we've provided the following guidance for DM's to consider:

For the purposes of a museum display, the creature's CR and size determine its object rarity and display size. These are outlined further in the tables in the next section on running your museum, but creatures' remains are typically considered to have the rarity outlined below:

entries.name: Rarity
entries: CR 0 to CR 5 Common CR 6 to CR 11 Uncommon CR 12 to CR 16 Rare CR 17 to CR 20 Very Rare CR 21 or higher Legendary There are some factors that may change a creature's remains' rarity. These are:

items: If the creature is not native to the museum's plane of existence and is not frequently found there (i.e.

entries: excluding commonly summoned creatures), its rarity is increased by one stage.

items: If a creature is not native to the museum's time period (i.e. has been transported from another time), its rarity is increased by one stage. Fossil remains are not subject to this modifier.
If the creature is a named unique creature (i.e. a named "boss" creature in the campaign), its rarity is increased by one stage.

entries: In order to prepare a carcass for display in a museum, the following criteria must be met:

items: The creature must leave substantial remains that can be collected (i.e. ghosts, air elementals, etc. aren't suitable).
The remains must be transported to the museum, either intact or cut into several pieces beforehand.

entries: - Players can either transport it themselves, or hire workers to assist them.

items: The museum must have space to house and prepare the carcass (or prepare at an appropriate place nearby).
The trophy's display size is typically one size larger than its actual size, subject to the DM's discretion (see the table below).

entries.name: Display Size
entries: Tiny or Small Small or Medium Medium Large Large Huge Huge Gargantuan Single part of a Large creature Medium Single part of a Huge creature Large Single part of a Gargantuan creature Huge It is important to establish what creatures' remains are appropriate to display in a museum in your world. Displaying humanoids is generally taboo, unless with the individual's permission before their death. Non-humanoid creatures with an intelligence score of 8 or higher are also generally seen as in poor-taste to display (if they are widely regarded as sapient). Intelligent creatures (such as dragons) may be an exception to this, if they weren't well-liked individuals, or if they willingly donated their remains.

If a museum is displaying remains that are taboo or in poor taste, players can expect protests at their museums and, ultimately, potentially riots that damage the building. DMs can consider these for plot points to tackle the ethics of museum displays in their campaigns.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: We believe that it is important that all of your players are having fun and are comfortable at the table. We recommend that you check with your players about what remains they might be comfortable/ uncomfortable with being displayed in a museum before implementing this system.

entries.name: Running a Museum
entries: Running a museum is an exciting prospect for players, but comes with a variety of challenges. Adding a museum system comes with a fair amount of extra bookkeeping for the DM and/or players. Below, we've provided two means to implement running a museum into your campaign. These are a facility compatible with the 5.5e Bastion system, and a standalone museum system. Of these two, we recommend using the 5.5e Bastion system, as it allows each player to contribute to the museum, while also providing other content for those who don't wish to run a museum.

Both of these systems allow players to generate significant income at the risk of having their artefacts and fossils stolen by burglars. DMs that are running economically tight campaigns can control how much money the party can generate by controlling the frequency at which they can acquire artefacts. However, some DMs may wish to cap the amount of profit the players' museum generates, justifying the cap with a local or regional tax or limited foot traffic. If so, we recommend the following weekly caps on profit:

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: If you're using the Bastion compatible system, the maximum revenue generation for a 36 square museum is about 16,000 gp. per week (with nothing but Legendary objects on display), so these caps are more for lower levels that get very lucky or if you're using the stand-alone system with no restriction on a player's museum size. While this might sound like a frighteningly large amount of income, keep in mind that it will take the average player party a very long time to build up their collections to that point and that they have the added responsibility of keeping the museum safe/running.
{@b optional Cap on proFit generation per week From museums, Based on party level.}
Iguanodon fossil as an example of a complete vertebrate fossil.

entries.name: Bastion Compatible Facility: Natural History Museum
A Brief Summary of This System

items: Players set up a Natural History Museum as a bastion room.
Museum Tours generate passive income per week, calculated via each display's rarity and size.
The DM can cap the revenue generated by the Museum Tours per week.
They can issue the Craft order to curate up to three objects, adding them to the facility.
They can issue the Trade order to sell off objects for 10% more than its normal price.
They can upgrade the security of the facility to detect and deter burglaries.
At the end of each week, the DM rolls in secret to see if a burglary will occur next week.

entries: To add an appropriate museum that you can house your fossils and artefacts in, use the {@b Natural History Museum} facility as described below.

entries.name: Natural History Museum
entries: {@b {@i Level 5 Facility}}

entries.name: Prerequisite
entries: at least one artefact, fossil, or trophy that can be displayed.

A Natural History Museum is a space that allows adventurers to curate and display their finds, as well share with their community the history of their region for a passive income. Multiple players can combine their Natural History Museum spaces to allow for larger, more complex, displays.

entries.name: Museum Tours
entries: Pilgrims, scholars, nobles, and commonfolk alike love to visit a Natural History Museum and their visits generate an income for you. The amount you generate is dependent on footfall, which is in turn dependent on the quality and quantity of objects on display. At the start of each week, your Natural History Museum gains income for each object that was displayed over the previous week, based on its rarity. The size of the display also affects how much gp. it raises each week.

entries.name: Per Week
entries: Common 2 gp.
Uncommon 10 gp.
Rare 50 gp.
Very Rare 150 gp.
Legendary 500 gp.

entries.name: Occupied
entries: Small or Medium 1 1x Large 4 3x Huge 9 6x Gargantuan 16 10x

entries.name: Craft: Curate Artefact, Fossil, or Trophy
entries: When you issue the Craft order to this facility, you may donate {@b up to three} fossils, minerals, artefacts, or trophies that you possess to be curated in your museum, so long as there is space to display them. These will be ready at the start of the next week. Each display in your Natural History Museum must have at least one adjacent 5 ft. square space for people to view the display, and there must be a continuous path between viewing spaces to an entrance/exit. All of the listed fossils, minerals, and artefacts have an associated display size and a trophy carcass' display sizes are usually one size bigger than their actual size (unless displaying a single body part). Below is a table that outlines the sizes of your displays, their space requirements, and the income multiplier that is applied to that object's.gp earned each week.

entries.name: Examples of Natural History Museum Display Layouts
entries: {@i These images show examples of how your natural history museum can be laid out if you want to use confined battlemaps. Alternatively, you can have the players populate a much larger room that has a limited number of "slots" for each display. These images were created with Dungeon Scrawl, a free online map making tool (https://dungeonscrawl.com, license on} {@b {@i page 1}}{@i ). We highly recommend using it to help design your Natural History Museum layouts.}

entries.name: Trade: Auction Artefact or Fossil
entries: When you issue the Trade order to this facility, you may sell one of your artefacts or fossils at an auction. At the start of the next week, the item is sold at 10% more than its normal value. During this time, you still gain the income from that object for being part of your Museum Tour.

entries.name: Enlarging the Facility
entries: You can enlarge your Natural History Museum from 16 squares to 32 squares by spending 2,000 gp. If you do so, the Natural History Museum can house more artefacts and therefore generates more foot traffic.

entries.name: Upgrading the Facility
entries: In addition to enlarging a Natural History Museum, players can spend gold to upgrade its defence against burglary. At the price of 15 gp. per square, an {@b Alarm System} can be permanently installed, but is only active if every square in your Natural History Museum is covered (240 gp. for 16 squares, 540 gp. for 32 squares). If triggered, this will magically alert the party if a burglary is being attempted, regardless of where they are.

Players can also hire additional {@b Guards} at the price of 5 gp. per square, per week (80 gp. per week for 16 squares, 180 gp. per week for 32 squares). These additional guards will deter some burglars (see the burglar stat blocks for more details).

Players can also install {@b Deterrents} at the price of 10 gp. per square, per week (160 gp. per week for 16 squares, 360 gp. per week for 32 squares). These increase the DC of skill checks needed by burglars (explained further on page 63) to steal from the Natural History Museum from 12 to 15.
The upgrades available to a museum are:

entries.name: Effect
entries: {@b Alarm System} 240 gp. (one-off)
540 gp. (one-off)
Alerts party to Burglary when it starts. Discard one of the 1s you roll from your Burglar Dice.
{@b Guards} 80 gp. per week 180 gp. per week Deters some burglars entirely. Discard one of the 1s you roll from your Burglar Dice.
{@b Deterrents} 160 gp. per week 360 gp. per week Burglary skill checks are increased to {@dc 15}. Discard one of the 1s you roll from your Burglar Dice.

entries.name: Weekly Event - Burglary
entries: In addition to any other events, at the end of each week, the DM rolls {@b in secret} to determine if a Burglary will be attempted against the museum. To do this, they roll a die for each object on display using the corresponding Burglary Die based on each object's rarity as outlined in the table here. If any Burglary Die rolls a 1 (after upgrade discards), a Burglary will be attempted (regardless of whether players are present or not). Alternatively, the DM may choose whether a Burglary occurs or not. See the Burglary rules on page 63 for more details.

entries.name: A Brief Summary of This System

items: The DM determines how a museum is set up and how much can be displayed in it.
The players deposit their objects to be displayed from the following week onwards.
The museum has a weekly running cost.
Museum tours generate passive income per week, calculated via each display's rarity and size.
The DM can cap the revenue generated by the museum per week.
At the end of each week, the DM rolls in secret to see if a burglary will occur next week.

entries: If you are not using the 5.5e Bastion rules, we've created an alternative standalone system for running a museum. Unlike the Bastion rules, this system does not provide strict guidance for the area of space available to your players. As such, it is up to the DM to determine what square footage of space is available to the players to set up their museum in, how much that will cost to set up, and how many objects can be displayed in the museum at any given time.

Once the party has purchased/organised the location for their museum (usually a hired space for just a few gp. per week), they can fill it with objects that they have found on their adventures. They can either arrange for these to be couriered (at their own risk!) or deposit them themselves. Once an artefact, fossil, mineral, or trophy has been passed to the museum, it will be prepared and displayed the following week.
Running a museum has an associated cost, revenue generation, and risks. These are determined once per in-game week, at the start of a week.

entries.name: Museum Running Costs
entries: At the start of each week, determine how much the museum costs to run. If the standard running costs cannot be paid,

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: We recommend allowing a maximum of one huge/ gargantuan display, two large displays, and eight small/medium displays. Beyond this, the passive income generated by the museum gets a bit silly.
no revenue is generated this week. If other costs (such as Tour Guides) cannot be paid, then no benefit is provided by them this week (although they can be resumed next week).
