Tour Guides, Guards, and Magical Security can be organised at any time when at least one player character is at the museum (or is in contact with someone who is) and these will be present from the following week onwards.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: Your museum can have a Commoner as staff to take payments, even if no one else is there, and deposit the money earned in a local bank or keep it within a secured safe in the museum. We recommend avoiding the temptation to have that money stolen.

entries.name: Benefit
entries: 10 gp. × number of items on display per week - Standard running costs Tour Guides 20 gp. per week The party may re-roll up to two random income dice.
Alerts party to Burglary when it starts. Discard one of the 1s you roll from your Burglar Dice.
15 gp. × number of items on display per week Alarm System Deters some burglars entirely. Discard one of the 1s you roll from your Burglar Dice.
Guards 10 gp. × number of items on display per week Burglary skill checks are increased to {@dc 15}. Discard one of the 1s you roll from your Burglar Dice.
Deterrents 20 gp. × number of items on display per week

entries.name: Museum Revenue Generation
entries: Your museum generates revenue based on the volume of foot traffic, which is in turn determined by the quality and quantity of objects on display in your museum. It generates a standard income, and a rolled variable income.
The standard income for running a museum is based on the quality, quantity, and size of your displays, determined at the start of each week and received at the end of each week:

entries.name: Per Week
entries: Common 2 gp.
Uncommon 10 gp.
Rare 50 gp.
Very Rare 150 gp.
Legendary 500 gp.

entries.name: Multiplier
entries: Small or Medium 1x Large 3x Huge 6x Gargantuan 10x

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: Remember that objects on display in a museum still have their normal value and can be sold at a later date.
Additionally, the party gains bonus income based on the rarest object on display in the museum. This is summarised in the table below:

entries.name: Revenue
entries: Common {@dice 1d4} gp.
Uncommon {@dice 3d10} gp.
Rare {@dice 4d20} gp.
Very Rare {@dice 2d100} gp.
Legendary {@dice 10d100} gp.

entries.name: Museum Burglary
entries: {@b :} At the start of each week, the DM rolls {@b in secret} to determine if a burglary will be attempted against the museum this week. To do this, they roll a die for each object on display using the corresponding Burglary Die based on its rarity as outlined in the table below. If any Burglary Die rolls a 1 (after any discards), a Burglary will be attempted (regardless of whether players are present or not). Alternatively, the DM may choose whether a Burglary occurs or not. See opposite for more details on how Burglaries work.

entries.name: A Brief Summary of This System

items: Once it has been determined that a Burglary will occur, the DM designs a burglary encounter.
They can use the Petty Robber, Hired Goon, Expert Thief, and/or Criminal Mastermind stat blocks presented here, as well as any others.
If the players are present, they can attempt to fight off or intercept the burglars.
If the players are absent and can't reach the museum within 2 hours, the burglars perform three skill checks to steal from the museum.
Check 1, get in: Intimidation, Persuasion, or Stealth {@dc 12}/15.
Check 2, grab the goods: Acrobatics, Athletics, or Sleight of Hand {@dc 12}/15.
Check 3, make your escape: Athletics, Intimidation, or Stealth {@dc 12}/15.
If all three checks are successful, randomly select an object for each burglar to steal. If only two checks are successful, half (rounded down) of the burglars steal randomly selected objects.

entries: As mentioned above for both museum systems, once a week the DM rolls {@b in secret} to determine whether a burglary will be attempted against the museum. They roll a die for each object on display using the corresponding Burglary Die based on each object's rarity. If any Burglary Die rolls a 1, a burglary will be attempted (regardless of whether players are present or not).

Additionally, each time an object is being couriered to the museum, rather than delivered by a player character, the DM may roll the corresponding Burglary Die for that object to see if it is intercepted by burglars before arriving. To reiterate, the Burglary Dice vs rarity are as follows: Common: {@dice d20}; Uncommon: {@dice d12}; Rare: {@dice d8}; Very Rare: {@dice d6}; Legendary: {@dice d4}.

Alternatively, the DM can simply decide whether/when a Burglary occurs. If you as a DM want a tighter control of their campaign's narrative and/or number of encounters, then we recommend this approach.

The DM can then follow the rules described here to design an encounter using the various burglar stat blocks provided, at a difficulty that is appropriate to the party's level and power, and choose a day or night over the next week in which the burglary attempt will be made.
{@b Once a burglary has been attempted, do not roll any Burglary Dice for the following week (as the museum is considered "too hot" to rob).}

entries.name: Burglary Encounter
entries: To build a Burglary Encounter first determine how many Petty Robbers, Hired Goons, Expert Thieves, Criminal Masterminds, and other NPCs are attempting to steal from the museum. We suggest that the encounter be designed as though it were an easy encounter for the players. Some examples are included below, although these may require re-balancing for your party's power or number of players, and the last one presented for levels 19 & 20 calculates as deadly (although players could likely kill most of the burglars quickly).

items: For Level 1-2 parties: 3 Petty Robbers
For Level 3-4 parties: 3 Petty Robbers and 1 Hired Goon
For Level 5-6 parties: 3 Petty Robbers and 2 Hired Goons
For Level 7-8 parties: 2 Petty Robbers, 1 Hired Goon, and 1 Expert Thief
For Level 9-10 parties: 2 Petty Robbers, 3 Hired Goons, and 1 Expert Thief
For Level 11-12 parties: 4 Petty Robbers, 2 Hired Goons, and 2 Expert Thieves
For Level 13-14 parties: 5 Petty Robbers, 4 Hired Goons, and 1 Criminal Mastermind
For Level 15-16 parties: 5 Petty Robbers, 6 Hired Goons, and 1 Criminal Mastermind
For Level 17-18 parties: 5 Petty Robbers, 6 Hired Goons and 2 Criminal Masterminds
For Level 19-20 parties: 6 Petty Robbers, 8 Hired Goons, and 3 Criminal Masterminds

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: We strongly recommend only using Criminal Masterminds and Expert Thieves if the player characters are able to intercept them, or if you've planned on a side-quest campaign for them to recover their stolen objects. It's not much fun if you put lots of hard work into getting cool stuff, then it just vanishes forever!

If the players are present, they may simply intercept the burglars and engage with them as with any normal combat encounter. If the players are absent (or perhaps just asleep), then {@b they have 2 hours to reach their museum to intercept the burglars}.

If they fail to reach their museum in time, the DM makes a series of three {@b Burglary Skill Checks} using a burglar of their choice and the skill check of their choice. Each skill check can be performed by a different burglar that is present and the skill checks represent the process of stealing from the museum. The standard DC for these skill checks is 12, although deterrents increase these to 15.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: If an object is ultimately stolen by a burglar, players should be given the opportunity later in the campaign to recover it - either via black market trading, or by stealing it back. This can make for an engaging vengeance-filled side quest!

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: If you randomly determine an object that a burglar can't carry, they waste their time trying to figure out how to get away with it and ultimately leave with nothing.

items: {@b Check 1, get in:} Intimidation, Persuasion, or Stealth {@dc 12}/15
{@b Check 2, grab the goods:} Acrobatics, Athletics, or Sleight of Hand {@dc 12}/15
{@b Check 3, make your escape:} Athletics, Intimidation, or Stealth {@dc 12}/15 Once the skill checks are completed, the Burglary is over and the burglars have escaped with their stolen objects.

entries: The next day, the players will then be informed that their museum has been burgled. The stolen objects will usually be available on the local black market a few days after they are stolen. The DM can determine whether they're being sold by the burglars themselves, or if they've exchanged hands several times before becoming available.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: If the first "get in" check fails and guards are present, they can optionally try to raise the alarm and contact the players about the Burglary. Players could provide the guards with a Sending Stone to ensure that they can be easily contacted.
Depending on how many of these skill checks are successful, results in the overall success of the Burglary and helps determine how many, if any, objects are stolen.
One or none of the skill checks are successful. The burglars failed to steal anything and fled.

entries.name: Failure
entries: Two of the skill checks are successful. Randomly select half of the burglars (rounded down). For each of those selected, randomly determine an object on display. The burglar steals that object if they can carry it.

entries.name: Partial Success
entries: All three of the skill checks are successful. For each burglar, randomly determine an object on display. The burglar steals that object if they can carry it.

entries.name: Burglary Npcs
entries: Below, we have provided four NPC stat blocks that can be used in concurrence with other official stat blocks (such as Bandit and Bandit leader) to commit burglaries. These stat blocks are tailor-made specifically for our Burglary system and each of them has unique traits that interact with that system. You can, of course, also use them elsewhere in your campaigns.

entries.name: Petty Robber
entries: Petty Robbers are the most common type of burglar. They differ from bandits in that they don't tend to attack people and are instead opportunistic thieves, preferring to steal from empty buildings or closed stores.

entries.name: Hired Goon
entries: Hired Goons are criminals who will undertake illegal tasks for others in nefarious contracts of employment. They tend to be physically strong individuals who are relatively well-trained, often disgraced former guards or soldiers.
However, they aren't very loyal and can sometimes be persuaded (either through intimidation or with bribes) to abandon their contract.

entries.name: Expert Thief
entries: Expert Thieves are professional criminals who make an excellent living stealing high-value items. They fit into the role of your typical cat-burglar and are extremely difficult for local authorities to catch. Several may be well-known in a region and have a nickname based on their calling card. Those individuals often compete to see who can steal the highest value object.

entries.name: Criminal Mastermind
entries: Criminal Masterminds are bombastic individuals that commit large scale heists for notoriety as much as for the loot. They are invariably iconic in their behaviour and appearance, choosing brightly coloured or themed costumes and taking a criminal alias. They vary greatly in their style and appearance, ranging from brutish hulks, to sleek acrobats, to calculating geniuses.

entries.name: Concluding Remarks
entries: While the systems described above allow you to include palaeontology in your games in its most realistic form (perhaps excluding the Criminal Mastermind!), it does not necessarily allow you to include the living prehistoric creatures themselves. One of the most common methods for doing that is time travel. However, we don't think you can explore time travel without including some discussion of its consequences. In the next section we explore its repercussions in depth and provide some systems that allow you to implement them into your campaigns.

data.name: Time Travel and the Butterfly Effect
entries: The curious tales of Dr Dhrolin's adventures through time during his last sabbatical have caught my attention. I certainly would like to embark on similar expeditions, although I must admit that the thought of tampering with the past leaves me uneasy... I doubt that he took such considerations before trudging around in our history.

In our first book, {@i Dr Dhrolin's Dictionary of Dinosaurs}, we introduced the Chronoficer ({@b page 28 in DDDD}) and some story hooks to help incorporate palaeontology into your campaigns through the medium of time travel. Adding time travel to a campaign world can be exciting, interesting, and potentially problematic, depending on how you approach this genre of storytelling.

In a very simplified summary, there are two ways to approach time travel in a campaign: either the PC and NPC actions in the past change the future (their present), or they don't. The latter of these offers the simplest approach to storytelling, allowing you to take the narrative stance that everything the PCs and NPCs are doing is already cemented in your story's timeline. Doing this greatly simplifies the narrative, freeing DMs to spend their time designing other parts of the campaign but can also drastically remove player agency if the players discover that there aren't chronological consequences for their actions.

The other approach to time travel arguably swings the pendulum too far in the other direction, giving PCs and NPCs the power to potentially overhaul the world with a series of simple actions, depending on how the DM structures cause and effect. This is due to the hypothesised real-life Butterfly Effect, coined by meteorologist Edward Norton Lorenz. {@i A butterfly flapping its wings on one side of the world may cause a tornado on the other side several weeks later}. In slightly less poetic terms, a small change in a deterministic nonlinear system can result in very large changes elsewhere, especially if given ample time. In time travel narratives, killing one small, apparently insignificant, animal could have a cascading effect in the food chain or for that animal's lineage (if it {@i Papilio antimachus (top), Ornithoptera priamu (right), and Ornithoptera victoriae (left)}
was going to reproduce). Over millions of years, this could fundamentally alter an entire ecosystem and subsequently the course of evolution as a whole.

If time travel to the past were possible in real life, it is unclear whether such an effect would actually occur. However, in a roleplaying campaign, we can choose whether it happen and to what extent. If you, as a DM, have the constitution to allow your players the freedom to fundamentally change your world through small actions, we've constructed some guidance in two separate approaches.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: If you're using time travel regularly and your players are using "normal" modern D&D playable species, it might be interesting to have the player characters transform into one of our prehistoric playable species while in the past (while retaining their original species traits) so that they can interact with past peoples without raising concerns.

These provide a framework to track what changes are being caused by the players and how to undo them, along with suggestions for the severity of those changes. We use some key terms to help us describe this guidance: a {@b cause} and an {@b effect}. The first thing to establish is what exactly your causes can be. These causes can then be assigned a label of {@b Major} or {@b Minor}, or a {@b Chrono-consequence Value}, to distinguish the impact they have on the timeline. Lets start by exploring causes and potential effects..

entries.name: A Brief Summary of This System

items: Player interactions with the past may trigger a "cause".
For each cause, either roll on the associated Major/Minor Effect tables or tally a Chrono-consequence Value for the party that increases with each cause.
Apply the changes from the associated Major/ Minor Effects table or apply the cumulative changes from the Chrono-consequence Cumulative Table to your world's future (the party's present).

entries: When determining the effects that are caused by PC and NPC actions, you can either roll on the corresponding {@b Minor/Major Effect table} each time they trigger a cause or keep a tally of the party's {@b Chrono-consequence Value}, increasing it by the associated value for each Cause.
We suggest that each of the following activities count as a single cause and has the corresponding Minor/Major effect or Chrono-consequence Value in the table below.
If you are using the Minor/Major effects, each time the party triggers a cause, roll on the corresponding table to determine the effect.

rows: Defeating a CR 2 or less creature in an encounter while in the past.
Defeating a CR 3 to 9 creature in an encounter while in the past.
Collecting resources for 30 minutes or more while in the past.
Damaging or disrupting at least a 15 ft. squared area of the environment (i.e. casting a destructive spell with an area of effect, or starting an out-of-control fire) while in the past.
Traveling for at least 2 hours and up to 8 hours while in the past.
Traveling for at least 8 hours and up to one day while in the past.
Defeating or saving a person in the past.
Informing people in the past about the future in detail.
Overthrowing a regional ruler or leader in the past.
Defeating a creature of CR 10 or higher while in the past.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: Feel free to adjust these causes as you see fit or use your own judgement to select a Minor/Major tag and/or Chrono-consequence Value for any activity that isn't listed here.

entries.name: Major Effect Table

rows: There are no noticeable changes to the world.
One cultural norm is now taboo and causes great offence to NPCs.
Replace Common (or whatever language is dominant in your world) with another previously rare language.
The main currency of your region has completely changed. Gold and silver coins are replaced by carved teeth, shells, or other coin types that renders the player's money valueless.
Select one common plant group in your world. It no longer exists. We suggest one very common group like grasses (including wheat, rice, barley, & oats), whose absence would be very noticeable.

Select one common animal group in your world. It no longer exists. We suggest a domesticated animal group like terrestrial ungulates (including horses, cows, deer, and pigs), whose absence would be very noticeable.
Add a new faction of NPCs to your world. They are vying for power just like any other faction.

Add a new humanoid species to your world. They intermingle and are present like any other existing species (we suggest using one of our prehistoric playable species, so long as they weren't already present in your world).
Add several Huge or Gargantuan creatures to your world that hunt humanoids (we suggest using our prehistoric creatures).
The series of events that led the party members on their adventure fundamentally changes. They may have been given a different task altogether.
Some of the NPCs that the party are familiar with no longer exist.
The environment is vastly different to before. Scorching deserts or tundra replace lush forests and vice versa.
Replace the plant life in your world with different groups of plants. Temperate deciduous forests become coniferous forests or bamboo forests, and grasslands are replaced by fern plains.

Select a major group of creatures in your world (i.e. mammals, birds, fish, dragons, goblinoids, etc.). Replace them with another major group of creatures that would not normally be present (i.e. dinosaurs, pterosaurs, marine reptiles, or a fantasy equivalent).
All NPC species are swapped to other species - they may be selected from the same pool of species (i.e. all dwarves could become elves and elves become dwarves), or determined randomly.
A major faction is replaced by a new faction with new ideologies and goals.
NPCs don't recognise or know the party. There is no record that they ever existed.
NPCs behave in extremely strange ways, doing things that are greatly offensive or confusing to you and being highly offended or confused by activities that you perceive as normal.
An entirely new civilisation replaces the one the party is familiar with. New factions, regions, cities, and NPCs exist in place of the old ones.
Civilisation as you know it never develops. Instead, the landscape is entirely feral with only scattered hunter-gatherer societies.

entries: *See the Designers' Note on page 77.

entries.name: Minor Effect Table

rows: There are no noticeable changes to the world.
A familiar plant species has different shaped leaves.
A familiar bird has a different sounding call.
A common smell in your world is replaced by another. For example, a specific food or flower smells different.
A familiar local insect has been replaced by a different one. For example, chirping common crickets are now screeching cicadas.
Wooden furniture and buildings are constructed out of a different coloured wood and floorboards creak with an unfamiliar tone.
One or two common humanoid species are a different size category (Small if they were Medium, or Medium if they were Small).
Water tastes unsettlingly different than how your players remember.
Local fruits that the players were familiar with are internally very different. For example, biting into an apple reveals the inside of an orange.
Uncommon eye colours are now quite common among NPCs in your world, or several humanoid species now have different pupil shapes.
The NPCs of your world have longer/shorter limbs or larger/smaller heads than before. This is noticeable to the players.

The players can't quite pinpoint the exact difference, but something is wrong with the world. It just feels... different. Trees don't quite sway in the same way, and other people talk in a subtly different accent.
Buildings and structures have a prominently different design style.
All plants are a slightly different shade of colour than the players would normally expect.
Select a language other than Common that is uncommonly spoken in your world. All NPCs that know that language replace it with another. For example, swap Draconic for Dwarvish.
Select two creatures in your world that have approximately the same CR but one is common and the other is rare to encounter. Swap their abundances, making the rare one common and the common one rare.
Select two humanoid species in your world that have differing abundances in your world and swap those abundances. NPCs of particular species may remain as they are.
Change the primary mode of transport used by people in your world. For example, horse and cart might be replaced by howdahs, or boats might be replaced by beast-drawn rafts or airships.
Add a small-to-medium sized bush to your world that is common (we suggest using one of our prehistoric plants).
Add a medium-to-large sized tree to your world that is common (we suggest using one of our prehistoric plants).
Add a new Small creature to your world that is uncommon, but ubiquitous (we suggest using one of our prehistoric creatures).
Add a new Large creature to your world that is uncommon, but ubiquitous (we suggest using one of our prehistoric creatures).
Add a Huge or Gargantuan predatory creature to your world's oceans (we suggest using one of our aquatic prehistoric creatures, like {@i Livyatan} ({@b page 264})).
Add a Huge or Gargantuan predatory creature to your world's forests that hunts at night (we suggest using one of our prehistoric creatures, like {@i Giganotosaurus} ({@b page 226})).
Add a Huge predatory flying creature to your world that wasn't present before (we suggest using one of our flying prehistoric creatures, like {@i Hatzegopteryx} ({@b page 86 in DDDD})).
Roll on the Major Effect table.
In addition to any other effects, NPCs don't recognise or know the party. There is no record that they ever existed.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: Rolling a 100 on this Minor Effects table is very impactful on storytelling. If you would rather not include it, instead select a Major Effect to replace it.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: The results marked with an asterisk (*) in the Major Effect Table fundamentally overhaul your world and might not be suitable for your campaign, unless you have undertaken significant preparation. If you do not wish to use these results, re-roll them until you get a different suitable result or select a different result.
If you are instead keeping a running tally of the party's {@b Chrono-consequence Value}, you can reference the table below to determine what effects are in play. This table is cumulative.

entries.name: A Brief Summary of This System

items: Players can attempt to repair the timeline.
Specific NPC factions can offer them quests to guide them in this process.
These are usually small and unusual tasks.
It is at the DM's discretion how many of these are required to repair the timeline, although each task can reduce the party's Chrono-consequence Value by {@dice 1d20} if you wish.

entries: Once players have established that their actions in the past have altered the future, their natural inclination will likely be to amend those errors. Below, we provide some plot hook ideas to allow players to resolve them, as well as some NPCs to provide guidance in that process.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: One exciting story twist could be that the adventuring party themselves were actually part of a divergent timeline and they learn at the last minute that if they restore the true timeline, they'll cease to exist (or be entirely different). This is a particularly interesting plot point if you're allowing players to use our custom playable species in a normal fantasy setting. It is a cruel twist for your players, but can make for an intense ending to a campaign. If they choose to repair the timeline at their own detriment, you could reward them with descriptions of simple peaceful lives as different species instead of their adventures, or throw them into an alternative reality for a future campaign.

In order to allow players to undo the damage that they have caused to the timeline, they need guidance, rather than acting randomly upon returning to the past. There are two ways in which this can be approached; either via information gained from a noninteractive source (like inscribed on an ancient temple) or from an interactive source (like discussing the situation with an NPC). The latter of these offers an interesting opportunity to flesh out your world by adding a faction or character that is semi-independent from the flow of time. This character or faction may play a significant role in the maintenance of a pre-set timeline, may be someone who is exceptional at predicting cause and effect, or may simply be a long-lived character that observes the world throughout their lifetime.

You can take inspiration from popular media about what such characters or factions may be like. Below, we have provided two ideas, which you can use directly or use as inspiration to design your own. These can be sought out by the players or simply come to them in their time of need.

entries.name: Circle of Cycles Druidic Order
entries: Members of the Circle of Cycles ({@b page 282 in DDDD}) are druids who venerate the passage of time itself. They seek to observe the world's long history with their own eyes and regularly commune with entities (be they ancestors, descendants, or natural spirits) from the past and future. The druid may also possess the capacity to commune with themselves from different periods of time, although the accuracy of their own long memory could disrupt the information they retrieve.

This affords them the rare ability to glimpse the ebb and flow of time, as well as determine which apparently insignificant events actually have profound long-term impacts. More senior members of the circle are able to divine specifics of those events and may actively attempt to control the timeline, depending on their disposition.

In either case, these druids offer a valuable source of information to repair disturbed timelines. However, they can be difficult to locate and even harder to convince to help. Given their exceptionally long lifespans, most Circle of Cycles druids are isolationist and esoteric. They tend to be hermits living deep in the wilds and those that do reside within a druidic grove may hibernate for centuries at a time, although some do partake in adventuring.

When including a senior druid from the Circle of Cycles, we recommend that they act as a quest-giving NPC who is willing to help the party, usually once convinced that they'll attempt to repair the timeline with or without the circle's help. These druids may also be aware that they have been altered by changes of events in some way and may be distressed by an uneasy strangeness of this false timeline.

entries.name: The Institution of Chronological Stability (ics) or the International Commission on Stratigraphy (ics)
entries: In many fictional universes, there is an authoritarian organisation that helps maintain a specific timeline (for example the TVA ({@i Marvel}), the Bronze Dragonflight ({@i World of Warcraft}), or The Department of Temporal Investigations ({@i Star Trek})). The actions of individuals from those organisations may seem brutal, inhumane, or simply odd as they attempt to maintain or repair their universe's timeline. This is typically because the current timeline is not seen as legitimate and therefore individuals within it are not considered real. Any methodology that successfully restores their perceived "correct" timeline can be justified with this thinking, making these individuals exceptionally dangerous foes.

We envision an organisation called the {@b Institution of Chronological Stability} (which we suppose would be the International Commission on Stratigraphy ({@b page 19}) in the real world) that can fulfil this role in your world. It can either operate outside of normal time, with agents moving between times at will (much like our Chronoficer ({@b page 28 in DDDD})), or as a cult-like organisation that has persisted for millennia, with members bound to the normal rules of time (as much as the players are), but following a strict guideline to help maintain the preferred timeline.

Two NPC types from this organisation are presented here, the ICS Enforcer and the ICS Officer. These characters represent the rank-and-file infantry of the Institution of Chronological Stability and might be tasked with attacking the players if they are perceived as damaging the "correct" timeline or assisting them in restoring it. This faction may even enlist the players to help repair the timeline and could be a major story point.

entries.name: Ics Enforcer
entries: The ICS Enforcers are low-ranking individuals from the Institution of Chronological Stability. They typically act as bodyguards for their higher-ranking ICS Officers and are the most common members of the Institution of Chronological Stability. They may also be tasked with capturing potential threats to the "correct" timeline.

entries.name: Ics Officer
entries: The ICS Officer is a mid-ranking individual from the Institution of Chronological Stability. These smart-dressed agents are stoic in their determination and typically very well-spoken. They wield strange technology that allows them to cast potent spells and have a habit of meticulously recording their assignments and any anomalies/events they observe in their Temporal Notepad. They may be tasked with negotiating with, or eliminating, major threats to the "correct" timeline.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: The Temporal Flak Armour and Temporal Baton are very strong gear rewards for defeating a CR 2 creature. If you don't want such rewarding drops, we suggest that these lose their magical properties when dropped.

entries.name: Quests to Repair the Timeline
entries: There are myriad ways in which your players can interact with the Circle of Cycles, ICS, or another group of NPCs, but each can be used to offer the opportunity to repair a disrupted timeline. Circle of Cycles druids may perform elaborate rituals to divine information in vague ways that the players need to decipher and execute, whereas officers of the ICS might have a stringent record of events that must be adhered to with accuracy. In either case, you may select or roll on the {@b Chrono-repair Tasks} table on page 83 to determine which tasks can be undertaken by the players to repair history.

The number of tasks that need to be completed in order to correct the timeline is entirely up to you. You could have a single pinpoint event correct everything, or the players may have to accumulate a value in a reverse manner to our Chrono-consequence Cumulative Table. If you do so, we suggest that each task reduces their Chrono-consequence value by {@dice 1d20}. Remember, these are just suggestions, and you can come up with your own wacky tasks that the players have to complete in a very specific way.

entries.name: Chrono-repair Tasks
entries: As an alternative to these options, you could have the players travel through time again to encounter themselves from earlier in the adventure. They could then engage with DM controlled versions of themselves, with the aim of preventing their past actions, either through persuasion or by incapacitating themselves. However, this is a risky approach, as you will need to determine the consequences for players killing their past selves.

entries.name: Concluding Remarks
entries: Now that we've covered how to implement various prehistoric elements into your games, we can finally get to the main content of this book - the prehistoric animals, plants, and environments themselves. To begin with, we will look at four holistic environments. These are real-world fossil locations that have dynamic and interesting environmental conditions, presented with some real-world plants and animals that were present within them.

rows: The players must pick up a specific object (i.e. a fallen fruit or a rock) and reposition it somewhere specific (we suggest 100 ft. away) without disturbing anything else.
The players must intervene in a fight between two Tiny creatures, ensuring that a specific one succeeds.
The players must harvest a specific plant or resource - picking a specific flower or collecting a specific object and returning to their own time with it.
The players must destroy everything within a specific 10 ft. square without disturbing anything else.
The players must collect the seed(s) of a specific plant and then plant them in a suitable patch of soil, then water the ground.
The players must catch and transfer an aquatic animal of a particular species from one body of water to another, while keeping it alive.
The players must place a piece of mechanical equipment on an altar at a specific location.
The players must capture a specific Tiny creature and set it adrift on a raft into the ocean.
The players must falsify a divine omen at a specific time and location that will convince a group of humanoids.
The players must track down a specific Small or Tiny creature that is sick or injured and heal it.
The players must seek out a humanoid isolated from others, frighten or shock them, then flee - leaving only a fleeting story of their strange presence.

The players must protect a specific humanoid creature from harm for a set duration, without killing any other creature. You may specify that they must not be seen by the humanoid while completing this task.
The players must find an NPC in the past that matches a specific description, then provide them with information about the future.
The players must donate a piece of metal equipment to a specific NPC in the past.
The players must ensure that some members of a specific species survive a disastrous event that is about to occur.
The players must slay every member of a specific species of creature (we suggest 30 or fewer animals).
The players must intervene in a fight between two Huge or Gargantuan creatures, ensuring that a specific one succeeds.
The players must slay a specific humanoid creature.
The players must slay a specific Huge or Gargantuan non-humanoid creature.
The players must destroy everything in a specific area (usually one with clear boundaries, like an island), burning all plant life to the ground and slaying all creatures.

entries.name: Preamble
entries: Much like in our first book {@i Dr Dhrolin's Dictionary of Dinosaurs}, we're presenting four holistic environments that Professor Primula has researched extensively on her adventures. Each holistic environment provides a reconstruction of a place that existed in the real world, with roleplaying rules for in-game environmental effects, based on their actual palaeoenvironment. We have populated each of these environments with five animal and four plant species, although they contained many more.

Each of these are accompanied by rules that let you interact with them in your roleplaying games. Like everything else based on the real world in our books, we've undertaken considerable research to ensure that these are as accurate, informative, and fun as possible.

In addition to these, each of our creatures is provided with symbols from our environmental icon system. This is a system of symbols associated with each animal that allow it to be easily correlated with appropriate environments, allowing you to populate your world with prehistoric creatures that {@i feel} right for that environment (because they are properly adapted for it!). Additionally, some of the mutations outlined on {@b pages 218-228} in {@i Dr Dhrolin's Dictionary of Dinosaurs} come with associated environmental icons, which can be used to adapt any creature (prehistoric or otherwise) to that specific environment.

Although historically dinosaurs and pterosaurs (and to a lesser extent other non-ice age prehistoric animals) have been depicted as largely inhabiting lush tropical environments populated by cycads and ferns, the truth is that they inhabited a wide variety of environments that existed throughout history. Plenty of dinosaurs and pterosaurs are found in places that were mountainous, arid, marshy, or even frigid, and had morphological and physiological adaptations that allowed them to thrive in these locations.

As such, we encourage you to "think outside of the box" when springing prehistoric animals on your party. Imagine a scene where the party are climbing the chilly slopes of an isolated mountain, only to be ambushed by a Yeti. Then, in its moment of roaring anger, the Yeti itself is ambushed by a large predatory feathered dinosaur, resulting in a completely unexpected combat encounter.
Image of "Pterodactyls" in a Liasic landscape from the book "The World before the Deluge" by Louis Figuier.

entries.name: Conifer Forest
entries: In {@i Dr Dhrolin's Dictionary of Dinosaurs} we followed this section with a table of all of our creatures, their associated environmental icons, and their CR. However, many of you asked us to instead put this table at the back of the book. We've listened and you can find the creature table for {@i Professor Primula's Portfolio of Palaeontology} on {@b pages 426-430}.

entries.name: La Brea Tar Pits
entries: The foul smell of carrion and bitumen in the air heralds one of the most dangerous natural phenomena that can form outside of direct volcanism. Tar pits are not to be underestimated. Although they are static traps that most humanoids can easily identify and work together to escape from if trodden in, other animals are not so savvy and their abundant corpses act as a carnivore trap - drawing in all manner of hungry predators. I strongly recommend avoiding such areas, unless you are particularly keen on a nasty fight!

entries.name: Background
entries: The La Brea Tar Pits are an unusual latest Pleistocene to Holocene geological phenomenon located in modern day Los Angeles, USA. They are a collection of pools of sticky tar that have persisted for thousands of years, trapping and preserving animals, plants, and microbes, providing an atypical fossil record of these organisms.

La Brea's oldest preserved remains date back to approximately 38,000 years ago, but it is still an active trap today and so new material is being added to the record even now. The pits themselves originate from seeping crude oil that reaches the surface. More volatile hydrocarbons then evaporate from this oil, leaving behind only the heaviest components, resulting in pools of asphalt (or bitumen). Over the course of thousands of years, this asphalt collected in pools deep enough to trap even large animals like mammoths, which would become stuck upon entering the pool and slowly sink. The asphalt itself inhibits the decay of submerged carcasses, preserving them remarkably well, while staining bone a dark brown to black colour.

Although it has been known to native North American peoples for thousands of years (who used the asphalt as an adhesive and caulking material for boats), the first written colonial record of La Brea was by Gaspar de Portolá in 1769, as part of a Spanish expedition, who described them as "springs of pitch" in his diary. The name "La Brea" is a direct translation from Spanish, meaning "The Tar", which results in its modern English name of "{@i The La Brea Tar Pits}" translating to "{@i The The Tar Tar Pits"}. Since their formally recorded discovery, the tar pits have been utilised to create a variety of construction materials and as tourist attractions. However, in 1901 William Orcutt identified the first fossil material yielded from the pits and later in 1913, George C. Page, the owner of the land that included the tar pits (Rancho La Brea), granted excavation rights to the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles. Palaeontological investigations of the pits continue to this day.

entries.name: Description
entries: La Brea's fossils offer a rare, detailed, glimpse into a holistic record of palaeoenvironmental change in North America through its relatively recent history. The earliest records from the pits show an overall wetter, cooler environment, although with rainfall largely restricted to winter months and an influx of winter snow meltwater from high-altitude hinterland regions. This resulted in a low-productivity floral community dominated by hardy coastal scrub plants that did not require year-round rain (i.e. sage, juniper, thistle, and ragweed). Despite these harsh conditions, the ecosystem preserved by La Brea is remarkably diverse, particularly with regards to its mammalian fauna (discussed further in Fossils).

Approximately 2,000 years ago, the environment around La Brea underwent a dramatic climatic shift. It became much warmer and drier, leading to the first regional wildfires. This time period also coincided with a dramatic increase in the human population, who would have also started (either accidentally or intentionally) many of these fires. In just a few hundred years, the ecosystem transitioned to the modern fire-adapted one we know California to be today. This rapid environmental shift resulted in the extinction of many of the large animals native to the region.

The pits themselves are a prominent feature within the local environment around La Brea. They functioned as a predator trap, snaring large and small animals alike, and allowing their partially exposed carcasses to rot openly. These animals were attracted to the pits by water floating on top of the tar, but found themselves unable to escape once trying to drink, later dying of hunger or thirst. The smell of this carrion attracted hungry predators and scavengers, who would attempt to feed on the partially exposed carcass, only to become ensnared themselves. This cycle could continue near-purpetually, with fresh carcasses being continually added to the trap, which in turn continued to lure other animals in. Interestingly, on cooler nights, the pits would have been more solidified and safer to scavenge from. In the latter 2,000 years, the number of animals becoming trapped in the pits likely increased as they approached in greater numbers in the hopes of finding food during the changing environmental conditions.

entries.name: Geology
entries: As a series of tar pits, La Brea doesn't really have its own geology in the same manner as other locations discussed in this book. Instead, its formation and history were shaped by the geology of the rocks that it originates from and interacts with. The origin of La Brea's hydrocarbons is the Miocene age oil-bearing Monterey Formation. This thick and extensive unit of rock was deposited in a marine environment and is composed of the remains of ancient microscopic plankton. With time, heat, and pressure, their remains matured into crude oil. Oil-bearing rocks are not uncommon, however, what allows for the formation of La Brea is the presence of other complex geology.

La Brea, and the surrounding Los Angeles, are located at the intersection between two systems of major geological faults. These are a series of east-west thrust faults that bound the Transverse Ranges (mountains that bisect the region) and the northwest trending San Andreas-type strike-slip faults caused by the Pacific Plate and the North American Plate scraping against each other. In essence, the geology of the region is that of an extremely productive oil-bearing rock with a complex series of tectonic faults that tear it and the surrounding rocks apart, creating subterranean breaks that allow crude oil to bubble up to the surface.

One geological component that does include the pits themselves is the periodic deposition of sediment carried by rivers and streams originating from the Santa Monica Mountains. These deposits covered some of the pits, sealing them beneath a layer of silt and sand, forming asphaltum deposits. It is these deposits that can be excavated with relative safety and are where many fossils are found.

entries.name: Fossils
entries: La Brea boasts a remarkable abundance and diversity of fossils. Millions of fossils have been extracted and hundreds of different species identified, with over 140 plant species and 420 animal species recorded. A very broad diversity of mammals are known, with horses and bison being among the most abundant, as well as American lions, badgers, bats, bears, camels, deer, dire wolves, dogs, foxes, a human, jaguars, llama, mammoths, mice, moles, pronghorns, pumas, rabbits, raccoons, rats, regular wolves, saber-toothed cats, skunks, sloths, squirrels, and tapirs, just to name a few. The human remains of La Brea are of a young woman who died of a fractured skull. She was found with some items that suggest she may have been buried there intentionally or ritualistically.

Other groups are slightly less diverse, but still impressively so. Birds include condors, crows, ducks, eagles, geese, hawks, owls, pigeons, seagulls, storks, turkeys, and vultures. Most of these likely landed on shimmering wet asphalt, mistaking it for water and were immediately trapped. This is a fate which also appears to have been shared by many semi-aquatic insects, like dragonflies. Reptiles and amphibians are rarer, but still abundant compared to other fossil sites. Lizards and snakes are the most common, although alligators, tortoises, and frogs are also present, along with rarer fish that may have been washed in during small-scale floods or carried by birds.
In the following pages, we have provided stat blocks for some of these animals; {@i Aenocyon}, {@i Mammuthus} (Columbian), {@i Paramylodon}, {@i Smilodon}, and {@i Teratornis}.
A tar seep with a layer of water covering it, forming a shallow pond.

entries.name: As a Roleplaying Environment
entries: The La Brea tar pits are a significant environmental hazard. The presence of numerous predators, crude oil, asphalt, and the potential for forest fires is not an amenable combination. Nevertheless, much like other hazardous regions (i.e. volcanos, deep ocean, etc.) they make for an interesting environment for players to explore.

In this environment, casual exploration and a simple misstep can result in inescapable death for a low-level character. As such, we strongly recommend making the presence of the tar pits abundantly clear with the strong smell of oil, carrion, and a visibly bubbling pool of tar. They also offer a suitable reason to concentrate large predators in a relatively small location - ensuring that the entire region is dangerous-to-deadly. In this section is a series of rules that capture the essence of these threats. Feel free to adjust damage numbers and DCs to match your party's needs, particularly with regards to the Sticky Tar's increasing difficulty with time.

entries.name: Sticky Tar
entries: The tar of La Brea is exceptionally dangerous. Stepping onto it can result in becoming stuck, and the more a creature struggles, the more its fate becomes sealed. Tar can either be {@b cured}, or {@b uncured}. Cured tar looks solid and crusty, whereas uncured tar is oily and gelatinous in appearance. Cured tar can be walked on by {@b Small and Tiny} creatures without issue (larger creatures break through the outer layer), whereas uncured tar is a threat to all creatures.

Any creature that starts its turn on or moves into tar that is unsafe for its size must succeed on a Strength saving throw or become {@condition restrained|XPHB|Restrained} by the tar. The DC for this saving throw is based on the size category of the creature: Tiny or smaller ({@dc 8}), Small ({@dc 10}), Medium ({@dc 12}), Large ({@dc 15}), Huge ({@dc 18}), Gargantuan or larger ({@dc 22}). A {@condition restrained|XPHB|Restrained} creature can use its Action to attempt to free itself with a successful Strength check, using the same DC as before, and on a success it is able to move up to 5 ft. However, for each successive failure of this check, the DC increases by 2. After 1 minute, a creature stuck in this manner will succumb to the tar and begin to suffocate in it.

entries.name: Predator Trap
entries: La Brea is a place of death. Carcasses lie rotting in unreachable pools of tar and starving predators stalk their margins. When encountering a carnivorous creature in La Brea, do not randomise its behaviour. Instead, assume that it will attack and fight to the death with any creature it sees as prey, and will flee from any other creature that it does not see as prey. Additionally, there should be at least twice as many large predators and scavengers around La Brea than would be expected for a normal environment.

entries.name: Flammable Hydrocarbons
entries: The tar contains flammable hydrocarbons. If flames come within 5 ft. of uncured tar, it will first detonate the methane on and around the pit. Each creature within 30 ft. of the pit must make a {@dc 16} Dexterity saving throw, taking {@dice 4d10} Fire damage on a failed save, or halve as much on a successful one.

The pit itself will then ignite and burn for up to 24 hours, causing any creature in it or within 5 ft. of it to take {@dice 1d10} Fire damage at the start of each of its turns (or every minute outside of combat). The tar is sticky and difficult to remove from a creature that is coated in it.

Once lit, these flames are very difficult to extinguish and will continue to burn even if splashed with water. Only very low temperatures, suffocation of the flames, or continuous flooding with water for 30 seconds will extinguish the fire.

entries.name: La Brea Tar PiTs FLora
entries: As La Brea is a relatively young fossil site, most (if not all) of the plants found within it are still alive today. In fact, some of these will be familiar to our North American readers as common plants that they've seen in life. As many plant remains were washed into the pits, a wide variety of plants can be found within it, including aquatic plants.

entries.name: Sagittaria sp.
entries: {@i Sagittaria} sp. is an extant (living today) pond-loving plant that has clusters of white and yellow flowers on small stems from a single larger stem (inflorescences) and bright green arrow-shaped leaves. It has a large edible potato-like tuber, which has historically been used by people native to the western coast of North America as a food source and has a bitter taste until cooked. This tuber floats in water, and so can be easily collected from ponds if the mud is disturbed.

entries.name: Tip of the Arrow
entries: This plant can be harvested, when doing so, either the root or the leaves may be selected (not both). If the roots are harvested, then one day's ration for one creature is recovered. If the leaves are harvested, then roll on the table below to determine what resource is gathered. {@dice 1d4} - result 1 - failed, nothing harvested 2 - Harvest {@dice 1d6} arrows 3 - Harvest {@dice 2d8} arrows 4 - Harvest {@dice 1d4} magical +1 arrows

entries.name: Sequoia sempervirens
entries: {@i Sequoia sempervirens} is an impressive tree species that is extant (living today) and is the world's tallest tree. Reaching ridiculous heights of up to 380 ft. tall and almost 30 ft. wide at the base. While often felled for logging, their sheer size makes them large enough to build houses (and even towns) on.

Inhabiting damp coastal regions, these giants are adapted to foggy moist conditions and their height helps stimulate fog formation, resulting in a damp, humid environment in the forests that they form. They are also extremely long-lived, with the oldest tree on record being over 2,200 years old.

entries.name: Forest Fog
entries: While within a forest and within 100 ft. of at least one Sequoia sempervirens, any plant based creature (i.e. Ents, Dryads, etc.) and any creature with spellcasting can cast the spell Fog Cloud as a Magic action without requiring a spell slot. A creature may do this a number of times equal to its Proficiency Bonus, then must finish a Long Rest to regain all expent uses.

entries.name: Sisyrinchium bellum
entries: {@i Sisyrinchium bellum} is an extant (living today) small herbaceous plant with bright purple or blue flowers. It is a perennial plant (lives for more than 2 years), growing in open grassy areas and high-altitude woodlands. In English, it has the common name of "Blue Eyed Grass" due to its exceedingly vivid flowers, and components of the plant have historically been used medicinally as a cure for indigestion.

entries.name: Blue-Eyed Boy
entries: Crushing the flowers of this plant into a paste and applying them to a creature's eyes gives that creature Truesight 10 ft. for the next 1 hour.

entries.name: Toxicodendron diversilobum
entries: {@i Toxicodendron diversilobum}, otherwise known as Poison Oak, is an extant (living today) shrub or tree-like vine with green leaves and small green flowers in the summer or red-brown leaves in the autumn (our illustration depicts summer-time flowers, but autumnal leaves to give an example of both seasons). It is a woodland plant that grows around the bases of trees and produces an oil that coats the surfaces of its leaves and stems. While not technically toxic, this oil triggers a strong allergic reaction in most people, resulting in extremely painful rashes.

entries.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: {@b {@i Poison Oak}}{@i. Any creature that touches this plant, or inhales smoke from this plant being burnt must succeed a DC 12 Constitution saving throw or become Poisoned for 24 hours.}

entries.name: Stuttgart Formation
entries: I had initially read of the poor weather conditions, but when we arrived at Stuttgart, I was utterly unprepared for the relentlessness of the rain. It rained, literally, non-stop day and night. Upon arrival, the ground was already soaked beyond description, a veritable swampland of mud and silt in all directions for hundreds of miles. Despite this, the region was full of life. Mussels and shellfish lined sodden riverbanks and early amphibians drifted down the overflowing waterways. Yet, there was an uneasy eeriness to this strange place. Unfamiliar reptiles lurked in the foggy mornings, with their hootings and grumblings masked by the torrent of rainfall. We never really felt... safe.

entries.name: Background
entries: The Stuttgart Formation is a Triassic (approximately 235-220 million years ago) sequence of rock, specifically Carnian in age, which is the earliest stage of the Late Triassic. It takes its name from the nearby German city of Stuttgart and crops out across southwestern Germany and northern Switzerland, with a handful of other outcrops elsewhere, like in northwestern Germany. It is part of the larger Triassic Keuper group, which spans most of Germany.

entries.name: Description
entries: The Stuttgart Formation was deposited in an extremely humid river delta, perhaps with some evidence of a slow marine ingression (sea flooding into the land), resulting in some brackish water conditions. The environment was particularly humid as it was deposited during the Carnian Pluvial Episode, which is a period of global warming caused by volcanism in the Triassic that greatly increased the amount of rainfall around the world. It replaced much of the global arid environments of the Triassic with hotter and more humid environments, causing significant and (possibly) near-constant rainfall in some areas. This resulted in very high levels of continental weathering and subsequent runoff, as well as the formation of soils that indicate that precipitation exceeded plant evapotranspiration. In short, many places developed hot tropical humid climates.

To say that the Stuttgart Formation was "wet", doesn't really convey the level of rainfall that the Carnian Pluvial Episode shows evidence for. Some science communicators state that it "rained for two million years straight" which, however hyperbolic, is not beyond the realm of possibility for the wettest regions. What is more important, however, is that this change in climate came during the Triassic, which is known for its particularly arid climate and harsh dry expanses. It is no surprise then that this time period also coincides with the rapid diversification of early dinosaurs, lepidosaurs, and possibly even the earliest mammals, as well as the rise of coccoliths and dinoflagellates in the oceans. These significant changes in the world's biota were likely caused by the rapid replacement of the hot, harsh, and arid environments of Triassic Pangea with lush, humid, and hotter jungles and rainforests.

entries.name: Geology
entries: The Stuttgart Formation is composed largely of fine-grained sandstones, siltstones, and mudstones. In the lowermost parts of the formation, the sandstones are cross-bedded and represent deposition in a very humid delta system with a large volume of flowing water. In the upper parts of the formation, this gives way to a lacustrine (lake) setting with sandstones and mudstones, again with repeated bouts of flooding. Interestingly, the uppermost part also has some indication of clearer and dry seasons, which may represent the tail-end of the Carnian Pluvial Episode and the transition to later, more familiar, Mesozoic climates.

entries.name: Fossils
entries: The fossil assemblage of the Stuttgart Formation is dominated by shelled invertebrates, particularly bivalved molluscs and bivalved crustaceans (Clam shrimp), which evidently lived in abundance in the rivers and deltas, as well as the remains of cycads and other plants that surrounded the riverways. Vertebrate fossils are noticeably rarer in the Stuttgart Formation, although it is of particular importance for temnospondyls, as six examples of this group are known from it - also evidently living within the rivers and deltas. Other vertebrate remains are rarer and often fragmentary, including reptiles, a therapsid (which may be {@i Woznikella}, an interpretation that we've followed in this book), and a small number of fish.

This restricted fish diversity may be indicative of fluctuating salinities and provides evidence towards a marine ingression event (or multiple events) that kept conditions unsuitable for a diverse array of fish. This is further supported by the abundance of {@i Mytilus} (mussels), which thrive in brackish estuarine waters.
In the following pages, we have provided stat blocks for some of these animals; {@i Dyoplax}, {@i Metoposaurus}, {@i Palaeobates}, {@i Woznikella}, and {@i Zanclodon.}

entries.name: As a Roleplaying Environment
entries: The Stuttgart Formation makes for an ideal setting for a roleplay-heavy mystery/horror campaign or story arc, with the environmental rules making it difficult for the characters to determine what is happening around them and to escape any dangers. Describing to players that it essentially never stops raining here and that you're never truly sure what lies just beyond the mist can invoke a sense of dread and fear that other environments lack, despite their dangers. We suggest building on this, but mixing in brief sightings/evidence of strange animals and gruesome predators lurking in the storms.

entries.name: Pluvial Episode
entries: Dim and dreary clouds cover the sky and a dense mist fills the waterlogged forest. It continually rains here, ranging from a light drizzle to a downpour. All creatures that are not sheltered from this weather effect have -5 to {@skill Perception} checks, as well as -5 to their passive Perception. Additionally, after completing a Long Rest, each creature in this region must make a {@dc 10} Charisma saving throw. On a failed save they have an additional -2 penalty to all other skill checks until their next Long Rest, as they succumb to the depressing weather (we call this debuff "being British").

entries.name: Sodden Earth
entries: For long periods of time, perhaps thousands of years, the ground of the Stuttgart Formation has been entirely saturated with water. It varies from washed out wet silt to deep squishy mud, but in any case, all of the natural ground is muddy difficult terrain.

entries.name: Sodden Carcasses
entries: The constantly wet conditions speed up the processes of decay and deterioration. Any carcass or dead body decays twice as fast as normal in this environment. Spells that target a dead body that must have been dead for less than a fixed duration of time (such as Revivify, Resurrection, and True Resurrection) have that duration halved.

entries.name: sTuTTgarT FormaTion FLora
entries: Despite the sodden conditions of the Stuttgart Formation, there are remains of many conifers and cycad trees that indicate that widespread forests not only persisted, but thrived in this environment.

entries.name: Desmiophyllum imhoffi
entries: {@i Desmiophyllum imhoffi} was a conifer tree with thin, pointed strap-like leaves arranged densely along its terminal branches. Aside from this physical description, very little is known about its evolutionary relationships and affinities with other conifers, and therefore what the rest of its anatomy may have been like. Our illustration here reconstructs this plant with a relatively high open canopy, based on modern Cupressales (cypresses), but future research may reveal that it had a different appearance.

entries.name: Optional Magical Rules
Expulsive Drinker
entries: Some Desmiophyllum imhoffi are magically adapted to wet conditions in such a manner that they absorb all water on contact and then violently expel excess water as a jet through pores in their leaves.

If a creature comes within 5 ft. of one of these Desmiophyllum imhoffi while it is raining (and it is always raining in the Stuttgart Formation), they trigger this expulsion and must make a {@dc 10} Dexterity saving throw, taking 3 ({@dice 1d4 + 1}) Cold damage on a failed save.

entries.name: Pagiophyllum foetterlei
entries: {@i Pagiophyllum foetterlei} was a conifer of unknown (or rather uncertain and variable) affinities, meaning that we don't fully understand its evolutionary relationships yet. It is most likely an araucarian (evergreen conifer) or cheirolepidiacean, which were a group of Triassic conifers that were particularly common in the Mesozoic. It had small pointed leaves, but otherwise its anatomy is largely unknown. Our reconstruction here is based on cheirolepidiacean affinities.

entries.name: Snaring Leaves
entries: A creature that comes within 5 ft. of this tree must succeed a {@dc 12} Dexterity saving throw or be {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} by Pagiophyllum foetterlei (escape {@dc 14}).

entries.name: Pterophyllum sp.
entries: {@i Pterophyllum} sp. was a small bennettitale plant (common shrubby and cycad-like seed plants from between the Permian and Cretaceous) with long (up to 8 in.), thin, feather-like leaves that formed rosettes at the end of its branches. It was an understory bush, potentially growing near (but not directly on) riverbanks and could form low-lying canopies if many bushes were growing together in a thicket. Male pollen organs had a frilly appearance and the female cones were wind pollinated. Once pollinated, the outer bracts and scales of the cone would wither and fall off, and a fibrous gynoecium (fruiting body) would grow in its place. This would later disintegrate, dropping seeds. Interestingly, {@i Pterophyllum} sp. has been used to help reconstruct ancient atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations by measuring the abundance of stomata on its leaves.

entries.name: Optional Magical Rules
Suffocating Suction
entries: Pterophyllum sp. fossils have been used to help reconstruct ancient atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations. Some Pterophyllum sp. have become retroactively enchanted by this future science, causing them to rapidly absorb oxygen and expel carbon dioxide.

If a creature comes within 5 ft. of one of these Pterophyllum sp., it triggers this ability and the area within a 20 ft. sphere from Pterophyllum sp. becomes devoid of oxygen, causing creatures that breathe air within it to begin to suffocate (with no saving throw, although they can hold their breath as normal). This effect persists for 1 hour, although creatures can freely leave the area and begin breathing again as normal.

entries.name: Dioonitocarpidium pennaeforme
entries: {@i Dioonitocarpidium pennaeforme} was a feathercone cycad tree with relatively large, stiff, pinnate leaves. These would have been arranged in a rosette around a large female seed cone with feather-shaped seed-leaves (also arranged in a rosette), all atop a thick, stout trunk.

entries.name: Feather-Forming Seeds
entries: If the seeds of this plant can be properly harvested ({@dc 5} {@skill Survival} check), then they can be crushed with water to create a potion that, when consumed, confers the effects of the Feather Fall spell (1st level) to the creature.

entries.name: Eumeralla Formation
entries: Trekking through the polar rift valleys is an arduous task in the best of seasons. However, doing so through the polar winter is an entirely different beast. One would think that the bitter cold and endless darkness is the primary threat. Yet, within certain valleys, stalking predatory dinosaurs hunt in the darkness and huge temnospondyl amphibians lie in wait. Don't be fooled by the stillness of the ice forest, for it is alive and hungry.

entries.name: Background
entries: The fossil locality known as "Dinosaur Cove" is a sequence of fossil bearing rocks from the Early Cretaceous of southern Victoria, Australia. Here, we focus specifically on the Eumeralla Formation, which is Aptian-Albian (Early Cretaceous) in age, approximately 106 million years old.

The first fossil dinosaurs were discovered at this site by William Ferguson in 1903, during an excavation in search of coal. This initial find was misidentified as a tooth, then later re-evaluated as a dinosaur claw fossil. About eighty years later, the abundance of fossils and prominence of the site prompted the establishment of a dedicated fossil hunting dig site, nicknamed "Dinoville", which persisted for a decade.

entries.name: Description
entries: In the Late Jurassic/Early Cretaceous, Australia was much further south than its modern latitude (75-80 degrees South) and partially within the Antarctic circle. Throughout the Early Cretaceous, it drifted further north away from Antarctica and this process created a great rift valley (a linear lowland between highlands/mountains, caused by geological rifting). It is within this rift valley that the Eumeralla Formation was deposited.

The environment during the Cretaceous within this polar latitude was very different from modern polar environments at similar latitudes. Instead of a frozen waste, the region was filled with a polar forest and was not permanently frozen. This is due to the overall warmer climate and greenhouse effects of the Cretaceous, resulting in a much warmer average global temperature. Nevertheless, the Eumeralla Formation was still relatively cold and oxygen isotope ratios suggest surface air temperatures close to an annual mean of 0°C (32°F), with evidence of seasonally frozen soils.

As the Eumeralla Formation was within the Antarctic circle, it experienced Polar Seasonality where the sun would never rise in winter and never set in summer. Each of these seasons lasted for a minimum of three months and resulted in extreme temperature differences, with winters being very cold and dark, and summers much warmer and brighter. This would have resulted in an environment that had extremes of activity - spring and summer bustling with life and new plant growth, then a frozen near-silent forest in winter.

entries.name: Geology
entries: As a whole, the Eumeralla Formation mostly consists of mudstones and sandstones, deposited fluvially (by a river system) within the rift valley. The sandstones were deposited in the high-velocity currents of a broad river (hundreds-to-thousands of ft. wide) and reach a thickness of up to 330 ft., whereas the mudstones represent channel-fills, indicating channels with much calmer conditions that slowly filled with sediment. Some units contain evidence of wind-driven rippling, further supporting the presence of very large rivers and perhaps areas where they opened up into wider shallow lake or swamp environments. Although much of these water bodies likely iced over during the winter, unfrozen water must have remained due to the presence of large numbers of aquatic animals.

Interspersed within the mudstone units are seams of coal, formed from ancient plant remains in these wet environments. Without these coals, William Ferguson may never have excavated the Eumeralla Formation and many of the animals of this locality might have remained undiscovered.

entries.name: Fossils
entries: A wide variety of vertebrate and plant fossils have been recovered from the Eumeralla Formation, although interestingly no invertebrate body fossils have been described yet (despite invertebrate trace fossil burrows being found). This is likely because many of the fossils are recovered from the high-energy sandstones and are often fragmentary. It is exceedingly rare for soft-bodied terrestrial invertebrates to be preserved in these types of sandstones, as the relative abundance of oxygen and high-energy results in them being destroyed by a combination of decay and physical damage. Perhaps some invertebrate remains will be recovered from the mudstone members at a later date as they were undoubtedly present within the environment.

Of the vertebrates found, dinosaurs are the most abundant, with over 1,500 specimens recovered. These include ankylosaurs, ornithopods, and a variety of theropods (including megaraptorids and a possible tyrannosaur). Most of these are preserved as fragmentary components, although one partial ornithopod skeleton is known. No sauropods are known from the Eumeralla Formation, which may be a result of its latitude as sauropod diversity generally decreases globally towards the poles.

Other reptiles are present, including a single crocodile, turtle, several indeterminate pterosaurs, and an indeterminate plesiosaur. Several fish are known, including a lungfish and ray-finned fish, as well as the primitive temnospondyl amphibians. There are alsoseveral species of semi-aquatic monotreme mammals (platypuses, echidnas, and their kin). In the following pages, we have provided stat blocks for some of these animals; {@i Australovenator}, {@i Ceratodus}, {@i Koolasuchus}, {@i Leaellynasaura}, and {@i Steropodon}.

entries.name: As a Roleplaying Environment
entries: The Eumeralla Formation makes for a compelling and unusual setting for a palaeontology-themed campaign/ arc. The extreme cold in winter and the unusual lighting conditions provide both excitement and notable hazards to players who may be expecting a more classic hot-jungle dinosaurian environment. These can result in challenging combat encounters and survival roleplaying, making the Eumeralla Formation an excellent twist on the usual prehistoric settings.

entries.name: Polar Seasonality
entries: Upon arrival in this environment, the DM may choose (or randomly determine) if the region is in summer or winter. Apply the environmental alterations described below based on that result. Alternatively, the region may be in the transition between these two extremes and be treated as a normal cold-to-temperate region.

{@b Polar Winter}: The region is in permanent darkness (lasting ~3 months) and is bitterly cold (although not as cold as modern polar regions). After each Long Rest, any creature not native to the environment that does not have Cold Resistance or Cold Immunity must make a {@dc 10} Constitution saving throw. On a failed save, they gain one level of Exhaustion. If a player character makes five successful saves against this check, they become immune to this effect for three months.
Additionally, most plant life is dormant and withered. Many creatures will be hibernating or desperately hungry - carnivores will attack creatures smaller than themselves on sight.

{@b Polar Summer}: The region is in permanent light (lasting ~3 months) and is temperate and mild. However, the lack of night makes resting difficult. At the start of each Long Rest, any creature not native to the environment must make a {@dc 10} Wisdom saving throw. On a failed save, they cannot rest for the entire period and instead only gain the benefits of a Short Rest. If a player makes five successful saves against this check, they become immune to this effect for three months.
Additionally, most plant life is active and in bloom. All native creatures will be highly active, although less hungry.

entries.name: Polar Madness
entries: If a humanoid fails three consecutive Polar Winter or Polar Summer saving throws, they become subject to Polar Madness. While under the effect of Polar Madness, their Proficiency Bonus becomes 0 and they must succeed a {@dc 10} Wisdom saving throw at the start of each round of combat or be {@condition frightened|XPHB|Frightened} of all enemy creatures for one round. This effect persists until they receive a Lesser Restoration, Greater Restoration, or similar effect, or until three months have elapsed (or if they become immune to the effects of Polar Winter / Polar Summer).
