entries.name: eumeraLLa FormaTion FLora
entries: Despite the long periods of darkness, forests were widespread around the Eumeralla Formation. These would have provided both shelter from the harsh winter weather and the chance for herbivores and omnivores to feed. In winter these would have been silent and eerie forests, whereas in summer, they would have erupted with life and activity, with animals and plants alike making the most of the warm sunshine.

entries.name: Ginkgoites australis
entries: {@i Ginkgoites australis} is a tree closely related to {@i Ginkgo apodes} ({@b page 42 in DDDD}) and is also a type of {@i Ginkgo} tree, although it likely had a more conical overall shape than a regular {@i Ginkgo}. This is a result of its larger, more deeply divided leaves, which would have turned bright yellow before being dropped for the dark winter months in the Eumeralla Formation.

entries.name: Mottled Shadows
entries: The leaves of some Ginkgoites australis cast a magical shadow effect that, with prolonged exposure, can leave a camouflaging mottled pattern on a creature. A creature that spends at least 10 minutes relatively still (i.e. sat or sleeping during a rest) under the shade of Ginkgoites australis (while in sunlight or moonlight) gains a mottled patterning and a +5 bonus to {@skill Stealth} checks that lasts for 24 hours.

entries.name: Carnoconites cranwellii
entries: {@i Carnoconites cranwellii} is the name given to a plant that has three different names assigned to three different components of it. In palaeobotany, leaves, pollen (♂), and seed cones (♀) each have their own taxonomic systems and a single organism may be assigned three names, one for each of these components, then one of them selected for the organism's overall name. For {@i Carnoconites cranwellii}, the leaves are called {@i Taeinopteris daintreei}, the male pollen organs are {@i Sahnia laxiphora}, and finally the female cones are {@i Carnoconites cranwellii}, which is also assigned to the whole plant. {@i Carnoconites cranwellii} was a pentoxylalean tree which had large, strap-like leaves that were borne in clusters on short shoots, similar to a {@i Ginkgo} tree. These leaves probably grew conically to take advantage of the low-angle of sunlight (due to the high latitude of the Eumeralla Formation) and were probably dropped during the dark winter months.

entries.name: Frightful Fruit
entries: Carnoconites cranwellii produces a fleshy fruit that, if harvested properly ({@dc 14} {@skill Survival} check), can be brewed into a magical poison. If the poison is consumed by a creature, that creature must succeed a {@dc 14} Wisdom saving throw or be {@condition frightened|XPHB|Frightened} of all other creatures for 12 hours (eating the fruit normally does not convey this effect). Additionally, the {@condition frightened|XPHB|Frightened} creature cannot take a Short or Long Rest for the duration of this effect.

entries.name: Brachyphyllum gippslandicum
entries: {@i Brachyphyllum gippslandicum} is an auraucarian tree that is similar in appearance and ecology to the extant (still living) members of {@i Araucaria}, otherwise known as the Monkey-Puzzle trees. While these modern Monkey-Puzzles are restricted to the Southern Hemisphere, they, and the closely related {@i Brachyphyllum gippslandicum}, had a global distribution in the Mesozoic where they grew in free-draining or rocky soils. Monkey-Puzzle trees take their name from their rough or spiky bark and leaves that make climbing difficult (coined by Charles Austin in 1834), and {@i Brachyphyllum gippslandicum} likely shared this trait. Although difficult to climb, its higher branches would have yielded seed cones filled with edible seeds.

entries.name: Monkey's Puzzle
entries: At the heart of some Brachyphyllum gippslandicum trees is a small archaic wooden puzzlebox trinket. This puzzlebox is only revealed if the tree is felled or destroyed. A creature can attempt to open this strange puzzle over the course of a Long Rest by succeeding on a {@dc 18} Intelligence check (or break it open with a {@dc 25} Strength check). Once opened, roll or pick from the table below to determine what is inside the puzzlebox.

rows: {@i The puzzlebox was boobytrapped. Each creature within 10 ft. of it must succeed a DC 16 Constitution saving throw or take 2d8 Poison damage and become Poisoned for 24 hours.}
{@i A cryptic treasure map (another DC 18 Intelligence check to decipher) that leads to}

entries.name: Cladophlebis biformis
entries: {@i Cladophlebis biformis} was an osmundaceous fern (a large group of widely distributed ferns that have naked sori and brightly coloured, stalked sporangia) that we have already discussed before in {@i Dr Dhrolin's Dictionary of Dinosaurs} ({@b page 63 in DDDD}), as it is also found in the Bahariya Formation. As we outlined there, this plant is a herbaceous fern that grows in damp soils and has several edible components, specifically its young fiddleheads (curled developing leaves) and its rhizome (underground stem). Here, we have provided alternative Optional Magical Rules specific to the species {@i biformis}. If you wish, you may use the rules in {@i Dr Dhrolin's Dictionary of Dinosaurs} instead.

entries.name: Seasonality Remedy
entries: Cladophlebis biformis' rhizome contains a natural magical compound that helps resist the effects of polar seasonality. If the roots are harvested and prepared as a tea ({@dc 10} {@skill Survival} check), when consumed by a creature it gains Advantage on Constitution/Wisdom saving throws to resist the effects of Polar Seasonality for 24 hours.

entries: Florin, R. 1936. Die fossilen Ginkgophyten von Franz-Joseph-Land nebst Eröterungen über vermeintliche Cordaitales mesozoischen Alters I. {@i Palaeontographica Abtheilung}, {@b 81}, 71-173.

entries.name: Wessex Formation
entries: As I reviewed the records of settlements established in the area commonly referred to as "Wessex" or "Wealden" by the locals (depending on provenance or mood, it seems), I happened across a strange pattern. Although the region boasted the same sort of dinosaurian threats as others, records indicate that most small settlements appear to have only lasted a couple of years at most. It seems that the undulating extremes in precipitation make agriculture particularly difficult in this region, despite the fertile soils. The hazard of wildfire-burnt crops and flood-drowned fields appears to be a sufficient deterrent, let alone the ever-present risk of dinosaur attack.

entries.name: Background
entries: The Wessex Formation is an Early Cretaceous (approximately 130 million years ago) sequence of rock from the southern coast of England and the English channel, and is within the Wealden Group (a collection of formations from the Cretaceous 140 - 125 million years ago). The Wessex Formation crops out most prominently on the isles of Wight and Purbeck and yields a vast diversity of fossil flora and fauna. Although not formally named until 1979, the formation was first described in 1816 by Thomas Webster and has been heavily studied for over two hundred years, including by famous early palaeontologists like William Buckland.

entries.name: Description
entries: The Wessex Formation was deposited in a lowland comprised of a series of floodplains, braided rivers, and coastal lagoons. Meandering rivers routinely formed oxbow lakes which led to isolated anoxic pools of stagnant water dotted around the landscape.

The region had distinctive wet and dry seasons, with considerable temperature differences between long, dry summers and short wet winters. These long, dry summers resulted in increased risk of wildfires, which would quickly sweep through desiccated scrub and the following short, wet winters were also prone to flash-flooding. This resulted in an environment of sudden hazards - peaceful for prolonged periods interspersed with rapid destruction of the landscape.

Overall, it was relatively warm compared to its modern setting and the climate was semi-arid, much more akin to a modern mediterranean shrubland than modern southern England. The surrounding landscape was largely covered in shrubby xerophytic (drought-resistant) ferns that could survive prolonged periods of drought, although the floodplains themselves had a wider diversity of foliage as the rivers continued to flow throughout the year.

entries.name: Geology
entries: The Wessex Formation is composed mainly of red mudstones with interbedded pale white/yellow sandstones deposited in rivers, lakes, and ponds, as well as across the floodplains during floods. These are interspersed with lignite deposits, which are layers of plant debris bed (often formed from swampy peats) that have matured (baked by heat and pressure) to form a combustible rock similar to coal, often referred to as "brown coal". These plant remains are also rich in pyrite, which is indicative of anoxic conditions at deposition and suggests that they were laid down in pools of stagnant water, likely the aforementioned oxbow lakes.

The Wessex Formation varies greatly in thickness. In its thickest parts, it is reported to reach an impressive 3,200 ft. in height, although it only reaches about 2,000 ft. in height on the Isle of Wight. In its thinnest places, the formation is only about 200 ft. thick.

entries.name: Fossils
entries: It is fair to say that the Wessex Formation is highly fossiliferous (yields a lot of fossils) as an extremely large number and diversity of organisms have been described from it. The overwhelming majority of these are fragmentary or preserved as isolated teeth, suggesting that most carcasses are exposed for some time before their burial, allowing scavengers and decay to break them up. Nevertheless, complete skeletons are known and, among dinosaurs alone, examples include {@i Hypsilophodon}, {@i Iguanodon}, {@i Polacanthus}, {@i Eotyrannus}, and {@i Neovenator}, which all likely represent animals caught up in flood events that were rapidly buried. For most of these animals, several closely related taxa are also reported as fragmentary material.

In addition to dinosaurs, a variety of pterosaurs, fish, turtles, frogs, salamanders, crocodiles, small mammals, arachnids, insects, and other arthropods are known, as well as a variety of plants including pines, ferns, tree ferns, and cypress trees. Of these, the diversity of mammals and amphibians have been particularly contributed to by the works of Steve Sweetman, who is famed for bulk processing huge volumes of sediment and identifying examples of new taxa from isolated teeth and bones. It should also be noted that some of the plant fossils preserve burnt components, providing further evidence for frequent wildfires.

In the following pages, we have provided stat blocks for some of these animals; {@i Barilium}, {@i Hypsilophodon}, {@i Istiodactylus}, {@i Neovenator}, and {@i Polacanthus}, however {@i Iguanodon} ({@b page 134 in DDDD}) can also be found here.

entries.name: As a Roleplaying Environment
entries: The Wessex Formation should generally be a pleasant, warm scrubby environment. This agreeable setting, however, is interspersed with periods of swift (but not total) destruction via flooding or wildfires. These are an ever-present hazard that makes the region particularly dangerous to spend prolonged periods in, although brief visits can often be harmless.

entries.name: Footprint Fossils
entries: Intermittent moist areas of clay-like mud can be found in the Wessex Formation, particularly along the riverbanks and coastline. These readily preserve the tracks of animals that walk through them. Any {@skill Survival} check to track another creature via its visible trail is made at Advantage while within the Wessex Formation.

entries.name: Seasonal Aridity
entries: When players first arrive at the Wessex Formation, choose (or randomly determine) if the region is experiencing a dry season or a wet season. If the season is dry, then fresh water will be scarce, with mud-cracked ground and mostly dried up riverbeds. Any standing water will be stagnant and pooled in oxbow lakes, and the region will be subject to the {@b Smouldering Wildfire} and {@b Sweeping Inferno} rules. If the season is wet, the rivers vary between being steady and strong to roaring torrents that are hazardous to cross (we suggest a {@dc 12} or greater {@skill Athletics} check). A storm rolls in each day (at a randomly determined time) during the wet season and the levees of the rivers will have a chance to break, creating a {@b Crevasse Splay}.

entries.name: Smouldering Wildfire
entries: Each day at midday during summer and while the party is within this environment, roll a {@dice d6}. On the roll of a 1, a smouldering wildfire ignites in a nearby area of your choosing. Every 10 minutes that the fire is left, it spreads to adjacent 5 ft. squares and the previous square remains smouldering. If a creature starts its turn within or enters an area that is a smouldering wildfire, it takes {@dice 1d4} Fire damage.
The smouldering wildfire is easily doused by a moderate amount of water, and isn't obviously visible. The only indication of its presence is puffy white smoke emanating from the dry foliage.

entries.name: Sweeping Inferno
entries: If a Smouldering Wildfire is left un-doused for 2-4 hours, it becomes a Sweeping Inferno. Any area currently occupied by the Smouldering Wildfire becomes engulfed in a Sweeping Inferno.
Every 30 seconds that the fire is left, it spreads to any un-burnt adjacent 5 ft. square and the previous square is left as a burnt husk, with plant life mostly charred to ashes.

Creatures that start their turn within 10 ft. of, or move within 10 ft. of, a Sweeping Inferno take {@dice 1d4} Fire damage and struggle to breathe. After 30 seconds they will begin to suffocate if they remain there any longer. If a creature starts its turn within or enters an area that is part of the Sweeping Inferno itself, it takes {@dice 2d10} Fire damage instead and begins to suffocate immediately.
A Sweeping Inferno is a large, clearly visible, fire that is difficult to douse. Most animals will flee across water to escape from it.

entries.name: Crevasse Splay
entries: After particularly heavy storms, the levees of the Wessex Formation have a chance to break, resulting in a torrent of water spreading across the floodplain and potentially burying creatures in mud. After each storm during the wet season, roll {@dice 1d6} and add 1 for each previous storm during that season where no levees broke. If the rolled value is 6 or higher, a levee breaks and a 200 ft. by 200 ft. area adjacent to the river is flooded with water and mud at a rate of 30 ft. per round over 7 rounds. We recommend rolling for initiative for creatures and having the water move at initiative 20 (losing ties).

Each creature caught by the torrent within that area takes {@dice 1d6} Bludgeoning damage and then must succeed a {@dc 10} Strength saving throw each round that it remains in the torrent, or be knocked {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone} and {@condition grappled|XPHB|Grappled} by mud. While {@condition prone|XPHB|Prone} in the mud, the creature begins to suffocate and can only unearth itself with a {@dc 14} Strength check. Both the torrent itself and the mud left behind are difficult terrain.

entries.name: Wessex FormaTion FLora
entries: The environmental destruction wrought across the Wessex Formation by its extreme weather means that its floral population must be able to survive such conditions. As such, it is largely populated by plants that are adapted to such devastation. Much of the flora present can either withstand the fires or flooding, or even utilises them as part of their reproductive cycle.

entries.name: Bevhalstia pebja
entries: {@i Bevhalstia pebja} was a small aquatic (or semi-aquatic) herbaceous plant that grew in simple single strands in the shallow ponds, streams, and marshes of the Early Cretaceous of Southern England. It grew to about 10 in. and was superficially similar to a buttercup ({@i Ranunculus bulbosus}). Its leaves and stems possessed some primitive fern-like characteristics, however it also had a much more advanced and complex flower-like reproductive system than ferns. Although the plant's evolutionary relationships are not fully resolved, it may have been a member of the liverworts (Marchantiophyta) or green algae. If dried, the leaves of {@i Bevhalstia pebja} were likely edible in the same manner as seaweed, although it probably tasted quite unpleasant.

entries.name: I Can't Believe It's Not Buttercups
entries: The flowers of Bevhalstia pebja can be harvested ({@dc 10} {@skill Survival} check) and crushed into a fine creamy paste that tastes like butter. When applied to a day's rations and consumed, a creature consuming it gains Advantage on Wisdom saving throws for the next 24 hours.

entries.name: Pityites solmsii
entries: {@i Pityites solmsii} was a pine tree that probably had long and large cones (based on coeval material). Although little is known about this tree, the presence of frequent fires within the Wessex Formation make it very likely to have been a fire adapted tree, similar to the Ponderosa Pine. The primary adaptation for fire resistance is thick bark that allows the tree to survive low-intensity fires unharmed, although the trade-off is that this bark can become easily infected by fungi and other parasites. As such, the tree becomes dependent on regular fires to sterilise the bark, ensuring that it remains healthy.

entries.name: Optional Magical Rules
Fiery Adaptations
entries: Pityites solmsii is adapted to inhabit regions that are routinely ravaged by wildfires. Its pinecones can be harvested ({@dc 5} {@skill Survival} check) and crushed with water to create a Potion of Fire Resistance.
Pityites solmsii itself has Resistance to Fire damage.

entries.name: Pseudofrenelopsis parceramosa
entries: {@i Pseudofrenelopsis parceramosa} was a coniferous tree that inhabited coastal areas and its genus dominated coastal woodlands across Europe, North America, and (probably) Korea during the Early Cretaceous. It was partially salt tolerant and had semi-succulent leaves and terminal stems. Its shoots were branching, smooth, segmented, cylindrical, and encircled by small, triangular leaves that acted like a sheath. The youngest shoots would have been edible if boiled and highly aromatic, giving off a strong smell. {@i Pseudofrenelopsis parceramosa} is one possible culprit for the famous fossil stumps near Lulworth Cove, which is a fossil forest preserved by limestone buildup around the trees' trunks.

entries.name: Sheathing Shoot Growth
entries: The shoots of Pseudofrenelopsis parceramosa can be found jutting out of the ground along the edges of coastal forests. If harvested correctly ({@dc 12} {@skill Survival} check), the shoots themselves provide one day's rations for one person, and their sheathing leaves can be picked off. When these leaves are placed on a creature's body, they form a magical protective layer that gives that creature Resistance to its choice of Bludgeoning, Piercing, or Slashing damage for 1 hour.

entries.name: Williamsonia margotiana
entries: {@i Williamsonia margotiana} was a bennettitalean (common shrubby and cycad-like seed plants between the Permian and Cretaceous) with large flower-like female cones, which would have attracted large pollinating insects and may have been edible when matured into the gynoecia (fruiting body). It had large, stiff, palm-like leaves and coarse branches. These branches would have been suitable for kindling, and its fruiting bodies were likely eaten by many herbivores.

entries.name: Serene Flowering
entries: The beauty of the large flowers of Williamsonia margotiana provide an aura of serenity and calm. If a creature finishes a Long Rest within 30 ft. of a flowering Williamsonia margotiana, that creature has Advantage on Constitution saving throws to maintain Concentration on a spell for the next 24 hours.

entries.name: Fantastic Fruit
entries: The fruits of Williamsonia margotiana can be harvested ({@dc 5} {@skill Survival} check) to provide two days' rations for one person or may be used during an {@skill Animal Handling} check with a herbivore to provide Advantage on that check.

entries.name: Laramidian Pacifist
entries: The majority of Laramidian society members are pacifists. These commonfolk commit to this ideology to ensure peace within their society and to help make other humanoid species feel safe in their company. Their calm demeanour and gentle attitude are in stark contrast to their fearsome appearance.

entries.name: Laramidian Moralist
entries: Laramidian Moralists are individuals who both commit to the pacifist ideology and also argue for/defend it fervently. They have a great interest in philosophical debate and are forethinkers in manners of morality. Generally, they are responsible for maintaining the Laramidian pacifist culture, despite their argumentative nature.

entries.name: Laramidian Cannibal Dissident
entries: Within Laramidian society, there are those who utterly reject the move towards pacifism. They believe that violence and bloodshed are fundamental to being a Laramidian, embracing their carnivorous nature in the most brutal ways; by committing acts of bloody murder and cannibalism. They live in the shadows or fringes of Laramidian society, sometimes as a double life, projecting a farce of pacifism in public.

entries.name: Neanderthal Hunter-gatherer
entries: Most Neanderthals are Hunter-Gatherers. Hardier than other commonfolk, they live in small bands of 25 or more individuals and have a nomadic lifestyle. As the name suggests, they forage and hunt to survive and can do so in particularly harsh, cold conditions.

entries.name: Neanderthal Elder Druid
entries: All Neanderthal bands are led by an Elder Druid. This individual is both the spiritual and political leader of the band and is typically centuries old. They use their connection to the land to guide their band, directing them to resources while generally avoiding contact with other humanoid species.

entries.name: Neanderthal Cave Painter
entries: Certain Neanderthals develop a talent for an unusual form of runic magic and may become Cave Painters. These Cave Painters ritualistically practice pictography to both keep records of their band's history and to create illustrations of power. Through these illustrations, they are able to conjure spiritual representations of creatures from their environment to defend themselves.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: The Neanderthal Hunter-Gatherer carries four spears, but will only ever throw up to three of them and will always retain one for melee combat.

entries.name: Phacopsian Scavenger
entries: In the cold depths, most Phacopsians eke out a living on scraps and detritus that drift down from the waters above. They are hardy individuals that can stomach most organic matter, but otherwise live docile lives in the crushing darkness.

entries.name: Phacopsian Pearl Carver
entries: Phacopsian Pearl Carvers are those Phacopsians who have dedicated themselves to self-improvement in all aspects of their life. They are proactive, intelligent individuals who ritualistically study Phacopsian history, culture, magic, and wellbeing. Through this study, they have learned a form of runic magic that utilises pearls as focal points of power.

entries.name: Phacopsian Abyssal Elder
entries: Abyssal Elders are ancient individuals who oversee Phacopsian society. Over the centuries, they have developed a powerful connection with the elements. They use this connection to ensure the safety of their people by creating whirling vortexes of water that eject unwanted visitors from their territory.

entries.name: Rhynchie Fishing Pirate
entries: Most Rhynchie are exceptional anglers. They spend long hours at sea fishing, reeling in enough to feed their communities and are able to sell off the excess. Some use this time at sea to engage in a double life, committing acts of piracy to earn extra coin while travelling between fishing spots, whereas others fully embrace the pirate lifestyle, joining pirate crews.

entries.name: Rhynchie Soothsayer
entries: Rhynchie Soothsayers are mystics and magicians who have dedicated their lives to reading fortunes, predicting futures, and interpreting omens. They usually do this in private chambers where visitors can pay to sit in attendance, or have their specific fortune read. Their mysteriousness can lead to them being treated with caution or fear by other Rhynchie.

entries.name: Rhynchie Buccaneer
entries: Rhynchie Buccaneers are individuals who have risen up in the ranks of a pirate crew to that of captain or first mate (or another notable position).
They are formidable combatants and capable commanders, able to garner the fierce loyalty of their crew.

We suggest that Rhynchie Soothsayer gives some vague descriptions of fortune/misfortune when Soothsaying, rather than describing the mechanics of this ability. If your players figure out how this system works, we suggest instead applying the effect randomly to the creature at some point during the next 24 hours.

entries.name: Sauropan Whelp
entries: Sauropan Whelps are the youngest members of a Sauropan caravan. They have few responsibilities within the caravan beyond basic cleaning and maintenance. They spend most of their time observing more senior members of the caravan, hoping to learn the skills necessary to one day lead their own caravan or have a lucrative trade.

entries.name: Sauropan Caravan Lugger
entries: Sauropan Caravan Luggers are those individuals who have earned the prestigious responsibility of pulling and pushing caravan carts. They are seen by members of their caravan as protectors and boast great physical strength. To be a Caravan Lugger is to be the beating heart of the caravan.

entries.name: Sauropan Caravan Matron
entries: All Caravans are led by a Sauropan Caravan Matron. This is an elder female Sauropan who has three primary roles within the caravan. She represents the caravan in political situations, she chooses the route and timing of the caravan's journeys, and she tends to the caravan's most precious cargo: their eggs. The Caravan Matron is the most respected member of the caravan.

entries.name: Machaeran Proletarian
entries: Proletarians are the Working Class members of Machaeran society and are the most common. They are the hard-working physical labourers that have built both the cities and industries that has allowed Machaeran society to thrive. They live in harsh conditions, sometimes in dire poverty, although are usually able to secure jobs working for the Bourgeoisie.

entries.name: Machaeran Bourgeoisie
entries: Bourgeoisie are the Middle Class members of Machaeran society. They are generally business and property owners or mid-to-high ranking officers within the military. They tend to interact directly with and employ Proletarians, but are also keen on striking deals with anyone in society, so long as it benefits them.

entries.name: Machaeran Aristocrat
entries: Aristocrats are the Upper Class members of Machaeran society and are the rarest. These ultra-wealthy elites live lives of excess in opulent palaces. Their wealth originates from commercial tithes tied to land usage, which are passed from generation to generation. They rarely see, let alone speak to, Proletarians and are out-of-touch with their societal issues, instead focusing on their own personal political problems.

entries.name: Subclasses
entries: For each subclass, rules are provided for both the 2014 (5th Edition) and 2024 (5.5 Edition) rules; traits marked for one edition appear only in that edition's version of the subclass.
